column2: Q1. Outline the gross structure of the eyeball.
column4: **Eyeball:** An oblate spheroid (fusion of two modified spheres), cystic organ. **Posterior larger sphere:** sclera, diameter 12 mm. **Anterior smaller sphere:** cornea, diameter 7.5 mm. **Anatomical landmarks:** (1) **Anterior pole** — central point of maximum convexity of anterior curvature. (2) **Posterior pole** — central point of maximum convexity of posterior curvature. (3) **Equator** — virtual line between anterior and posterior poles at the greatest circumference: *geometric equator* (exact midpoint between poles), *anatomical equator* (tilted slightly backward temporally, forward nasally, due to temporal bulge of sclera), *surgical equator* (greatest circumference in coronal plane). (4) **Axes:** *optical axis* (through centre of cornea and lens, ends on nasal side of fovea), *visual axis* (fixation point → nodal point → fovea), *fixation axis* (fixation point → centre of rotation). (5) **Visual angles:** *angle kappa* (between visual axis and pupillary plane — only one clinically measurable; positive = pseudoexotropia, negative = pseudoesotropia), *angle alpha* (optical axis vs visual axis at nodal point), *angle gamma* (optical axis vs fixation axis at centre of rotation). **Dimensions:** AP 24 mm, horizontal 23.5 mm, vertical 23 mm, circumference 75 mm. **Weight:** ~7 g; volume ~6.5 ml. **Coats:** (a) Outer fibrous — cornea (anterior 1/6, transparent, +44D, strongest optical media), sclera (posterior 5/6, opaque), limbus (junction; contains limbal stem cells; bulbar conjunctiva firmly attached here). (b) Middle vascular — iris, ciliary body, choroid. (c) Inner nervous — retina. **Segments:** anterior segment (cornea to lens) contains anterior chamber (depth 3.0 mm, 0.25 ml aqueous; bounded anteriorly by corneal endothelium, posteriorly by iris and part of ciliary body; angle of AC at junction) and posterior chamber (triangular, 0.6 ml aqueous; bounded by iris, ciliary body, lens, zonules). Posterior segment contains vitreous, retina, choroid, optic nerve head. **Applied:** aqueous drains through trabecular meshwork at AC angle — closure causes angle-closure glaucoma; shallow AC = increased risk of closure; AC deeper in myopes, shallower in hypermetropes.

column2: Q2. Describe the layers of cornea. What are the factors maintaining corneal transparency?
column4: **Cornea:** Transparent, avascular anterior 1/6 of outer fibrous coat. **Dimensions:** elliptical anteriorly (11 mm), circular posteriorly (11.5 mm); radius of curvature 7.8 mm (anterior) / 6.5 mm (posterior); central thickness 0.52 mm, peripheral 0.67 mm. **Refractive power:** anterior +48D, posterior −5D, net +43D (¾ of total refractive power of eye). **Refractive index:** 1.37. **Layers (anterior → posterior):** (1) **Epithelium** — stratified squamous non-keratinised, 5–6 layers: flattened superficial, 2–3 layers of wing/umbrella cells, tall columnar basal cells; continuous with bulbar conjunctival epithelium at limbus. (2) **Bowman's membrane** — acellular condensed collagen fibrils; binds stroma to epithelial basement membrane; does not regenerate (heals by scarring). (3) **Stroma / substantia propria** — 90% of corneal thickness (~0.5 mm); lamellae parallel to each other and to corneal plane, alternating layers at right angles; each lamella contains collagen fibrils (types I and V) in a matrix of proteoglycans (chondroitin sulphate and keratan sulphate); between lamellae lie keratocytes, wandering macrophages, histiocytes, few leucocytes. (4) **Pre-Descemet's membrane (Dua's layer)** — discovered 2013 by Dr. Harminder Singh Dua; 45 μm thick acellular structure anterior to Descemet's; very strong, impervious to air; acts as a guide during DALK. (5) **Descemet's membrane** — strong homogeneous basement membrane of corneal endothelium; collagen and glycoproteins; ends peripherally as Schwalbe's line; resistant to chemical agents, trauma and infection — in terminal corneal perforation, descemetocele maintains eyeball integrity; normally under tension, when torn curls on itself (Descemet's detachment). (6) **Endothelium** — single layer of mainly hexagonal cells; mosaic appearance on slit lamp; density ~3000 cells/mm², decreases with age; cell loss compensated by polymegathism and migration; contains active pump mechanism keeping cornea dehydrated; corneal decompensation occurs only after 75% endothelial loss. **Blood supply:** avascular; small loops from anterior ciliary vessels invade up to 1 mm of periphery. **Nerve supply:** long ciliary nerves (V1 → nasociliary → long ciliary); 60–80 myelinated fibres enter cornea, lose myelin 1–2 mm in, form stromal plexus → subepithelial plexus → intraepithelial plexus; central posterior cornea, Descemet's and endothelium have no nerves; innervation highest centrally, decreases peripherally. **Corneal transparency — anatomical factors:** (1) homogeneity of refractive index between epithelium and precorneal tear film; (2) **Maurice's lattice theory** — regular lattice arrangement of collagen fibrils so scattered light is destroyed by mutual interference; transparent if fibrils separated by < wavelength of light (4000–7000 Å); (3) **Goldmann–Benedek theory** — corneal fibrils < half wavelength of light (~2000 Å); (4) avascularity except 1 mm peripheral loops. **Physiological factors (relative dehydration, 78% water):** (1) barrier function of epithelium and endothelium (tight junctions); (2) evaporation from corneal surface; (3) endothelial pumps (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, Na⁺/H⁺ ATPase, bicarbonate-dependent ATPase); (4) corneal crystallins (water-soluble proteins); (5) swelling pressure countering imbibition — in vivo imbibition pressure must be less than swelling pressure to maintain transparency; (6) normal IOP.

column2: Q3. Describe with a suitable diagram the anatomy of sclera.
column4: **Sclera:** Posterior 5/6 of outer fibrous coat of eyeball. **Coverings:** outer surface covered by Tenon's capsule; anterior surface by bulbar conjunctiva. **Thickness:** thinner in children than adults; thinner in females than males; ~1 mm posteriorly, progressively thinner anteriorly; thinnest at insertion of extraocular muscles (~0.8 mm); ~0.8 mm around limbus. **Histology (outer → inner):** (1) **Episcleral layer** — densely vascularised thin connective tissue covering sclera proper; continuous with Tenon's capsule anteriorly. (2) **Sclera proper** — thick avascular layer of collagen fibres in haphazard arrangement (unlike cornea); mucopolysaccharide plugging between fibrils; few fibroblasts. (3) **Lamina fusca** — innermost pigmented part; fuses with uveal tissue; pigmented cells give brownish colour. **Special areas:** (1) **Lamina cribrosa** — sieve-like posterior sclera pierced by optic nerve fibres. (2) **Scleral sulcus** — furrow-like indentation at anterior limbus containing Schlemm's canal. (3) **Scleral spur** — anterior-most sclera ends as a circular flange posterior to Schlemm's canal, wedge-shaped in cross section. **Applied importance:** trabecular meshwork extends from Schwalbe's line to scleral spur; longitudinal ciliary muscle fibres attach to scleral spur. **Scleral apertures:** (1) **Anterior** (3–4 mm posterior to limbus) — transmit anterior ciliary vessels, long and short ciliary nerves. (2) **Middle** (4–7 mm posterior to equator) — transmit vortex veins (venae vorticosae). (3) **Posterior** (around lamina cribrosa) — transmit long and short ciliary nerves and vessels. **Nerve supply:** anterior apertures — long ciliary nerves; posterior to equator — short ciliary nerves. **Blood supply:** anterior and posterior ciliary vessels.

column2: Q4. Describe with a suitable diagram the anatomy of limbus.
column4: **Limbus:** Circumcorneal junctional zone between conjunctiva, cornea and sclera. **Anatomically — two junctions:** (1) **Sclerocorneal junction** — uniform corneal collagen fibrils become irregular, turning outer fibrous coat opaque. (2) **Conjunctivocorneal junction** — substantia propria of conjunctiva ends but conjunctival epithelium becomes several layers thick and continues with corneal epithelium; limbal epithelial cells irregularly arranged, contain melanin (unlike cornea). **Surgically:** limb is a 2 mm wide circumcorneal transitional zone between cornea and sclera. **Anterior → posterior landmarks:** (1) **Anterior limbal border** — anterior-most landmark; prominent ridge formed by insertion of conjunctiva and Tenon's capsule into cornea; Bowman's membrane terminates underneath. (2) **Blue limbal zone/area** — translucent bluish zone from anterior limbal border to mid limbal line; visible only after dissecting conjunctiva and Tenon's fascia; breadth varies by quadrant — superior 1 mm, inferior 0.8 mm, nasal and temporal 0.4 mm (due to non-uniform attachment of conjunctivo-Tenon's complex). (3) **Mid limbal line** — imaginary junction between blue and white zones; Descemet's membrane terminates underneath as Schwalbe's line. (4) **White limbal zone/area** — 1 mm circumcorneal white area between mid limbal line and posterior limbal border; trabecular meshwork underneath; width constant. (5) **Posterior limbal border** — circumcorneal border ~1 mm posterior to mid limbal line; scleral spur underneath. **Applied importance:** (1) **Cataract surgery** — SICS sclerocorneal tunnel incision at mid limbal line avoids trabecular meshwork, ciliary body and bleeding/hyphaema; clear corneal incision in phacoemulsification at or anterior to anterior limbal border (higher risk of Descemet's stripping). (2) **Glaucoma filtration surgery** — trabecular meshwork accessed through mid limbal line. (3) Excessive cauterisation of limbal area damages limbal stem cells → postoperative dry eye. (4) Superior quadrant preferred for surgical approach because blue and white limbal zones are widest (1 mm).

column2: Q5. Outline the anatomy of uvea. (Or: Macroscopic and microscopic structure of iris / ciliary body / choroid)
column4: **Uvea:** Middle vascular coat of eyeball; from anterior to posterior — iris, ciliary body, choroid. **IRIS:** Diaphragm-like thin circular disc with central aperture (pupil); diameter 12 mm, thickness 0.5 mm; pupil 3–4 mm under normal conditions; peripheral iris attached to middle of anterior surface of ciliary body (root of iris). *Macroscopic — anterior surface:* collarette (zigzag line at attachment of developmental pupillary margin); **ciliary zone** (root to collarette) — radial streaks (underlying radial vessels), crypts (pothole-like depressions from segmental lack of superficial layer), contraction furrows (concentric lines prominent on dilatation); **pupillary zone** (collarette to pupillary frill) — smooth and flat; **pupillary frills** (slight extension of posterior pigmented epithelium around pupillary margin). *Posterior surface:* apparently smooth, dark brown or blackish; on higher magnification — Schwalbe's radial furrows (finer, begin 1–1.5 mm from pupillary border, narrow and deep, become broad and shallow toward root), circular furrows (cross radial at regular intervals). *Microscopic (anterior → posterior):* (1) anterior limiting membrane (condensed stroma with fibroblasts and melanocytes; deficiency causes crypts; pigmentation decides iris colour); (2) iris stroma (loose collagen with mucopolysaccharide ground substance; contains sphincter pupillae — circular band in pupillary zone, parasympathetic via III; dilator pupillae — posterior stroma, cervical sympathetic, dilates pupil; vessels from circulus arteriosus majoris; melanocytes, fibroblasts, lymphocytes, macrophages); (3) anterior non-pigmented epithelial layer (continuation of pigment epithelial layer of retina and ciliary body; no melanocytes; dilator pupillae originates here); (4) posterior pigmented epithelial layer (continuation of sensory retina after ora serrata; columnar pigmented cells; extends at pupillary margin to form pupillary frill). *Applied:* iris weakest at root — iridodialysis after blunt trauma (D-shaped pupil); tamsulosin thins iris stroma (floppy iris syndrome); pseudoexfoliation → poor pupillary dilatation. **CILIARY BODY:** Middle portion of vascular coat; from ora serrata to angle of AC. *Macroscopic:* triangular in cross-section; inner part in angle of AC (ciliary body band) and posterior chamber; root of iris arises from middle; outer part blends with sclera forming suprachoroidal space; inner part has **pars plicata** (anterior 2–2.5 mm with ciliary processes) and **pars plana** (posterior smooth part, 3 mm nasal, 5 mm temporal). *Microscopic (outward → inward):* (1) supraciliary lamina (outermost condensed stroma, continuation of suprachoroidal lamina, merges with anterior limiting membrane of iris); (2) stroma (collagenous connective tissue with ciliary muscle — non-striated, three parts: longitudinal/meridional, radial, circular; parasympathetic via short ciliary nerves from ciliary ganglion; longitudinal fibres draw choroid forward and open trabecular meshwork increasing aqueous outflow); pigment cells, lymphocytes, macrophages, major arterial circle from anastomosis of long posterior ciliary and anterior ciliary arteries; (3) pigmented epithelium (continuation of RPE; continues as anterior non-pigmented epithelium of iris); (4) non-pigmented epithelium (continuation of sensory retina after ora serrata; continues as posterior pigmented epithelium of iris); (5) internal limiting membrane (continuation of retinal ILM). **Ciliary processes:** 70–80 white finger-like projections from pars plicata; each ~2 mm long, 0.5 mm diameter; secrete aqueous humour. **CHOROID:** Posterior-most part of middle vascular coat; from ora serrata to optic nerve head. *Macroscopic:* smooth brownish inner surface in close apposition with RPE; rough outer surface with sclera; thicker near posterior pole. *Microscopic (outside → inside):* (1) lamina fusca/suprachoroidal lamina (thin condensed collagen, melanocytes, fibroblasts; suprachoroidal space between this and sclera contains long and short posterior ciliary vessels and nerves; anteriorly continues as supraciliary lamina); (2) choroidal stroma (loose collagen, elastic, reticular fibrils; cellular components — melanocytes, macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells; vascular component — Haller's layer (outer, large vessels) and Sattler's layer (inner, medium vessels); calibre reduces from outside inwards); (3) choriocapillary layer (rich network of fenestrated capillaries in non-overlapping lobules; nourishes RPE and outer sensory retina); (4) Bruch's membrane/lamina vitrea (multi-strata innermost layer between choriocapillaries and RPE; five layers on EM — basement membrane of RPE, inner collagen, middle elastic, outer collagen, basement membrane of choriocapillaries). *Applied:* choriocapillaries + Bruch's membrane form blood-retinal barrier; Bruch's thickens with age → drusen → dry AMD; in choroidal neovascularisation, Bruch's is broken down by inward-growing choroidal vessels (common in pathological myopia).

column2: Q6. Outline the anatomy of blood-ocular barrier with a suitable diagram. (Or: Blood-retinal barrier)
column4: **Definition:** Anatomical barriers at cellular level preventing proteins and large molecules and blood corpuscles from entering ocular cavities, maintaining clarity of refractive media. **Components:** (1) **Anterior blood-aqueous barrier** — formed by tight junctions (zonula occludens and zonula adherens) between inner non-pigmented epithelium of ciliary body; non-fenestrated capillary endothelium also acts as blood-aqueous barrier. (2) **Posterior blood-retinal barrier** — two parts: **inner blood-retinal barrier** (tight junctions between endothelial cells of retinal capillaries) and **outer blood-retinal barrier** (tight junctions between retinal pigment epithelial cells). **Applied importance:** (1) Barriers are not rigid — medium-sized hydrophilic molecules (urea, creatinine, carbohydrates) penetrate slowly. (2) Lipophilic substances penetrate better even with higher molecular weight. (3) Most systemically administered antibiotics do not cross the barriers → in endophthalmitis, antibiotics must be given by intravitreal injection. (4) In acute IOP rise, IV mannitol is given — a hyperosmotic agent that does not cross the barrier, accumulates in extracellular spaces, causes osmotic withdrawal of water mainly from vitreous → reduces IOP. (5) Fragile barriers break down in: infections/inflammations, trauma (blunt and penetrating), intraocular surgery/interventions, chemical burn, thermal burn, radiation exposure, and pharmacological agents (prostaglandin analogues used for glaucoma). On breakdown, proteins, antibodies and macrophages leak from plasma into aqueous and vitreous → intraocular inflammation (uveitis).

column2: Q7. With a suitable diagram outline the anatomy of the angle of the anterior chamber.
column4: **Angle of anterior chamber:** Site from which aqueous humour drains out of the eye. **Gonioscopy:** Clinical method for viewing angle structures. **Structures from posterior to anterior:** (1) **Ciliary body band** — anterior-most part of ciliary body between scleral spur and root of iris; dark brown or greyish. (2) **Scleral spur** — prominent posterior part of scleral sulcus; appears as a white line on gonioscopy; meridional/longitudinal fibres of ciliary muscle attach over it. (3) **Trabecular meshwork** — sieve-like structure covering scleral spur and converting it into tunnel (Schlemm's canal); non-pigmented at birth, pigmentation increases with age; hyaluronic acid main endogenous GAG. Parts (inward → outward): (a) **uveal meshwork** — innermost, from ciliary body base to Schwalbe's line; 2–3 layers, irregular pores; EM: outer cellular layer, middle basement membrane, central collagenous core; (b) **corneoscleral meshwork** — middle portion, from scleral spur to lateral wall of scleral sulcus; elliptical pores become progressively smaller approaching Schlemm's canal; (c) **juxtacanalicular meshwork** — outermost, in apposition with Schlemm's canal; 2–5 layers of connective tissue cells in extracellular matrix, lined on both sides by endothelium; outer endothelium forms inner wall of Schlemm's canal; inner endothelium continues as endothelium of corneoscleral meshwork. **Schlemm's canal** — endothelial-lined oval channel formed by trabecular meshwork covering scleral sulcus; collector channels (25–30) leave Schlemm's canal and drain into episcleral veins; two systems — **direct** (short intrascleral course, terminate directly in episcleral veins) and **indirect** (form intrascleral and episcleral venous plexuses before draining). Episcleral veins drain into cavernous sinus via anterior ciliary and superior ophthalmic veins. (4) **Schwalbe's line** — prominent end of Descemet's membrane; marks end of AC angle anteriorly. **Applied:** (1) In myopes, root of iris originates lower → wider ciliary body band; in hypermetropes, originates higher → narrower. (2) In blunt trauma, ciliary body band becomes abnormally wide → angle recession glaucoma. (3) In angle-closure glaucoma, angle anatomically/physiologically closed; Shaffer's grading system most common. (4) In paediatric glaucoma, developmental dysgenesis causes root of iris to cover trabecular meshwork → buphthalmos.

column2: Q8. Discuss the theories of aqueous humour formation
column5: **Source:** Plasma in capillary network of ciliary processes. **Site:** Ciliary processes in pars plicata of ciliary body. **Mechanism of formation — three processes:** (1) **Ultrafiltration** — passive transport mediated by hydrostatic pressure; fluid filtered from capillary walls of ciliary processes and loose connective tissue = **dialysate**; accumulates behind epithelium of ciliary processes. (2) **Secretion** — active transport; after dialysate enters pigment epithelium, active transport of Na⁺, Cl⁻, K⁺, ascorbic acid, amino acids, bicarbonates from stroma into cells; done by Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump, calcium ion channels, voltage-gated ion channels, carbonic anhydrase enzyme transport mechanism. (3) **Diffusion** — passive transport mediated by osmotic gradient created by active transport (secretion); diffusion of plasma constituents (principally water) across blood-aqueous barrier into posterior chamber; sodium primarily responsible for osmotic gradient for water movement. **Anterior chamber aqueous** resembles plasma more closely than posterior chamber aqueous due to diffusional exchange of ions (Na⁺/K⁺/Cl⁻) from surrounding structures (ciliary body, iris, lens, cornea) during circulation. **Steps:** (1) creation of stromal pool by ultrafiltration; (2) active transport of stromal filtrate across non-pigmented epithelium by secretion; (3) passive transport across non-pigmented epithelium along osmotic gradient created by secretion. **Control of aqueous formation:** passive transport depends on blood pressure, IOP, plasma osmotic pressure; dense adrenergic innervation of ciliary processes increases vessel permeability; vasopressin (ADH) increases active Na⁺ transport; adenyl cyclase influences active transport via Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase. **Drainage:** Aqueous from ciliary processes → posterior chamber → across pupil → anterior chamber → **trabecular outflow (70–80%)** through trabecular meshwork → Schlemm's canal → collector channels → episcleral veins, and **uveoscleral outflow (20–30%)** into suprachoroidal space across ciliary body → venous circulation of sclera, ciliary body, orbit. **Trabecular outflow mechanisms:** (1) **passive filter mechanisms** — vacuolation theory (large intraendothelial vacuoles/vesicles open and close intermittently), pores in endothelial cells (~20,000 pores, diameter up to 3 μm), Sondermann's channels (transtrabecular small tubules), contractile microfilaments reducing resistance to flow into Schlemm's canal; (2) **active pump mechanisms (biomechanical pump)** — circumferential aqueous valves at Schlemm's canal, ocular pulse, blinking rate, ocular movements — influence trabecular meshwork flexibility → active mechanisms. **Applied:** uveoscleral outflow occurs mostly at night (9 pm) → prostaglandin analogues prescribed at night.

column2: Q9. Describe the anatomy and physiology of the lens.
column4: **Gross anatomy:** Transparent, biconvex, crystalline structure between iris and vitreous, sitting in a saucer-shaped depression (patellar fossa). **Related structures:** (1) **Retrolental space (Berger's space)** — potential space inside the ligamentum hyaloideo-capsulare (Wieger's ligament), a circular ligament intimately connecting anterior hyaloid face and posterior lens surface. (2) **Suspensory ligament of lens (zonules of Zinn / ciliary zonules)** — series of fibres from ciliary body to lens, holding lens in position and facilitating accommodation. (3) **Anterior hyaloid face.** **Dimensions:** equator where anterior and posterior surfaces meet; equatorial diameter 9–10 mm; anterior radius of curvature 10 mm; posterior radius of curvature 6 mm; weight and thickness variable with age. **Refractive index:** 1.39. **Total dioptric power:** 15–16D. **Accommodative power:** at birth 14–16D; 25 years 7–8D; 50 years 1–2D (causing presbyopia). **Development:** from lens placode and vesicle derived from surface ectoderm. **Lamellar structure (inner → outer):** embryonic nucleus, fetal nucleus, infantile nucleus, adult nucleus, anterior and posterior lens capsule, anterior lens epithelium. **A. Anterior and posterior lens capsule:** thin transparent hyaline collagenous membrane completely covering lens matter; anterior thicker than posterior; thickest at pre-equatorial area, thinnest at posterior pole. **B. Anterior lens epithelium:** single layer of nucleated cuboidal epithelium; all metabolic, synthetic and transport processes occur; no posterior epithelial cells (used up during development). Zones: (1) central zone — flat, metabolically stable cuboidal cells, slowly reduces with age; metaplasia produces anterior subcapsular cataract and glaucoma flecken; (2) intermediate zone — becomes more cylindrical toward periphery, round central nucleus, metabolically stable, extremely susceptible to radiation; dysplasia leads to posterior subcapsular cataract; (3) germinative equatorial zone — metabolically active columnar cells, lifelong dividing; new cells migrate posteriorly to form lens fibres. **C. Embryonic nucleus:** primary lens fibres from posterior wall of lens vesicle, formed within first 3 months of gestation. **D. Fetal nucleus:** lens fibres from 3 months gestation to birth; meet around sutures — Y-shaped anteriorly, inverted Y-shaped posteriorly. **E. Infantile nucleus:** fibres from birth to puberty. **F. Adult nucleus:** fibres from puberty to rest of life; asymmetric fibre growth produces complicated dendritic pattern instead of simple Y-shaped sutures. **Surgical anatomy (anterior → posterior):** anterior capsule, anterior cortical matter, epinuclear sheet, central hard nucleus, posterior cortical matter, posterior capsule. **Nuclear grading (colour):** whitish/green-yellow → yellow → amber → brown → black. **Lens transparency — causes:** (1) avascularity; (2) semipermeable lens capsule; (3) single-layered anterior epithelium; (4) lens fibres — tightly packed, lack organelles; (5) lens proteins — aquaporin MIP26/aquaporin 0 maintains water balance by controlling water and glycerol transport; (6) cell membranes of lens fibres have pump mechanisms regulating electrolyte and water balance, maintaining relative dehydration; (7) high concentration of reduced glutathione maintains proteins in reduced state; (8) nature and structure of lens proteins. **Lens metabolism:** avascular, dependent on aqueous humour for ATP; water and electrolyte transport via Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump and osmotic passive transport; amino acids actively transported into lens at anterior epithelial cells; simple and facilitated diffusion of glucose at anterior and posterior lens surfaces; some nutrients from vitreous. **ATP generation — glucose metabolism:** glycolysis (80% of glucose, lactic acid end product, 0.2 mol ATP/mol glucose); Kreb's cycle (15%, CO₂ + H₂O, 36 mol ATP/mol glucose); pentose shunt; sorbitol pathway (lactic acid end product, pivotal in sugar cataract development). **Lens proteins:** highest protein content of any structure; soluble (>80%: α-crystallin (highest mol weight), β-crystallin, γ-crystallin (monomer)); insoluble (<20%: polymer, chemically albuminoids).

column2: Q10. Describe the anatomy of conjunctiva.
column4: **Gross anatomy:** mucous membrane lining posterior surface of eyelids and anterior aspect of eyeball; begins at limbus, ends at lid margin; encloses conjunctival cul-de-sac open in front at palpebral fissure. **Embryology:** from surface ectoderm lining developing eyelids and eyeball. **Parts:** (1) **Palpebral conjunctiva** — lining inner surface of eyelids. *Tarsal (orbital) conjunctiva:* firmly adherent to whole tarsal plate in upper lid, only half width in lower lid; thin, transparent, highly vascular. *Marginal conjunctiva:* from lid margin up to 2 mm on inner side; ends at sulcus subtarsalis (shallow groove); transition zone between skin and conjunctiva proper. (2) **Forniceal conjunctiva** — continuous circular cul-de-sac joining bulbar and palpebral; broken medially by caruncle and plica semilunaris. *Superior fornix:* at level of superior orbital margin; fascial sheaths of LPS and SR attached, help maintain recess during upper eyelid movement. *Inferior fornix:* till 8 mm below inferior limbus near inferior orbital margin; fascial sheath of IO and IR attached. *Lateral fornix:* extends beyond equator, 14 mm from lateral limbus. *Medial fornix:* shallow, interrupted by caruncle and plica semilunaris, remains occupied by lacus lacrimalis (tear lake). (3) **Bulbar conjunctiva** — thin, transparent, loosely attached; 3 mm ridge around cornea = limbal conjunctiva. **Plica semilunaris:** pinkish crescentic fold in medial canthus, represents nictitating membrane of lower animals. **Caruncle:** small ovoid pinkish mass medial to plica, modified skin. **Histology — two layers:** (1) epithelium (nature varies by region): tarsal — bilayered (superficial columnar, basal cuboidal); forniceal and bulbar — three-layered (superficial columnar, middle polyhedral, basal cuboidal); marginal — 5-layered non-keratinised stratified squamous; limbal — multi-layered (8–10) stratified squamous; form papillae of palisades of Vogt. (2) adenoid layer — lymphoid, lymphocytes in fine connective tissue reticulum, most developed in fornices. (3) fibrous layer — meshwork of collagen and elastic fibres, contains neurovascular supply. Adenoid + fibrous = substantia propria. **Glands and special cells:** goblet cells (between epithelial cells throughout; secret mucinous layer of tear film); crypts of Henle (between tarsal plates and fornices; immunological role); glands of Krause (subconjunctival connective tissue in fornices; accessory lacrimal); glands of Wolfring (upper border of superior tarsus, lower border of inferior tarsus; accessory lacrimal); melanocytes (in epithelium; racial pigmentation); Langerhans cells (in epithelium; immunological, especially in corneal allograft rejection). **Blood supply:** arterial — peripheral arterial arcade of eyelids, marginal arterial arcade, anterior ciliary arteries; venous — into venous plexus of eyelids and anterior ciliary veins. **Lymphatics:** lateral half → preauricular; medial half → submandibular. **Nerve supply:** circumcorneal zone by long ciliary branches; rest by supra/infra-trochlear, supraorbital, lacrimal, frontal nerves. **Applied:** conjunctival chemosis more common in bulbar (loosely attached); foreign body in superior fornix seen by double eversion; incision through superior fornix in orbitotomy opens plane between LPS and SR; conjunctiva, Tenon's capsule and episcleral tissue fused at limbus — preferred site for firm hold during ocular surgery; excessive cauterisation during SICS destroys goblet cells → postoperative dry eye.

column2: Q11. Briefly outline the anatomy of vitreous humour. (Or: Anatomy of vitreous base)
column4: **Definition:** Transparent, hydrophobic gel-like connective tissue bounded anteriorly by lens and ciliary body and posteriorly by retina; optical media and support for globular structure from inside. **Weight:** ~4 g; volume ~4 cc; 99% water. **Gross anatomy — three parts:** (1) **Hyaloid layer/membrane** — outermost condensed part; (a) **anterior hyaloid membrane** — covers anterior vitreous ~1.5 mm from ora serrata; close apposition with pars plana, ciliary processes, ciliary zonules, posterior lens capsule; central 9 mm diameter ring-shaped attachment to posterior lens capsule = hyaloideo-capsular ligament of Wieger; **Berger's space / patellar fossa / retrolental space** = potential space between posterior capsule and anterior hyaloid membrane within this ring; attachments — retrolental ligament (ligamentum hyaloideo-capsulare, lens ↔ anterior hyaloid), hyalociliary zonules and coronary ligament (anterior hyaloid ↔ pars plicata), median ligament (anterior hyaloid ↔ pars plana); (b) **posterior hyaloid membrane** — posterior condensed part from vitreous base to optic nerve head; clinically indistinguishable from retinal ILM. (2) **Cortical vitreous** — peripheral ~100 μm; metabolic centre; contains hyalocytes (synthesise hyaluronic acid). (3) **Medullary vitreous** — central core; less fibrillary than cortical, no cellular component; **Cloquet's canal / hyaloid canal** runs through centre, connects optic disc with posterior pole of lens, 1–2 mm wide, walls formed by condensed vitreous. **Vitreous tracts (fine sheet-like condensed vitreous, concentric onion-peel arrangement of adult vitreous):** (1) **tractus retrolentalis** — innermost tract connecting posterior lens capsule with optic nerve head; (2) **tractus coronaries** — coronary ligament of anterior hyaloid attaches with ciliary processes, connects coronary ligament with retina; (3) **tractus medianus** — connects median ligament of anterior hyaloid with retina; (4) **tractus preretinalis** — outermost tract connecting ora serrata with posterior retina. **Vitreous zones:** tractus retrolentalis and tractus preretinalis divide vitreous into three optically distinct zones: (1) **retrolental zone** — central, bounded anteriorly by patellar fossa and posterior lens capsule, circumferentially by tractus retrolentalis; Cloquet's canal runs through centre; (2) **intermediate zone** — bounded anteriorly by pars plana; between tractus retrolentalis and tractus preretinalis; contains tractus coronaries and tractus medianus; (3) **preretinal zone** — between tractus preretinalis and retina. **Vitreous attachments (firm):** around ora serrata (vitreous base), optic nerve head, fovea, posterior pole of crystalline lens. **Vitreous base:** 4 mm wide strongest attachment of vitreous with pars plana and peripheral retina at ora serrata; includes 1.5–2 mm of pars plana adjoining ora serrata and 2 mm (temporal) / 3 mm (nasal) of peripheral retina posterior to ora serrata. **Microscopic:** collagen fibres from vitreous inserted at right angles to pars plana and retinal ILM; in rest of vitreoretinal interface, collagen fibres parallel to retinal ILM; this right-angular ultrastructural arrangement converts vitreous base into three-dimensional zone; complex interdigitations of vitreal collagen fibres with reticular fibres of basement membrane of non-pigmented epithelium of ciliary body; degenerative remodelling of retina — through focal gaps in retinal ILM, vitreous collagen fibres adhere firmly with plasma membrane of retinal glial cells; focal contributions by hemidesmosomes in ILM and Müller cells. **Applied:** (1) blunt trauma — retinal breaks may occur at vitreous base → retinal detachment; (2) with age, vitreous liquifies → posterior vitreous detachment; complete PVD → circular ring (Weiss ring) in front of optic disc; incomplete PVD → vitreoretinal traction → retinal breaks and detachment; (3) during pars plana vitrectomy, PVD must be surgically induced for complete vitreous removal and to prevent iatrogenic vitreoretinal traction; (4) in vascular retinal disorders (diabetic retinopathy, retinal venous occlusion), retinal ischaemia → neovascularisation → vitreous haemorrhage.

column2: Q12. Outline the gross anatomy and microscopic structure of retina. (Or: Short note on layers of rods and cones)
column4: **Definition:** Thin, transparent, innermost neural coat of eyeball; normally purplish-red; thickest at posterior pole (0.56 mm), thinner at ora serrata (0.1 mm); surface area 266 sq mm. **GROSS ANATOMY — three zones:** (1) **Optic disc/optic nerve head** — 1.5 mm diameter well-defined circular area where all retinal layers except nerve fibre layer and choroid terminate; nerve fibres pass through lamina cribrosa of sclera and form optic nerve trunk; appears whitish due to lamina cribrosa, medullated nerve fibres and absence of choroidal tissue; **cup** = central depression/pit; central retinal vessels emerge through centre of cup; rest of disc around cup = **neuroretinal rim (NRR)**; at centre of cup nerve fibres thinnest → more shiny white; grey dots at centre of cup reflect non-medullated nerve fibres. *Applied:* vertical cup-disc ratio (VCDR) important in glaucoma — increase in cup size, thinning of NRR; optic nerve carries meningeal covering of brain (direct outpouching of CNS) — any raised ICT → papilloedema; optic nerve inflammation → optic neuritis (potentially blinding); complete loss of retinal nerve fibres → chalky white disc with poor/no vision = optic atrophy. (2) **Macula lutea** — central 1.5 mm diameter retina at posterior pole, temporal to optic nerve head, appears relatively darker. **Fovea centralis:** 1.85 mm diameter, 0.25 mm thick central depressed part; central 5° of visual field. **Foveola:** 0.35 mm diameter central floor of fovea; 3 mm (approx 2 disc diameters) from temporal margin of optic nerve head, 1 mm below horizontal meridian. **Umbo:** tiny depression in centre of foveola (foveolar reflex). **Foveal avascular zone (FAZ):** avascular part of fovea centralis excluding foveolar area; delineated by FFA. (3) **Peripheral retina** — near periphery (1.5 mm around macula), mid periphery (3 mm wide zone around near periphery, more on nasal side), far periphery (rest till ora serrata). **Ora serrata** — serrated wavy peripheral margin where retina ends and ciliary body starts; 2.1 mm temporal, 0.8 mm nasal. **MICROSCOPIC STRUCTURE (outside → inwards):** (1) **Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)** — single layer of pigmented hexagonal cells; non-uniform pigmentation → granular fundus appearance; at fovea, taller, thinner cells with coarse granules → darker fovea; firmly adherent to Bruch's, loosely to rods and cones. *Applied:* potential space between RPE and sensory retina = subretinal space; retinal detachment = separation of RPE from sensory retina; subretinal fluid; RPE pumps out water and ions; light junctions between RPE cells = outer blood-retinal barrier; nutrient transport; mechanical support to photoreceptors; optical absorption of light; photoreceptor renewal and vitamin A metabolism. (2) **Layers of rods and cones** — photoreceptors converting light to visual impulse. **Rods (120 million):** contain rhodopsin, responsible for scotopic (low illumination) and peripheral vision; absent at foveal centre for 0.35 mm (rod-free zone); correspond to central 1.25° of visual field; large numbers in a ring ~5.6 mm from fovea. **Cones (6.5 million):** responsible for photopic (high illumination) and colour vision; highest density at fovea, rapidly decreases outside; nasal quadrant has more cones than temporal; inferior quadrant more than superior. **Ultrastructure of photoreceptors:** central cell body with nucleus, cell process extending into outer plexiform layer, inner and outer segments (form photoreceptor layer); oriented perpendicular to retinal surface. **Rod cells:** highly refractive cylindrical transversely striated outer segment with lamellar lipoprotein discs; rhodopsin pigment inside discs and on surface; inner segment with outer ellipsoid zone (numerous mitochondria) and inner myoid zone (organelles and glycogen); outer and inner segments connected by cilium; outer rod fibre pierces external limiting membrane; inner rod fibre ends as swollen bulb = rod spherule; rod granule = dense nucleus in outer nuclear layer; length 40–60 μm. **Cone cells:** outer segment conical, shorter than rods; lamellar discs narrower than rod discs; contain iodopsin; inner segment and connecting cilium similar to rods; no outer cone fibre — inner segment directly forms cone cell body; stout inner cone fibre ends with lateral processes = cone feet / cone pedicles. **Inter-photoreceptor matrix:** complex connective tissue with GAGs, glycoproteins, proteoglycans, proteins filling space between photoreceptor outer segments and RPE; protein = interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP), produced by photoreceptors, transports retinoids between RPE and photoreceptors (visual cycle); matrix helps photoreceptor alignment, prevents retinal detachment, performs phagocytosis, molecular transport. (3) **External limiting membrane** — fenestrated from optic nerve head edges to ora serrata; pierced by photoreceptor cells; not a true basement membrane. (4) **Outer nuclear layer** — multi-layer, primarily cell bodies with nuclei of rods and cones; cone nuclei dominate in foveal region, rod nuclei elsewhere; cone nuclei larger than rod. (5) **Outer plexiform layer** — synapses between four cellular components: rod spherules, cone feet/pedicles, dendrites of bipolar cells, processes of horizontal cells; thickest at macula (Henle's layer); first-order neurons of visual pathway begin here. (6) **Inner nuclear layer** — thin, absent at fovea; contains: **bipolar cells** (first-order neurons of visual pathway; cell body and nucleus here, dendrites synapse with rods, cones, horizontal cells in outer plexiform layer; morphology and synaptic relationships vary); **horizontal cells** (flat horizontally oriented cells with numerous processes in outer plexiform layer; type A synapse with cones, type B with rods); **amacrine cells** (pyriform, innermost part of inner nuclear layer; single process synapses with bipolar axons and/or ganglion dendrites in inner plexiform layer); **Müller cells** (fibres from cell body connect external and internal limiting membranes; anatomical support and metabolism; no optical function; ELM formed by outer fibres of Müller cells and cell membranes of photoreceptors; ILM formed solely by inner fibres of Müller cells); **glial cells** (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia; structural integrity). (7) **Inner plexiform layer** — synapses of bipolar axons, ganglion cell dendrites and soma, amacrine cell processes; absent at foveola. (8) **Ganglion cell layer** — cell bodies with nuclei of ganglion cells (second-order neurons of visual pathway); 6–8 layers at macula; bilayered temporal to optic disc; unilayered elsewhere; absent at foveola; monosynaptic ganglion cells predominate centrally, polysynaptic peripherally. (9) **Nerve fibre layer / stratum opticum** — unmyelinated axons of ganglion cells; converge at optic nerve head, pass through lamina cribrosa, become myelinated and form optic nerve trunk; runs parallel to retinal surface (unlike other perpendicular layers). Disposition: nasal quadrant — superior and inferior radiating fibres directly to optic disc; temporal quadrant — **papillomacular bundle** (fibres from macula) directly to disc, **arcuate bundle** (fibres from rest of temporal retina) arch above and below then reach disc. *Applied:* early glaucomatous damage in arcuate fibres → isolated scotoma; complete loss of arcuate fibres → ring scotoma; while converging at optic disc, peripheral deep fibres occupy superficial part of disc, central superficial fibres lie deeper; papilloedema appears first in thicker nasal quadrant. (10) **Internal limiting membrane** — true basement membrane, interface between retina and vitreous; peripheral vitreous fibrils merge with it. *Applied:* during macular hole surgery, ILM stained and peeled off for structural rearrangement of photoreceptors to bridge anatomical gap at macula.

column2: Q13. Describe the pathway of the optic nerve with its lesions.
column4: **Visual pathway:** retina → optic nerve → optic chiasma → optic tract → LGB → optic radiation → visual cortex. **Optic nerve (2nd cranial nerve):** also contains afferent fibres of light reflex; extends from optic disc to optic chiasma; backward continuation of RNFL of retina, 1.2 million axons from ganglion cells; morphologically and embryologically comparable to a sensory nerve. **Parts:** (1) **Intraocular** — shortest, 1 mm deep × 1.5 mm vertical; ophthalmoscopically visible portion is disc; axons from NFL make orthogonal turn and pass through lamina cribrosa to appear as intraorbital part. (2) **Intraorbital** — from back of eyeball to optic foramina at orbital apex; 25–30 mm; surrounded by tough annulus of Zinn at orbital apex; covered by meningeal sheath; SR and MR fuse with ON sheath → painful ocular movements in retrobulbar optic neuritis. (3) **Intracanalicular** — 6 mm; closely related to ophthalmic artery; sphenoid and ethmoid sinuses lie medial, separated by thin bony plate → sinusitis → retrobulbar neuritis; dura mater fuses with periosteum; ON fixed to optic canal. (4) **Intracranial** — 5–16 mm; unites with contralateral optic nerve to form optic chiasma; travels superior to diaphragma sellae and cavernous sinus. **Meningeal sheaths:** intracanalicular and intraorbital part — 3 coverings; intracranial part — only pia mater; subarachnoid space around ON is continuous with subarachnoid space of brain and contains CSF. **Optic chiasma:** flattened structure 12 mm horizontally × 8 mm AP; lies over diaphragma sellae and cavernous sinus in middle cranial fossa; fibres from nasal half of each retina cross to contralateral optic tract; temporal halves remain ipsilateral; **prefixed** 10%, **central** 80%, **postfixed**. **Optic tract:** cylindrical bundle of nerve fibres from temporal half of retina of same eye and nasal half of retina of opposite eye; ends in LGB; pupillary reflex fibres pass onto superior colliculi through superior brachium. **LGB:** six layers of neurons (grey matter) alternating with white matter (optic fibres); second-order neurons relay here. **Optic radiation (geniculocalcarine pathway):** from LGB to visual cortex; 'optic peduncle' of Wernicke; pass forward and then laterally; **inferior fibres** (upper visual fields) first sweep anteroinferiorly in **Meyer's loop** around anterior tip of temporal horn of lateral ventricle and temporal lobe; **superior fibres** (inferior visual field) proceed directly posteriorly through parietal lobe to visual cortex. **Visual cortex:** medial aspect of occipital lobe in and near calcarine fissure; visuopsychic area (peristriate 18, parastriate 19), visuosensory area (striate area 17); stria of Gennari identifies visual cortex section. **Arrangement of nerve fibres:** (a) **retina** — superior/nasal/inferior; macula → straight to temporal pathway optic disc as PMB; temporal retina → arch above and below PMB as SAF and IAF. (b) **Optic nerve head** — fibres peripheral lie deep in retina but occupy most peripheral part of disc; fibres originating closer to retina lie superficial in retina but occupy central portion of disc. (c) **Distal region** (behind eye) vs **proximal region** — upper temporal, upper nasal, macular, lower temporal, lower nasal; macular fibres centrally located. (d) **Optic tract** — upper retinal, macular, lower retinal. (e) **LGB** — upper retinal, lower retinal fibres. (f) **Optic radiation** — upper uniocular, upper peripheral, upper macular; lower uniocular, lower peripheral, lower macular. (g) **Visual cortex** — upper peripheral, upper macular, lower macular, lower peripheral. **Lesions (implied by arrangement):** complete lesion of ON → ipsilateral blindness; chiasmal lesion → bitemporal hemianopia; optic tract lesion → contralateral homonymous hemianopia; Meyer's loop → contralateral superior quadrantanopia; parietal radiation → contralateral inferior quadrantanopia; occipital cortex → contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

column2: Q14. Outline the blood supply of the eyeball with suitable diagrams. (Or: Course and applied importance of central retinal artery / Long and short posterior ciliary artery / Venous drainage)
column4: **Ophthalmic artery:** principal source of blood supply for eyeball and orbit; arises from medial side of 5th bend of internal carotid artery immediately after leaving roof of cavernous sinus; lies inferior to optic nerve. **Course:** passes through optic canal within dural sheath of optic nerve, lies inferior; at orbital apex comes out of dural sheath, lies lateral to optic nerve and medial to oculomotor and abducens nerves; moves forward and upward in central or retrobulbar space; crosses optic nerve lateral to medial, runs below superior rectus; nasociliary nerve and superior ophthalmic vein accompany; moves toward maxillary process of frontal bone between MR and SO; comes out into peripheral orbital space; terminates at medial end of upper eyelid giving two terminal branches — **dorsal nasal artery** and **supratrochlear artery**. **Branches:** (1) **Central retinal artery** — arises from ophthalmic artery near optic foramen; runs wavy forward, adherent to dural sheath below optic nerve; 10–15 mm behind eyeball, bends upward and pierces dura and arachnoid (1st bend); bends forward in subarachnoid space and runs short distance inferior to optic nerve (2nd bend); bends upward at right angle to pierce pia mater and reaches centre of optic nerve, surrounded by pial vessels and sympathetic nerve plexus (nerve of Tiedemann) — 3rd bend; in centre of optic nerve, bends forward and runs to lamina cribrosa, pierces it to enter eyeball through centre of optic nerve head — 4th bend; at physiological cup covered by thin connective tissue of Kuhnt — 5th bend; at junction of physiological cup and neuroretinal rim, artery or terminal branches bend. **Terminal branches:** superior retinal artery (→ superior nasal and superior temporal retinal arteries) and inferior retinal artery (→ inferior nasal and inferior temporal retinal arteries); all four divide dichotomously toward ora serrata, ending without anastomosis (end arteries). **Blood supply of retina:** outer four layers (till outer nuclear layer) from choriocapillaries; outer plexiform partially from central retinal artery and partially from choriocapillaries; inner six layers from central retinal arteries — **dual blood supply**. **Macula** from superior and inferior temporal retinal arteries by small twigs. **Cilioretinal artery:** sometimes vessel from ciliary plexus arises at temporal margin of optic disc and supplies it — with cilioretinal artery, central vision saved in central retinal artery occlusion. **Fovea** on avascular zone (FAZ) — during FFA, FAZ delineates as dark hypofluorescent circular zone (no dye reaches), 500 μm diameter. **Retinal capillaries:** arterioles from four terminal branches dip vertically into retinal tissue, form two networks — superficial capillary network at NFL; deep capillary network at inner nuclear layer and outer plexiform layer (more extensive). In parafoveal region, three-layered; absent at FAZ; peripapillary region four-layered (thicker NFL). (2) **Lacrimal artery** — from ophthalmic artery lateral to optic nerve just after coming out from dural sheath; runs along upper border of LR with lacrimal nerve; gives lateral palpebral artery which anastomoses with medial palpebral artery to form superior and inferior palpebral arcades supplying eyelids and conjunctiva. (3) **Long and short posterior ciliary arteries** — **long posterior ciliary arteries:** two in number; each from ophthalmic artery below optic nerve; go forward and pierce sclera one on lateral, one on medial aspect of optic nerve; move forward between sclera and choroid, reach ciliary body; terminate in iris after anastomosing with anterior ciliary arteries to form **major arterial circle of iris (circulus arteriosus iridis major)**. **Short posterior ciliary arteries:** each long posterior ciliary gives 10–20 short posterior ciliary arteries; before piercing sclera, anastomose in circular fashion giving **circle of Zinn** (in sclera, closely surrounds optic nerve); supply optic nerve, optic nerve head, lamina cribrosa; sometimes gives a short straight branch to macula entering eyeball through temporal disc margin = **cilioretinal artery**; pierce sclera and give rich plexus of choroidal vasculature. **Anterior ciliary arteries:** from ophthalmic artery arise lateral and medial muscular branches supplying extraocular muscles; muscular branches supplying four recti give anterior ciliary arteries — seven in number (two from each rectus except LR which gives one); run on both sides of tendons; ~4 mm from limbus pierce sclera; enter iris, terminate after anastomosing with long posterior ciliary arteries to form circulus arteriosus iridis major. (4) **Other branches:** supraorbital (upper eyelid and scalp); medial palpebral (two, anastomose with lateral palpebral to form palpebral arcades); anterior and posterior ethmoidal (ethmoidal air sinuses); dorsal nasal (terminal; lacrimal sac; anastomoses with facial artery); supratrochlear (terminal; medial forehead). **VENOUS SUPPLY:** Superior venous network (above levator palpebrae superioris) and inferior venous network (above orbital floor). (1) **Superior ophthalmic vein:** superior and inferior roots in superomedial part of anterior orbit above LPS tendon receive communication from angular vein, join to form superior ophthalmic vein; runs toward orbital apex in superomedial peripheral space with ophthalmic artery; receives tributaries corresponding to ophthalmic artery branches (posterior ciliary, anterior and posterior ethmoidal veins); joins inferior ophthalmic vein near superior orbital fissure; passes through SOF to drain into cavernous sinus. (2) **Inferior ophthalmic vein:** from inferior venous plexus at anterior orbital floor; communicates with pterygoid venous plexus and anterior facial vein; joins superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus. (3) **Middle ophthalmic vein:** from inferior venous network at inferior border of LR; drains into cavernous sinus; seen in 20%. (4) **Medial ophthalmic vein:** not routinely present; near superior orbital vein in medial peripheral space; shadows superior ophthalmic vein. (5) **Angular vein:** from confluence of supratrochlear and supraorbital veins; after communicating with superior and inferior roots of SOV, runs along lateral wall of nose ~8 mm from medial canthus crossing medial edge of medial palpebral ligament; lies lateral to angular artery; continues as facial vein. *Applied:* in DCR/DCT (lacrimal sac surgeries), angular vein sometimes injured inadvertently → profuse intraoperative bleeding.

column2: Q15. Briefly discuss the anatomy of precorneal tear film.
column4: **History:** First demonstrated in 1928 by Fischer; in 1946 Wolff described detailed structure and coined the term 'precorneal tear film'. **Three layers (outside → inwards):** (1) **Lipid layer** — outermost; secreted by meibomian, Zeiss and Moll glands; 0.1 μm thick (thickness increases with decrease in palpebral fissure width); prevents rapid evaporation of aqueous component; contains low-polarity lipids, fluidic at body temperature, high molecular weight. (2) **Aqueous layer** — middle; secreted by lacrimal gland and accessory lacrimal glands of Krause and Wolfring; thickness 10 μm; constitutes 60% of tear film volume; main proteins — lactoferrin, prealbumin, lysozymes, immunoglobulins; also glucose, urea, ionic inorganic salts; low viscosity. (3) **Mucin layer** — innermost; secreted by conjunctival goblet cells; mucins adsorbed on cell membrane of hydrophobic corneal epithelial cells; mucins anchored by cell membrane microvillae convert hydrophobic corneal epithelial surface into hydrophilic surface on which aqueous layer spreads; thickness 30 μm (thickest layer). **Functions:** makes corneal surface smoother by filling surface irregularities (essential for refraction); lubrication, nutrition and immunity of ocular surface; washes away debris, toxins and foreign bodies; provides oxygen to avascular cornea. **Summary:** lipid layer prevents rapid evaporation; aqueous layer provides lubrication, nutrition and immunity; mucin layer helps anchor tear film over cornea.

column2: Differences between granulomatous and non-granulomatous uveitis.
column4: | Feature | Granulomatous uveitis | Non-granulomatous uveitis | |---|---|---| | **Onset and course** | Usually insidious onset with chronic course | Usually acute onset and short course | | **Symptoms** | Mild persistent symptoms with relatively less ciliary congestion | Severe symptoms with pain and higher degree of ciliary congestion | | **AC reaction** | Mild to moderate if not associated with acute attack | Severe reaction with higher grades of AC cells and flare, sometimes fibrinous exudates | | **Keratic precipitates (KPs)** | Large or medium-sized, crenated-bordered, waxy or pigmented KPs (mutton fat) | Fine granular KPs | | **Iris nodules** | Koeppe's, Busacca's nodules or Berlin's nodules in angle of anterior chamber | No such nodules | | **Anatomic involvement** | Intermediate and posterior uveal involvement is common | Usually anterior uvea involved | | **Causes** | Granulomatous infectious or non-infectious causes (TB, leprosy, sarcoidosis) | Usually idiopathic or immunologic | | **Treatment** | Treatment of cause (systemic) along with ocular immunosuppression and cycloplegia | Usually ocular immunosuppressives and cycloplegics |

column2: Differences between chalazion and stye.
column4: | Feature | Chalazion | Stye (hordeolum) | |---|---|---| | **Definition** | Chronic lipo-granulomatous inflammation of meibomian gland | Acute suppurative inflammation of gland of Zeiss or Moll | | **Symptoms** | Pain, redness, swelling — signs of inflammation usually absent or mild | Pain, redness, swelling — signs of inflammation present | | **Site of lesion** | Round or oval swelling in eyelid; usually away from lid margin | Near the lid margin | | **Pus-point** | No pus-point usually noted | Pus-point at the root of eyelashes | | **Adenopathy** | No such association | Pre-auricular, sub-mandibular adenopathy may be noted | | **Treatment** | Surgical — incision and curettage | Conservative — systemic antibiotics with hot compression, sometimes epilation of involved eyelash |

column2: Differences between phthisis bulbi and atrophic bulbi.
column4: | Feature | Phthisis bulbi | Atrophic bulbi | |---|---|---| | **Shape of eyeball** | Usually irregular in shape | Usually quadrilateral in shape | | **Cause** | Severe open globe injury or inflammation (endophthalmitis, panophthalmitis) | Long-standing iridocyclitis, uveitis causing ciliary shutdown | | **Anatomy (external, intermediate, internal coats)** | Disorganised/disrupted | Can be distinguished separately | | **Calcification** | Definite chances of calcification | Rare chances |

column2: Differences between squamous blepharitis and ulcerative blepharitis.
column4: | Feature | Squamous blepharitis | Ulcerative blepharitis | |---|---|---| | **Lid margin appearance** | Reddish (congestion) with white scales | Yellowish crusts at eyelash roots | | **Swelling** | May be little swollen | Thickened and distorted | | **Erythema/oedema/telangiectasia** | Less | More | | **Eyelashes** | Matted near roots, may be absent in some places or distorted | Small ulceration, may be associated with bleeding | | **Corneal changes** | Not associated with any changes | May be associated with infiltrates, phlyctenules, scarring (in long-standing cases) | | **Underlying margin (after removal of scales)** | Dry, no bleeding | Dry but no bleeding |

column2: Differences between internal and external hordeolum.
column4: | Feature | Internal hordeolum | External hordeolum | |---|---|---| | **Definition** | Acute suppurative inflammation of meibomian gland or pre-existing chalazion | Acute suppurative inflammation of gland of Zeiss or Moll | | **Pus-point and eyelash** | Away from lid margin and eyelash not involved | Near lid margin and eyelash involved | | **Tenderness/swelling** | Away from lid margin and whole tarsal plate area may be involved diffusely | Maximum tenderness and swelling in lid margin | | **H/O previous swelling** | May be there | Usually no such history | | **Treatment** | Conservative treatment with chalazion incision and curettage later | Conservative treatment with epilation of involved eyelashes |

column2: Differences between superficial and deep corneal neovascularisation.
column4: | Feature | Superficial neovascularisation | Deep neovascularisation | |---|---|---| | **Colour and texture of blood vessels** | Bright red and well-defined | Greyish red and ill-defined | | **Crossing limbus** | Continuous over the limbus into the conjunctiva | End abruptly near limbus | | **Anatomical disposition** | Between epithelium and Bowman's membrane | Between stroma and Descemet's membrane | | **Corneal surface** | Raised at places of blood vessels | Deep stromal involvement with smooth surface | | **Branching pattern** | Arborescent — branches run in radial fashion | Acute-angled branches — run in dichotomous fashion | | **Role of anti-VEGF** | No such role | Anti-VEGF has role |

column2: Differences between corneal degeneration and corneal dystrophy.
column4: | Feature | Corneal degeneration | Corneal dystrophy | |---|---|---| | **Inheritance** | Non-hereditary | Hereditary | | **Laterality** | Unilateral or may be bilateral | Always bilateral | | **Corneal thickness** | Usually normal; thinning of cornea in involved area in some long-standing cases | Thinning of cornea in involved area | | **Age** | Younger (usually) | Older (usually) | | **Classification** | According to cause (primary, secondary, associated with metabolic disturbances) | According to involvement of corneal layers | | **H/O previous disease/environmental factors/aging** | May or may not be associated with degeneration — previous disease: band-shaped keratopathy; environmental factors: climatic droplet keratopathy; aging process: arcus senilis | Not associated with dystrophy |

column2: Differences between seclusio pupillae and occlusio pupillae.
column4: | Feature | Seclusio pupillae | Occlusio pupillae | |---|---|---| | **Definition** | 360° posterior synechiae causing complete obstruction of aqueous flow through pupil | Complete occlusion of pupil by organised exudates across entire pupillary area | | **Mechanism** | Adhesion of pupillary margin to anterior lens capsule | Organised inflammatory exudate fills the whole pupillary area | | **Condition of peripheral anterior chamber** | If associated with exudates filled in posterior chamber, iris retraction may lead to deepening of peripheral AC | Peripheral AC usually not deepened in the same manner | | **Stage of uveitis** | Typically seen in chronic/recurrent anterior uveitis | Typically seen in severe fibrinous uveitis | | **Consequence** | Iris bombe → secondary angle-closure glaucoma | Secondary glaucoma due to pupillary block |

column2: Differences between phacomorphic and phacolytic glaucoma.
column4: | Feature | Phacomorphic glaucoma | Phacolytic glaucoma | |---|---|---| | **Cause** | Intumescent crystalline lens due to rapid development of cataract with intact capsule or water imbibition after ruptured capsule by trauma | Crystalline lens protein-induced inflammation and blocking of trabecular meshwork by macrophages after engulfing lens protein | | **Anterior chamber and pupil** | Extremely shallow with rigid pupil | Deep AC with lens matter in AC, keratic precipitates on endothelium, free and active pupil | | **Condition of angle** | Closed angle | Open angle | | **Anterior capsule status** | Taut and bulging anteriorly | Wrinkled and shrunken | | **Surgical challenges** | Due to shallow anterior chamber and intumescent/hard dense nucleus | Due to friable wrinkled anterior capsule and free-floating nucleus |

column2: Differences between optic neuritis and papilloedema.
column4: | Feature | Optic neuritis | Papilloedema | |---|---|---| | **Age/Gender** | Middle-aged females more affected | Any age and gender; no predisposition | | **Laterality** | Usually unilateral; bilateral in neuromyelitis optica | By definition bilateral | | **Cause** | Idiopathic, isolated demyelinating, associated with multiple sclerosis, infective causes | Raised ICP due to any intracranial cause (tumour, haemorrhage, meningitis, hypervitaminosis A/D especially in children) | | **Classification/types** | Retrobulbar optic neuritis, papillitis, neuro-retinitis | No such types | | **Ocular symptoms** | Decreased vision or blurring, pain specifically with eye movement | Blurring of vision, symptoms due to intracranial cause | | **Associated symptoms** | Altered perception of moving objects (Pulfrich phenomenon), worsening with exercise and increased body temperature (Uhthoff sign) | Headache, nausea, vomiting, diplopia (may be due to sixth nerve palsy) | | **Visual acuity** | Affected more, even up to PL only | Affected less, usually 6/6–6/18 | | **Features of optic nerve dysfunction** | Defective colour vision, reduced contrast sensitivity, significant visual field and VEP changes | Only found in long-standing cases where optic atrophy sets in | | **RAPD** | Present in involved eye | Absent | | **Fundus changes** | May be normal in retrobulbar optic neuritis; in papillitis — disc hyperaemia, small haemorrhagic spots, oedema (max 2–3D on direct ophthalmoscope); neuro-retinitis — associated with macular star or macular fan | Disc more hyperemic, haemorrhages and oedema (up to 6D on direct ophthalmoscope) | | **Treatment** | IV steroid followed by oral steroids; neuro-retinitis treated with IV antibiotics; treatment of MS | Treatment of cause of raised ICP; stoppage of vitamin intake etc. | | **Prognosis** | Good in demyelinating cases, worse in infective neuro-retinitis | Depends on prognosis of intracranial cause |

column2: Differences between penetrating and anterior lamellar keratoplasty.
column4: | Feature | Penetrating keratoplasty | Anterior lamellar keratoplasty | |---|---|---| | **Indications** | Opacity of any type or corneal ulcer, even in cases of keratoconus | Anterior corneal disorders, opacity not perforating, formed in corneal ulcer | | **Donor cornea** | Fresh cornea always preferred | May be done with older tissue with healthy status | | **Surgical technique** | Easier than lamellar procedure; open globe surgery | Technically difficult; closed globe surgery | | **Intra-op/Post-op complications** | More; graft failure and rejection rate also high | Less chance of the same, but interface complications more | | **Prognosis** | Early results may be good but long-term outcome determined by graft failure or rejection | Early results may not be as good as penetrating but long-term prognosis better |

column2: Differences between conjunctival congestion and ciliary congestion.
column4: | Feature | Conjunctival congestion | Ciliary congestion | |---|---|---| | **Colour** | Bright red | Dusky red or pink | | **Origin of vessels** | Posterior conjunctival vessels | Anterior ciliary vessels | | **Anatomical area** | Whole conjunctiva may be involved, usually away from cornea | Circumcorneal | | **Branching pattern** | Random branching of congested vessels | Radial disposition | | **Effect of digital pressure or sympathomimetic drops (10% phenylephrine)** | Blanches | Never blanches | | **Significance** | Conjunctival inflammation, hyperaemia | Deeper structure pathology (iridocyclitis, iritis, keratitis) |

column2: Differences between true pterygium and pseudopterygium.
column4: | Feature | True pterygium | Pseudopterygium | |---|---|---| | **Laterality** | Usually bilateral involvement | May be unilateral or bilateral | | **Age** | Environmental factors (high altitude), limbal stem cell degeneration due to UV light, tear film instability | At any age; post-inflammatory fibrotic response; limbal stem cell deficiency may have some role | | **Anatomical area** | Subconjunctival elastotic degeneration; interpalpebral area, nasal or temporal side of cornea | Superficial inflammatory process; from any side onto the cornea | | **Nature** | Progressive, stationary or regressive | Usually static | | **Probe test** | Under the pterygium, probe cannot be passed as there is no gap between pterygium and underlying eyeball | Easily passed as there is a gap between pseudopterygium and eyeball | | **Treatment** | Conjunctivo-limbal autograft (limbal stem cell deficiency covered by limbal tissue from same or other eye), amniotic membrane grafting, pterygium extended removal followed by extended conjunctival transplantation (PERFECT) | Simple excision with conjunctival autograft may be helpful in some cases; amniotic membrane grafting, cultured limbal stem cell transplantation in extensive cases |

column2: Differences between concomitant squint and paralytic squint.
column4: | Feature | Concomitant squint | Paralytic squint | |---|---|---| | **Deviation** | Equal in all directions of gaze | Variable in different directions of gaze | | **Etiology** | Usually developmental | Usually acquired due to disease (thyroid eye disease, raised ICP) or trauma | | **Age** | Infants, toddlers, children | Usually elderly age group but can occur at any age | | **False localisation of object** | Absent | Present | | **Head posture** | May be present | Normal | | **Diplopia** | Usually absent (as it is developmental, diplopia usually taken care of by developing brain by different mechanisms) | Present | | **Extraocular movement** | Normal without restriction | Restricted in direction of involved paralyzed muscle | | **Angle of deviation (AoD)** | Primary AoD = Secondary AoD | Secondary AoD > Primary AoD | | **Treatment/prognosis** | Surgically can be corrected with good prognosis | Diplopia can be avoided by occlusion but surgical correction can be done in long-standing cases where spontaneous recovery failed |

column2: Differences between episcleritis and scleritis.
column4: | Feature | Episcleritis | Scleritis | |---|---|---| | **Definition** | Inflammation of episcleral tissue | Inflammation of sclera | | **Depth** | Superficial | Deeper layer | | **Symptoms** | Redness with mild pain or discomfort, usually no dimness of vision | Severe pain, redness, dimness of vision | | **Signs of uveitis** | Common | Present | | **Other signs** | Less tender, bright red subconjunctival congestion which blanches on pressure | Severely tender bluish red or red nodular involvement, never blanches on pressure | | **Blanching of blood vessels** | No definite complications noted | No such blanching | | **10% phenylephrine (PHE) test** | No such blanching | No such blanching | | **Complications** | Usually good | Thinning of sclera, staphyloma, exudative retinal detachment, cystoid macular oedema, even localised perforation upon minor trauma | | **Treatment** | No definite treatment required; artificial tear substitute, topical NSAID, topical low-potent steroid in non-responding cases | Systemic and topical steroids; treatment of cause (TB, connective tissue disorders) if found | | **Prognosis** | Usually good | Usually poor |

column2: Differences between primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) and primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG).
column4: | Feature | POAG | PACG | |---|---|---| | **Incidence** | Male = female, more chance in myopic | Female > male, more in hypermetropic | | **Status of angle** | Wide open | Closed or narrow according to stage | | **Cause of raised IOP** | Conformational changes in angle structures causing less drainage; unknown | Angle narrowing causes hindrance in aqueous drainage | | **Symptoms** | Dull boring headache or eye pain, frequent change in near glasses, peripheral field loss in late stage | Coloured halos, eye pain mainly in evening (due to mid-dilated pupil in dusk causing pupillary block), nausea/vomiting, painful dimness of vision, redness, photophobia, lacrimation in acute attack | | **Precipitation of acute attack** | Absent | Present (ACG) | | **Treatment** | Topical antiglaucoma medication, sometimes systemic; trabeculectomy depending on response to topical medication, number of drugs, combination | Diagnosed cases treated with topical pilocarpine 2%, Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy or surgical iridectomy in both eyes, lens extraction with IOL; ACG treated with systemic medication along with LPI/SI of both eyes; surgical — trabeculectomy depending on degree of synechial angle closure and response to initial treatment |

column2: Differences between pseudophakia and aphakia.
column4: | Feature | Pseudophakia | Aphakia | |---|---|---| | **Definition** | Eyeball with artificial lens (usually PCIOL after uncomplicated cataract surgery) | Eyeball without any lens — no IOL after cataract surgery (complicated surgery with posterior capsular rupture or pre-existing posterior capsular/capsule-zonular dehiscence so that IOL placement support not available) | | **Refractive status** | Depending on biometry (may be no refractive error for distance) and surgery-induced astigmatism | High hypermetropia usually (except high myopia pre-operatively) plus surgery-induced astigmatism | | **Pupillary area** | Shiny glistening reflex with presence of 3rd Purkinje's image | Jet black pupillary reflex with absence of 3rd Purkinje's image | | **Pupil shape** | Usually round | Usually distorted | | **Posterior capsule and anterior vitreous face** | Usually intact | Usually disturbed | | **Uveal reaction** | Less | Less | | **Chances of complication (raised IOP, corneal decompensation)** | Very less | More | | **Visual rehabilitation** | Not challenging | Challenging; secondary IOL to be planned accordingly |

column2: Differences between posterior chamber IOL (PCIOL) and anterior chamber IOL (ACIOL).
column4: | Feature | PCIOL | ACIOL | |---|---|---| | **Implantation site** | Posterior chamber (behind iris) — in the capsular bag or ciliary sulcus | Anterior chamber (in front of iris) | | **Types** | Rigid PCIOL (SICS); foldable PCIOL; intraocular contact lens (ICL) for refractive surgery | Closed-loop ACIOL (more complications, no longer used); open-loop Kelman Multiflex III | | **Design** | Modified C-loop haptics; optic with dialing hole | Open-loop modified haptics | | **Advantages** | Most physiologically accurate placement of IOL; less chance of bullous keratopathy, secondary glaucoma | Safe and economic option for better visual rehabilitation than aphakic glass in cases after ICCE or ECCE with no capsular support for IOL placement | | **Pre-requisite for implantation** | Adequate support of capsular bag | Complete anterior vitrectomy; pilocarpine-aided intraoperative miosis; surgical iridectomy (peripheral) | | **Complications** | Displacement of IOL from capsular bag; partial implantation of IOL in capsular bag and partially in sulcus (post-op lenticular astigmatism); opacification of optic | Secondary glaucoma; uveitis (recurrent and intractable); pseudophakic bullous keratopathy | | **Post-operative mydriasis** | May be done for better inspection of posterior chamber and/or posterior segment | Contraindicated as it will lead to drop of ACIOL into vitreous cavity |
