column2: Differences between primary and secondary acquired cholesteatoma (ocular context — corneal/conjunctival surface lesions).
column4: The primary/secondary distinction applies mainly to cholesteatoma of the ear; in ophthalmology the analogous comparison is between **primary** and **secondary** acquired surface lesions of cornea/conjunctiva (e.g., limbal stem cell deficiency-related keratinisation). **Primary** = arises de novo from the tissue itself without preceding identifiable insult; **secondary** = arises after a known preceding insult (trauma, chemical injury, chronic inflammation, surgery). Primary lesions tend to be bilateral, slowly progressive, and without identifiable trigger; secondary lesions are unilateral or asymmetric, arise at the site of the prior insult, and progression correlates with the severity of the inciting event. Treatment differs — primary requires addressing the underlying dystrophic/limbal deficiency process (limbal stem cell transplantation, amniotic membrane grafting); secondary requires removal of the inciting factor and reconstruction of the damaged surface.

column2: Differences between acute and chronic dacryocystitis.
column4: | Feature | Acute dacryocystitis | Chronic dacryocystitis | |---|---|---| | **Definition** | Acute suppurative inflammation of lacrimal sac | Chronic inflammation of lacrimal drainage pathway mostly due to partial/complete mechanical obstruction | | **Onset** | Sudden, painful, red, hot, tender swelling in sac region | Gradual, mostly painless swelling below inner canthus | | **Systemic features** | Fever, malaise | Usually absent | | **Discharge** | Frank pus on pressure (pyocele) | Clear fluid (catarrhal), milky gelatinous (mucocele), or pus (pyocele) | | **Complications** | Lacrimal abscess, fistula formation, orbital cellulitis | Recurrent conjunctivitis, epiphora, dacryocystitis flare-ups | | **Treatment** | Systemic antibiotics, topical antibiotics, analgesics; drainage if abscess; DCR/DCT later | DCR (conventional, endoscopic, CDCR) or DCT if sac fibrosed |

column2: Differences between anterior and posterior uveitis.
column4: | Feature | Anterior uveitis | Posterior uveitis | |---|---|---| | **Site of inflammation** | Iris and pars plicata of ciliary body | Choroid and retina (vitreous involvement common) | | **Symptoms** | Pain, photophobia, redness, lacrimation, dimness of vision | Painless floaters, dimness of vision, metamorphopsia | | **Signs** | Circumcorneal congestion, AC cells and flare, KPs, posterior synechiae, iris nodules, hypopyon | Vitritis, retinal/choroidal infiltrates, vasculitis, retinitis, choroiditis, macular oedema | | **Complications** | Complicated cataract, secondary glaucoma (seclusio/occlusio), band keratopathy, phthisis bulbi | CMO, retinal detachment, retinal scarring, optic atrophy, epiretinal membrane | | **Investigations** | CBC, ESR, ANA, RA factor, ACE, HLA B27, Mantoux | FFA, OCT, serology (toxoplasma, CMV, syphilis, TB), chest X-ray, ACE, HIV | | **Treatment** | Topical steroids, cycloplegics, IOP-lowering drugs; systemic steroids if severe/refractory | Systemic steroids, immunosuppressives, intravitreal anti-VEGF/steroid, specific antimicrobial therapy |

column2: Differences between benign and malignant eyelid tumours.
column4: | Feature | Benign eyelid tumours | Malignant eyelid tumours | |---|---|---| | **Growth** | Slow-growing, stable, or may regress | Rapidly progressive, enlarging | | **Ulceration** | Usually intact overlying skin | Centrally ulcerated with heaped-up pearly margins (BCC); friable, bleeds on touch (SCC) | | **Margins** | Well-defined | Ill-defined, indurated beyond visible margin | | **Loss of eyelashes** | Absent | Present | | **Telangiectasia** | Absent | Present over lesion | | **Fixity to deeper tissues** | Mobile | Fixed to underlying tarsus/orbit in advanced cases | | **Regional lymph nodes** | Not involved | May be involved (SCC, sebaceous carcinoma) | | **Metastasis** | None | Present in aggressive/malignant tumours | | **Treatment** | Excision if cosmetic or functional impairment | Wide excision with frozen section/Mohs micrographic surgery ± reconstruction; radiotherapy/chemotherapy for advanced lesions |

column2: Differences between mature and immature cataract.
column4: | Feature | Immature cataract | Mature cataract | |---|---|---| | **Lens appearance** | Partially opacified, greyish | Milky white or pearly, completely opacified | | **Iris shadow** | Present | Absent | | **Visual acuity** | Mild–moderate reduction | Marked reduction, often HM/PL only | | **Fundus view** | Partially visible | Not visible | | **Purkinje images** | First three fused; fourth may or may not be seen | First three fused; fourth absent | | **Coloured halos** | Present (due to prismatic dispersion) | Absent | | **B-scan** | Not routinely required | Required before surgery to rule out posterior segment pathology | | **Surgical urgency** | Elective | Elective but earlier if intumescent/hypermature |

column2: Differences between hypermetropia and presbyopia.
column4: | Feature | Hypermetropia | Presbyopia | |---|---|---| | **Nature** | Refractive error — parallel rays focus behind retina with accommodation at rest | Physiological insufficiency of accommodation due to age | | **Age** | Present since childhood (may be latent and manifest later) | Begins after 40 years | | **Cause** | Axial (short eyeball), curvatural, index, positional, or absence of lens | Decreased lens elasticity and ciliary muscle power | | **Far vision** | Blurred | Normal | | **Near vision** | Blurred if manifest; may be compensated by accommodation | Blurred | | **Symptoms** | Asthenopia (tiredness, headache, watering, photophobia) | Difficulty in near vision, headache, squinting, need for more light | | **Refraction** | Hypermetropic | Emmetropic or as per pre-existing refractive status | | **Correction** | Convex (plus) lens — full cycloplegic correction | Convex (plus) near addition (e.g., +1.00 to +3.00 D depending on age) |

column2: Differences between myopia and hypermetropia.
column4: | Feature | Myopia | Hypermetropia | |---|---|---| | **Definition** | Parallel rays focus in front of retina (accommodation at rest) | Parallel rays focus behind retina (accommodation at rest) | | **Far point** | Finite | Infinity or beyond | | **Eyeball** | Long (axial myopia) | Short (axial hypermetropia) | | **Anterior chamber** | Deep | Shallow | | **Fundus** | Tessellated, myopic crescent, posterior staphyloma (high myopia) | Shot-silk retina, pseudopapillitis (small crowded disc) | | **Symptoms** | Diminished far vision, asthenopia, floaters, pseudoproptosis | Asthenopia, diminished near and distance vision (near worse in low hypermetropia) | | **Complications** | Retinal detachment, CNVM, lattice degeneration, complicated cataract | Amblyopia, accommodative convergent squint, angle-closure glaucoma risk | | **Correction** | Concave (minus) spherical lens | Convex (plus) spherical lens |

column2: Differences between anisometropia and aniseikonia.
column4: | Feature | Anisometropia | Aniseikonia | |---|---|---| | **Definition** | Unequal total refraction between two eyes | Unequal size of retinal images in two eyes | | **Cause** | Differential growth, uniocular aphakia, pseudophakia with wrong biometry, asymmetric age-related changes | Anisometropia (mainly), unequal axial length, IOL-related magnification differences, retinal causes | | **Symptoms** | Asthenopia, headache, anisometropic amblyopia, diplopia in high anisometropia | Diplopia, asthenopia, difficulty in depth perception, headache | | **Significance** | > 4D becomes clinically significant | Retinal image size difference > 5% becomes symptomatic | | **Treatment** | Spectacles (tolerated up to 4D), contact lenses (> 4D), aniseikonic glasses, refractive surgery, IOL exchange, patching for amblyopia | Aniseikonic glasses, contact lenses, refractive surgery, iseikonic lens design |

column2: Differences between corneal ulcer and corneal abrasion.
column4: | Feature | Corneal ulcer | Corneal abrasion | |---|---|---| | **Definition** | Loss of corneal epithelium with involvement of underlying stroma (infective or non-infective) | Loss of superficial corneal epithelium only, without stromal involvement | | **Cause** | Bacterial, fungal, viral, protozoal infection; trophic (exposure, neurotrophic); autoimmune (Mooren's, PUK) | Mechanical trauma, foreign body, contact lens, chemical injury | | **Symptoms** | Pain, redness, photophobia, lacrimation, dimness of vision, foreign body sensation | Severe pain, foreign body sensation, lacrimation, photophobia, blepharospasm | | **Signs** | Stromal infiltrate, overhanging margins, peri-ulcer oedema, hypopyon (in severe), AC reaction | Epithelial defect, no stromal infiltrate; fluorescein staining shows epithelial defect | | **Healing** | Heals with scarring (nebula, macula, leucoma) | Heals completely within 24–72 hours without scarring | | **Complications** | Descemetocele, perforation, endophthalmitis, secondary glaucoma, adherent leucoma | Recurrent corneal erosion, secondary infection (if untreated) | | **Treatment** | Antimicrobial therapy (per cause), cycloplegics, supportive; surgical if impending perforation | Topical antibiotic ointment, pressure patch, bandage contact lens for recurrent erosion |

column2: Differences between hypopyon and hyphema.
column4: | Feature | Hypopyon | Hyphema | |---|---|---| | **Definition** | Collection of pus (WBCs, sterile or infected) in anterior chamber | Collection of blood in anterior chamber | | **Appearance** | Whitish/yellowish layer with flat or convex border, settles inferiorly | Reddish layer, settles inferiorly; may be clot (8-ball hyphema) | | **Cause** | Severe corneal ulcer, endophthalmitis, severe anterior uveitis, fungal infection | Ocular trauma, post-operative, rubeosis iridis, intraocular tumours, blood dyscrasias | | **Associated signs** | Corneal ulcer, hypopyon level, AC cells and flare, severe inflammation | Traumatic signs, elevated IOP, corneal blood staining (late) | | **Grading** | Not formally graded (descriptive) | Graded I–IV (microhyphema, 1/3, 1/3–1/2, >1/2, 8-ball) | | **Complications** | Endophthalmitis, panophthalmitis, secondary glaucoma, corneal perforation | Secondary glaucoma, corneal blood staining, secondary haemorrhage, optic atrophy | | **Treatment** | Topical/systemic antibiotics, antifungal if indicated, cycloplegics, steroids (careful), IOP control, surgical drainage if severe | Bed rest, head elevation, cycloplegics, IOP control, avoid antiplatelets/NSAIDs, surgical paracentesis if indicated |

column2: Long case documentation: Mature/immature senile cataract.
column4: **History:** chief complaints — dimness of vision in affected eye (LE/RE) for ___ months; rainbow/coloured halos (immature cataract only) for same duration; white spot in black portion of eye (mature cataract only). **History of present illness:** patient was seeing well ___ months back; then developed dimness of vision in affected eye — gradual onset, painless, progressive. No history of pain, redness, lacrimation, swelling or trauma. **Past history — medical:** diabetes mellitus (duration, therapy, compliance); hypertension (duration, therapy, compliance); ischaemic heart disease on antiplatelets/anticoagulants; COPD on inhalers/oral steroids; claustrophobia or generalised anxiety disorder; cardiac arrhythmia. **Past history — ocular:** known glaucoma (duration, anti-glaucoma medications, laser therapy, filtration surgery); pre-existing diabetic retinopathy (anti-VEGF, vitrectomy); prior retinal disorders (retinal occlusions, therapy); prior refraction (pathological myopia, high hypermetropia, high astigmatism); dry eye on regular lubricants; other ocular comorbidity. **Ocular examination — vision:** immature cataract — pin hole 6/36 to 6/60, field not assessable, colour vision not assessable; mature cataract — HM or PL with accurate/inaccurate PR, field not assessable, colour vision not assessable. **Structural assessment:** ocular adnexa (lids, lacrimal sac) normal (mention any abnormality in lacrimal sac area); cornea clear (mention corneal opacity or arcus senilis); anterior chamber normal depth (deep in pathological myopia; shallow in high hypermetropia, intumescent cataract); iris normal; iris shadow present (immature) or absent (mature); pupils circular 3–4 mm direct and consensual light reflex present; lens greyish (immature) or milky white/pearly (mature); Purkinje images — first three fused, fourth may or may not be seen depending on grade; digital tension comparable bilaterally. **Summary:** ___ year old lady/gentleman presented with gradual onset painless progressive loss of vision for ___ years/months. Diabetic/non-diabetic, hypertensive/normotensive, with or without ocular history. On ocular examination, VA ___. Iris shadow present/absent. Milky white/greyish white pupillary reflex. First three fused Purkinje images seen. **Provisional diagnosis:** mature/immature senile cataract of left/right eye.

column2: Long case documentation: Pseudophakia (with/without PCO).
column4: **Patient particulars, chief complaint:** routine check-up after cataract surgery (pseudophakia without PCO); dimness of vision in RE/LE (pseudophakia with PCO); foreign body sensation in RE/LE. **History of present illness:** for pseudophakia without PCO — patient underwent cataract surgery (ECCE/SICS/phacoemulsification) in RE/LE about ___ months/weeks/days back; came for routine follow-up or refraction; foreign body sensation in affected eye from immediate post-operative period; no history of pain, swelling, watering or trauma since surgery. For pseudophakia with PCO — patient underwent cataract surgery about ___ months/years back (duration long; mention type if recalled); satisfactory visual rehabilitation after surgery; for past 3 months dimness of vision in operated eye — gradual onset, painless, progressive; no history of pain, swelling, redness or trauma. **Past history:** same as mature/immature cataract. **Ocular examination — vision:** no PCO — 6/9 N6 (RE/LE); with PCO — 6/36 N24 (RE/LE). Field — comparable with examiner by confrontation (no PCO); not assessable (with PCO). Colour vision — normal (no PCO); not assessable (with PCO). **Structural assessment:** all points normal; shiny glass-like reflex in pupillary area. If duration of cataract surgery within 6 months, mention scar mark; otherwise write no visible scar mark. **Scar mark by type:** SICS — frown or linear scar mark seen in superior limbus, covered by conjunctiva scar; mention if suture or suture marks; mention if gaping of wound or iris prolapse. Conventional ECCE — scar mark seen along limbus from 10 o'clock to 2 o'clock closed with interrupted sutures (mention number). Phacoemulsification — clear corneal main incision scar mark; right and left paracentesis scars (may not always be seen). **Note:** even if pseudophakia with PCO, do not mention PCO if examined with torch light only. **Provisional diagnosis:** pseudophakia (RE/LE).

column2: Long case documentation: Aphakia.
column4: **Chief complaint:** dimness of vision in RE/LE both for near and distance since cataract surgery ___ years/months/days ago; foreign body sensation since cataract surgery; lacrimation. **History of present illness:** patient underwent cataract surgery ___ years/months/days ago (mention type if recalled); in immediate post-operative days patient did not regain useful vision; associated history of pain and lacrimation since cataract surgery; no history of trauma. **Past history:** same as mature/immature cataract. **Ocular examination — vision:** VA 6/60 or less; near vision not assessable; field not assessable; colour vision not assessable. **Structural assessment:** all points normal except — mention and document scar mark if operation done < 6 months (as in pseudophakia); deep anterior chamber; iridodonesis present; mention any abnormality of iris and pupil (iridodialysis, updrawn pupil); jet black pupil; only fused first two Purkinje images seen. **Provisional diagnosis:** aphakia (RE/LE).

column2: Short case documentation: Corneal opacity.
column4: **History:** name, age, gender, occupation, religion, date of admission, date of examination. **Chief complaints:** white spot in front of RE/LE for last ___ months/years; dimness of vision for last ___ months/years. **History of present illness (various scenarios):** (1) post-trauma — apparently healthy ___ months/years back, developed sudden onset pain/redness/photophobia/watering following trauma with entry of foreign body during work; treated with multiple eye drops; after recovery noticed white spot in front of RE/LE with Dv hampering daily activity or cosmetically unacceptable; Dv same/increased/decreased. (2) post-systemic illness — history of weakness of one side of face/body with movement/gait abnormalities, or hospitalisation for chronic disease; developed white spots in RE/LE/BE mainly in lower segment with redness, watering, photophobia; treated with multiple eye drops; residual white spot with Dv. (3) post-contact lens — sudden onset pain/redness/photophobia/watering following removal/wearing of contact lens; treated with multiple eye drops; residual white spot with Dv. (4) post-pterygium surgery — small curtain-like reddish thing in front of RE/LE; operated; developed white spots mainly in nasal/temporal part; Dv non-progressive but cosmetically unacceptable. (5) post-refractive surgery — similar spots/high refractive error treated by surgery; developed white spot with pain/redness/photophobia/watering; residual white spot with Dv. (6) post-inflammatory — sudden onset pain/redness/photophobia/watering involving mainly ___ segment; treated with multiple eye drops; residual white spot with Dv; H/O joint pain/arthritis. (7) congenital — white spot since childhood, non-progressive, not associated with pain/redness/photophobia/watering; no family history; Dv non-progressive but cosmetically unacceptable. (8) hereditary — white spot since childhood, non-progressive, but associated with waxing-waning pain/redness/photophobia/watering; similar history in first-degree relative; temporary Dv but cosmetically unacceptable. **Important negative history to mention; known medical/surgical history — DM/HTN/corneal surgery. O/E (RE/LE):** number (single/two/multiple); site (central/paracentral/peripheral); shape (round/oval/rhomboid); size (A × C mm); surface (raised/excavated/smooth regular with other parts of cornea); character (nebula/macula/leucoma); pigmentation (Y/N); vascularisation (Y/N); if leucoma — adherent/non-adherent; pupil; diagram (must); corneal sensation — comparing with other eye. **Provisional diagnosis:** (single/two/multiple), (nebula/macula/leucoma) type of (central/paracentral/peripheral) corneal opacity of (RE/LE), with (normal/diminished) corneal sensation, most probably ___.

column2: Short case documentation: Pterygium.
column4: **Chief complaint:** reddish-white/whitish-red spot in front of RE/LE for last ___ months/years with intermittent redness; reddish-white/whitish-red spot in front of RE/LE for last ___ months/years with intermittent redness following surgery for similar illness in same area of RE/LE few years back; dimness of vision for last ___ months/years in RE/LE. **History of present illness:** apparently healthy ___ months/years back, noticed yellowish spot in RE/LE in nasal/temporal aspect of cornea; then developed insidious onset gradually progressive whitish-red/white curtain-like fleshy thing in nasal/temporal side of RE/LE; treated with multiple eye drops; noticed gradual increase in size toward centre with intermittent redness relieved by eye drops ± Dv hampering daily activity or cosmetically unacceptable. Alternatively — sudden onset pain/redness/photophobia/watering following burn injury to RE/LE; treated with multiple eye drops; residual fleshy lesion with Dv. Alternatively — H/O surgery for similar illness; no difficulty for ___ months/years; then recurrent redness in same area with similar curtain-like fleshy thing in front of RE/LE, gradually progressive. **Important negative history to mention; known medical/surgical history — DM/HTN/pterygium surgery. O/E (RE/LE):** nature (occurrence) — primary/recurrent (as per history); site (nasal/temporal); shape (oval/tongue-shaped); size (A × C mm in cornea); surface (raised/smooth regular with other parts of cornea); character (progressive/vascularised reddish OR regressive/non-vascularised whitish); collection of lymphocytes in front of tongue (+nt under slit lamp = progressive; −nt under slit lamp = regressive); pigmentation (Y/N); diagram (must); corneal sensation — comparing with other eye; pupil. **Provisional diagnosis:** (primary/recurrent), (progressive/regressive), (nasal/temporal) pterygium in (RE/LE) ± inflammation.

column2: Short case documentation: Epiphora due to chronic dacryocystitis.
column4: **Chief complaint:** watering from RE/LE for last ___ months/years; swelling near nasal side of RE/LE for last ___ months/years. **History of present illness:** apparently healthy ___ months/years back, noticed watering from RE/LE with occasional morning stickiness of RE/LE; recurrent redness of RE/LE relieved by eye drops from ophthalmologist; watering and stickiness increased during cough and cold, decreased after drops. Swelling near RE/LE medial canthus for last ___ months/years, soft and painless; swelling increased during cough and cold, relieved by hot compress or external pressure which expresses muco-pus or serous fluid; swelling and sticky discharge causing social discomfort. Alternatively — H/O surgery for similar illness; no difficulty for ___ months/years; then recurrent redness, watering and stickiness from same eye for last ___ months/years; increased during cough and cold, decreased after drops. **Important negative history to mention; known medical/surgical history — DM/HTN/DCR surgery. O/E (RE/LE) swelling — inspection:** site near medial canthus; shape (oval/round); size (A × C cm); surface (rough/smooth regular with adjacent skin/reddish tense); pigmentation, scar mark. **Palpation — superficial:** tenderness present/absent; temperature increased/not increased. **Deep:** surface smooth/rough/lobulated; margin diffuse/well-demarcated; mobility mobile/immobile; fixity to skin/bone/not fixed; tenderness present/absent; compressibility (with evacuation of fluid) present/absent. **Syringing (through lower puncta):** late regurgitation of sero-mucus fluid through upper puncta with hard stop on further propagation of cannula. **Known medical/surgical history:** DM/HTN/DCR surgery. **Provisional diagnosis:** epiphora most probably due to chronic dacryocystitis (Rt/Lt) side with conjunctival congestion (RE/LE).

column2: Short case documentation: Chalazion.
column4: **Chief complaint:** swelling in upper/lower lid (RE/LE) for last ___ months/years; Dv for last ___ months/years. **History of present illness:** apparently healthy ___ months/years back, noticed small swelling in upper/lower lid (RE/LE), initially painful with redness of eye; pain and redness subsided after treatment by local doctor; swelling remained in same site with occasional pain and increasing size; swelling decreased with hot compress and antibiotic ointment, increased with frequent rubbing. Alternatively — Dv for last ___ months/years perceived by patient as swelling increases; increased size of swelling causes drooping of upper eyelid. Alternatively — H/O surgery for similar illness before in same/other eye; no difficulty for ___ months/years; then recurrent redness, watering and stickiness with swelling from same eye for last ___ months/years in upper/lower lid (RE/LE). **Important negative history to mention; known medical/surgical history. O/E (RE/LE) swelling — inspection:** site (upper/lower lid RE/LE — medial 1/3rd or middle 1/3rd or lateral 1/3rd); shape (oval/round); size (A × C mm); surface (rough/smooth regular with adjacent skin/reddish tense); pigmentation, scar mark. **Palpation — superficial:** tenderness present/absent; temperature increased/not increased. **Deep:** surface smooth/rough; mobility mobile/immobile; fixity to skin/bone/not fixed; tenderness present/absent; compressibility (with evacuation of fluid) present/absent. **Transillumination:** absent. **Conjunctiva:** congestion/no congestion. **Cornea and pupil:** ___. **Known medical/surgical history:** DM/HTN/chalazion surgery. **Provisional diagnosis:** primary/recurrent chalazion of (RE/LE) upper/lower lid with/without inflammation at present.

column2: Short case documentation: Subconjunctival haemorrhage.

column2: Explain why: In small children atropine should be applied in ointment form.
column4: In small children atropine ointment is preferred over atropine drops because drops drain through the lacrimal passage to nasal mucosa, which is highly vascular. From nasal mucosa the drug is absorbed into systemic circulation and produces **anticholinergic side effects** — fever, hot flushes, tachycardia. The baby may become restless, creating a different critical situation. If ointment form is used, chances of similar events are much less due to **less systemic absorption**.

column2: Explain why: Genetic counselling is important in retinoblastoma.
column4: The retinoblastoma gene is **80% penetrant**. (1) In patients with positive family history, **40% of siblings** are at risk of developing RB, and **40% of offspring** of the affected patient may develop RB. (2) In patients with no family history of RB, if the affected child has **unilateral RB**, 1% of siblings are at risk and 8% of offspring may develop RB. (3) In **bilateral RB** with no positive family history, 6% of siblings and 40% of offspring may develop RB. So, genetic counselling of the parents is important in retinoblastoma.
