column2: Q1. Define myopia. Classify it and describe its clinical features and treatment.
column4: **Definition:** Refractive error in which parallel rays of light coming from infinity are focused in front of retina, with accommodation at rest. **Symptoms:** Diminution of far vision, asthenopia, floaters, pseudoproptosis (large eyeballs appearing to bulge). **Signs:** pseudoeso deviation (high myopia due to negative angle kappa), deep anterior chamber, increased prevalence of nuclear and posterior subcapsular cataract, decreased ocular rigidity. **Fundus findings (only in high myopia):** temporal myopic crescent, tessellated/tigroid fundus, tilted optic disc, posterior staphyloma, lacquer cracks, Foster-Fuchs spots, peripheral lattice degeneration, vitreous degeneration with posterior detachment. **Etiological classification:** (1) **Axial myopia** — commonest; increased AP length of eyeball; 1 mm increase = 3D myopia. (2) **Curvatural myopia** — increased curvature of cornea, lens or both. (3) **Positional myopia** — anterior displacement of crystalline lens. (4) **Index myopia** — increased refractive index of crystalline lens (nuclear cataract). **Clinical classification:** (1) **Congenital myopia** — present since birth, usually unilateral (anisometropia), associated with convergent squint, may have other congenital anomalies. (2) **Simple myopia** — commonest variety; develops and slowly progresses after birth with age; sharpest rise in school-going age (school myopia); occurs between 6–10 years, increases till 18–20 years @ ~0.50 D/year; does not exceed 6–8D. (3) **Pathological myopia** — degenerative/progressive; starts at 5–10 years; rapid progression during early adult life; > 6D or axial length > 26 mm; associated with degenerative changes; prone to long-term complications (retinal detachment, CNVM). (4) **Acquired myopia** — post-traumatic, drug-induced, space myopia, consecutive myopia, night myopia. **Optics:** infinite far point becomes finite; convergence insufficiency. **Treatment — optical:** prescription of appropriate **concave spherical lens** by objective and subjective refraction (glasses or contact lens); slight under-correction preferred. **Surgical:** radial keratotomy (obsolete); clear lens extraction (only in pathological myopia); phakic refractive lens; femto-second laser-based surgeries (RELEX, SMILE); excimer laser-based surgeries (PRK, LASIK) — aim is to flatten/decrease central corneal curvature by photoablation of corneal stroma. **Special note:** genetic predisposition; prevalence more in children with both parents myopic.

column2: Q2. Write short notes on pathological myopia.
column4: **Definition:** Rapidly progressive variant of myopia beginning at 5–10 years, progressing rapidly, usually associated with degenerative changes in the eye. **Etiology:** rapid axial growth of eyeball beyond normal biological variations of development; genetic factors play a major role — more growth in retina, thinning of sclera, increased axial length, degeneration of choroid, degeneration of retina, degeneration of vitreous. **Symptoms:** defective and poor-quality vision; muscae volitantes (floaters); night blindness. **Signs:** prominent eyeball, large corneas, deep anterior chamber, large pupils. **Fundus:** Foster-Fuchs spot, subretinal neovascularisation, choroidal haemorrhage, white atrophic patches, CNVM, posterior staphyloma. **Peripheral retina:** large and pale, temporal myopic crescent (may encircle entire disc; traction band may be present on nasal side), degenerations like lattice and cystoid common, breaks in long-standing cases. **Vitreous:** liquefaction, Weiss ring (complete PVD), vitreous opacities. **Complications:** retinal detachment, complicated cataract, spontaneous vitreous haemorrhage, CNVM, strabismus. **Treatment principle:** optical/surgical correction makes patient free from spectacles but does NOT insulate against long-term complications due to retinal/choroidal/vitreous degeneration; counsel for premonition signs of RD and regular long-term follow-up. **Optical:** minimum power acceptance with maximum visual benefit; concave spherical lens of appropriate dioptre; contact lens better (avoids peripheral distortion and minification of image); low or zero drop IOL. **Surgical:** refractive lens exchange / clear lens extraction with phacoemulsification; phakic refractive lens implantation (appropriate dioptre IOL in sulcus with crystalline lens in situ).

column2: Q3. Define hypermetropia. Classify it and describe its clinical features and treatment.
column4: **Definition:** Refractive error in which parallel rays of light coming from infinity are focused behind retina, with accommodation at rest. **Symptoms:** asthenopic symptoms (tiredness of eye, frontotemporal headache, watering, photophobia due to sustained accommodation); dimness of both near and distance vision. Low hypermetropia — near vision more defective than distance; high hypermetropia — both equally defective. **Signs:** shallow AC, small pupils, small corneas, small AP length of eyeballs; **shot-silk appearance** of retina (more bright, reflects more light); small optic disc with ill-defined margins and more vascularity mimicking papillitis (pseudopapillitis). **Classification:** (1) **Axial hypermetropia** — commonest; normal biological variation; axial length < 1 mm than normal = +3D. (2) **Curvatural** — decreased curvature of cornea/lens. (3) **Index** — due to cortical cataract. (4) **Positional** — posterior subluxation of lens. (5) **Congenital/acquired** — due to developmental/acquired conditions outside normal biological variation (e.g., aphakia). (6) **Due to paralysis of accommodation** — III nerve palsy (internal ophthalmoplegia). (7) **Consecutive hypermetropia** — surgically over-corrected myopia. **Components:** Total hypermetropia = latent + manifest. **Latent:** amount normally corrected by inherent ciliary muscle tone (~1D); disclosed during objective refraction after total cycloplegia. **Manifest:** corrected by inherent ciliary muscle tone; subdivided into **facultative** (correctable by accommodative effort) and **absolute** (not correctable by accommodative effort). **Treatment — optical:** convex spherical lens; full spherical correction provided; total hypermetropia found out after cycloplegia (especially children); contact lens preferred in unilateral high hypermetropia. **Surgical — cornea-based:** (1) incisional refractive surgery — hexagonal keratotomy (corrects low-moderate). (2) excimer laser-based — hyperopic PRK, hyperopic epi-LASIK (preferred over PRK), hyperopic LASIK (corrects 1–8D), hyperopic c-LASIK (better than conventional). (3) other non-laser and laser-based — thermal laser keratoplasty (Thulium-Holmium-Chromium:YAG laser, corrects up to 2.5D), conductive keratoplasty (radiofrequency energy, non-laser, shrinks corneal tissue). **Lens-based:** hyperopic lens exchange (for high hypermetropia in presbyopic age); phakic refractive lens (specially designed IOL in sulcus with in-situ crystalline lens). **Complications:** recurrent blepharitis/chalazion (children); **amblyopia** (anisometropic/strabismic/ametropic — mandatory amblyopia treatment in children; more risk than other refractive errors); accommodative convergent squint; primary angle-closure glaucoma risk.

column2: Q4. Define aphakia. Describe its optical considerations
column4: clinical features and treatment.
column6: **Definition:** High degree of hypermetropic state where crystalline lens is absent from pupillary area and does not take part in refraction. **Optical considerations:** absence of crystalline lens → total dioptric power decreases from +60D to +44D → parallel rays focus behind retina → state of high hypermetropia with total loss of accommodation. **Causes:** (1) **Congenital** — absence since birth (rare). (2) **Traumatic** — traumatic extrusion of lens; post-traumatic absorption of lens matter (especially children); posterior dislocation of lens into vitreous (optical aphakia). (3) **Surgical** — after ICCE/complicated ECCE (commonest cause). **Symptoms:** dimness of vision for far and near. **Signs:** **iridodonesis** (tremulous iris due to loss of lens support), deep AC, jet black pupil, absence of IIIrd and IVth Purkinje images, scar mark in surgical aphakia (limbus/sclera depending on cataract surgery type). **Optical treatment:** +10D spherical with cylindrical correction (spectacles or contact lens); image magnification over spectacles (30%) → anisokonia and loss of binocular vision; spherical aberration (2.5%) → pin cushion distortion; prismatic aberration → **roving ring scotoma / jack-in-the-box phenomenon**; restricted field of vision (50% restriction in all quadrants); chromatic aberration (due to absence of natural colour filter of crystalline lens); cosmetic issues. **Surgical treatment:** (1) **Intraocular lens implantation** — **PCIOL (0% magnification — treatment of choice):** scleral-fixated PCIOL (10% magnification preferred), iris-supported PCIOL, sulcus placement of PCIOL (in cases where capsular bag is intact); **ACIOL** (not recommended). (2) **Refractive corneal surgery** — keratophakia/epikeratophakia (still under trial): refractive lenticule from donor cornea transplanted in aphakic eye. **Special notes:** spectacle correction of unilateral aphakia → diplopia due to anisocoria; difficulty in hand-eye coordination due to image magnification; Snellen's VA in spectacle-corrected aphakia theoretically better than actual VA due to image magnification; progressive/multifocal glasses better than conventional bifocals.

column2: Q5. Define astigmatism. Classify it and describe its clinical features and treatment.
column4: **Definition:** Refractive error in which refraction varies in different meridians of eye, and light rays fail to converge in a point focus but form focal lines. **Classification — regular astigmatism** (refractive power changes uniformly from one meridian to another, forming two principal meridians) vs **irregular astigmatism** (non-uniform change, multiple meridians, beyond geometric analysis). **Regular — by relationship between two principal meridians:** (1) **with-the-rule** — vertical meridian more curved; angle between meridians 90°; (2) **against-the-rule** — horizontal meridian more curved; 90°; (3) **oblique** — two principal meridians not horizontal/vertical but at right angles (45° & 135°); (4) **bioblique** — two principal meridians not at right angles. **By optics of two principal meridians:** (1) **Simple astigmatism** — one meridian focused on retina; other either **simple myopic** (in front) or **simple hypermetropic** (behind). (2) **Compound astigmatism** — both meridians in front (**compound myopic**) or behind (**compound hypermetropic** — most common type) but at different points. (3) **Mixed astigmatism** — one meridian in front (myopic), one behind (hypermetropic); least visually troublesome. **Symptoms:** blurring of vision with distortion of images; asthenopic symptoms; tilting of head; squinting/half-closure of eyelids. **Clinical pearls:** asthenopic symptoms more with astigmatism than spherical ametropia; low astigmatism produces more marked symptoms; with-the-rule produces clearer vision but more symptoms; hypermetropic astigmatism more symptomatic than same amount of myopic astigmatism. **Signs:** retinoscopy reveals two different powers in two principal meridians (regular); irregular pupillary reflex (irregular); slit lamp may reveal keratoconus. **Etiology:** corneal astigmatism, lenticular astigmatism, retinal astigmatism. **Treatment — optical:** myopic → concave cylindrical lens; hypermetropic → convex cylindrical lens; may be spectacle or contact lens; < 0.50D → treat only if symptomatic; high astigmatism → under-correction initially, then follow-up and adjustments; principal meridians determined by refractometer or objective refraction plus astigmatic & Jackson's cross cylinder tests. **Surgical — cornea-based:** (1) incisional — astigmatic keratotomy (transverse arcuate cuts 5–7 mm away from pupil; flattens steep meridian; corrects up to 4–6D astigmatism); limbal relaxing incision (corrects 1–2D). (2) laser ablation — PRK, astigmatic LASIK. **Lens-based:** toric IOL implantation after cataract surgery in presbyopic age group.

column2: Q6. Define presbyopia. Describe its pathophysiology
column5: **Definition:** Physiological phenomenon beginning after 40 years of age resulting in physiological insufficiency of accommodation due to reduced amplitude leading to progressive deterioration of near vision. **Pathophysiology:** in emmetropic eye, far point at infinity; near point varies with age — 7 cm at 10 years, 25 cm at 40 years, 33 cm at 45 years; amplitude of accommodation decreases with age (14D at 10 years → 4D at 40 years). Beyond 40 years, near point of accommodation recedes beyond normal reading distance due to: (a) age-related lenticular changes — decreased elasticity of lens capsule, cataractogenesis making lens stiff; (b) age-related decline in ciliary muscle power. **Symptoms:** difficulty in near vision, diplopia during near vision, asthenopic symptoms. **Signs:** assessment of near point of accommodation (NPA) and amplitude by RAF rule / Prince rule, minus lens (concave) measurement, push-up test. **Optical correction:** both monocularly and binocularly; dynamic retinoscopy to assess accommodative response; convex lens of appropriate power; near add — difference between distance correction and convex lens needed for near vision; 45 years: +1.00–1.25 Dsph; 50 years: +1.50–1.75 Dsph; 55 years: +2.00–2.25 Dsph; 60 years: +2.50–3.00 Dsph; adjust for working distance; intermediate add = half near add; glasses as reading glasses, D-bifocal, multifocal; weakest convex lens with clear near vision prescribed (over-correction causes asthenopia). **Surgical — cornea-based:** monovision conductive keratoplasty, monovision LASIK (one eye distance, other near), presbyopic bifocal LASIK (two concentric zones for distance and near), presbyopic multifocal LASIK (multiple independently calculated ablations at different optical zones), corneal inlay placement with femtosecond laser. **Lens-based:** refractive lens exchange with accommodative IOLs; monovision with IOL. **Sclera-based:** still under clinical trials.

column2: Q7. Define accommodation. Describe ocular changes
column4: assessment and anomalies.
column6: **Definition:** Physiological phenomenon by which diverging rays from a near object are focused on retina; converging power of eye increases by augmenting the power of crystalline lens via increased anterior curvature by ciliary muscle action. **Ocular changes:** ciliary muscle contracts → ciliary ring diameter decreases → zonules relax (decreased tension) → equatorial diameter of lens decreases → axial diameter (thickness) increases → anterior curvature increases (posterior curvature no change) → total dioptric power of lens increases. **Terminologies:** (1) **Far point (punctum remotum)** — farthest point where objects can be seen clearly. (2) **Near point (punctum proximum)** — nearest point where small objects can be seen clearly. (3) **Range of accommodation** — distance between near and far point. (4) **Amplitude of accommodation (A)** — difference between dioptric power needed to focus at near point (P) and far point (R); A = P − R = 1/Near point (m) − 1/Far point (m). (5) **Depth of field** — range of distance from eye within which an object appears clear without accommodation change. (6) **Depth of focus** — range at retina within which an object may move with clarity. **Assessment:** NPA and amplitude measured by Prince's rule / RAF rule, concave (minus) lens, push-up test (patient needs full refractive correction; measure monocularly and binocularly); accommodative response by dynamic retinoscopy. **Anomalies — diminished accommodation:** physiological (presbyopia), pharmacological (cycloplegia), pathological (inertia, paralysis, insufficiency, ill-sustained accommodation). **Increased accommodation:** excessive accommodation, spasm of accommodation.

column2: Q8. Define anisometropia. Describe its etiology
column4: optical considerations and treatment.
column6: **Definition:** Optical condition where total refraction between two eyes is unequal; > 4D becomes a clinical concern due to considerable difference between retinal images. **Etiology — congenital:** differential growth of two eyeballs; **acquired:** uniocular aphakia (after cataract surgery), pseudophakia with wrong biometry, asymmetric age-related changes. **Classification:** (1) **Simple anisometropia** — one eye emmetropic, other myopic (**simple myopic**) or hypermetropic (**simple hypermetropic**); simple astigmatic — one emmetropic, other astigmatic. (2) **Compound anisometropia** — both eyes myopic (**compound myopic**) or hypermetropic (**compound hypermetropic**); compound astigmatic — both astigmatic. (3) **Mixed anisometropia (antimetropia)** — one eye myopic, other hypermetropic. **Optical considerations:** binocular single vision present if < 3D anisometropia; **uniocular vision** in very high anisometropia (one eye develops); **alternate vision** in mixed anisometropia (hypermetropic eye for distance, myopic eye for near); risk of **anisometropic amblyopia**. **Treatment — optical:** corrective spectacles tolerated up to 4D; contact lens for > 4D; **aniseikonic glass** (corrects image size disparity); alternate eye patching according to age for amblyopia. **Surgical — cornea-based:** refractive corneal surgeries for myopia, hypermetropia, astigmatism. **Lens-based:** refractive lens exchange, phakic IOL insertion, secondary IOL insertion for uniocular aphakia, pseudophakic IOL exchange for wrong biometry (not well tolerated).

column2: Q9. Define cycloplegics. Describe their uses
column5: **Definition:** Drugs that react with postsynaptic muscarinic receptors and block acetylcholine action, thus paralysing iris sphincter; due to unopposed action of dilator muscle, there is pupillary dilatation (mydriasis). **Uses:** (1) **Diagnostic** — examination of peripheral lens and posterior segment (use drugs of shorter duration); (2) **Therapeutic** — iritis in adults (paralyses ciliary muscle → maintains full cycloplegia, relieves pain of iridocyclitis — atropine longer duration); (3) **Refraction** — inhibits accommodation so accurate refraction in children (atropine and cyclopentolate approved). **Stop atropine if:** local — irritation, swelling, maceration of eyelid and conjunctival hyperaemia; systemic (especially children) — fever, tachycardia, constipation, urinary retention (mild → discontinuation; severe → IV physostigmine). **Use of adrenergic drugs with cycloplegics:** co-administration of mydriatic (α1 agonist, e.g., phenylephrine) with cycloplegic causes sustained iris dilatation (paralysis of sphincter pupillae + stronger dilator action). **Comparison table (onset/duration):** phenylephrine (α1 agonist) — 30–60 min onset, 3–5 hours duration; atropine sulphate — 45–120 min, 7–14 days; scopolamine — 30–60 min, 4–7 days; tropicamide — 20–40 min, 4–6 hours.

column2: Q10. Describe the methods of determination of visual acuity.
column4: **Basic considerations:** visual angle = angle subtended at nodal point by physical dimensions of object in visual field; a visual angle of ≥ 1 minute required to make two points clear and discreet. **Visual acuity** = reciprocal of the minimum resolvable visual angle measured in minutes of arc for a standard test pattern. **Components:** (1) minimum visible (detection of object); (2) minimum separable (location relative to another object); (3) minimum resolvable (ability to distinguish > 1 identifying feature). Clinical practice measures **minimum resolvable** — threshold between 30 seconds to 1 minute of arc. **Types of tests:** (A) **Detection acuity** — dot visual acuity, Catford drum, candy bead, STYCAR graded balls. (B) **Recognition acuity** — direction identification (Snellen's E chart, Landolt's C chart), letter identification (Snellen's, Sheridan's, ETDRS, HOTV), picture identification (Allen's picture card, miniature toy, domino cards), picture identification on behavior (Cardiff acuity cards, Bailey-Hall cereal). (C) **Resolution acuity** — optokinetic nystagmus, preferential looking, visually evoked response. **Technique — distant VA (children > 5 years and adults):** Snellen's letter/E/C charts (E/C for illiterate); series of black capitals on white board, each progressively diminishing; at given distance each letter subtends 5 minutes at nodal point; top line read at 60 m; subsequent lines from 36, 24, 18, 12, 9, 6 m; patient at 6 m from chart; chart well illuminated; each eye tested separately; recorded as fraction — numerator = distance from chart, denominator = distance at which normal person reads same line; if top line unreadable → reduce distance (5/60, 4/60, 3/60, 2/60, 1/60); if top line unreadable at 1 m → count fingers (CF); if CF not possible → hand movements (HM+); if HM not perceived → perception of light (PL). **Near VA:** each eye separately; chart at comfortable reading distance; Jaeger's chart (J1–J7); Roman test types (N5, N6, N8, N10, N12, N18, N36, N48); Snellen's near vision chart (~1/17 of normal size). **Limitations:** detects foveal vision at one level of illumination/adaptation at one distance; testing in children difficult, observer variance in interpretation.

column2: Q11. Define colour vision. Describe the physiology of colour vision and colour vision tests.
column4: **Definition:** Perceptual phenomenon of human eye to discriminate between different colours when light rays of different wavelengths excite different groups of cone cells in retina. All colours are proportionate admixture of three primary colours: red (723–645 nm), green (576–492 nm), blue (492–450 nm). **Attributes:** (1) **Hue** — permits colour to be classified as red, yellow, green, blue or intermediate; determined by dominant wavelength of visible spectrum. (2) **Lightness/brightness** — determined by luminosity of component wavelength; maximum under photopic, minimum under scotopic conditions — **Purkynje shift**. (3) **Saturation** — white light + amount of particular wavelength = resultant non-white colour; inverse of amount of particular colour added; more saturation → sharper colour; less → faded. **Physiology:** trichromatic at retina (trichromatic theory); opponent colour theory at ganglion cells and LGB; hierarchical arrangement of colour-coded cells in striate cortex. **Retinal level:** blue-sensitive cones (cyanolabe, short wavelength), green-sensitive cones (chlorolabe, medium wavelength), red-sensitive cones (erythrolabe, long wavelength); colour determined by relative proportion of impulse generation by these three cone systems. **Ganglion cell layer:** opponent colour cells (successive colour contrast) and double opponent cells (simultaneous colour contrast); combination of exclusive colours (reddish green) does not exist. **LGB:** colour perception mediated by parvocellular part (60% spectrally opponent cells). **Striate cortex and above:** relayed to layer IVc by parvocellular LGB; spectrally opponent and double opponent cells; stimulus relayed to blobs of layers II & III; hierarchical arrangement of complex and hypercomplex colour-coded cells; passes to visual association area; final relay in lingual and fusiform gyri of occipital lobe (specialised colour perception area). **Colour blindness:** anomaly (defective colour perception) vs anopia (absent colour perception). **Genetics:** chromosome 7 — blue cone gene; chromosome Xq — red and green cones. **Congenital (X-linked recessive):** anomalous trichromatic (protanomalous — defective red; deuteranomalous — defective green; tritanomalous — defective blue); dichromatic (protanopia — absent red; deuteranopia — absent green; tritanopia — absent blue); achromatopsia (rare — cone monochromatism, rod monochromatism autosomal recessive total colour blindness). **Acquired:** due to damage to macula or optic nerve (disease or drugs) — blue-red (CSCR, macular oedema); red-green (optic nerve disease or compression); blue blindness (nuclear cataract). **Tests:** (A) **Ishihara pseudoisochromatic chart** — most frequently used screening; 24 plates; 1–17 with dots showing central number; 18–24 with wiggly lines to trace; plates 1 & 24 control; read at 75 cm with natural light; ≥ 10 correct = normal; ≤ 7 = deficient; 8–9 = indeterminate; confirm with 100-hue or anomaloscope. (B) **City University test, spectroscopic test** — one central + four peripheral; closest hue matched. (C) **Hardy-Rand-Rittler** — similar to Ishihara. (D) **Lantern test** — coloured lanterns; obsolete. (E) **Farnsworth-Munsell 100-hue** — 85 caps in four racks; rearrange in ascending colour progression; recorded on circular chart; total error score: 0–16 superior, 17–100 average, > 100 low. (F) **Nagel's anomaloscope** — match between mixture colour and test colour; four matches: Rayleigh (yellow test / red-green mixture — detects red-green deficiencies), Engelking-Tredelenburg (blue test / blue-green mixture — blue-yellow), Pickford-Lakowski (blue-yellow), Moreland (blue-yellow); currently digital anomaloscope with RGB primaries in CRT widely available.

column2: Q12. Describe the preoperative evaluation of a patient for refractive surgery.
column4: **Selection of patient:** (1) patients younger than 18 years not suitable; (2) refraction stable for at least 1 year; (3) exact reason for surgery — cosmetic, occupational, contact lens intolerance; (4) counselling regarding choice of procedure (each corrects a particular range); (5) refractive surgery has direct effect on occupation — e.g., radial keratotomy avoided in night drivers due to glare risk; (6) avoid in pre-existing ocular diseases; (7) valid written informed consent. **Absolute contraindications:** immunosuppression, known glaucoma, keratoconus, active keratitis, scarred cornea, connective tissue disorders, corneal warp due to contact lens use, retinal vascular diseases. **Relative contraindications:** severe dry eye, one-eyed, blepharitis, ocular surface disorder. **Preoperative examinations:** (1) slit lamp biomicroscopy (rule out absolute/relative contraindications in anterior segment); (2) indirect ophthalmoscopy and +90D lens (rule out pre-existing posterior segment pathology); (3) cycloplegic refraction (especially younger patients); (4) mesopic (low light) pupillary diameter measurement (~6 mm) — laser ablation zone diameter must be less than this to prevent glare and halos; (5) applanation tonometry (rule out glaucoma); (6) Pentacam (comprehensive anterior segment analyser) — rule out keratoconus; (7) pachymetry — cornea-based procedures contraindicated in thin corneas.

column2: Q13. Write short notes on excimer laser.
column4: **Principle:** Excited dimer. Excited state — atoms A and B form a stable molecule; LASER energy emission; ground state — atoms mutually repulsive. In excimer laser, ground state does not exist, so after LASER emission molecules automatically return to excited state. **Composition:** rare gas halides; choice of laser wavelength determined by gas mixture — ArF: 193 nm; KrF: 248 nm; XeF: 351 nm. **Characteristics:** (1) high corneal tissue absorption coefficient — suitable for surface ablation; (2) poor tissue penetration; (3) minimal thermal effect due to short pulse duration; (4) reproducible and repeatable energy emission; (5) emitted energy sufficient to ablate 4–7 mm diameter central cornea, 0.2–0.3 mm depth precision, ideal penetration at Argon F 193 nm, 10 μm-wide incision up to 95% corneal stromal thickness; (6) limited penetration → minimal damage to deeper stroma and endothelium; (7) no penetration to anterior chamber. **Generations:** 1st — broad irregular beams; 2nd — scanning slit, thinner beam; 3rd — scanning spot; 4th — wavefront technology and eye trackers. **Uses:** PRK, LASIK, phototherapeutic keratectomy for band-shaped keratopathy.

column2: Q14. Write short notes on femtosecond laser.
column4: **LASER:** Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation — coherent, directional, monochromatic light that can be precisely focused into a small spot. **Principle:** optically transparent refractive layers (cornea, lens) do not absorb electromagnetic radiation in visible/infrared spectrum at low power densities, allowing light to pass without alteration; at higher power densities, they absorb light energy → plasma generation → tissue disruption. Nd:YAG has nanosecond (10⁻⁹) pulse duration → photodisruption with zone of collateral damage > 100 μm. By shortening pulse duration from nanosecond (10⁻⁹) to picosecond (10⁻¹²) to femtosecond (10⁻¹⁵), zone of collateral damage reduced to 1 μm. **Femtosecond laser:** focused infrared laser, wavelength 1053 nm; ultrafast pulses of 100 fs; solid-state Nd:Glass laser generated from titanium sapphire; non-visible, becomes visible when combined with helium; machine — IntraLase FSL. **Mechanism:** very low energy settings due to very short pulse duration and rapid pulse repetition; energy absorbed by target tissue → plasma formation; free electrons and ionised molecules rapidly expand → cavitation bubbles; force of cavitation bubbles creates tissue separation. **Uses — diagnostic:** UHR-OCT (increases axial resolution to 1–3 μm); SHG imaging (3-D image acquisition through full corneal thickness). **Therapeutic — corneal and refractive surgery:** creating corneal flap for LASIK, lamellar keratoplasty, creating channels for INTACS, penetrating keratoplasty. **LASIK advantages:** greater accuracy of flap design, thin yet stable flaps, fewer flap complications, better centration, stronger flap adherence, less IOP rise during suction, fewer higher-order aberrations, less dry eyes, less epithelial ingrowth, better contrast sensitivity. **LASIK disadvantages:** suction breaks, incomplete flaps, transient light sensitivity, persistent bubbles in stroma, harder to lift flaps, granular bed. **Other uses:** PK (penetrating keratoplasty — donor corneal button preparation), DALK, DSAEK, astigmatic keratotomy after suture lysis in PK, INTACS (intrastromal corneal ring segments), collagen cross-linking (riboflavin injection), presbyopia (INTRACOR, lentotomy, corneal inlays), FSL-assisted corneal biopsy. **Cataract surgery:** corneal incision and limbal relaxing incision, paracentesis, capsulorhexis, lens fragmentation. **Cataract contraindications for FSL use:** deep-set orbits, tremors/poor docking, dementia, anterior basement membrane dystrophy, trauma/contact lens-induced scars, ocular surface disease, poor dilatation, increased IOP/glaucoma, dense PSC (relative). **Cataract advantages:** more square corneal incision (resistant to leakage), incision can be planned per pre-existing astigmatism (astigmatically neutral), more circular/stronger/precisely planned rhexis (less PCO, more accurate refractive outcome), lens fragmentation (less phaco energy and time). **Cataract disadvantages:** high cost, moving patient between 2 rooms/2 laser delivery systems (for LASIK), questionable efficacy in very hard cataract, electron microscopy shows rhexis irregularity, creeds steady lens (contraindicated in zonular dialysis). **Glaucoma:** SLT (selective laser trabeculoplasty — full-thickness ablation channels through TM with minimum surrounding tissue damage), guarded filtration surgery (more precise scleral incision), deep sclerotomy (superficial and deep partial-thickness scleral flaps). **PDT:** replaces diode laser; ICG-guided FSL application in CNVM and melanomas. **Endo-canalicular DCR:** more effective bony ostium creation.

column2: Q15. Define amblyopia. Describe its mechanism
column4: types and management.
column6: **Definition:** Developmental disorder due to defective spatial visual processing in central visual pathway in brain, leading to decreased visual acuity without any identifiable local ophthalmic structural or pathological cause. **Mechanism:** (1) chronic blurr image at fovea due to stimulation deprivation or unbalanced extreme refractive error; (2) abnormal binocular interaction in strabismus. **Characteristics of vision:** (1) > 2 Snellen line difference in BCVA (> 1 log unit); (2) crowding phenomenon; (3) less degradation of visual acuity, rather improvement with neutral density filter; (4) decreased contrast sensitivity, vernier acuity, grating acuity, spatial localisation; (5) decreased saccade amplitude and impaired pursuit movements. **Types:** (1) **strabismic** — abnormal binocular interaction due to misalignment of visual axes; (2) **anisometropic** — difference in refractive error, usually hypermetropia in BE, as little as 1D; (2) **ametropic** — history of symmetrical refractive error in two eyes; (3) **meridional** — > 1D uncorrected astigmatism in U/L or B/L persisting beyond period of emmetropisation in early childhood; (4) **stimulus deprivation** — due to media opacities (e.g., cataract). **Critical period:** 0–8 years, first 3 years most critical; for anisometropic amblyopia may be longer into teens where good binocular function is present; plasticity decreases: visual association area > primary visual cortex > LGB neurones. **Work-up:** determine aetiology — history/refraction/cover test/visuoscopy (fixation pattern), anterior and posterior segment, pupils, colour vision; rule out organic cause — history/neutrality filter/HVF/VEP. **Treatment goals:** attain binocular single vision, no difference in BCVA between two eyes, better contrast sensitivity and spatial localisation, normal saccade and pursuit movement. **Specific treatment strategies — should continue both pre and post operative period:** (1) **occlusion** — elastoplast/opticlude/spectacle lens with neutral density filters/nail polish/extended wear large-diameter fogging contact lens; full-time patching (all waking hours) till signs of amblyopia reversal; part-time (5 hours/day); 1–2 hours/day for maintenance till 9 years; regimen 2 days up to 2 years, 3 days up to 3 years, etc.; follow-up weekly for 1 year, 2-weekly for 2 years, 3-weekly for 4/5/6 years; above 6 years ratio 6:1; complications — occlusion amblyopia of dominant eye (difficult to reverse). (2) **penalisation** — partial occlusion forcing amblyopic eye to use for distance/near work by artificially disadvantaging normal eye: optical (over-correct with plus lens) or pharmacological (atropine once daily for mild hypermetropic; requires prior correction of squint with prisms or surgery). (3) **pleoptics** — bleaching peripheral retina with powerful light, stimulation of macula with flashes; no longer popular. (4) **CAM vision stimulator** — discs of various spatial frequencies rotated slowly before amblyopic eye with dominant eye occluded; no longer popular. (5) **levodopa/carbidopa** — increases dopaminergic transmission in retina and visual cortex; may be adjuvant to occlusion. (6) **active vision therapy/home vision therapy** — requires parents and child cooperation. **Correct specific aetiology:** refractive error, media opacities, strabismus surgery.

column2: Q1. Define entropion. Classify it and describe pathophysiology and treatment.
column4: **Definition:** Inward turning of eyelid margin. **Classification:** (1) **Congenital** — rare birth defect; may be associated with microphthalmos; affects lower lid. (2) **Spastic** — seen in old people; affects lower lid; most common. (3) **Senile/involutional** — age-related; affects lower lid. (4) **Cicatricial** — seen in trachoma, burns, membranous conjunctivitis. (5) **Mechanical** — due to orbital countertraction; seen in phthisis bulbi, enophthalmos, post enucleation or evisceration. **Pathophysiology (senile):** (1) **horizontal lid laxity** — stretching of canthal tendons and tarsal plate; (2) **vertical lid instability** — weakness of lower lid retractors; (3) **over-riding of orbicularis** — pretarsal orbicularis over-ridden by preseptal during lid closure, moves lower border of tarsal plate away from globe and upper border toward globe; (4) **orbital septum laxity** — prolapse of orbital fat into lower lid. **Treatment:** (1) lubricant drops and ointment; (2) taping of eyelids; (3) bandage soft contact lens; (4) orbicularis chemodenervation with botulinum toxin injection. **Correction of vertical lid instability and over-riding:** (a) transverse everting sutures — prevents over-riding of orbicularis, high relapse rate, useful in old debilitated patients; (b) Weiss procedure — full-thickness horizontal lid splitting + everting sutures, durable; (c) Lester Jones procedure — lower lid retractor reinsertion, more durable than Weiss, for recurrent cases. **Correction of horizontal lid laxity:** lateral canthal sling or lateral pentagonal full-thickness excision (tightens lower lid, opposes it against globe). **Complications:** corneal abrasion or more severe ulceration due to constant rubbing of inwardly turned eyelashes (**pseudotrichiasis**).

column2: Q2. Define ectropion. Classify it and describe pathophysiology and treatment.
column4: **Definition:** Outward turning of eyelid margins. **Classification:** (1) **Senile/involutional** — most common; affects lower lid of elderly. (2) **Paralytic** — paralysis of ipsilateral VII nerve; associated with lagophthalmos, Bell's palsy, head injury, middle ear infections. (3) **Cicatricial** — secondary to chemical burn, thermal burn, lacerated eyelid injury, skin ulcers; can involve both lids. (4) **Mechanical** — tumors on/near lid margin, proptosis. (5) **Spastic** — rare. **Pathophysiology (involutional):** (1) **horizontal lid laxity** — demonstrated by snap test; (2) **lateral canthal tendon laxity** — rounded appearance of lateral canthus, ability to pull lower lid medially > 2 mm; (3) **medial canthal tendon laxity**. **Paralytic ectropion:** paralysis of ipsilateral VII nerve → lagophthalmos → exposure keratopathy, malposition of inferior punctum, lacrimal pump failure. **Treatment — involutional:** (1) lateral tarsal strip procedure — shortens lateral canthal tendon, reattaches to lateral orbital rim; (2) excision of tarso-conjunctival pentagon — may be combined with lateral tarsal strip to remove localised areas of misdirected lashes or keratinised conjunctiva. **Paralytic — temporary:** lubrication, bandage soft contact lens, botulinum toxin into LPS to induce temporary ptosis, temporary tarsorrhaphy. **Permanent:** (a) medial canthoplasty — eyelids sutured medial to lacrimal puncta (shortens palpebral aperture, corrects ectropion); (b) lateral tarsal strip — corrects residual ectropion after medial canthoplasty; (c) limited lateral tarsorrhaphy; (d) levator disinsertion — lowers upper eyelid, corrects lagophthalmos. **Complications:** persistent epiphora, exacerbation of ocular surface disease, chronic conjunctivitis of exposed conjunctiva → thickening and keratinisation.

column2: Q3. Define blepharitis. Classify it and describe clinical features and treatment.
column4: **Definition:** Chronic inflammation of eyelid margins. **Classification:** (1) **Anterior blepharitis** — related to chronic infective elements; more amenable to treatment. **Staphylococcal** — abnormal cell-mediated response to cell wall components of Staph aureus; more marked in atopic dermatitis. **Seborrheic** — strongly associated with generalised seborrheic dermatitis (scalp, nasolabial folds, skin behind ears and sternum). (2) **Posterior blepharitis** — meibomian gland dysfunction; more persistent and chronic inflammatory condition than anterior; commonly associated with acne rosacea. (3) **Mixed blepharitis.** **Demodex mite:** extremely common hair follicle and sebaceous gland dwelling mite — *D. folliculorum longus* (anterior blepharitis); *D. folliculorum brevis* (posterior blepharitis). **Symptoms:** poor correlation between severity of symptoms and signs; burning, grittiness, mild photophobia, crusting and redness of eyelids with remissions and exacerbations. **Signs — anterior (staphylococcal):** soft deposit on eyelashes, loss of lashes, distortion/trichiasis strongly present, lid margin ulceration and notching present, hordeolum present, meibomian cyst absent, phlyctenular conjunctivitis present, tear film foaming absent, dry eye present, corneal punctate erosions/vascularisation/infiltrates may be associated. **Anterior (seborrheic):** hard deposit, no loss of lash, no distortion, no ulceration, no notching, hordeolum present, meibomian cyst absent, phlyctenular conjunctivitis absent, dry eye present. **Posterior:** pouting of meibomian gland orifices, expression of tooth-paste-like material, lid transillumination shows gland loss, cystic dilation of obstructed meibomian ducts. **Treatment:** (1) lid hygiene — warm compression, crust removal, mechanical expression of meibomian secretions, soap/alcohol-impregnated pads for lid scrubbing; (2) eye ointment azithromycin/erythromycin/bacitracin/fusidic acid; (3) tab doxycycline 100 mg BDPC × 1 week, followed by ODPC × 6–24 weeks depending on response (more effective in posterior blepharitis); (4) low-potency topical steroids (fluorometholone 0.1% / loteprednol) 1 drop QDS × 1 week for substantial local inflammation; (5) tear substitutes for dry eye; (6) demodex — 50% tea tree oil scrub, 5% tea tree oil ointment, topical permethrin or oral/topical ivermectin. Permanent cure unlikely, but symptom control usually possible.

column2: Q4. Define internal hordeolum. Describe its etiology
column5: **Definition:** Suppurative inflammation of a previously blocked meibomian gland. **Predisposing factors:** more common in children and young adults; uncorrected refractive error or ocular strain due to muscle imbalance; metabolic diseases like diabetes; excessive alcohol consumption; chronic blepharitis; habitual rubbing of eyes or fingering of eyelids and nose; chronic debility. **Causative organism:** most commonly Staphylococcus aureus. **Pathogenesis:** primary infection of a blocked meibomian gland OR secondary infection of a chalazion. **Symptoms:** acute pain, swelling of involved eyelid, redness, watering, photophobia. **Note:** because inflamed meibomian glands lie deep within the tarsal plate, stretch pain in internal hordeolum is much more severe than external hordeolum. **Signs:** localised firm red tender swelling with marked chemosis of affected lids and tarsal conjunctiva (seen on everting lid); pus point as yellowish area on swelling away from root of cilia near grey line (contrast to external hordeolum). **Treatment — general:** local hot fomentation 2–3 times/day, maintenance of eyelid hygiene, glycaemic control if diabetic. **Medical:** eyedrop moxifloxacin 1 drop 3–4 times/day (or any other fourth-generation fluoroquinolone), eye ointment moxifloxacin/gatifloxacin at bedtime, tab amoxicillin + clavulanic acid 625 mg TDPC × 5 days (or tab cefepime 500 mg BDPC × 5 days), tab ibuprofen 400 mg BDPC × 3 days and SOS thereafter, tab ranitidine 150 mg / pantoprazole 40 mg BDAC × 5 days, management of blepharitis if present. **Surgical:** in non-resolving cases, drainage with vertical incision over swelling on conjunctival surface.

column2: Q5. Write short notes on chalazion operation.
column4: **Principle of surgery:** similar to incision and drainage of abscess; vertical incision only severs the affected meibomian duct, whereas transverse incision cuts many unrelated ducts → evaporative dry eye (lack of superficial oily layer of tear film). **Indications:** persistent chalazion after conservative management, multiple chalazion, large chalazion causing mechanical ptosis, internal hordeolum with abscess formation, cosmetic reason, recurrent chalazion. **Anaesthesia:** surface with 4% lignocaine eye drop; local infiltration with 2% lignocaine with adrenaline into eyelid around chalazion. **Surgical steps:** (1) chalazion forceps introduced with fenestrated plate toward tarsal conjunctiva, affected lid everted; adjustable screw rotated to fix chalazion within fenestrated plate (self-retaining, haemostatic); (2) vertical incision given; (3) all contents of chalazion scooped out thoroughly through chalazion scoop by rotatory movement; (4) forceps removed, lid position normalised, gentle pressure from skin surface by cotton bud for 2–5 minutes for haemostasis; (5) eye pad and bandage for a few hours. **Postoperative advice:** no water to incision site; local warm fomentation; eye ointment moxifloxacin at incision site and fornices at bedtime × 7 days; eyedrop moxifloxacin 1 drop QDS × 7 days; tab ibuprofen 400 mg BDPC × 3 days and SOS; systemic antibiotics may be given. **Complications — intraoperative:** through-and-through lid laceration, disinsertion of tarsal plate, injury to eyeball (rare). **Postoperative:** infection, recurrence due to incomplete removal, evaporative dry eye. **Special notes:** oral tetracycline postoperatively for patients with blepharitis, acne rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis; expressed material must be sent for histopathological diagnosis to rule out malignancy in recurrent chalazion.

column2: Q6. Define preseptal cellulitis. Describe its pathogenesis
column5: **Definition:** Inflammatory disease of infectious origin affecting subcutaneous tissue of upper eyelid and ocular adnexa anterior to orbital septum. **Pathogenesis:** local foci (acute hordeolum, dacryocystitis), external foci (local trauma, hematoma), endogenous spread (upper respiratory tract, middle ear); usually bacterial — Staph aureus, S. pyogenes. **Symptoms:** pain, conjunctival congestion, lacrimation, swelling of eyelids and adnexa. **Signs:** swelling of upper eyelids and adnexa with signs of acute inflammation; mechanical ptosis of upper eyelid; ocular movements full in all directions; vision normal; pupils reacting; eyeball position normal; no proptosis; mild conjunctival congestion. **Investigations:** (1) complete hemogram — neutrophilic leucocytosis with elevated ESR; (2) FBS/PPBS for adults to rule out hyperglycaemia; (3) recurrent cases — rule out immunosuppression; (4) locate source of infection after subsidence of acute inflammation (lacrimal sac, paranasal sinus, hordeolum); (5) CT scan of orbit with contrast if necessary — not routine, done in poorly responding cases or diagnostic dilemmas (opacification anterior to orbital septum; tissues posterior to septum normal). **Treatment:** (1) tab co-amoxiclav 625 mg TDPC × 5 days (or 1000 mg BDPC × 5 days); (2) tab ibuprofen/serratiopeptidase 1 tab BDPC × 5 days for pain and swelling; (3) IV antibiotics rarely needed (severe cases).

column2: Q7. Define ptosis. Classify it
column5: **Definition:** Abnormal lower position of upper eyelid (drooping). Normally upper eyelid covers upper 2 mm of cornea from superior limbus; lower eyelid just touches inferior limbus. **Classification — by cause:** (1) **Neurogenic** — III nerve paralysis (LPS palsy), Horner's syndrome (Müller's muscle palsy). (2) **Myogenic** — LPS myopathy (congenital), neuromuscular junction disorders (myasthenia gravis, acquired), myotonic dystrophy, progressive external ophthalmoplegia. (3) **Aponeurotic** — weakness of LPS aponeurosis, mostly age-related. (4) **Mechanical** — by mass/SOL/inflammatory swelling (large chalazion, lid tumours, preseptal cellulitis). **By age of onset:** **congenital** (present since birth, absence of lid crease, may be unilateral/bilateral) vs **acquired** (presents after birth; may be neurogenic, myogenic, aponeurotic or mechanical). **Pseudoptosis — differential:** post-enucleation/evisceration/lid-sparing exenteration, brow ptosis, dermatocalasis, contralateral lid retraction, ipsilateral hypotropia. **Clinical evaluation:** (1) **MRD1** — distance between midpoint of upper eyelid margin and reflection of torch light at centre of cornea (Hirschberg reflex); normal 4–4.5 mm. (2) **MRD2** — lower eyelid; normal 5–5.5 mm. (3) **MRD3** — MRD1 in upgaze. **Levator function:** measured with thumb on ipsilateral eyebrow (negates frontalis), eyes in downgaze, patient looks up; normal ≥ 15 mm, good 12–14 mm, fair 5–11 mm, poor ≤ 4 mm. (4) **Palpebral fissure** — males 7–10 mm, females 8–12 mm. (5) **Amount of ptosis** — mild up to 2 mm, moderate 2–3 mm, severe ≥ 4 mm. (6) **Upper lid crease** — males 8 mm, females 10 mm; absent in congenital ptosis; higher in aponeurotic ptosis. (7) **Pretarsal show.** (8) **Fatigability** — maintain upgaze 30 seconds without blinking; progressive drooping in myasthenia gravis. (9) **Cogan twitch sign** — overshoot of upper eyelid in myasthenia gravis. (10) **Ocular motility** — detect associated paralytic strabismus. (11) **Corneal sensation** — absent in any quadrant indicates V nerve dysfunction. (12) **Bell's phenomenon** — good (> 2/3 of cornea rotates and disappears), fair (1/3–2/3), poor (< 1/3); good Bell's is essential for frontalis sling surgery. (13) **Jaw winking** — congenital ptosis, variable outcome. **Investigations:** mainly to rule out myasthenia gravis — ice pack test (transient improvement), edrophonium test (with atropine premedication and resuscitation), serum Ach receptor antibody, RNST and SFEMG, thoracic CT/MRI for thymoma. **Treatment — MG:** anticholinesterase (pyridostigmine, neostigmine) initially; steroids/immunosuppressives in severe; therapeutic plasma exchange in selected cases; managed with neurologist. **III nerve palsy:** at least 6 months stability with minimal strabismus before surgery; botulinum toxin temporary. **Congenital ptosis with strabismus:** strabismus surgery first, 6 months later ptosis correction. **Surgical options for congenital ptosis:** (1) **Fasanella-Servat procedure** — conjunctiva-Müller resection; mild ptosis with ≥ 10 mm LPS action; 2–3 mm correction maximum; transconjunctival approach (no scarring). (2) **Levator resection** — strengthening LPS by shortening; mild-moderate ptosis with ≥ 5 mm LPS action; transcutaneous through lid crease; transconjunctival approach also possible. (3) **Frontalis sling surgery/brow suspension** — suspension of tarsal plate with frontalis muscle by non-absorbable thread; severe ptosis with poor LPS action (< 4 mm); Marcus Gunn ptosis, blepharophimosis syndrome, ptosis with III nerve palsy, failed levator resection; sling materials — autologous fascia lata (ideal but requires second-site harvesting), silicone (most commonly used), prolene; contraindicated in poor Bell's phenomenon.

column2: Q8. Define lid lag. Describe its features and causes.
column4: **Definition:** Static situation where the position of upper eyelid of affected eye is at a higher level than normal eye with the globe in downgaze. **Features:** (1) seen mainly in thyroid orbitopathy; (2) early stages — secondary to sympathomimetic response of eyelid muscles; (3) late stages — due to (a) fibrosis of superior rectus-LPS muscle complex, (b) to counteract fibrosis of inferior rectus, SR-LPS complex remains in sustained contraction; (4) in late stage of thyroid orbitopathy, may be associated with proptosis. **Lid retraction (upper and lower eyelid position):** upper eyelid at or higher than superior limbus; lower eyelid below inferior limbus causing inferior scleral show. **Causes of lid retraction:** thyroid orbitopathy; congenital (Duane's, Down's syndrome, idiopathic); mechanical (surgical overcorrection, scarring of eyelid skin); neurogenic (VII nerve palsy, Marcus-Gunn jaw winking, Parinaud syndrome, Parkinsonism, hydrocephalus, sympathomimetic drops); miscellaneous (hepatic failure — Summer skill sign).

column2: Q9. Discuss the signs
column3: symptoms and management of chronic dacryocystitis.
column5: **Definition:** Chronic inflammation of lacrimal drainage pathway mostly due to partial or complete mechanical obstruction. **Stage 1 — chronic catarrhal dacryocystitis:** symptoms — mild to moderate epiphora, mild inner canthal congestion; signs — syringing reveals NLD partial/complete blockade, regurgitation of clear fluid or few fibrinous mucoid flakes; dacryocystography reveals NLD blockade with normal-sized lacrimal sac. **Stage 2 — lacrimal mucocele:** constant epiphora, swelling below inner canthus; signs — milky gelatinous fluid regurgitates from lower punctum on pressing swelling; **encysted mucocele** — opening of both canaliculi into sac blocked due to continued infection, so regurgitation test negative. **Stage 3 — chronic suppurative dacryocystitis (pyocele):** constant epiphora, recurrent conjunctivitis, swelling below inner canthus; signs — mild erythema over swelling, on pressure frank purulent discharge from lower punctum; if opening to both canaliculi blocked, **encysted pyocele** occurs. **Stage 4 — chronic fibrotic stage:** constant epiphora, recurrent non-resolving conjunctivitis, swelling of sac resolves; dacryocystography reveals very small fibrotic sac with irregular mucosal folds. **Investigations:** (1) **Probing** — hard stop = NLD obstruction; soft stop = canalicular obstruction. (2) **Syringing** — partial obstruction: saline passes with considerable pressure; common canalicular or individual canalicular obstruction: reflux of saline through same or opposite punctum; NLD obstruction: reflux through opposite punctum. (3) **Regurgitation test** — clear fluid (chronic catarrhal), milky gelatinous (mucocele), frank pus (pyocele). (4) **Jones' dye test I & II** — I detects partial lacrimal drainage pathway obstruction from causes of primary hyperlacrimation; II detects partial lacrimal drainage pathway obstruction from lacrimal pump failure. (5) **Dacryocystography** — documents exact site, nature, extent of block and condition of sac. (6) **Radionucleotide dacryocystography** — non-invasive functional efficiency. **Systemic investigations:** CBC (leukocytosis = inflammation; Hb = anaemic status), FBS/PPBS/HbA1c (rule out diabetes), cardiovascular assessment (fitness for surgery). **Treatment:** **NLD obstruction — complete/total:** observation mainly, DCR; **partial NLD:** dilatation, dacryoplasty (may be attempted), prophylactic DCR; **canalicular obstruction:** conjunctivo-dacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) with Jones' tube through medial canthus into nose below middle meatus of nose. **Dacryocystectomy (DCT)** — removal of sac; indicated when DCR not possible or failed multiple times: fibrotic sac with no potential for anastomosis, tuberculosis, leprosy, mycotic sac infection, carcinoma of lacrimal sac, carcinoma of nasopharynx, atrophic rhinitis.

column2: Q10. Write short notes on syringing of lacrimal passage.
column4: **Purpose:** detect lacrimal outflow passage obstruction and anomalies. **Procedure:** lower punctum dilated with Nettleship punctum dilator; blunt-tipped curved 26G cannula inserted into punctum and lower canaliculi; saline injected for irrigation. **Interpretation:** (1) fluid flows into nasal cavity and throat → **patent lacrimal apparatus (no obstruction);** causes of watering — hypersecretion, lacrimal pump failure, partial obstruction. (2) regurgitation of fluid → obstruction present in lacrimal drainage pathway; probing with Bowman's lacrimal probe: **hard stop** = nasolacrimal duct obstruction; **soft stop** = canalicular block — upper/lower canalicular block: regurgitation from same punctum; common canalicular block: regurgitation from opposite punctum. **When syringing is inconclusive → Jones' dye test.** **Jones dye test I:** 2% fluorescein instilled into conjunctival sac, cotton bud soaked in anaesthetic placed inside nose — **positive** (fluorescein staining on bud): patent and functional drainage, watering due to hypersecretion; **negative** (no staining): partial obstruction or lacrimal pump failure. **Jones dye test II:** fluorescein-stained fluid irrigated through lower punctum with bud in nose — **positive** (staining on bud): partial obstruction; **negative** (no staining): lacrimal pump failure. **Management options by site:** (1) upper/lower canalicular obstruction — CDCR with Jones' tube; (2) common canalicular obstruction — canaliculo-dacryocystorhinostomy or intubation DCR with silicone tube; (3) NLD obstruction — conventional DCR; (4) partial NLD obstruction — pressure syringing with antibiotics.

column2: Q11. Define epiphora. Describe its causes
column5: **Definition:** Overflow of tears at the eyelid margin. **Causes:** **Hypersecretion** — secondary to anterior segment disease (misdirected cilia, dry eye (paradoxical watering), inflammation — conjunctivitis/keratitis). **Defective drainage** — (a) malposition of lacrimal puncta (entropion/ectropion); (b) obstruction at any point from punctal region to valve of Hasner; (c) lacrimal pump failure secondary to lower lid laxity or weakness of orbicularis (facial nerve palsy). **Evaluation:** (1) elucidation of proper history; (2) external examination + slit lamp — detect anterior segment pathology, punctal stenosis/malposition, misdirected cilia, palpation of lacrimal sac (ROPLAS); (3) **fluorescein disappearance test** — one drop of 2% fluorescein in fornices, inspect under cobalt blue after 5–10 minutes; prolonged retention = defective lacrimal drainage; (4) syringing and probing — as above; (5) Jones' dye test I and II. **Management options:** (1) upper/lower canalicular obstruction — CDCR with Jones' tube; (2) common canalicular obstruction — canaliculo-DCR or intubation DCR with silicone tube; (3) NLD obstruction — conventional DCR; (4) partial NLD obstruction — pressure syringing with antibiotics; (5) hypersecretion — treat underlying anterior segment disease; (6) lacrimal pump failure — address lid laxity/weakness.

column2: Q12. Define acute dacryocystitis. Describe pathophysiology
column5: **Definition:** Acute suppurative inflammation of lacrimal sac. **Pathophysiology:** infection from infected paranasal sinuses, surrounding bones and soft tissues, caries teeth in upper jaw, or acute exacerbation of chronic dacryocystitis. **Causative organisms:** Streptococcus haemolyticus, Staphylococcus, Pneumococcus. **Clinical features — stage 1 (cellulitis):** painful swelling in sac region — red, hot, firm, tender; systemic symptoms of fever and malaise; epiphora; redness and oedema spreading to lids and cheek. **Stage 2 (lacrimal abscess):** pus-filled distended sac with pericystic swelling → large fluctuant lacrimal abscess; pus point usually below and laterally (due to gravitation of pus). **Stage 3 (fistula formation):** pus from progressively increasing abscess discharges outside, creating **external fistula** typically located below the medial palpebral ligament; **internal fistula** — rarely, abscess opens into nasal cavity. **Treatment:** (1) **Drugs for acute inflammation** — systemic antibiotics (tab amoxicillin + clavulanic acid 625 mg TDPC × 5 days); topical antibiotic drops and ointment (eyedrop moxifloxacin QDS; eye ointment moxifloxacin/gatifloxacin/chloramphenicol TDS on affected eye and over inflamed sac area); systemic anti-inflammatory analgesics (tab ibuprofen BDPC × 3 days). (2) **Stage of lacrimal abscess** — drain pus by small external incision to prevent external fistula. (3) Later, depending on sac condition — dacryocystectomy or DCR. (4) **External fistula** — complete fistulectomy followed by DCR or DCT. (5) **Preferred in some centres** — endoscopic DCR drains pus nasally and creates alternative tear drainage pathway.

column2: Q13. Write short notes on dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).
column4: **Principle:** create an alternate tear drainage pathway by constructing a communication between lacrimal sac and nasal cavity through the middle meatus. **Indications:** chronic dacryocystitis due to nasolacrimal duct obstruction. **Anaesthesia:** (1) local infiltrative blocks — infra-trochlear, infra-orbital, dorsal nasal, anterior ethmoidal (transcaruncular); (2) general anaesthesia in children. **Surgical steps:** nasal pack given to control nasal mucosal bleed. (1) **Incision** — curved along anterior lacrimal crest OR straight 8 mm medial to medial canthus; 2.5–3 cm long. (2) **Exposure of medial palpebral ligament and anterior lacrimal crest** — blunt dissection; MPL cut or retracted. (3) **Dissection of lacrimal sac** — periosteum separated from anterior lacrimal crest; sac reflected laterally to expose lacrimal fossa. (4) **Exposure of nasal mucosa** — 10 × 15 mm bony ostium created by removing bones forming lacrimal fossa, exposing nasal mucosa. (5) **Fashioning and suturing of flaps** — efficacy comparable for both flap techniques (H-shaped or U-shaped); flaps sutured with 6-0 vicryl. (6) **Closure of wound** — MPL sutured to periosteum; orbicularis 6-0 vicryl; skin 6-0 silk. (7) Nasal pack removed after 24–48 hours. **Complications — intraoperative:** bleeding (most common; sources — inadvertent nasal mucosal injury, angular vein, surrounding paranasal sinuses), injury/desiccation of lacrimal sac, injury/desiccation of nasal mucosa. **Postoperative:** reactionary nasal bleeding, infection, failed DCR (non-patency of new pathway). **Contraindications — absolute:** nasopharyngeal carcinoma, atrophic rhinitis, malignancy of lacrimal sac. **Relative:** extremes of age, gross DNS or other nasal pathologies (polyps).

column2: Q14. Write short notes on eyelid tumours.
column4: **Benign tumours:** (1) **Melanocytic nevus** — brown/pigmented macule or plaque on eyelids; **congenital** (rare, small, uniform colour, kissing/split nevus involves corresponding upper and lower eyelid areas, giant hairy nevus has 15% malignant transformation risk); **acquired** (histological location decides appearance and malignant potential — junctional nevus: uniformly brown macule/plaque, low malignant potential, young people; compound nevus: uniformly light tan-brown papules, low malignant potential, middle-aged; intradermal nevus: papillomatous lesion with little pigmentation, dilated vessels, protruding eyelashes, no malignant potential, old age). Management: observation; complete surgical excision for cosmetic reasons or suspected malignant transformation. (2) **Capillary haemangioma (strawberry nevus)** — most common benign vascular tumour of infancy; raised bright red lesion, unilateral, predilection for upper eyelid, blanches on pressure, increases on crying, mechanical ptosis; more common in male; may have orbital extension; visceral haemangiomas ruled out. Histology: proliferation of vascular channels of varying size in dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Management: 30% resolve by 3 years, 70% by 7 years; indications for intervention — amblyopia, compressive optic neuropathy, exposure keratopathy, recurrent infection, cosmetic blemish; modalities — laser (superficial lesions), intralesional triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg/ml (1–2 ml), systemic beta-blockers (oral propranolol 2–3 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses), surgical debulking (late inactive stage only due to high risk of bleeding); systemic steroids if large orbital extension. (3) **Port-wine stain (nevus flammeus/cavernous haemangioma)** — rare congenital benign vascular neoplasm associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome; sharply demarcated soft pink patch, does not blanch on pressure, lesion does not grow with age but colour darkens, overlying skin becomes hypertrophied/friable/bleeds on touch/prone to infection; trisystem disease (face, leptomeninges, eye) = Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalo-trigeminal angiomatosis); bisystem (face + eyes/leptomeninges); prone to paediatric glaucoma. Management: laser therapy, photodynamic therapy. (4) **Pyogenic granuloma** — rapidly progressing vascular polypoidal lesion; induced by trauma, infection, surgery, or idiopathic; treated by complete excision. (5) **Xanthelasma** — multiple yellowish subcutaneous plaques usually on medial upper eyelid; associated with elevated serum cholesterol; treated by laser or complete surgical excision for cosmetic blemish. (6) **Neurofibroma** — typically affects upper eyelid producing S-shaped deformity. **Pre-malignant tumours:** Xeroderma pigmentosa (AR) — prone to BCC, SCC, melanoma; Gorlin-Goltz syndrome (AD) — naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome; Bazex syndrome (X-linked) — prone to pre-malignant conditions; Muir-Torre syndrome (AD) — prone to BCC, sebaceous gland carcinoma, keratoacanthoma. **Malignant tumours:** (1) **Basal cell carcinoma** — most common malignant eyelid tumour; slow-growing, locally invasive, non-metastasising; site — lower eyelid (most common), medial canthus (second, more prone to invade orbit and paranasal sinus, difficult to manage), upper eyelid (third), lateral canthus (fourth). Clinical types: nodulo-ulcerative (rodent ulcer — pearly raised rolled edges, small overlying dilated blood vessels/telangiectasias, centrally ulcerated); sclerosing (indurated plaque invading dermis and epidermis, margins not delineable, mimics chronic blepharitis). Histopathology: from basal layer cells of epidermis; downward migration and proliferation of basophilic basal cells; lobules from epidermis to dermis; pallisading of basal cells at periphery. (2) **Squamous cell carcinoma** — relatively less common but more aggressive; potential to invade regional lymph nodes and perineural spread to intracranial cavity via orbit. Predisposing factors: fair skin, chronic sun exposure, actinic keratosis, Bowen's disease (intraepidermal carcinoma/carcinoma in situ), immunocompromised. Site: lower eyelid and lid margins. Clinical types: ulcerating SCC, cutaneous horn (hyperkeratotic nodule with crusting, hard erosions and fissures; underlying invasive SCC). Histology: from squamous layer; proliferation of atypical dysplastic epithelial cells of variable sizes throughout dermis; keratin pearls and intercellular bridges (desmosomes) in well-differentiated tumours. (3) **Sebaceous gland carcinoma** — slow-growing rare malignant eyelid tumour from meibomian gland, mostly elderly females, potential for pagetoid spread. Site: mostly upper eyelid. Clinical types: nodular (discreet hard nodule within tarsal plate — mistaken as meibomitis or chronic posterior blepharitis), spreading/infiltrating sac (diffuse thickening of lid margins due to dermis infiltration — mistaken as chalazion); yellowish discolouration of tumour mass due to lipid deposition is highly suggestive. Histology: lobules of cells with large hyperchromatic nuclei, multiple foamy vacuoles containing lipids. (4) **Melanoma** — potentially lethal rare eyelid malignant tumour; features suggestive: increase in existing pigmented size with irregular margins, asymmetrical shape, recent onset of large pigmented lesion (> 6 mm), recent change of colour, presence of multiple colours. Lentigo maligna (melanoma in situ / Hutchinson freckle) — slow-expanding pigmented macule with irregular border; superficial spreading melanoma — plaque with irregular margins and variable pigmentation; nodular melanoma — dark nodule surrounded by normal skin. (5) **Keratoacanthoma** — fair-complexioned individual with prolonged chronic sun exposure; also may occur with immunosuppressive therapy; lesion grows rapidly within weeks but involutes spontaneously by 1 year; histopathology mimics SCC — irregular thickened epidermal cells surrounded by acanthotic squamous epithelium; **shoulder formation** (sharp transition from thickened to normal epidermal cells); by 1 year, involuted lesion becomes a large scar. (6) **Merkel cell carcinoma** — Merkel cells are sensory cutaneous receptors sensing light touch; cutaneous neuroendocrine highly malignant tumour usually on upper eyelid of older individuals; morphologically violaceous well-demarcated nodule with intact overlying skin; 50% patients have metastatic spread at presentation. (7) **Kaposi sarcoma** — vascular tumours typically in AIDS patients; pinkish/red-violet to brown colour spectrum nodular lesion, may be found anywhere in both upper and lower eyelids; histopathology shows proliferation of spindle cells with vascular channels and inflammatory cells; usually mistaken as haematoma or nevus if history not taken. **Approach to eyelid neoplasm:** history (prior/existing skin cancer, chronic sun exposure, radiation/chemotherapy, tobacco, fair skin/red hair/blue iris, immunosuppression); clinical signs of malignancy (rapid painless growth, sudden ulceration/bleeding/crusting/pigmentary change/drainage, destruction of normal eyelid architecture, loss of eyelashes, fine telangiectasias, loss of fine cutaneous crinkles, heaped-up pearly translucent margins with central ulceration); before surgery — palpable induration beyond visible margin, lesions near lacrimal puncta, bony involvement, regional lymph nodes, perineural spread (V and VII). **Management — biopsy:** incisional (approachable part, local/distant spread) vs excisional (entire lesion with 4 mm clear margin). **Before biopsy:** MRI orbit, PNS and brain with contrast if clinical suspicion of local spread. **Two strategies for confirmation of complete clearance:** (1) **intraoperative frozen section** — HPE of margins of excised specimen; if tumour cells present → wider excision till clear; if absent → proceed to reconstruction; (2) **Mohs micrographic surgery** — layer-by-layer excision and intraoperative HPE creates micrographic map of tumour edge; time-consuming but more accurate; particularly useful for diffuse growth and indistinct margins (sclerosing BCC, recurrent tumours). **Eyelid reconstruction:** defect < 1/3 → layer-by-layer direct closure with/without lateral cantholysis; 1/3–1/2 → Tenzel semi-circular rotational flap for anterior lamellar reconstruction + posterior lamellar reconstruction by amniotic membrane, buccal mucosa, or tarso-conjunctival graft; > 50% → challenging, requires advancement + rotational flaps; **Cutler-Beard lid sharing surgery** is good option for upper eyelid > 50% reconstruction. **Principles of total/subtotal eyelid reconstruction:** replace posterior lamella (tarso-conjunctiva), replace anterior lamella (orbicularis + skin).

column2: Q1. Define orbital cellulitis. Describe etiology
column4: complications and management.
column6: **Definition:** Potentially life-threatening infection of soft tissues behind orbital septum; mostly children and immunocompromised. **Pathogenesis:** extension of preseptal cellulitis through internal orbital septum; local spread from sinusitis (mostly ethmoid); local spread from dacryocystitis; post-surgical; orbital foreign body; midfacial or dental infection; post-traumatic; haematogenous spread from middle ear or respiratory tract. **Common agents:** S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, S. pyogenes, H. influenzae. **Symptoms:** systemic — fever, malaise; ocular — severe pain, rapidly deteriorating visual impairment, proptosis, swelling of eyelids and ocular adnexa. **Signs:** tender warm red periorbital and lid oedema; mechanical ptosis; conjunctival chemosis and congestion; proptosis (usually lateral and downward, obscured by mechanical ptosis); RAPD positive or fixed mid-dilated if optic nerve involvement; painful ophthalmoplegia; severe visual impairment. **Investigations:** same as preseptal cellulitis plus blood culture and antibiotic sensitivity; CT scan of orbit and paranasal sinuses with contrast — opacifications both anterior and posterior to orbital septum, eyeball laterally rotated, opacification of paranasal sinuses, opacification inside orbit obscuring delineation of optic nerve and soft tissues, orbital foreign bodies may be seen. **Treatment:** (1) hospital admission in consultation with otorhinolaryngologist and physician/paediatrician; (2) **antimicrobial therapy** — IV ceftazidime 1 g IV BD to start with; may escalate to 2 g IV TDS in life-threatening/immunocompromised; children 75–150 mg/kg/day IV divided every 8 hours; oral metronidazole — adults 500–750 mg TDS for 5–10 days; children (> 8 weeks) 7.5 mg/kg every 8 hours; children (< 8 weeks) 7.5 mg/kg every 12 hours (added for anaerobic coverage); in poor responders, escalate IV antibiotics per blood culture sensitivity in consultation with physician and critical care; IV antibiotics continued till patient apyrexial for 4 days; (3) monitoring — optic nerve conduction every 4 hours (pupillary light reflexes, bedside visual acuity, colour vision); monitor signs of intracranial spread; (4) indications for surgical intervention — subperiosteal abscess (usually medial orbital wall), rapidly progressing proptosis due to pus in orbital spaces, diagnostic dilemmas with poor response to antimicrobial therapy requiring biopsy; (5) MRI of orbit may be required in diagnostic dilemma or poor response to IV antimicrobials (metallic orbit foreign body must be ruled out). **Complications — ocular:** central retinal artery or vein occlusion by infective emboli, optic neuropathy, exposure keratopathy, panophthalmitis. **Systemic:** meningitis, brain abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, septic shock.

column2: Q2. Write short notes on cavernous sinus thrombosis.
column4: **Definition:** Clinical condition due to formation of thrombus within cavernous sinus — septic or aseptic. **Septic CST:** rapidly evolving thrombophlebitis with infectious origin; source — middle third of face, sinuses, ear, teeth, oral cavity. **Aseptic CST:** thrombotic process as a result of trauma, iatrogenic or prothrombotic conditions. **Symptoms — systemic:** rapid onset severe headache, malaise, nausea, vomiting, fever. **Ocular:** U/L or B/L rapid-onset proptosis, periorbital oedema, chemosis, ptosis, decreased vision, decreased ocular motility. **Signs — systemic:** congestion of facial veins, facial oedema, hyperthermia, septicaemia, haemodynamic instability. **Ocular:** U/L or B/L axial proptosis, conjunctival chemosis, acute onset ptosis, features of III/IV/VI nerve palsy, reduced corneal reflex, hypo/hyperaesthesia in distribution of ophthalmic and maxillary nerve. **Investigations:** blood — CBC, CRP, blood culture; contrast-enhanced high-resolution CT; contrast-enhanced MRI and MR venography; LP and CSF analysis. **Treatment:** (1) **antibiotics — broad spectrum:** inj meropenem 1 g IV stat and TDS; inj piperacillin + tazobactam 4.5 g TDS; inj linezolid 600 mg IV BD; vancomycin for MRSA; then oral — faropenem 200 mg BD, third-generation cephalosporin. (2) **anticoagulants** — role debatable; early institution may be beneficial. (3) **fungal** (Aspergillus most common; also Mucor, Rhizopus, Cryptococcus, Candida) — liposomal amphotericin B (5–10 mg/kg/day) × 3 weeks then oral posaconazole 400 mg BD; for aspergillosis — voriconazole. (4) **oral steroids** — reduce nerve dysfunction. (5) **aseptic CST** — surgical neurosurgical intervention required.

column2: Q3. Classify orbital tumours. Describe orbital dermoid cyst.
column4: **Classification — benign:** cystic (dermoid cyst, dacryops, sinus mucocele, encephalocele); vascular (orbital varices, lymphangioma, capillary haemangioma, cavernous haemangioma); lacrimal gland (pleomorphic adenoma); neural (optic nerve glioma, optic nerve sheath meningioma, neurofibroma). **Malignant:** lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, metastatic tumours, lacrimal gland carcinoma, orbital invasion of adjacent malignant tumours. **ORBITAL DERMOID CYST:** **Definition** — choristoma (histologically normal tissue in abnormal location); **Pathophysiology** — subcutaneous displacement of ectodermal tissue along embryonic lines of closure; **Pathology** — fibrous wall lined by keratinised stratified squamous epithelium; contains dermal appendages (sweat glands, sebaceous glands, hair follicles); appears like skin. **Types:** superficial (anterior to orbital septum) vs deep (posterior to orbital septum). **Symptoms:** superficial dermoid — painless nodule, most commonly superotemporal orbit, in infancy; deep dermoid — gradually increasing non-axial proptosis in adolescents/adults. **Signs:** superficial — firm mobile non-tender 1–2 cm mass, posterior margin easily palpable; deep — posterior margin not palpable. **Investigations:** contrast CT scan of orbit — well-circumscribed heterogeneous lesion; deep dermoids may be associated with surrounding bone remodelling and rarely intracranial extension. **Treatment:** small lesion — observation; progressively increasing with proptosis/eyeball compression/dystopia — excisional biopsy with intention to remove entire mass (iatrogenic rupture → granulomatous inflammation of surrounding tissue); ruptured dermoids with orbital cellulitis — systemic steroids.

column2: Q4. Write short notes on capillary haemangioma of the orbit.
column4: **Definition:** Most common neoplasm of orbit and periorbital area among children; more common in girls; hamartoma (disorganised overgrowth of normal mature tissue) due to proliferation of vascular endothelial cells. **Symptoms:** clinical presentation varies from small isolated lesion with no symptoms to large disfiguring SOL causing visual impairment and systemic complications. **Signs:** **superficial tumours** — haemangiomatous involvement of palpebral or inferior conjunctiva (common), no bruit, no pulsation, cutaneous lesions = strawberry nevus, preseptal location, dark blue or purple; deep orbital involvement must be ruled out by orbital imaging in all superficial cases. **Deep orbital tumours** — unilateral proptosis, no bruit, no pulsation. **Investigations:** MRI (preferred) or CT scan of orbit; no bony erosion; enlargement of orbital cavity may be seen in long-standing large deep orbital lesions; extraconal mass may have finger-like posterior expansions. **Treatment:** (1) resolves spontaneously — 30% by 3 years, 70% by 7 years; diagnosis for 3–6 months, phase of rapid growth, phase of natural resolution. (2) **Indications for treatment:** exposure keratopathy, optic nerve compression, amblyopia high risk (occlusion, strabismus, lesion-induced refractive error). (3) **Modalities:** oral beta-blockers in conjunction with paediatrician; topical timolol maleate (beta-blocker, no systemic side effect); intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (2 ml of 40 mg/ml) or betamethasone (2 ml of 4 mg/ml) — regression begins by 2 weeks, may repeat twice with 2-month gap; deep orbital injection avoided due to risk of central retinal artery occlusion; systemic steroids for sight-threatening large orbital lesions; topical clobetasol propionate cream for large cutaneous lesions; interferon-2a and vincristine for steroid-resistant sight-threatening mass; local resection reserved for late resistant non-resolving cases; laser embolisation for superficial tumours < 2 mm thickness. (4) **Complications:** Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (life-threatening thrombocytopenia in large multiple lesions with visceral involvement; 50% mortality); PHACE syndrome (large disfiguring facial haemangioma).
