column2: What are the causes of red eye? Write clinical features and management of any one cause.
column4: **Adnexal causes:** trichiasis, distichiasis, floppy eyelid syndrome, entropion, ectropion, lagophthalmos, blepharitis, meibomitis, acne rosacea, dacryocystitis. **Conjunctival causes:** ophthalmia neonatorum, conjunctivitis (bacterial, viral, chemical, atopic, vernal), subconjunctival haemorrhage, inflamed pinguecula, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis, conjunctival foreign body, symblepharon, Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN, conjunctival neoplasm. **Corneal causes:** corneal foreign body, contact lens-induced, recurrent corneal erosions, pterygium, UV or chemical burn. **Others:** trauma, post-operative dry eye syndrome, endophthalmitis, acute anterior uveitis, dry eye syndrome, episcleritis, scleritis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, carotid-cavernous fistula, cluster headache. **Acute anterior uveitis (detailed example) — definition:** acute inflammation of uveal tissue from iris to pars plicata of ciliary body (iritis: predominant iris; iridocyclitis: equal involvement; anterior cyclitis: predominant pars plicata). **Symptoms:** dull aching throbbing pain worsening at night (referred by V1 branches to forehead and scalp), redness, photophobia, blepharospasm, lacrimation, dimness of vision. **Signs:** circumcorneal congestion (deep vessels radiating from limbus, do not blanch with phenylephrine), mild lid oedema, corneal oedema due to toxic endothelitis, aqueous cells and flare, keratic precipitates (pathognomonic), posterior synechiae with festooned pupils, iris bombe, hypopyon (sterile pus), muddy iris. **Complications:** complicated cataract (polychromatic lustre, rapid progression), secondary glaucoma (hypertensive early due to clogging of trabecular meshwork; late due to seclusio/occlusio pupillae), cyclitic membrane, retinochoroiditis progression, CME, macular hole, epiretinal membrane, macular scar, exudative RD, papillitis, band-shaped keratopathy, phthisis bulbi. **Management:** (1) **investigations** — CBC, ESR/CRP, FBS/PPBS/HbA1c, uric acid, serology (syphilis, toxoplasmosis, histoplasmosis), ANA/Rh factor/LE cells/serum ACE (sarcoidosis), RA factor/anti-CCP (rheumatoid arthritis); urine and stool; chest X-ray, X-ray PNS/SIJ/lumbar spine, CT thorax, MRI brain; skin tests (tuberculin, Kveim, toxoplasmin, lepromin, pathergy). (2) **general** — local hot fomentation, dark goggles. (3) **topical** — 1% atropine TDS or 2% homatropine BD × 2–3 weeks (relieves ciliary spasm, prevents synechiae, reduces exudation, brings more antibodies); 1% prednisolone acetate 1 drop 6–8 times/day, tapered over 3–4 weeks (alternatives: dexamethasone/loteprednol/fluorometholone; anterior sub-Tenon injection in severe cases). (4) **systemic** — tab prednisolone 1 mg/kg OD after breakfast for 2 weeks, tapered over 6–8 weeks (intractable cases); immunosuppressives (methotrexate/cyclophosphamide/chlorambucil/azathioprine) in steroid-resistant cases with physician; specific treatment of cause (TB, syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rheumatological) with physician; if no cause, full course of broad-spectrum antibiotics.

column2: Write short notes on viral conjunctivitis.
column4: **Definition:** inflammation of conjunctiva due to viral infection; since viral infection mostly involves epithelium of both conjunctiva and cornea, termed 'keratoconjunctivitis'. **Agents:** adenovirus, coronavirus, herpes simplex, herpes zoster, poxvirus, myxovirus, paramyxovirus, arbovirus. Some cause more conjunctival involvement (pharyngoconjunctival fever), some predominantly affect cornea (HSV). **Three clinical forms:** (1) **Acute serous conjunctivitis** — typically mild-grade viral infection; minimal congestion with watery discharge and boggy conjunctival chemosis; self-limiting; broad-spectrum topical antibiotics (fluoroquinolones) for 7–10 days to prevent secondary bacterial infection. (2) **Acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis** — enterovirus type 70 (Picornaviridae, RNA virus); extremely contagious, transmitted by hand-to-eye contact; very short incubation (1–2 days); symptoms — pain, redness, lid chemosis, photophobia, transient blurring; signs — lid oedema, multiple haemorrhages in bulbar conjunctiva with mild follicular hyperplasia, fine epithelial keratitis, periauricular (occasionally) lymphadenopathy; self-limiting with 5–7 day course; no specific treatment (topical fluoroquinolones to prevent secondary infection); epidemic potential (epidemic haemorrhagic conjunctivitis) — general cleanliness measures to prevent person-to-person transmission. (3) **Acute follicular conjunctivitis** — acute conjunctivitis with severe follicular hyperplasia mainly at lower palpebral conjunctiva and lower fornix; symptoms — redness, watering, mucoid discharge, mild photophobia, foreign body sensation; signs — multiple follicles in lower palpebral conjunctiva and lower fornix as compared to upper lid. **Etiological classification:** epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (adenovirus 8, 19, 37 — highly contagious, epidemic potential, incubation 8 days, virus shed from eyes for 2–3 weeks, three stages: acute serous → acute follicular → acute pseudomembranous; associated SPK and periauricular lymphadenopathy; treated symptomatically, topical adenine arabinoside (Ara-A) may be effective); Newcastle conjunctivitis (Newcastle virus; rare; contact with diseased owls; mainly affects poultry workers); pharyngoconjunctival fever (adenovirus 3 and 7; primarily affects children; epidemic potential; systemic symptoms of fever, pharyngitis, periauricular lymphadenopathy); herpes simplex (HSV type 1; spreads by kissing/close personal contact; typical form — follicular conjunctivitis with primary vesicular lesions of face and lids; atypical form — without vesicular lesions; dendritic keratitis may or may not be associated; treated with topical acyclovir eye ointment 5 times/day × 2–3 weeks). **Chlamydial (inclusion) conjunctivitis:** sexually active young adults; Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D–K; contaminated swimming pool water important source; treated with topical 1% tetracycline eye ointment + oral tetracycline 250 mg BDPC × 3–4 weeks.

column2: Write short notes on phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis.
column4: **Definition:** inflammatory response of conjunctiva and cornea due to delayed hypersensitivity response to some endogenous allergens. **Epidemiology:** peak age 3–15 years; higher incidence among girls; more common in malnourished children; more common in overcrowded/unhygienic conditions; higher in spring and summer. **Causative allergens:** staphylococcal proteins most common; previously tubercular proteins common; doubtful association — Moraxella proteins, helminthic proteins. **Pathogenesis:** delayed hypersensitivity response to endogenous allergens → nodule formation → necrosis of apex → ulcer formation → floor covered with granulation tissue → healing with minimal scarring. **Symptoms:** photophobia, lacrimation, blepharospasm. **Signs — phlyctenular conjunctivitis:** simple phlyctenular (solitary pinkish-white nodule with surrounding conjunctival hyperaemia on bulbar conjunctiva near limbus); necrotising (very large phlycten with central necrosis and ulceration); miliary (multiple phlyctens arranged in ring around limbus with surrounding global conjunctivitis; may proceed to ring ulcer). **Phlyctenular keratitis:** (a) **ulcerative keratitis** — scrofulous ulcer (self-limiting superficial infiltrative keratitis; marginal ulcer from breakdown of limbal phlycten; no clear space between ulcer margin and limbus; long axis perpendicular to limbus; heals without residual opacity); fascicular ulcer (solitary superficial ulcer with prominent parallel leash of blood vessels; leaves band-shaped opacity on healing); miliary ulcer (multiple small ulcers scattered over cornea or part of it; may coalesce to ring ulcer). (b) **diffuse infiltrative keratitis** — self-limiting; heals spontaneously in 8–10 days without residual opacity. **Investigations:** CBC, ESR (infective status); stool for OPC (helminthic infestation); chest X-ray PA (TB); sputum for AFB and Mantoux test (TB); systemic examination for infective foci — ENT, dental, physician. **Treatment — ocular:** eye drop dexamethasone/betamethasone, severe cases prednisolone acetate (excellent result); topical antibiotics if secondary bacterial infection; topical cycloplegics if corneal involvement. **Systemic:** ATT if active TB focus found; systemic antibiotics for staphylococcal infection; deworming for antihelminthic infestation. **General supportive:** high-protein diet + vitamin A, C, D for malnutrition; local warm compression; preservative-free topical artificial tear substitute.

column2: Write short notes on xerosis of conjunctiva.
column4: **Definition:** normal conjunctiva kept moist by tear secretion; xerosis is a symptomatic clinical condition in which conjunctiva becomes dry and lustreless. **Etiology and manifestations:** (1) **Parenchymal conjunctival xerosis** — due to cicatricial disorganisation of conjunctiva; seen in all ages; marked dryness, thickening and scarring, keratinisation; causes — destructive interstitial conjunctivitis (trachoma, diphtheritic membranous conjunctivitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, ocular pemphigus, thermal burn, radiation burn, chemical burn), conjunctival exposure (proptosis, lagophthalmos, facial palsy, ectropion). (2) **Epithelial xerosis** — hypovitaminosis A; usually in children; associated with night blindness; may progress to complete loss of vision; history of measles. **Treatment:** (1) treatment of cause in parenchymal conjunctival xerosis; (2) vitamin A supplementation as per WHO recommendations in epithelial xerosis; (3) topical artificial tear substitutes.

column2: Define trachoma. Describe its pathogenesis
column4: WHO grading
column7: **Definition:** potentially blinding infectious disease of eye caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars A, B, Ba, C). **Pathogenesis:** poverty + overcrowding + poor hygiene → re-infection cycles within communities → recurrent infection elicits chronic cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity (Type IV) to chlamydial antigens → chronic inflammation of ocular surface and eyelids → loss of vision. **Clinical features:** (1) **Active inflammatory stage** — commonly in pre-school children; mixed follicular or papillary conjunctivitis with superior epithelial keratitis and pannus formation in superior cornea. (2) **Chronic cicatricial stage** — commonly in middle-aged people; upper tarsal conjunctivitis scars; **Herbert pits** (shallow depressions near limbus); trichiasis, distichiasis, cicatricial entropion; corneal scarring and opacification. **WHO grading:** TF — follicular trachomatous inflammation: ≥ 5 follicles > 0.5 mm on superior tarsal plate; TI — intense trachomatous inflammation: diffuse involvement of superior tarsal conjunctiva obscuring > 50% of deep tarsal vessels; TS — trachomatous conjunctival scarring; TT — trachomatous trichiasis: at least one eyelash touching globe; CO — corneal opacity involving part of pupillary margin. **Management — SAFE strategy:** **S** — surgery for trichiasis, distichiasis, entropion; **A** — antibiotics for active disease: drug of choice — tablet azithromycin 20 mg/kg single dose; others — tablet erythromycin 500 mg BD × 14 days, tab doxycycline 100 mg BD × 10 days, topical 1% tetracycline ointment; antibiotics administered to patient and all family members; single course followed by annual antibiotic retreatment to affected communities; **F** — maintenance of facial hygiene; **E** — improvement of sanitation, water supply and other environmental risk factors. **Current Indian scenario — WHO criteria for trachoma elimination:** (1) prevalence of TF stage among 1–9 years children < 5%; (2) prevalence of TT stage in > 15 years < 2/1000 population. **National Trachoma Prevalence study findings:** TF not a public health problem in any endemic unit in India (mass antibiotic administration no longer required); TT prevalence > 0.2% in four endemic units — public health-level trichiasis surgery intervention required for complete elimination.

column2: Write short notes on vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) / spring catarrh.
column4: **Definition:** recurrent, bilateral, interstitial, self-limiting allergic inflammation of conjunctiva mediated by both IgE and cell-mediated immune mechanisms, with periodic seasonal incidence. **Epidemiology:** more common in 4–20 years; boys more predisposed; more common in summer (warm weather conjunctivitis); more prevalent in tropical climate; patients with atopic diseases (eczema, asthma) commonly associated. **Etiopathogenesis:** generalised background of atopy → T-helper lymphocyte alteration → aggravated Type-I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction → clinical manifestations of vernal conjunctivitis. **Symptoms:** marked itching and burning sensation (worse in warm humid atmosphere), ropy discharge, mild photophobia. **Signs — conjunctival involvement:** (1) **palpebral disease** — hard flat-topped macropapillae arranged in 'cobblestone' or 'pavement stone' pattern with conjunctival hyperaemia. (2) **bulbar disease** — Horner-Tranta spots (discrete whitish raised dots), gelatinous membrane around limbus, dusky-red congestion of bulbar conjunctiva. (3) **mixed form** — combined features. **Corneal involvement — vernal keratopathy:** (a) punctate epithelial keratitis in superior cornea; (b) epithelial erosion due to coalescing punctate lesions; (c) vernal corneal plaques due to coating of epithelial macroerosion areas with exudates; (d) ulcerative keratitis (shield ulcer — shallow transverse ulcer in upper part of cornea, difficult to heal, complicated with secondary bacterial infection); (e) ring scar due to subepithelial scarring; (f) pseudogerontoxon/Cupid's bow due to recurrent limbal disease. **Treatment — general:** local cold compress, lid hygiene, air-conditioned atmosphere, dark goggles, allergen avoidance (identified by patch test), bandage soft contact lens for persistent epithelial erosions. **Local:** (1) topical steroids — 0.1% fluorometholone, 0.2/0.5% loteprednol etabonate, 0.5/0.1% prednisolone acetate (severe exacerbations and severe keratopathy); start 1 drop 2-hourly × 7 days, then QDS × 2 weeks; IOP monitoring; minimal use due to risk of steroid-induced glaucoma; hydrocortisone ointment at bedtime; (2) topical NSAIDs (ketorolac); (3) topical mast cell stabilisers (nedocromil sodium, sodium cromoglycate, lodoxamide) 1 drop 5 times/day — slow onset but long-term use; (4) antihistamines — alcaftadine, bepotastine, olopatadine (dual acting); (5) topical fourth-generation fluoroquinolones for severe keratopathy; (6) E/D cyclosporine 0.5% BD or 0.03% at HS; (7) preservative-free artificial tear substitutes; (8) 0.5% topical N-acetylcysteine (mucolytic in plaque keratopathy). **Systemic:** oral antihistamines (loratadine/levocetirizine) at bedtime; short course oral steroids in severe non-responsive. **Surgical:** supratarsal steroid injection (0.1 ml triamcinolone 40 mg/ml or dexamethasone 4 mg/ml) in severe non-remitting palpebral disease or non-compliant; superficial keratectomy for plaques/shield ulcers; amniotic membrane transplantation for slowly responsive shield ulcer.

column2: Write short notes on pterygium.
column4: **Definition:** degenerative and hyperplastic condition of conjunctiva where a wing-shaped fold of degenerative conjunctival tissue encroaches on cornea from either side within interpalpebral fissure. **Pathophysiology — risk factors:** hot climate, predominant outdoor work, exposure to UV rays, exposure to dry heat, exposure to high wind, excessive dust. Subconjunctival tissue undergoes elastotic degeneration → proliferates as subepithelial vascularised granulation tissue → enters cornea from limbus → destroys corneal epithelium, Bowman's layer and superficial stroma. **Symptoms:** foreign body sensation, defective vision due to astigmatism, cosmetic issues. **Signs:** primary (usually nasal; old age; male); double pterygium (both nasal and temporal in single eye); **head** (apical part on cornea), **cap** (semilunar whitish infiltrate in front of head), **body** (scleral part between limbus and canthus), **Stocker's line** (deposition of iron anterior to advancing head in limbal area). **Classification — by progression:** progressive (thick, fleshy, vascular) vs regressive (thin, atrophic, attenuated, minimal vascularity; no typical head-neck morphology). **By extent of involvement:** type I (< 2 mm corneal involvement), type II (2–4 mm), type III (> 4 mm). **By occurrence:** primary (first time) vs recurrent (after primary excision). **Medical treatment:** topical tear substitutes (foreign body sensation), topical steroids and antibiotics (associated inflammation), UV-protective spectacles/sunglasses. **Surgical indications:** causing visual disturbance, progressive pterygium encroaching over visual axis, cosmetic blemish. **Surgical techniques:** (1) pterygium excision with bare sclera in situ (high recurrence); (2) pterygium excision with conjunctival limbal autografting (CLAU) — autografting with sutures or without sutures (autoblood technique, tissue adhesives); (3) pterygium excision with amniotic membrane transplantation and 0.02% topical mitomycin C; (4) lamellar keratoplasty in cases with deep stromal involvement. **Differential diagnosis:** **pseudo-pterygium** — fold of bulbar conjunctiva attached to cornea as result of acute inflammation; can occur at any age/any site; does not progress; probe can be passed under neck. **Complications:** recurrent inflammation, cystic degeneration, rarely neoplastic changes.

column2: Write short notes on recurrent pterygium.
column4: **Definition:** pterygium is degenerative/hyperplastic condition of conjunctiva where wing-shaped fold encroaches over cornea from either side within interpalpebral fissure; said to be recurrent when it reappears after primary excision. **Causes:** pterygium excision with bare sclera in situ; pterygium excision with failed conjunctival limbal autograft; excessive UV radiation exposure; progressive limbal stem cell insufficiency; incomplete removal of pterygium. **Management principle:** (1) surgical exploration and complete excision with free conjunctival limbal autografting; (2) autograft augmented with prior topical antimetabolite application on scleral bed and excised edges; (3) autograft secured with stay sutures, tissue adhesives or autoblood technique; (4) when insufficient normal conjunctival tissue or conjunctival tissue must be preserved (e.g., trabeculectomy), amniotic membrane used for grafting; (5) recurrent recalcitrant pterygium with deep stromal bed involvement — lamellar keratoplasty (DALK). **Surgical steps:** (1) antiseptic dressing and draping; (2) topical anaesthesia with proparacaine; (3) meticulous dissection of head from corneal tissue with No. 15 blade or crescent knife; (4) dissection of body from scleral bed with complete removal of subepithelial degenerative tissue and excision of pterygium; special care to prevent injury to lateral/medial recti; no cautery of scleral bed; (5) bare scleral bed; graft conjunctival tissue harvested from temporal quadrant; superior quadrant conjunctiva usually preserved for future surgical use; harvest only conjunctiva and not Tenon's sheath (subconjunctival saline injection helpful); (6) securing graft — sutures (causes irritation), fibrin glue (expensive), patient's own blood (commonly done). **Special note:** topical 0.02% mitomycin C application on scleral bed for few minutes before CLAU or amniotic membrane graft prevents recurrence. **Complications:** failure of graft due to cystic degeneration or over-use of topical mitomycin or cauterisation of scleral bed; graft shrinkage; subgraft granulation tissue formation.

column2: Define symblepharon. Describe pathophysiology
column5: **Definition:** pathological condition where eyelids become abnormally adherent to eyeball. **Pathophysiology:** thermal burn, chemical injury, membranous conjunctivitis, injury, systemic conditions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) → raw surface of palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva → healing of both apposed surfaces → adhesions between palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva → adhesions can even occur between palpebral conjunctiva and cornea. **Symptoms:** diplopia, lagophthalmos, cosmetic issues, restricted ocular movements, restrictive strabismus. **Classification:** (1) **anterior symblepharon** — adhesions in anterior part only; (2) **posterior symblepharon** — adhesions in fornices only; (3) **total symblepharon** — adhesions completely between palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva, extending up to cornea in certain cases. **Treatment — prophylactic:** lubricant-coated glass rod sweeping in fornices several times a day; large-size therapeutic soft contact lens. **Curative:** (1) mild — symblepharectomy with mobilisation of surrounding conjunctiva; (2) severe — symblepharectomy with buccal mucosal graft or amniotic membrane transplantation.

column2: Write short notes on bacterial corneal ulcer.
column4: **Symptoms:** pain, foreign body sensation, epiphora, redness, photophobia, dimness of vision. **Signs:** eyelids — swelling, blepharospasm; conjunctiva — chemosis and congestion; cornea — yellowish-white area of ulcer (oval or irregular), peri-ulcer stromal oedema (no ulcer), floor/base covered with necrotic material, margins swollen and overhanging. **Characteristic by causative agent:** (1) **Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus** — oval, densely opaque, peri-ulcer clear cornea. (2) **Pseudomonas** — rapid progression with high risk of perforation, irregular margin, peri-ulcer ground-glass appearance, greenish mucopurulent exudation due to liquefactive necrosis. (3) **Enterobacteria** — shallow ulcer, ring-shaped peri-ulcer corneal infiltrate. **General features:** hypopyon with toxin-induced sterile acute uveitis; IOP sometimes raised due to associated inflammatory glaucoma. **Investigations:** PPBS (recurrent ulcer); complete urine and stool examination (children — parasitic infestation); lacrimal sac patency (chronic dacryocystitis); microbiological examination (before antimicrobials) — 2% xylocaine/proparacaine, scraping from base and margins separately with modified Kimura spatula or 20G needle; gram stain and Giemsa (bacterial nature), 10% KOH mount (hyphae vs non-hyphae fungi), calcofluor white stain (fungal filaments under fluorescence microscope), culture on blood agar (aerobes), Sabouraud's dextrose agar (fungi), biochemical tests for bacterial species. **Treatment:** (1) **antimicrobials — initial therapy till culture sensitivity:** cefazolin 5% + tobramycin 1.3% fortified eye drops every 5 min for 30 min, then every 15 min for 2 hours, OR vancomycin 5% + fluoroquinolone 0.3% ciprofloxacin/0.5% moxifloxacin every hour for 48 hours; topical antimicrobials continued if favourable response; poor response after 48 hours → modify per culture sensitivity; systemic antibiotics only in fulminating cases with impending perforation (oral ciprofloxacin/aminoglycosides/cephalosporins). (2) **cycloplegics** — 2% homatropine BD, 1% atropine TDS (relieves ciliary spasm pain, brings more antibiotics to aqueous humour by increasing blood supply to anterior uvea, reduces anterior uveitis and hypopyon). (3) Tab ibuprofen 400 mg / tab paracetamol 500 mg SOS. (4) **general** — dark goggles, hot fomentation, protection from dust/water/trauma. **Complications:** acute anterior uveitis, secondary glaucoma (inflammatory angle closure by fibrinous exudates), descemetocele (impending perforation), perforation of corneal ulcer (decreased pain, aqueous comes out, prolapse of iris, anterior staphyloma), complications of perforated ulcer (subluxation/anterior dislocation of lens, anterior capsular cataract, corneal fistula, endophthalmitis/panophthalmitis → phthisis bulbi, expulsive choroidal haemorrhage), corneal scarring.

column2: Write short notes on hypopyon corneal ulcer.
column4: **Definition:** characteristic corneal ulcer caused by pneumococcus species; also called 'ulcer serpens'. **Source of infection:** exogenous; most commonly chronic dacryocystitis. **Symptoms:** pain, foreign body sensation, epiphora, redness, photophobia, dimness of vision. **Signs:** **ulcer serpens** — one edge progresses rapidly while other edge shows cicatrisation; disc-shaped ulcer at centre of cornea; iridocyclitis; associated hypopyon that increases rapidly leading to secondary glaucoma. **Pathogenesis:** bacteria enter breached corneal epithelium → exogenous source → characteristic ulcer serpens formation → bacterial toxins diffuse into anterior chamber → severe iridocyclitis → leucocytes gravitate to bottom of anterior chamber → **hypopyon** (essentially sterile). **Differential diagnosis:** corneal ulcer with hypopyon caused by staphylococci, streptococci, gonococci, Pseudomonas, Moraxella. **Management:** same as bacterial corneal ulcer.

column2: Write short notes on non-healing corneal ulcer.
column4: **Definition:** corneal ulcer progressing despite adequate therapy. **Etiology — local causes:** impacted foreign body, misdirected eyelashes, chronic dacryocystitis, any long-standing cause of raised IOP, antimicrobial resistance, inadequate therapy, incorrect etiological diagnosis, non-compliant patient, lagophthalmos. **Systemic causes:** uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, severe anaemia, malnutrition, chronic debilitating diseases, patients on long-standing systemic or topical corticosteroids. **Investigations:** same as bacterial ulcer plus aimed at ruling out causes of non-healing. **Treatment:** (1) antimicrobials per sensitivity; (2) rest same as bacterial ulcer; (3) cycloplegics same; (4) **IOP-lowering agents** — eyedrop timolol maleate 0.5% BD; latanoprost or other prostaglandin analogue avoided; (5) slit-lamp biomicroscopy-guided removal of foreign body with 26G needle under topical anaesthesia; (6) slit-lamp biomicroscopy-guided mechanical debridement of ulcer base with spatula or 26G needle under topical anaesthesia; (7) cauterisation of ulcer with carbolic acid or trichloroacetic acid in advanced non-healing; (8) 360° conjunctival peritomy to prevent excessive corneal vascularisation hindering healing; (9) bandage soft contact lens.

column2: Describe management of corneal ulcer with impending perforation.
column4: **Definition:** slit-lamp biomicroscopic identification of a descemetocele is the sign of any corneal ulcer impending perforation. **General measures:** avoidance of straining; strict bed rest; eye pressure bandage till definitive treatment initiated; counselling for guarded visual prognosis. **Specific measures:** (1) **IOP-lowering agents** — tab acetazolamide 250 mg QDS PO; infusion mannitol 20% 300 ml stat followed by 100 ml IV TDS; E/D timolol maleate 0.5% 1 drop BD; therapeutic paracentesis if all IOP-lowering drug measures fail. (2) **Temporary measures** — bandage soft contact lens; cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive to seal probable site of impending perforation; hooding of site of impending corneal perforation by conjunctival flap (entire cornea may be covered if required); amniotic membrane transplantation over site of impending perforation. (3) **Permanent measure** — penetrating therapeutic tectonic corneal transplantation in large corneal ulcers impending perforation not manageable with other options; in fungal corneal ulcer post-therapeutic keratoplasty, postoperative topical steroids avoided or used judiciously. (4) **Antimicrobial therapy** — same as corneal ulcer treatment.

column2: Write short notes on superficial punctate keratitis (SPK).
column4: **Definition:** small, multiple, spot-like lesions in superficial corneal layers due to various infective and non-infective causes. **Infective causes:** viral infections (herpes zoster ophthalmicus, adenovirus, herpes simplex, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, pharyngoconjunctival fever); chlamydial (trachoma, inclusion conjunctivitis); staphylococcal toxin; chronic blepharitis. **Non-infective causes:** vernal keratoconjunctivitis; trophic lesions (exposure keratitis, neuroparalytic keratitis); drug-induced (idoxuridine); dermatological diseases (acne rosacea, pemphigoid); dry-eye disorders; idiopathic — Thygeson's SPK, Theodore's superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis; photophthalmia due to UV exposure (311–290 nm); lagophthalmos; aberrant eyelashes; entropion; floppy eyelid syndrome; prolonged contact lens wear. **Location gives clue to cause:** superior — VKC, chlamydia, floppy eyelid, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis; interpalpebral — dry eye, reduced corneal sensation; diffuse — photophthalmia, drug toxicity, viral & bacterial infection, prolonged contact lens wear; inferior — chronic blepharitis, lagophthalmos, aberrant eyelashes, entropion. **Symptoms:** photophobia, lacrimation, ocular pain, conjunctival redness. **Signs (slit lamp under cobalt blue after fluorescein):** (a) punctate epithelial lesions; (b) punctate subepithelial lesions; (c) combined punctate epithelial and subepithelial lesion; (d) filamentary lesions — stain well with rose bengal, most common cause dry eye. **Treatment:** (1) **general ocular therapy** — liberal use of preservative-free artificial tear substitutes as topical drops and ointments at bedtime; topical steroids (marked suppressive effect); bandage soft contact lens. (2) **specific therapy** — identify specific cause and treat medically or surgically.

column2: Write short notes on contact lens.
column4: **Definition:** artificial lens placed in opposition with anterior corneal surface for optical, therapeutic, diagnostic or cosmetic purposes. **Indications — optical:** correcting refractive errors (absolute indications — anisometropia, unilateral/bilateral aphakia especially children, high myopia, irregular astigmatism especially keratoconus). **Therapeutic and operative:** corneal ulcer impending perforation, bullous keratopathy, filamentous keratopathy, recurrent corneal erosion syndrome, aniridia, coloboma, oculocutaneous albinism, as vehicle for drug delivery in glaucoma, opaque contact lenses for occlusion therapy in amblyopia, to seal small corneal perforation. **Diagnostic:** gonioscopy, goniotomy for congenital glaucoma, ERG, Goldmann's three-mirror fundus examination, vitrectomy, endocular photocoagulation. **Cosmetic and occupational:** corneal opacity, haptic contact lens in mild ptosis, cosmetic scleral lens in phthisis bulbi, pilots, actors, sports personalities. **Contraindications:** mental incompetence, chronic dacryocystitis, chronic blepharitis, recurrent hordeolum, severe dry eye, corneal dystrophies and degenerations, recurrent episcleritis/scleritis/iridocyclitis. **Types:** (1) **Hard (PMMA)** — light weight, non-toxic, durable, cheap; impermeable to O₂; can cause corneal abrasions; hydrophobic → tear film instability; not used nowadays (poor patient tolerance). (2) **Rigid gas permeable** — silicon acrylate copolymer of PMMA or cellulose acetate butyrate (CAB, thermoplastic from wood); semi-soft, permeable to oxygen; better tolerated than PMMA. (3) **Soft** — hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA); 1–2 mm larger than corneal diameter; soft, O₂-permeable, well tolerated; cannot correct astigmatism > 2D; less longevity; inferior optical quality; more corneal infections; most frequently prescribed in clinical practice. **Parts:** front curve/central anterior curve (determines power); base curve/central posterior curve (fits anterior corneal surface); peripheral curves (tear reservoir, acts as ski for lens movements); edge (polished/blended union of peripheral posterior and anterior curves); optical zone diameter; overall diameter; power (posterior vertex power in diameter); tint (colour). **Contact lens fitting:** after insertion, lens in eye environment evaluated — maintains 0.5–1.0 mm movement with ocular movements; good centration; no conjunctival vessel/scleral compression; stable visual acuity with/without blinking; sharp retinoscopic reflex and keratometric mires before/after blinking; wait 10–20 minutes for settling of lens under slit lamp. **Complications — ocular:** corneal (SPK, epithelial oedema and microcysts, epithelial abrasions, 3 and 9 o'clock corneal staining due to tear flow disruption, sterile corneal infiltrates, corneal neovascularisation, microbial keratitis — bacterial/acanthamoeba); conjunctival (giant papillary conjunctivitis, allergic conjunctivitis, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis). **Contact lens complications:** discolouration, physical damage, lens loss, lens deposits (protein/lipid). **Contact lens care:** wetting solutions (coat lens uniformly before use, minimize friction, buffer/cushion replaced by tear); cleaning solutions (detergent to remove tear film and deposits, bactericidal); storage/soaking solutions (antiseptic bactericidal, keeps lens hydrated); rewetting solutions (artificial tear substitutes used to alleviate discomfort while wearing). **Advantages over spectacles:** irregular corneal astigmatism corrected; normal field of vision; no peripheral prismatic aberrations of thick spectacles; binocular vision retained in high anisometropia; more cosmetic acceptance.

column2: Write short notes on adherent leucoma.
column4: **Definition:** leucomatous corneal opacity is full-thickness corneal opacity through which no underlying structures of anterior chamber are visible; becomes adherent leucoma when iris tissue is incorporated within the corneal scar without corneal ectatic changes. **Causes:** perforated corneal ulcer, full-thickness corneal penetrating injury, iatrogenic surgical wounds. **Pathogenesis:** perforation of corneal ulcer OR penetrating corneal wound → iris tissue plugs into corneal defect with or without prolapse into exterior → wound healing starts with organisation of incarcerated iris tissue → corneal scar formation with incorporation of iris tissue → adherent leucoma. Note: chance of development is less if perforation is central (absence of iris tissue in pupillary zone). **Symptoms:** dimness of vision (due to central opacity or astigmatism from peripheral opacity), cosmetic blemish. **Signs:** vision PL (+) with accurate/inaccurate PR; irregular pupils; central leucomatous corneal opacity with iris tissue adhered; brown pigmentation; deep vascularisation. **Investigations:** PPBS (glycaemic control); ECG, BP (cardiological fitness); USG B-scan (posterior segment, vitreous opacities, retinal detachment); syringing (rule out infective foci in lacrimal sac); biometry (if triple procedure planned — cataract extraction + IOL + corneal transplantation). **Treatment:** (1) peripheral adherent leucoma with no cosmetic blemish, acceptable vision, no posterior segment pathology → no treatment required. (2) central adherent leucoma with normal posterior segment → synechiotomy with penetrating keratoplasty (PKP); with significant cataract → triple procedure (synechiotomy with PKP + open-sky cataract extraction + PCIOL in-the-bag); deep vascularisation is a poor prognostic marker for successful PKP; prior adequate control of raised IOP due to secondary glaucoma. (3) no visual prognosis with cosmetic blemish → corneal tattooing (temporary; 4% gold chloride + 2% hydrazine hydrate for brown; 2% platinum chloride + 2% hydrazine hydrate for black; automated tattoo gun under topical anaesthesia); matching cosmetic soft contact lens. (4) No PL with cosmetic blemish → enucleation with intraorbital implant and customised prosthetic eye shell. **Complications:** secondary angle-closure glaucoma (blockade of AC angle), recurrent iridocyclitis, failed PKP, phthisis bulbi.

column2: Enumerate the causes of corneal oedema.
column4: (1) **Infective** — keratitis, corneal ulcer. (2) **Degenerative** — corneal dystrophies, acute hydrops in keratoconus. (3) **Endothelial dysfunction** — trauma, post-intraocular surgery. (4) **Corneal graft failure.** (5) **Any cause of acute sudden rise in IOP.**

column2: Define dry eye. Describe its pathophysiology
column4: investigations
column7: **Definition (TFOS DEWS II):** multifactorial disease of tears and ocular surface characterised by loss of homeostasis of tear film, accompanied by ocular symptoms, in which tear film instability and hyperosmolarity, ocular surface inflammation and damage, and neurosensory abnormalities play etiological roles. **Pathophysiology:** interplay of inter-related mechanisms — ocular surface, internal factors (hormonal status, neural reflex), external factors (environment, relative humidity, medications). **Classification (DEWS 2007):** (1) **Aqueous-deficient** — Sjogren syndrome (primary, secondary); non-Sjogren syndrome (lacrimal deficiency, lacrimal gland duct obstruction, reflex hyposecretion, systemic drugs). (2) **Evaporative** — intrinsic (meibomian gland dysfunction due to posterior blepharitis, contact lens use, refractive surgery, low blink rate, drug-induced antihistamines/beta-blockers/antispasmodics/diuretics) and extrinsic (vitamin A deficiency, preservatives of topical medications, contact lens wear, computer use). Mechanisms may overlap. **Investigations (poor correlation between symptoms and clinical tests; reliability improves with severity; performed in order):** (1) **TBUT** — fluorescein strip, patient blinks, time between last blink and first dry spot under cobalt blue; < 10 seconds highly suspicious of evaporative dry eye. (2) **Schirmer test** — Whatman #41 filter paper (35 mm), folded 5 mm, inserted at junction of middle and outer third of lower eyelid; without anaesthetic (Schirmer 1) — measures basic + reflex secretion; > 10 mm normal; with anaesthetic (Schirmer 2) — measures basic secretion only; > 6 mm normal. (3) **Ocular surface staining** — fluorescein (punctate epithelial erosions under cobalt blue as green); rose bengal 1% (dead/devitalised cells and mucous, red-free filter, preceded by anaesthesia, excess dye washed out because of stinging); lissamine green (same as rose bengal, less irritation). (4) **Fluorescein clearance test** — 5 μl fluorescein, residual dye measured by Schirmer strip at lower lateral eyelid margin; delayed clearance in dry eye. (5) **Tear film osmolarity** — normal threshold 305–316 mOsm/L; does not correlate with symptoms but correlates well with management efficacy; measured by Clifton and vapour pressure osmometers; TearLab better (micro-electrode, no contact with surface to prevent reflex tearing). (6) **Phenol red thread test** — pH-sensitive dye-impregnated thread placed on lower lid; colour change yellow → red after 15 seconds; < 6 mm = dry eye. (7) **Tear meniscometry** — quantifies height of tear film meniscus from lower lid margin. (8) **Impression cytology** — cellulose acetate filter paper applied on ocular surface to remove superficial epithelium; histological/immunohistochemical/molecular analysis. **Severity grading scheme (DEWS):** level 1 (mild/episodic under environmental stress), level 2 (moderate episodic or chronic), level 3 (severe frequent/constant without stress), level 4 (severe disabling constant); discomfort, visual symptoms, conjunctival injection, conjunctival/corneal staining, corneal/tear signs, lid/meibomian glands, TFBUT, Schirmer score increase with level. Treatment applied in graded approach. **Treatment — Level 1:** information/education/communication, lifestyle review to minimize low blink rate activities (20-20-20 rule), avoid dry/dusty environment and air-conditioned rooms, awareness of LASIK exacerbating dry eye, compliance, eliminate systemic/topical medications contributing to dry eye, preserved artificial tear substitutes, eyelid therapy (warm compress, lid hygiene, control of blepharitis, correction of lid position, lateral tarsorrhaphy in extreme cases). **Level 2:** non-preserved ATS only (drops/gels/ointments), anti-inflammatory agents (topical steroids, topical cyclosporine, oral omega fatty acids), treatment of meibomian gland dysfunction, temporary punctal occlusion, moisture chamber spectacles. **Level 3:** autologous or umbilical cord serum eye drops, contact lens, permanent punctal occlusion, systemic anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs, steroids), ocular surface reconstruction surgery with amniotic membrane transplantation, ocular stem cell transplantation.

column2: Write short notes on artificial tear substitutes.
column4: **Definition:** tear replacement agents manufactured artificially to include ingredients addressing each deranged aspect of dysfunctional tear film. **Classification by degree of interaction with human eye:** (1) **Wetting agents** — enhance tear film viscosity and lubricate ocular surface for short time. (2) **Demulcents** — improve tear film quality and quantity for longer time. (3) **Multiple-action tear substitutes** — lubricate and influence ocular surface to counteract dry eye disease pathology. (4) **Ocular surface modulators** — influence ocular surface to counteract dry eye pathology. **Composition:** active ingredients (demulcents — water-soluble polymers protecting and lubricating mucous membrane); biologically active excipients (complement active ingredients); preservatives (reduce risk of microbial contamination). **Active ingredients (max 3 per preparation):** (a) cellulose derivatives 0.2–2.5% — CMC, HPMC, HMC, MC (increase viscosity and stabilise tear film); (b) liquid polyols 0.2–1% — PEG 300, PEG 400, propylene glycol (reduce hyperosmolarity, retain water ~3× own weight, form protective layer over ocular surface); (c) polymers — carbomer, PVA 0.1–4%, povidone 0.1–2% (incorporate into lipid layer, prevent aqueous evaporation, prolong tear film retention time); (d) dextran 70 (0.1%) — improves mechanical strength of tear film; (e) gelatin (0.01%) — gelling agent. **Biologically active excipients:** osmoprotectants (prevent corneal epithelial cell apoptosis, prevent autophagy, promote epithelial cell growth, prevent inflammation and shrinkage, reduce osmotic stress — e.g., L-carnosine); humectants/hygroscopic agents (retain water multiple times own weight; hyaluronic acid, hydroxypropyl guar — improve cellular adhesion, prolonged adherence to ocular surface by mimicking mucin layer, actively cross-link at pH > 7); oil-based agents and surfactants (polar and non-polar lipids, mineral oils — produce positively charged nano-droplets that bind negatively charged epithelial cells); electrolytes (Na⁺/K⁺/Cl⁻/Mg²⁺/Ca²⁺ — maintain osmotic balance and pH); antioxidants and buffers (scavenge free radicals); wound healing agents (high molecular weight hyaluronic acid, high molecular weight lysine). **Preservatives:** maximum efficacy when preservative-free in unit doses or specialised multi-dose vials; complete elimination challenging due to cost; detergent type (more ocular surface toxicity — polyhexamethylene biguanide, EDTA); oxidative type (less toxic — Polyquad, sorbitol); ionic buffer system; disappearing preservatives (sodium perborate, stabilised oxychloro complex — decompose spontaneously into hydrogen, oxygen, water on contact with ocular surface). **Principle of ATS use:** choose by ingredients — demulcents for aqueous tear film deficiency, humectants for evaporative dry eye or oil-based agents, osmoprotectants for hypermolarity-induced dry eye, osmoprotectants + humectants for dry eye with corneal epithelial damage; choose by severity (high viscosity = prolonged retention, more severe disease); frequency 4–6 times/day during waking hours; step-ladder approach (start with one agent, add another as required).

column2: Write short notes on punctal occlusion.
column4: **Principle:** preserves natural tears and prolongs artificial tear substitute action by reducing tear film drainage; mostly used for keratoconjunctivitis sicca patients with poor response to ATS. **Types:** (1) **Temporary** — self-dissolving (few weeks) collagen plugs inserted into inferior puncta; patient reviewed after 2 weeks; if significant improvement, plan permanent inferior punctal occlusion. (2) **Reversible** — inferior punctal occlusion by silicone plugs; kept for 2–6 months; complications — self-extrusion, distal migration. (3) **Permanent** — for severe dry eye who have shown improvement with temporary occlusion; thermal or laser cauterisation of proximal canaliculi; all four canaliculi should not be done in same sitting.

column2: Enumerate the causes of corneal blindness.
column4: (1) **Infective** — post-keratitis/corneal ulcer/trachoma corneal scar formation. (2) **Trauma** — post-traumatic corneal rupture leading to corneal scar along visual axis. (3) **Degenerative** — corneal scarring along visual axis due to progressive pterygium; corneal scarring due to corneal dystrophies and degenerations. (4) **Iatrogenic** — corneal scarring due to post-intraocular surgery, bullous keratopathy, corneal graft rejection.

column2: Write short notes on keratoplasty.
column4: **Definition:** operative procedure in which patient's diseased cornea is replaced by healthy and clear donor corneal tissue, either in part or entirely. **Indications by expected outcome:** **optical** (visual improvement — bullous keratopathy, corneal dystrophies, advanced keratoconus); **therapeutic** (replacing inflamed cornea not responding to conventional antimicrobial therapy — corneal ulcer due to multidrug-resistant organisms); **tectonic** (restoring structural integrity — corneal ulcer impending perforation, penetrating corneal injury with tissue loss); **cosmetic** (improving appearance with no expected visual improvement). **By nature of keratoplasty:** **penetrating keratoplasty (PKP)** — can be done for any indication (optical, therapeutic, tectonic, cosmetic); **lamellar keratoplasty** — principally done for optical reasons: (a) anterior lamellar keratoplasty — superficial anterior lamellar keratoplasty (SALK, ~10% superficial stroma replaced), deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK, 80–90% stromal tissue replaced leaving healthy endothelium and Descemet's); (b) posterior lamellar keratoplasty/endothelial keratoplasty — Descemet's stripping endothelial keratoplasty (DSEK), Descemet's stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK, along with Descemet's and endothelium a small amount of posterior stroma harvested), Descemet's membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK, only Descemet's membrane and endothelium harvested); for Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy, aphakic bullous keratopathy, posterior polymorphous dystrophy, iridocorneal endothelial syndrome. **Other types:** rotational autokeratoplasty (patient's own cornea cut and rotated to transfer pupillary area from small opacity to peripheral zone); contralateral keratoplasty (corneas of two eyes exchanged — opaque but visual cornea of one eye replaces clear but blind cornea of other). **Complications — early:** flat anterior chamber, endophthalmitis, secondary glaucoma, iris prolapse, primary graft failure. **Late:** graft rejection (endothelial rejection line with subepithelial infiltrates — Khodadoust line demarcates healthy and diseased endothelium; epithelial rejection line with subepithelial infiltrates — Kayes dot; sudden-onset full-thickness stromal haze; diffuse KPs with Descemet's folds); irregular/high regular astigmatism.

column2: Write short notes on donor corneal tissue preservation.
column4: **Donor corneal tissue** must be removed within 6 hours of death by whole globe enucleation or sclero-corneal button; tissue always associated with blood sample of donor; brought to eye bank maintaining cold chain. **Evaluation for suitability:** (1) slit lamp biomicroscopy and gradation (grade I–V); (2) specular microscopy — endothelial cell count and morphology; (3) microbiological evaluation of donor tissue; (4) serological tests of collected blood for HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis. After evaluation, tissue may be utilised immediately or preserved. **Preservation by duration — short-term (24–96 hours):** (a) **moist chamber method** — enucleated whole globe in moist chamber at 4°C in refrigerator up to 24 hours; (b) **McCarey-Kaufman (M-K) medium** — pinkish; tissue culture (TC)-199, 5% dextran-40, HEPES buffer, gentamycin 0.1 mg/ml; pH 7.4; sclero-corneal button; up to 96 hours. **Intermediate-term (up to 2 weeks):** 2.5% chondroitin sulphate, 1% dextran, ascorbic acid, vitamin B12, ATP precursors, gentamycin, streptomycin; sclero-corneal button; preservation at 4°C. **Long-term (up to 1 year):** (a) **glycerine preservation** — up to 3–4 weeks; tissue nonviable for transplantation but suitable for research; (b) **organ culture method** — up to 35 days at 30–37°C; tissue remains viable for transplantation; (c) **cryopreservation** — up to 1 year at −70°C; tissue remains viable for transplantation.

column2: Write short notes on tarsorrhaphy.
column4: **Surgical principle:** narrowing of palpebral aperture or almost closing it, by surgically creating adhesions between apposing parts of lid margins. **Indications:** (1) **temporary (paramedian/lateral):** to protect cornea in VII nerve palsy, neuroparalytic keratitis, assist healing of indolent corneal ulcer, corneal ulcer impending perforation, assist healing of skin grafts on eyelids; (2) **permanent (lateral):** established VII nerve palsy with no chance of recovery, neuroparalytic keratitis with severe loss of sensation, abnormal length of palpebral fissure. **Anaesthesia:** surface with 4% lignocaine eye drops; local infiltration with 2% lignocaine with adrenaline. **Surgical steps:** (1) 5 mm-long incision site marked on corresponding parts of upper and lower eyelid margins, 3 mm on either side of midline; (2) incision 2 mm deep along marked site, marginal epithelium excised (care not to damage ciliary line anteriorly and sharp lid border posteriorly); (3) lid margins apposed with two double-armed 6-0 silk mattress sutures passed through rubber bolsters. **Follow-up:** sutures and rubber bolsters removed after 7–10 days; release of temporary tarsorrhaphy after 6–12 weeks by putting small artery forceps or muscle hook through bridge between two lids and cutting with surgical blade/scissors. **Complications — intraoperative:** injury to root of cilia, injury to tarsal plate, intraocular injury while passing mattress sutures or during release of temporary tarsorrhaphy. **Postoperative:** failed tarsorrhaphy with release of eyelids, eyelid skin necrosis due to tight mattress sutures, infection, dry eyes due to meibomian duct injury. **Recent advances:** triangular flap of skin and orbicularis excised from lower lid and corresponding tarsoconjunctival flap from upper lid, then both lids sutured with mattress technique over rubber bolsters.

column2: Write short notes on removal of corneal foreign body.
column4: **Nature of foreign bodies — non-organic:** inert (glass, plastics, porcelain, gold, silver, platinum, titanium); less reactive (aluminium frequently gets powdered, zinc/nickel/mercury/max lead to local suppuration); iron and copper (undergo electrolytic dissociation leading to long-term degeneration). **Organic:** tend to produce proliferative reaction with granulation tissue formation — vegetable matter (risk of fungal infection), wood, dislodged eyelashes, caterpillar hair (has ability to penetrate intact cornea and fan out — ophthalmia nodosa). **Evaluation under slit lamp:** (1) approximate time — > 24 hours poorer prognosis, risk of perforation/migration; < 24 hours good prognosis; (2) topical proparacaine judiciously (risk of corneal melt in severely decompensated corneas); (3) lid speculum/retractors depending on periocular chemosis severity; (4) systemic analgesia depending on pain; (5) under diffuse and focused parallelepiped illumination — chemical nature, depth and extent of corneal involvement noted and documented with colour coding; (6) superior fornix (by double eversion) and inferior fornix inspected for additional foreign bodies; (7) attempt to measure IOP if tolerable and no perforation/impending risk; (8) Seidel test to identify perforation in doubtful cases. **Removal techniques:** (1) **continuous irrigation and mechanical removal** with moist cotton swab — first step; majority of recent and superficial foreign bodies successfully removed; (2) **with 26G needle** — under slit lamp or operating microscope; bevel parallel to corneal plane; needle attached to tuberculin syringe for better control; rust rings dislodged meticulously; central corneal foreign bodies and rust rings require aggressive removal for better visual rehabilitation; (3) **with Alger brush/rotating corneal burr** — flicks out foreign body; more aggressively removes rust rings with minimal surrounding tissue injury; (4) **removal of full-thickness foreign bodies/foreign bodies involving > 80–90% corneal stroma** — in OT with operating microscope; attempt to remove after incising with No. 15 blade or 3.2 mm keratome; high risk of intraocular migration with corneal perforation. **Management of corneal perforation:** small perforations — cyanoacrylate tissue glue + bandage contact lens; large perforations — suturing with 10-0 nylon + anterior chamber reformation with air or BSS; very large tissue defect — tectonic penetrating keratoplasty. **Caterpillar hair removal:** potential to penetrate intact cornea if left unremoved; usually multiple and difficult to recognise; removal of all caterpillar hair from fornices and ocular adnexa mandatory. **Post-removal care and follow-up:** topical fourth-generation fluoroquinolone for ≥ 7 days (eyedrop + eye ointment); secondary anterior uveitis possible in incomplete rust ring removal or large foreign bodies — topical cycloplegics; antifungal topical applications in vegetable matter foreign bodies; liberal preservative-free tear substitute; systemic analgesics; topical and systemic IOP-lowering drugs for impending corneal perforation; dilated fundus examination with slit lamp and indirect ophthalmoscopy to detect intraocular foreign body if media clear; in non-clear media, USG B-scan and CT scan of orbit; MRI orbit avoided especially in suspected metallic foreign bodies. **Prognosis:** small nonmetallic foreign bodies heal with clear cornea; large foreign bodies heal with corneal opacities (if central may require DALK later for full visual recovery); if corneal perforation, risk of endophthalmitis; bomb blast injuries → multiple small corneal foreign bodies at various depths — individually not removable, may require anterior lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty.

column2: Write short notes on eye banking.
column4: **Definition:** organisation dealing with collection, storage and distribution of cornea for corneal transplantation, research and supply of eye tissue for other ophthalmological purposes. **Functions:** (1) activities to promote eye donation by increasing awareness among general population; (2) maintenance and follow-up of register enlisting names of people who have pledged for eye donation; (3) collection of donated eyes from deceased; (4) receiving, evaluating and processing donor eyes; (5) preservation of donor tissue for short-term, intermediate-term, long-term; (6) distribution of donor tissues to corneal surgeons; (7) research activities and training of ophthalmic personnel. **Types of eye banking organisations — three tier:** eye bank (functions for collection, evaluation, storage, distribution of corneal tissue + awareness promotion); eye bank training centre (all functions of eye bank with additional training facilities for all levels of personnel); eyebank increase (harvesting corneal tissue and blood for serology from donor; safe transportation of collected samples to parent eye bank; promotion of eye donation awareness among community). **Eyebank personnel:** eye bank technician (enucleates donor eyes, maintains eye collection kits, tissue preservation, record upkeep, maintains asepsis in eyebank); eye bank manager (qualified ophthalmologist, head of eye bank operations); clerk-cum-storekeeper (record upkeep, communication with prospective donors and their families, communication with EDCs and other EBs, distribution of corneas to surgeons or other eye banks); medical social worker (not mandatory, may be voluntary worker, promotes awareness for voluntary eye donation); driver-cum-projectionist (runs and maintains eye bank vehicle, screens films to promote eye donation in community).
