column2: Write short notes on episcleritis.
column4: **Definition:** Inflammatory condition of episclera–conjunctiva–Tenon capsule complex (episclera = layer of connective tissue between scleral stroma and Tenon capsule). Idiopathic, benign, recurrent, bilateral condition; middle-aged females and children (gender-neutral prevalence). **Disease association — ocular:** dry eye disease, prolonged contact lens wear. **Systemic:** rheumatoid arthritis, gout, rosacea, inflammatory bowel disease, herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Systemic evaluation must be done in all cases of recurrent episcleritis. **Clinical features:** (1) **Simple episcleritis (more common)** — symptoms: grittiness, photophobia, bilateral red eye; interpalpebral sectoral involvement; triangular shape with base at limbus; underlying sclera normal. (2) **Nodular episcleritis** — symptoms same but more aggravated; tender red vascular nodule in interpalpebral area with surrounding congestion and chemosis. **Treatment:** (1) **mild cases** — cold compress; E/D 0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose (refrigerated) 1 drop 4–6 times in affected eye for 2 weeks. (2) **moderate to severe** — with ATS a weak topical steroid is preferred: E/D loteprednol 1 drop QDS × 2 weeks then taper over 2 weeks; E/D nepafenac/diclofenac (NSAIDs) 1 drop TDS × 2 weeks (less effective); tab ibuprofen 200 mg TDPC or tab indomethacin TDPC in severe cases.

column2: Write short notes on scleritis.
column4: **Definition:** Inflammatory (mostly non-infective immune-mediated) condition involving entire scleral thickness; rare disease; scleritis is mostly the initial manifestation of underlying immunological systemic disease. **Classification:** inflammatory changes in anterior and posterior disease are identical and may be present separately or simultaneously. **Anterior scleritis — non-necrotising diffuse:** more common in females in 5th decade; redness and pain radiating to face and temple; diurnal variation (symptoms improve later in the day); dimness of vision; vascular congestion generalised or localised to one quadrant (typically superior under cover of upper eyelid); as oedema resolves, affected area takes greyish-blue appearance due to increased scleral translucency (rearrangement of scleral fibres rather than decreased thickness); associated secondary glaucoma, anterior uveitis, eyelid chemosis; resolves over ~6 years with recurrent episodes; long-term visual prognosis good. **Non-necrotising nodular:** most cases have past H/O herpes zoster ophthalmicus; multiple deep-blue coloured immobile nodules in interpalpebral area close to limbus; if untreated, nodules expand and coalesce leading to necrotising scleritis; if treated early, heal with small atrophic scar; commonly misdiagnosed as nodular episcleritis (scleritis nodules are darker, immobile, and on slit lamp there is elevation of anterior scleral surface). **Necrotising:** occurs in patients ≥ 60 years; aggressive form requiring systemic immunotherapy to preserve vision and eyeball; severe pain radiating to temple, brow, jaw with poor response to analgesics; in rheumatoid arthritis, vaso-occlusive necrotising scleritis seen; patches of scleral oedema coalesce and lead to scleral necrosis; in polyarteritis nodosa, disease progresses within 24 hours; iatrogenic scleritis starts at surgical site within 3 weeks but remains localised to one sector; severe dimness of vision. **Posterior scleritis:** potentially blinding; occurs in patients < 40 years; severe dimness of vision; pain does not correlate well with severity of inflammation; choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachment, choroidal detachment (uveal effusion), disc oedema, myositis-induced diplopia and painful ocular movements, mild proptosis and ptosis. **Investigations:** CBC (raised ESR in RA, anaemia, eosinophilia in PAN); CRP, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP; ANA (PAN), ANCA (Wegener's); serum uric acid; syphilis serology; Lyme serology; HBsAg (PAN); antiphospholipid antibodies; Mantoux/chest X-ray/sputum AFB/TB Quantiferon Gold; HRCT chest (sarcoidosis); HLA B27 and X-ray LS spine (ankylosing spondylitis); anterior segment angiography (scleral non-perfusion in necrotising scleritis); USG B-scan (posterior scleritis — increased scleral thickness, fluid between sclera and Tenon's fascia giving 'T' sign — stem of T is optic nerve shadow, head is collected fluid). **Treatment:** (1) topical steroids (non-necrotising, relieve symptoms and scleral oedema); (2) systemic NSAIDs (selected non-necrotising); (3) systemic steroids — tab prednisolone 1–1.5 mg/kg single dose at 8 AM fast; pulse methyl prednisolone 0.5–4 g/day IV × 3 days in severe cases; (4) **immunomodulators** — indications: poor response to steroids, steroid-responsive patients, long-term measure to avoid steroid adverse effects, immediately indicated as first-line in RA/PAN/GPA/relapsing polychondritis; agents — tab methotrexate 12.5–50 mg once weekly + tab folic acid 1 mg/day (avoid alcohol, monitor CBC/LFT weekly), tab azathioprine 1–2.5 mg/kg/day (risk of leukopenia), tab mycophenolate mofetil 2–3 g/day in 2 divided doses, tab cyclophosphamide 1–2 mg/kg/day, tab cyclosporine 2.5–5 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses; **biologicals** — etanercept (dimeric fusion protein, 25 mg SC twice weekly; adverse: reactivated TB, opportunistic infections, uveitis, demyelinating disease, malignancy); infliximab (chimeric monoclonal antibody to TNF-α, 3–10 mg/kg IV at 4–8 week intervals; adverse: same as etanercept + heart failure aggravation + lupus-like symptoms); adalimumab (humanised IgG antibody to TNF-α, 20–40 mg SC weekly; adverse: same as infliximab); **rituximab** (B-cell inhibitor — chimeric antibody to CD-20; 500–1000 mg IV repeated 2 cycles at 2-week interval; most promising agent, most preferred).

column2: Write short notes on scleromalacia perforans.
column4: **Definition:** specific type of scleritis affecting elderly women with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis; progressive scleral thinning without inflammation; 'pseudo' nomenclature because it rarely causes perforation of eyeball. **Symptoms:** normal vision (except age-related cataract or coexisting ocular disease); no pain; nonspecific irritation; dry eye symptoms. **Signs:** necrotic bluish scleral plaques near limbus (usually superior) coalesce to form large necrotic area; bluish colour due to exposure of underlying uveal tissue secondary to scleral thinning. **Treatment — mainly symptomatic:** frequent lubricating agent (CMC, sodium hyaluronate); protection from ocular trauma; control of systemic disease; **periocular injection of steroids or topical cyclosporin is contraindicated**; scleral patch grafting in advanced cases with impending scleral perforation. **Differential diagnosis:** senile scleromalacia, scleral hyaline plaque.

column2: Describe ocular manifestations of important connective tissue diseases and immunological diseases.
column4: **Rheumatoid arthritis:** most common systemic disorder associated with all forms of immune-mediated scleritis; keratoconjunctivitis sicca (secondary Sjogren syndrome); peripheral ulcerative keratitis. **Granulomatosis with polyangiitis:** scleritis, peripheral ulcerative keratitis, occlusive retinal vasculitis, idiopathic orbital inflammation, nasolacrimal duct obstruction, dacryocystitis, conjunctivitis. **Relapsing polychondritis:** scleritis, anterior uveitis. **Polyarteritis nodosa:** same as granulomatosis with polyangiitis. **Crohn's disease:** acute episcleritis, acute anterior uveitis, marginal keratitis; commonest ocular manifestation — conjunctivitis, idiopathic orbital inflammation, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, rarely scleritis. **Infectious scleritis (rare):** herpes zoster, tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis, Lyme disease, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Nocardia.
column6: Ocular Manifestations of Connective Tissue Diseases

column2: Write short notes on staphyloma.
column4: **Definition:** localised bulging of outer coat of eyeball (corneal or scleral) lined by uveal tissue inside. **Types:** (1) **Anterior staphyloma** — after corneal perforation, outpouching of pseudocornea formed by organised exudates and fibrous tissue, with iris plastered behind; causes: old ruptured cornea; special note: usually prognosis very poor; eye turns phthisical with time; if no PL — enucleation may be done. (2) **Intercalary staphyloma** — localised bulge in limbal area lined by root of iris and anterior part of ciliary body; causes: inappropriate healing of perforating limbal injury, inappropriate healing of ruptured peripheral corneal ulcer; may develop secondary angle-closure glaucoma; defective vision due to irregular corneal astigmatism; localised staphylectomy may be attempted with guarded visual prognosis. (3) **Ciliary staphyloma** — bulge of weak sclera about 2–3 mm away from limbus extending up to 8 mm behind limbus, lined entirely by ciliary body; causes: inappropriate healing of perforating injury, scleritis, developmental glaucoma, end-stage glaucoma; treatment of cause; very poor visual prognosis. (4) **Equatorial staphyloma** — bulge of sclera lined by choroid in equatorial region; causes: scleritis, end-stage glaucoma, advanced pathological myopia; commonly occurs in regions where sclera is perforated by vortex veins. (5) **Posterior staphyloma** — bulge of weak sclera lined by choroid behind equator; causes: pathological myopia (most common), posterior scleritis, perforating injuries near posterior pole; diagnosed by direct/indirect ophthalmoscopy and 90D examination; direct ophthalmoscopy focuses floor of staphyloma with more minus lenses than margins; morphologically excavated area with retinal vessels dipping into it.

column2: Define endophthalmitis. Describe etiology
column5: **Definition:** inflammation of inner two coats of eyeball (uvea and retina) with deposition of exudates in vitreous cavity, anterior and posterior chamber. **Etiology — infective causes:** (1) exogenous infection following intraocular surgeries, penetrating trauma, perforated corneal ulcer; (2) endogenous/metastatic endophthalmitis — microorganism carried from infective foci elsewhere (carries tooth); more common in immunocompromised; (3) secondary infection from ocular adnexa (lacrimal sac infections, orbital cellulitis). **Agents — bacterial:** gram-positive cocci (Staphylococcus aureus and epidermidis, streptococci, pneumococci); bacilli (Pseudomonas, Corynebacterium); others (Propionibacterium acnes, Actinomyces). **Fungal:** Aspergillus, Fusarium, Candida. **Non-infective causes:** (1) post-operative sterile endophthalmitis — immunological reaction to chemicals adherent to IOL, instruments, retained viscoelastic; (2) post-traumatic with retained intraocular foreign body; (3) lens protein-induced sterile endophthalmitis in neglected Morgagnian cataract (**phacoanaphylactic endophthalmitis**); (4) masquerade syndrome in intraocular tumours (retinoblastoma). Acute post-operative endophthalmitis is the most catastrophic post-operative complication after cataract surgery (incidence 0.1%). **By onset:** **acute** (within 1–7 days post-op; staphylococci most common); **delayed** (weeks to months; fungal or Propionibacterium acnes). **Symptoms:** severe dimness of vision, ocular pain, photophobia, lacrimation. **Signs:** swelling of eyelids, conjunctival chemosis, yellow pupillary reflex, edges of operative wound yellow and necrotic, hypopyon in anterior chamber, corneal oedema; on indirect ophthalmoscope fundus not visible usually; USG B-scan shows hyperechoic reflection in vitreous cavity suggesting exudates; in advanced cases associated retinal detachment. **Prophylaxis:** 5% povidone iodine into conjunctival cul-de-sac for 3 minutes before surgery; scrupulous antiseptic dressing and disposable surgical drapes; pre-operative treatment of infective foci in ocular adnexa and face; strict perioperative glycaemic control; pre-operative topical antibiotic prophylaxis (4th-generation fluoroquinolones) 3–5 days before surgery; intracameral preservative-free moxifloxacin or cefuroxime before wound closure; proper apposition of all wounds. **Treatment (EVS):** (1) **intravitreal antimicrobial injection** — ceftazidime 2 mg/0.1 ml (gram-negative), vancomycin 2 mg/0.1 ml (gram-positive including MRSA); alternative amikacin 0.4 mg/0.1 ml (more toxic to retina); sampling of vitreous and aqueous before injection; injection slowly into mid-vitreous with 25G needle; ceftazidime/amikacin diluted with sterile water, vancomycin with normal saline. (2) **pars plana vitrectomy** — surgical removal of exudate-filled vitreous prevents retinal damage. (3) **supportive** — subconjunctival vancomycin and ceftazidime (doubtful benefit); topical antibiotics (limited posterior penetration); tab moxifloxacin 400 mg OD × 10 days, tab clarithromycin 500 mg BD × 10 days (culture-negative infections); oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg after 12–24 hours of antimicrobial therapy (severe cases, no fungal elements, systemic contraindications ruled out); periocular dexamethasone/triamcinolone alternative; eye drop 0.1% dexamethasone 2-hourly for severe anterior segment inflammation; topical cycloplegics; intravitreal steroid avoided; IV antibiotics have no role. (4) **follow-up (EVS):** only PL or worse — immediate pars plana vitrectomy; better than PL — intravitreal antibiotic injection + vitreous sampling; reassess after 48 hours; no improvement or worsening — repeat intravitreal injection per culture sensitivity; symptomatic improvement — immediate pars plana vitrectomy if severe; if immediate vitrectomy facilities unavailable — first dose of intravitreal injection and vitreous sampling regardless of presenting vision; repeat amikacin/aminoglycosides avoided (retinal toxicity); EVS protocol exclusively for acute post-operative endophthalmitis; delayed-onset Propionibacterium acnes — does not respond to intravitreal antibiotics, requires pars plana vitrectomy with IOL removal; secondary IOL implantation later. **Complications — resolved:** persistent vitreous opacities, maculopathy with ERM and CMO, chronic uveitis, secondary glaucoma, retinal detachment. **Non-resolving:** panophthalmitis, phthisis bulbi.

column2: Write short notes on panophthalmitis.
column4: **Definition:** acute purulent infection of all three coats of eyeball including Tenon's fascia. **Etiopathogenesis:** purulent anterior + posterior segment inflammation → follows very short stage of endophthalmitis → infection involves sclera and starts to spread in periocular tissue → panophthalmitis. Most commonly acute bacterial: gram-positive cocci (Staph aureus, Staph epidermidis, Streptococcus, Pneumococcus); bacilli (Pseudomonas, Corynebacterium); others (Actinomyces). **Symptoms — systemic:** headache, fever, myalgia, fatigue, generalised sepsis in children and immunocompromised adults. **Ocular:** complete loss of vision (no PL), profuse lacrimation and purulent discharge, severe ocular pain, severe redness and swelling, pain on ocular movements. **Signs:** vision no PL; eyelids and ocular adnexa marked chemosis and hyperaemia; conjunctiva marked chemosis with ciliary and conjunctival congestion; cornea hazy and oedematous with no further visibility or hazy view of pus-filled anterior segment; slight proptosis with grossly restricted and painful ocular movements; IOP initially higher due to pus-filled distension until globe perforation at limbus. **Investigations:** blood — complete hemogram/ESR/CRP (systemic spread), FBS/PPBS/HbA1c (glycaemic status); neuro-orbital imaging with CT and MR of brain and orbit (rule out intracranial spread, cavernous sinus involvement, orbital spread). **Treatment — no visual prognosis:** (1) **conservative** — broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately: inj ceftriaxone 1 g IV BD × 5–7 days followed by oral third-generation cephalosporins; systemic anti-inflammatory and analgesic — tab ibuprofen 400 mg BDPC × 5 days and SOS; topical reconstituted ceftazidime + vancomycin with/without 4th-gen fluoroquinolones (limited value); systemic and topical IOP-lowering drugs (limited role); topical cycloplegics for symptomatic relief. (2) **surgical** — **evisceration with intraorbital acrylic ball implantation and conformer placement** in fornices; followed by removal of conformer after 3 months and placement of customised artificial eye shell for ideal cosmetic outcome; indications: intractable pain despite conservative treatment, systemic spread, intracranial spread, patient wants evisceration for cosmetic/symptomatic reasons; role of conformer: prevents fornical contraction; acrylic implants cheaper with better results than hydroxyapatite. **Special note:** **enucleation is contraindicated in panophthalmitis** due to high risk of intracranial spread through severed end of optic nerve and its meningeal coverings.

column2: Write short notes on evisceration.
column4: **Principle of surgery:** removal of contents of eyeball leaving behind variable amount of scleral coat. **Indications:** panophthalmitis, expulsive choroidal haemorrhage, bleeding anterior staphyloma. **Anaesthesia:** general anaesthesia preferred (psychologically traumatic); if contraindicated — peribulbar/retrobulbar block with lignocaine + bupivacaine + hyaluronidase + adrenaline + topical proparacaine + IM diazepam/voveran. **Surgical steps:** (1) 360° peritomy; (2) sclerocorneal button cut out leaving globe open with contents; (3) evisceration scoop introduced between sclera and uveal tissue, whole content removed by repeated sweeping; all uveal tissue must be removed especially around vortex veins and optic disc; adequate haemostasis; structures scooped out — lens, vitreous, whole uveal tissue, whole retina; (4) after soaking scleral cavity with alcohol, largest implant that can fit into scleral cavity chosen by intraoperative trial and error; **flower petal sclerotomies** for best size of implant for better cosmetic outcome; (5) intraorbital implants — porous (hydroxyapatite) or non-porous (silicone, acrylic); non-porous cheaper with better long-term cosmetic outcome; (6) wound closed in layers — scleral frill closure, posterior Tenon closure, anterior Tenon and conjunctival closure; (7) conformer placed in fornix, temporary tarsorrhaphy done; (8) 3 months later conformer replaced by customised prosthetic eyeball matching other eye cosmetically. **Frill evisceration:** only 3 mm scleral frill kept around optic nerve, rest removed; extraocular muscles separately cut and sutured later at fornices for better prosthetic eye movement. **Complications — intraoperative:** profuse bleeding, scleral laceration in thin/necrosed sclera. **Postoperative:** sympathetic ophthalmia (very rare) in other eye — directly proportional to amount of retained uveal tissue; infection of socket; deep superior sulcus (small orbital implant); ptosis; implant-related (extrusion, exposure, migration); weeping and oedematous socket; pyogenic granuloma; contracted socket (high risk if no implant). **Contraindications:** painful blind eye/disfigured eye due to risk of sympathetic ophthalmia from retained ocular tissue (relative); **absolute contraindication — intraocular malignancies (retinoblastoma, melanoma)** due to risk of local and distant spread.

column2: Write short notes on enucleation.
column4: **Surgical principle:** excision of entire eyeball after cutting it off from optic nerve stump. **Indications — absolute:** retinoblastoma, malignant melanoma. **Relative:** painful blind eye nonresponsive to conservative therapy; phthisis bulbi for cosmetic purposes; anterior staphyloma for cosmetic purposes; mutilating ocular injuries; for cadaveric corneal harvestation. **Anaesthesia:** adults — peribulbar/retrobulbar block (lignocaine + bupivacaine + hyaluronidase + adrenaline); children — general anaesthesia. **Surgical steps:** (1) 360° peritomy, careful separation of anterior Tenon's fascia around limbus up to equator until recti exposed; (2) each rectus identified and hooked; two sutures placed on muscle tendon — one proximal (anchoring), one distal (stay suture to prevent retraction into orbital cavity, used later for myoconjunctival technique); muscle cut between two sutures; recti cut in order SLIM (superior, lateral, inferior, medial); (3) eyeball prolapsed out of orbital cavity by stretching and pushing eye speculum down; anchoring sutures maintain outward pull; enucleation scissors introduced through medial aspect as optic nerve cut ≥ 10 mm away from posterior pole; enucleation spoon introduced from lateral side to hold optic nerve and stabilise globe; structures cut — optic nerve with meningeal sheaths, central retinal artery and vein, two long posterior ciliary arteries, two long ciliary veins, short posterior ciliary vessels and nerves, two oblique muscles; (4) intraorbital implant placed (porous hydroxyapatite or non-porous silicone/acrylic; non-porous cheaper with less complications); (5) wound closed in layers — posterior Tenon closure, anterior Tenon closure, conjunctival closure vertically (preserve fornices); (6) conformer of adequate size placed in fornices, temporary tarsorrhaphy done; (7) customised prosthetic eye shell placed after 6 weeks; (8) **myoconjunctival technique** — cut ends of severed recti held with stay sutures passed outside; after wound closure, recti fixated with opposite fornices; produces best post-operative prosthetic eye movement. **Complications — intraoperative:** profuse bleeding, globe perforation and mutilation, slippage of EOM into orbital cavity. **Postoperative:** enophthalmos, deep superior sulcus, ptosis, contracted socket, implant-related (extrusion, erosion, migration), weeping and oedematous socket, pyogenic socket granuloma. **Contraindication:** **panophthalmitis** due to risk of spread of infection intracranially through cut end of meninges around severed optic nerve stump. **Special note:** in intraocular tumours (retinoblastoma) at least 10 mm optic nerve stump should remain with eyeball — central retinal artery enters optic nerve at this distance; histopathologic examination of optic nerve end provides information about extraocular vascular spread enabling future chemoradiation planning.

column2: Write short notes on acute anterior uveitis.
column4: **Definition:** acute inflammatory disease of uveal tissue from iris up to pars plicata of ciliary body. **Iritis:** predominant iris involvement; **iridocyclitis:** equal involvement of iris and pars plicata; **anterior cyclitis:** predominant pars plicata involvement. **Symptoms:** dull aching throbbing pain worsening at night (referred by V1 branches to forehead and scalp), redness, photophobia and blepharospasm, lacrimation, dimness of vision. **Signs:** lid oedema, circumcorneal congestion (deep vessels radiating from limbus, no blanching with phenylephrine, fill from limbus to fornices), corneal oedema due to toxic endothelitis, aqueous cells and flare, keratic precipitates (pathognomonic), posterior synechiae with festooned pupils, iris bombe, hypopyon (sterile pus), muddy iris, increased IOP. **Signs needing special mention:** (a) **aqueous cells** — clumps of inflammatory cells in anterior chamber; graded under 1 mm × 1 mm slit lamp beam as per SUN into '0' to '4+'; (b) **aqueous flare** — earliest sign; leaked protein particles from damaged blood vessels into aqueous humour; Brownian movements/Tyndall phenomenon; graded per SUN '0' to '4+'; (c) **iris nodules** (granulomatous uveitis) — Koeppe's nodules at pupillary border; Busacca's nodules near collarette; (d) **posterior synechiae** — adhesions between posterior iris surface and anterior lens capsule due to organisation of fibrin-rich exudates; segmental, ring/annular, total; (e) **ectropion pupillae** — eversion of pupillary margin due to contraction of fibrinous exudate; (f) **festooned pupil** — irregular pupil shape due to posterior synechiae; (g) **occlusio pupillae** — complete occlusion of pupil by organised exudates. **Complications:** complicated cataract (polychromatic lustre, rapid maturity), secondary glaucoma (early hypertensive due to clogging of trabecular meshwork; late due to seclusio/occlusio pupillae), cyclitic membrane, retinochoroiditis progression, CMO, macular hole, ERM, macular scar, exudative RD, papillitis, band-shaped keratopathy, phthisis bulbi (final end stage), bread-crumb uveitis. **Investigations:** (a) **hematological** — CBC, ESR/CRP (inflammation), FBS/PPBS/HbA1c (glycaemic), uric acid (gout), serological tests (syphilis, toxoplasmosis, histoplasmosis), ANA/Rh factor/LE cells/serum ACE (sarcoidosis), RA factor/anti-CCP (RA); (b) **urine** — routine microscopic (UTI); (c) **stool** — routine microscopic (parasitic infestation); (d) **radiological** — chest X-ray PA (sarcoidosis, TB), X-ray PNS/SIJ/lumbar spine, CT thorax (sarcoidosis), MRI brain (sarcoidosis, lymphoma, demyelination); (e) **skin tests** — tuberculin, Kveim, toxoplasmin, lepromin, pathergy (Behcet's). **Treatment:** (a) **general** — local hot fomentation, dark goggles (reduce photophobia and blepharospasm); (b) **topical** — 1% atropine TDS or 2% homatropine BD × 2–3 weeks (relieves ciliary spasm, prevents synechiae, reduces exudation, brings more antibodies); 1% prednisolone acetate 1 drop 6–8 times/day (alternatives: dexamethasone/loteprednol/fluorometholone; taper over 3–4 weeks; anterior sub-Tenon injection in severe); (c) **systemic** — tab prednisolone 1 mg/kg OD after breakfast × 2 weeks, tapered over 6–8 weeks (intractable, resistant to topical; regular follow-up for steroid-induced glaucoma); immunosuppressives (methotrexate/cyclophosphamide/chlorambucil/azathioprine) in steroid-resistant cases with physician; (d) **specific treatment of cause** — for TB, syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rheumatological diseases with physician; if no cause found, full course of broad-spectrum antibiotics may be helpful (non-granulomatous cases).

column2: Write short notes on keratic precipitates.
column4: **Definition:** pathognomonic sign of anterior uveitis; proteinaceous cellular deposits at the back of cornea; arranged in triangular fashion occupying centre and inferior part of cornea because of aqueous humour convection current. **Types:** (1) **mutton fat KP** — seen in granulomatous uveitis; epithelioid cells and macrophages; large, thick, fluffy, lardaceous; greasy/waxy appearance. (2) **granular KP** — non-granulomatous uveitis; mainly lymphocytes; small, discreet, dirty white; irregular arrangement; usually large numbers. (3) **stellate KP** — seen in Fuchs' heterochromic iridocyclitis, herpetic iritis, CMV retinitis; spread over entire corneal endothelium; endothelial dusting. (4) **old KP** — mostly in healed uveitis; all other three forms turn into old KP; fewer in number; old mutton-fat KP become hyalinized forming ground-glass appearance. **Clinical significance:** nature and distribution of KPs give clue to granulomatous or non-granulomatous origin; fine KPs indicate herpetic or Fuchs' iridocyclitis; resolution of KPs is a clinical sign for acute anterior uveitis responding to current treatment; old KPs with complicated cataract indicate past episodes of untreated or poorly responded uveitis; presence of old KPs gives clinical indication for compromised endothelial cells.

column2: Write short notes on ring synechiae.
column4: **Definition:** clinical sign seen in eyes with past history of repeated attacks of acute anterior uveitis, where 360° adhesions of pupillary margin to anterior lens capsule are seen. **Pathogenesis:** repeated attacks of acute anterior uveitis (ill-treated/untreated/poorly responding to steroids) → aggregation of inflammatory exudates from iris vessels at pupillary margin → fibrinous exudates cause adhesion of 360° pupillary margin with anterior lens capsule → no circulation of aqueous from posterior to anterior chamber (seclusio pupillae) → collection of aqueous behind iris causing anterior bowing of iris (**iris bombe**) → rise in IOP → secondary glaucoma. **Clinical significance:** ring synechiae indicates recurrent anterior uveitis leading to high chance of secondary glaucoma and complicated cataract development; presence in a case of complicated cataract makes pre-operative posterior segment evaluation very difficult; pupils become mechanically non-reacting to light — impedance in clinical assessment of optic nerve; cataract operation more challenging — mechanical synechiolysis with pupillary expanding devices like iris hooks required. **Treatment:** treat acute anterior uveitis if actively present clinically; strong mydriatics may release entire synechiae or partially in recent-onset cases; in iris bombe formation without acute congestive attack — simple YAG laser iridotomy may release pupillary block; in acute congestive glaucoma attack — IV, oral and topical IOP-lowering agents per protocol, and YAG laser iridotomy as soon as corneal clarity ensures.

column2: Write short notes on posterior synechiae.
column4: **Definition:** physical adhesions between posterior surface of iris and any of the following — anterior capsule of crystalline lens (most common), anterior surface of posterior chamber IOL, capsular bag (anterior capsular rim or posterior capsule) in aphakia after ECCE, anterior hyaloid face (rarely). **Morphological types:** (1) **segmental/partial/incomplete** — adhesions at some points or places; if involving more than 2–3 segments → **festooned pupil**. (2) **annular posterior synechiae/ring synechiae** — 360° adhesion of pupillary margin to anterior lens capsule → non-circulation of aqueous from posterior to anterior chamber → trapping of aqueous behind iris → **iris bombe** → secondary glaucoma. (3) **total posterior synechiae** — total plastering of entire posterior iris surface with anterior lens capsule; rarely in long-standing or recurrent anterior uveitis; anterior chamber deeper compared to other eye; results in secondary glaucoma due to aqueous non-circulation. **Causes:** acute anterior uveitis, recurrent anterior uveitis, long-standing posterior uveitis, ocular trauma (traumatic uveitis). **Complications:** secondary glaucoma, complicated cataract. **Management — with active inflammation:** control inflammation with topical steroids, cycloplegics and IOP-lowering drugs; investigate systemic causes; no surgical intervention for synechiolysis unless inflammation controlled; in acute rise in IOP, YAG laser peripheral iridotomy may be attempted; if failed, surgical iridotomy with perioperative IOP control with IV mannitol. **Without active inflammation — indications for surgical intervention:** (a) **complicated cataract** — synechiolysis with iris repositor aided by viscoelastic devices; pupillary dilatation by pupillary expansion devices like iris hooks; cataract extraction with PCIOL implantation by phacoemulsification or ECCE depending on corneal clarity; (b) **secondary glaucoma** — surgical iridotomy with YAG laser peripheral iridotomy; pupiloplasty + cataract extraction. **Special notes:** segmental posterior synechiae without secondary glaucoma or complicated cataract — topical homatropine or atropine; non-responsive — subconjunctival injection of mydricaine (lignocaine + adrenaline + atropine) to break formed synechiae; no surgical intervention except emergency iridotomy should be performed unless ocular inflammation is controlled; topical PG analogues avoided for IOP control (cause uveitis); pre-operative topical steroid coverage for any planned surgical intervention.

column2: Write short notes on buphthalmos.
column4: **Definition:** clinical term used to refer to enlarged eyeballs with large cloudy corneas seen typically in children affected by paediatric glaucoma before the age of 3 years. **Classification:** **primary congenital/developmental glaucoma** (without ocular/systemic abnormalities) — newborn glaucoma (true congenital, child born with glaucoma), infantile glaucoma (manifests within 3 years), juvenile glaucoma (manifests after 3 years, usually 10–35 years). **Secondary congenital/developmental glaucoma with associated ocular abnormalities:** iridodysgenesis (aniridia, familial iris hypoplasia, congenital nanophthalmos); iridocorneal dysgenesis (Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome, Peter's anomaly). **Secondary glaucomas associated with systemic anomaly:** chromosomal anomalies (Down's, Edward, Turner); phacomatoses (Sturge-Weber, neurofibromatosis); syndromes with ectopia lentis (Marfan, Weill-Marchesani, homocystinuria); metabolic syndromes (Lowe, Hurler, Zellweger). **Symptoms (classical triad):** lacrimation, photophobia, blepharospasm. **Signs:** large cornea (diameter > 13 mm); thin blue sclera due to exposure of underlying uveal tissue; diffuse corneal oedema; **Haab's striae** (breaks in Descemet's membrane); thin iris with iridodonesis and atrophic patches; anteriorly flattened lens; deep anterior chamber; optic disc reversible cupping; diffuse stromal corneal oedema. **Evaluation under anaesthesia:** measurement of IOP (handheld Perkin's tonometer), corneal diameter, gonioscopy, portable slit lamp, stereoscopic examination of optic nerve head and posterior segment. **Treatment — medical (temporary, before examination and surgery):** hyperosmotic agents, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, topical beta-blockers; **contraindicated drugs:** miotics (paradoxical IOP increase), alpha-2 agonists (CNS depression), PG analogues (prone to uveitis). **Surgical — mainstay:** **clear cornea** — goniotomy (ab interno approach; goniotomy knife inserted under gonioscopic guidance, 75° incision at AC angle midway between root of iris and Schwalbe's line); **hazy cornea** — trabeculotomy (ab externo approach; trabeculotome inserted into Schlemm's canal after dissecting from limbal approach; breaks inner wall over one quarter on each side); trabeculectomy with antimetabolites (filtration surgery); combined trabeculotomy and trabeculectomy (gold standard); glaucoma drainage devices (calcitrant cases). **Visual rehabilitation:** lifelong follow-up; cycloplegic refraction per age; management of amblyopia (axial myopia); visual rehabilitation according to retained BCVA.

column2: Write short notes on phacomorphic glaucoma.
column4: **Definition:** acute secondary angle-closure glaucoma caused by intumescent cataractous lens or anterior subluxation/dislocation of crystalline lens or due to congenital spherophakia (**phacotopic glaucoma**). **Etiopathogenesis:** rapid maturation of cataract leads to stage of intumescence (capsular bag swells with liquefied cataractous lens) → swollen lens pushes iris forward and obliterates angle → pupillary block develops → iris bombe due to aqueous accumulation in posterior chamber → secondary acute angle-closure glaucoma. **Less commonly:** crystalline lens becoming anteriorly subluxated pushes iris forward causing secondary acute angle-closure; microspherophakic lens dislocates anteriorly and physically obliterates pupillary aperture → pupillary block → secondary acute angle-closure. **Symptoms — systemic:** nausea, vomiting; **ocular:** pain, rapidly progressing dimness of vision, redness, photophobia, lacrimation. **Signs:** mid-dilated fixed pupil; corneal oedema; ciliary congestion; no fundal reflex due to intumescent white cataract; iridocorneal contact and iris bombe formation leads to secondary angle-closure; swollen intumescent lens pushing iris forward; small and spherical lens; anteriorly dislocated/subluxated microspherophakic lens pushing iris leading to secondary angle-closure (mechanical pupillary block). **Treatment — medical (immediate IOP control before cataract surgery):** IV 20% mannitol 300 ml IV stat and SOS before surgery; tab acetazolamide 500 mg stat and BDPC till surgery; E/D 0.05% timolol maleate 1 drop BD. **Laser iridotomy:** if cornea clear and sufficient pre-operative IOP reduction not achieved by maximal medical therapy, laser iridotomy may be attempted for mechanical relief of pupillary block. **Cataract extraction with PCIOL insertion — definitive management:** accurate biometry (if not possible, keratometric values of other eye); adequate pre-operative IOP control (else risk of expulsive choroidal haemorrhage); adequate pupillary dilatation (pupillary expanding devices/rings if inadequate); pre-operative USG B-scan; phacoemulsification preferred over ECCE where cornea minimally decompensated (minimal ultrasonic power protects endothelium); capsulorrhexis tends to extend peripherally due to high intracapsular pressure; capsular bag dialysis may occur requiring capsular support devices; high viscoelastic devices prevent corneal endothelial damage; attempt for in-the-bag PCIOL; post-operative uveitis aggressively controlled with potent topical steroids under cover of topical IOP-lowering drugs; in decompensated corneas increased chance of post-operative pseudophakic bullous keratopathy.

column2: Write short notes on trabeculectomy.
column4: **Principle:** first described by Cairns in 1968; partial-thickness filtering surgery; creates an iatrogenic fistula connecting anterior chamber with subconjunctival space leading to alternate pathway of aqueous drainage. **IOP-lowering mechanism:** aqueous flows from anterior chamber through transtrabecular iatrogenic fistula into subconjunctival space where either transconjunctival filtration or absorption into subconjunctival lymphatics occurs; increased aqueous drainage causes IOP reduction. **Indications:** (1) primary angle-closure glaucoma where peripheral laser iridotomy and medical management failed and there is extensive (> 270°) peripheral anterior synechiae; (2) primary open-angle glaucoma where IOP not controlled with medical management; (3) congenital and developmental glaucoma — combined trabeculotomy and trabeculectomy is treatment of choice; (4) secondary glaucomas not controlled medically; (5) glaucoma patients non-compliant to medical therapy. **Surgical steps:** (1) peribulbar block anaesthesia with antiseptic dressing and draping similar to cataract surgery; (2) **pre-operative prerequisites** — IOP medically reduced to < 30 mmHg; pre-operative control of inflammation with topical steroids; E/D 1% pilocarpine pre-operatively for adequate intraoperative miosis; topical pre-operative antibiotics (4th-generation fluoroquinolones); (3) exposure of scleral tissue with minimal cauterisation; (4) limbal-based (or fornix-based) conjunctival flap with careful dissection of underlying Tenon's fascia; (5) exposed deeper sclera with bluish hue of underlying Schlemm's canal and trabecular meshwork; (6) half-thickness 5 mm × 5 mm quadrangular limbal-based scleral flap reflected; (7) 4 mm × 2 mm narrow strip of deep sclera with underlying Schlemm's canal and trabecular meshwork excised with crescent knife or trabeculectomy punch (Kelly's punch); (8) peripheral surgical iridotomy through the wound; (9) scleral flap replaced and sutured with 10-0 nylon; (10) conjunctival flap sutured with 10-0 nylon; adjustable sutures help post-operative suture tightening/loosening depending on filtration adequacy; (11) application of topical antimetabolites like mitomycin C for 2 minutes between scleral flap and Tenon's capsule in: high risk of filtration failure or previously failed filtration, complicated secondary glaucomas (post-uveitic, neovascular), glaucoma with aphakia. **Post-operative evaluation:** superior conjunctival bleb formation, peripheral patent iridotomy opening, formed anterior chamber with normal IOP; in hyperfiltration — AC shallow or collapsed with significantly low IOP; in hypofiltration — collapsed bleb with deep AC and raised IOP. **Complications — intraoperative:** hyphaema due to iris damage, damage to lens, amputation of scleral flap, choroidal injury leading to malignant glaucoma. **Postoperative:** blebitis, post-operative endophthalmitis, failed filtration with fibrosed collapsed bleb, post-operative cataract, malignant glaucoma. **Contraindications:** developmental glaucoma due to Sturge-Weber syndrome, malignant glaucoma, lens-induced glaucoma (as primary therapy). **Recent advances:** conventional trabeculectomy augmented with 6 mm × 1 mm collagen implant insertion as alternative to antimetabolite use; sutureless trabeculectomy by creating 4 mm × 4 mm valvular sclerocorneal tunnel.

column2: Describe visual field changes in primary open-angle glaucoma.
column4: **Background:** glaucomatous field defect has characteristics — defects appear clinically only if at least 40% axonal loss has happened; defect physiologically corresponds to area of nerve fibre layer or optic nerve head damage; field changes progress in characteristic pattern if etiopathogenesis not controlled. **Anatomical basis:** retinal nerve fibre layer distribution to optic disc follows pattern — nasal retina (superior and inferior nasal retinal fibres), temporal retina (superior and inferior arcuate fibres), macula (papillomacular bundle); papillomacular fibres remain central; arcuate fibres occupy superior and inferior temporal part of optic disc and are most sensitive to glaucomatous damage. **Morphology of field changes:** (1) **isopter contraction** — earliest visual field defect; generalised constriction of central and peripheral visual fields. (2) **baring of blind spot** — inward curving of central 30° boundary of central visual field excluding area of blind spot; non-specific with limited diagnostic value. (3) **paracentral scotoma** — small wing-shaped scotoma appears in superior or inferior hemifield in area extending above and below blind spot between 10° and 20° of fixation point (arcuate area/Bjerrum's area). (4) **Seidel's scotoma** — paracentral scotomas coalesce with blind spot; resultant sickle-shaped scotoma. (5) **arcuate/Bjerrum's scotoma** — scotoma reaches horizontal line either above or below fixation point occupying almost entire arcuate area. (6) **ring/double arcuate scotoma** — two arcuate scotomas from superior and inferior hemifield join forming ring. (7) **Roenne's central nasal step** — superior and inferior arcuate scotomas do not coalesce symmetrically at horizontal line (different arcs) — sharp right-angled defect at horizontal meridian. (8) **Roenne's peripheral nasal step** — unequal constriction of peripheral isopter causes sharp right-angled defect at horizontal meridian in peripheral 60° visual field (60°–80°). (9) **advanced glaucomatous field defect** — **tubular vision** (small island of central vision remaining; decreases radially until complete extinguishing); **temporal island** (small island of vision in temporal visual field which extinguishes at end, turning patient to No PL). **Applied:** tested by Humphrey's standard automated perimeter (static perimeter); tests retinal sensitivity of predesignated points in superior and inferior hemifield in central 24° or 30°; obtained retinal sensitivities compared statistically with standard retinal sensitivities matched for age, race, ethnicity; field changes must match corresponding areas of retinal ganglion cell damage; glaucoma is a 'silent killer of sight' (central vision goes at the end) — early detection of field defects key to diagnosis; efficacy of glaucoma management monitored by progression of visual defects.

column2: Define IOP. Discuss conditions where IOP is low.
column4: **Definition:** Intraocular pressure is the pressure exerted by intraocular fluids on the coats of the eyeball. **Normal IOP:** 10–21 mmHg (mean 16 ± 2.5 mmHg). The dynamic equilibrium between aqueous humour formation and drainage is the key contributor in maintaining normal IOP. **Conditions with low IOP:** (1) **Post-operative wound leak** — immediate post-operative shallow anterior chamber with very low IOP; diagnosed by Seidel's test (drop of fluorescein into lower fornix, patient blinks, incision examined under cobalt blue — fluorescein diluted by aqueous at leaking site); treatment — small leakage: conservative with pressure bandage and oral acetazolamide; larger: suturing wound with 10-0 nylon and AC reformation with air. (2) **Over-filtering bleb after trabeculectomy** — causes: bleb leakage through inadvertent buttonhole, insufficient resistance to outflow at lamellar scleral flap, inadequate closure of conjunctival flap; **scleral flap leak** — low IOP, well-formed bleb, negative Seidel's test; **bleb leak** — low IOP, flat bleb, positive Seidel's test; Descemet's folds in cornea due to low IOP; treatment depends on cause and degree of shallowing — small leakage observed with E/D atropine to prevent peripheral anterior synechiae and reduce risk of malignant glaucoma; temporary conjunctival tamponade with large-diameter soft bandage contact lens, collagen shield/Simmon's shell, pressure bandage; resuturing conjunctival sutures or tightening adjustable sutures; if persistent shallowing — AC formed with viscoelastic. (3) **Retinal detachment** — IOP lower by about 5 mmHg compared to normal; extremely low may indicate associated choroidal detachment; IOP low because of abnormal posterior aqueous outflow in addition to normal anterior pathways; sudden painless loss of vision; diagnosis — RAPD +ve, indirect ophthalmoscopy if media clear, USG B-scan if media opaque; treatment — scleral buckling (external), pars plana vitrectomy (internal). (4) **Choroidal detachment/choroidal effusion** — causes: persistent post-operative hypotony (especially after glaucoma filtering surgery), posterior uveitis, posterior scleritis, choroidal tumours, drugs (acetazolamide, topiramate), trauma; low IOP due to ciliary body detachment; media clear — indirect ophthalmoscopy shows brown, convex, smooth, relatively immobile elevations not extending to posterior pole (limited by vortex veins), can extend anterior beyond ora serrata; media hazy — USG B-scan; large kissing choroidal detachments may obscure view; treatment of cause + full-thickness or partial-thickness sclerotomies. (5) **Penetrating/perforating ocular injury** — penetrating: full-thickness wound; perforating: two full-thickness wounds (entry + exit); diagnosed by slit lamp; posterior segment evaluation by indirect ophthalmoscopy; USG B-scan if hazy (posterior segment, intraocular foreign body); X-ray orbit and CT scan to rule out/localise intraocular foreign body; urgent surgical intervention depending on site and nature. (6) **Following blunt trauma** — temporary cessation of aqueous secretion by ciliary body (**ciliary shock**). (7) **Cyclodialysis cleft** — abnormal pathway between AC and suprachoroidal space from disruption of ciliary body attachment from scleral spur (traumatic/iatrogenic); diagnosed in clear media by gonioscopy and anterior segment OCT; in opaque media by UBM; treatment — conservative (topical cycloplegics and steroids), laser (high-energy argon laser to produce local inflammation and scarring closure), surgical (direct cyclopexy through partial-thickness limbal scleral graft). (8) **Other important causes** — phthisis bulbi (ciliary shutdown), post-cryotherapy to reduce ocular pain in end-stage glaucoma, severe dehydration, pregnancy, anaesthetic drug-induced.

column2: Write short notes on anti-glaucoma drugs.
column4: **Classification:** (1) **Prostaglandin analogues** — latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost, unoprostone. (2) **Beta-blockers** — non-selective: timolol, levobunolol, carteolol; selective: betaxolol. (3) **Sympathomimetics** — non-selective: epinephrine, dipivefrine; selective α2 agonists: brimonidine, apraclonidine, clonidine. (4) **Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors** — topical: dorzolamide, brinzolamide; oral: acetazolamide. (5) **Cholinergic** — directly acting: pilocarpine; anticholinesterase: echothiophate, physostigmine; dual action: carbachol. (6) **Hyperosmotic agents** — oral: glycerol, isosorbide; IV: mannitol. (7) **Neuroprotective drugs** — antioxidants, calcium channel blockers, nitric oxide synthetase inhibitor, NMDA antagonists, vasodilators. **Mechanism of action:** (a) **drugs increasing trabecular outflow** — cholinergic (pilocarpine), bimatoprost, non-selective sympathomimetics (epinephrine, dipivefrine); (b) **drugs increasing uveoscleral outflow** — all prostaglandin analogues, non-selective sympathomimetics, selective sympathomimetics (brimonidine, apraclonidine); (c) **drugs decreasing aqueous production** — carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, beta-blockers, non-selective and selective sympathomimetics acting on alpha receptors in ciliary process (brimonidine); (d) **hyperosmotic agents** — increase plasma tonicity, create osmotic gradient between blood and vitreous, draw water out of eyeball, lower IOP. **Adverse effects:** (1) **Prostaglandin analogues** — ocular: conjunctival hyperaemia, eyelash lengthening/thickening/increased number, hyperpigmentation of iris and periorbital skin, anterior uveitis, increased severity/recurrence of herpetic keratitis; systemic: headache, migraine precipitation, skin rash, possible teratogenicity (avoid in pregnancy). (2) **Sympathomimetics** — ocular: conjunctival hyperaemia/pigmentation, allergic blepharoconjunctivitis, mydriasis, CMO in aphakia; systemic: hypertension, tachycardia, headache, palpitation, tremor, nervousness/anxiety. (3) **Beta-blockers** — ocular: conjunctival hyperaemia, SPK, corneal anaesthesia; systemic: cardiovascular (bradyarrhythmia, heart failure), respiratory (bronchospasm, airway obstruction in asthmatics), CNS (depression, anxiety, confusion, syncope), others (decreased libido, skin rash, alopecia). (4) **Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors** — mainly systemic: paraesthesias around fingers/toes/hands/feet/mouth, increased urinary frequency, hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia, metabolic acidosis, GI symptoms (abdominal discomfort, gastric irritation, metallic taste, diarrhoea), sulphonamide-related (renal calculi, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, blood dyscrasia, teratogenic effects). (5) **Parasympathomimetics** — ocular (miosis-related): decreased visual acuity, impairment of night vision, contraction of visual field, frontal headache, retinal detachment, cataract, iris cyst, iritis, follicular conjunctivitis; systemic: bradycardia, increased sweating, hypersalivation; **Scoline apnoea** — only with irreversible anticholinesterases where patient does not resume normal respiration after termination of general anaesthesia. (6) **Hyperosmotic agents** — generalised dehydration, pulmonary oedema, heart failure, cerebral oedema, subdural haematoma. **Drug interactions and special notes:** PG analogues have additive interaction with pilocarpine and timolol; topical beta-blockers show **short-term escape** (after initial dramatic response, significant loss of response 3–4 weeks later due to down-regulation of β-receptor) and **long-term escape** (slow decline in IOP reduction beginning 3 months to 1 year after starting treatment); pilocarpine used in both POAG (contraction of ciliary muscles, facilitates aqueous outflow) and PACG (contraction of sphincter pupillae, opens angle); neuroprotective drugs independently prevent apoptosis of retinal ganglion cells and optic nerve fibres.

column2: Write short notes on acute attack of primary angle-closure glaucoma.
column4: **History:** acute attack is a sight-threatening emergency; occurs due to sudden total angle closure leading to severe rise in IOP; patient may have past history of intermittent attacks of subacute glaucoma. **Symptoms:** pain, nausea/vomiting, rapidly progressive diminution of vision, redness, photophobia, lacrimation. **Signs:** lid oedematous; conjunctiva chemosed and congested (ciliary + conjunctival vessels); cornea oedematous; anterior chamber shallow with cells and flare; angle of anterior chamber closed; iris discoloured; pupil unreactive to light, mid-dilated, vertically oval; IOP markedly elevated (40–70 mmHg); optic nerve head oedematous and hyperaemic; fellow eye shows shallow anterior chamber and narrow angle. **Management:** (1) **diagnosis** — clinical. (2) **medical** — supine position; measure IOP: if > 40 mmHg → IV mannitol 20% 1 g/kg body weight; IV acetazolamide 500 mg; E/D pilocarpine 2% every 30 minutes × 2 hours; E/D timolol 0.5% BD; E/D prednisolone acetate 1% QID; oral acetazolamide 250 mg QDS; analgesic + antiemetics. If < 40 mmHg → E/D pilocarpine 2% every 30 minutes; E/D timolol 0.5% BD; E/D prednisolone acetate 1% QID; oral acetazolamide 250 mg QDS. (3) **prophylactic treatment of normal fellow eye** — prophylactic laser peripheral iridotomy after instillation of 1% pilocarpine. (4) **surgical — peripheral iridotomy:** when peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) < 50% of AC angle → peripheral iridotomy; when PAS > 50% → filtration surgery; failure with medical therapy or non-compliance → clear lens extraction.

column2: Define glaucoma. Describe symptoms
column3: signs and management of primary open-angle glaucoma.
column5: **Definition:** chronic progressive optic neuropathy with characteristic loss of ganglion cells and corresponding defects in visual field, with or without raised IOP. **Key features:** primary (no cause), open angle, optic nerve head changes, corresponding visual field changes, raised IOP. **Diagnosis — clinical features:** family H/O glaucoma (10% siblings, 4% offspring), cigarette smoking, diabetes, hypertension, thyrotoxicosis associated with increased risk; symptoms usually asymptomatic, mild headache or eyeache, frequent change in presbyopic glasses, delayed dark adaptation. **Investigations:** tonometry — IOP (applanation method of choice), diurnal variation test; gonioscopy — open angle; slit lamp with 90D; perimetry — visual field change; nerve fibre layer analysis (NFLA); provocative test (water drinking) for borderline cases. **Anterior segment signs:** normal; sluggish pupillary reaction; IOP changes — early diurnal variation, suspicious > 5 mmHg, diagnostic > 8 mmHg; late IOP > 21 mmHg (usually 30–45 mmHg). **Optic nerve head changes (stereotactic with 90D/78D lens gives 3-D view):** early optic atrophy — vertically oval cup, large cup > 0.6 (VCDR), asymmetry between 2 eyes > 0.2, splinter haemorrhage, atrophy of retinal nerve fibre layer; advanced — marked cupping VCDR 0.7–0.9, thinning of neuroretinal rim (NRR), nasal shifting of retinal vessel (bayonetting sign), pulsation of retinal arterioles, lamellar dot sign, deeply excavated disc, appears white, destruction of all NRR. **Visual field changes:** early — isopter contraction, baring of blind spot, paracentral scotoma, arcuate scotoma; late — double arcuate scotoma with nasal step of Roenne, peripheral field defect; advanced — tubular vision; final interpretation only after repeating fields twice. **Management:** (1) **identification of target pressure** for each patient (below which glaucomatous damage is not likely to progress) — 16–18 for mild damage, 12–14 for severe damage. (2) **medical** — single drug therapy, combination therapy, monitoring of therapy. (3) **laser trabeculoplasty** — ALT (argon laser), SLT (selective), diode; indications: IOP control not achieved by maximal medical therapy, as primary therapy when non-compliant to medical therapy, as adjuvant to reduce number/dosage/frequency of drugs. (4) **surgical — trabeculectomy (filtration surgery):** indications: IOP control not achieved by medical and laser therapy, non-compliant patient, advanced glaucomatous field defect. (5) **follow-up:** history and examination for adverse reactions of anti-glaucoma drugs, target pressure, IOP measurement, optic nerve head evaluation, patient education for compliance.

column2: Write short notes on tonometry.
column4: **Definition:** indirect way of measuring IOP by tonometers specially designed for the purpose. **Types:** (1) **Indentation/impression tonometry** — Schiotz tonometer. (2) **Applanation tonometry** — Goldmann, Perkin's, pneumatic, air-puff, pulse air, tono-pen. **Indentation tonometer:** principle — a soft eye will be indented more than a hard eye with a plunger; conversion of Pt (artificially raised IOP after placement of plunger) to Po (resting IOP) obtained from modified Friedenwald nomogram conversion table. Parts — scale for reading (if initial reading < 3, additional weights in increasing proportion must be added), deflection needle, plunger (moves freely and exerts weight), weight (5.5 g to start with, followed by 7.5, 10, 15 g), handle for holding, footplate rests on cornea. Reading obtained from scale is used to derive IOP in mmHg from conversion table as per plunger weight used. **Applanation tonometer:** principle — **Imbert-Fick law:** pressure (P) inside a sphere (eyeball) = force (N) required to flatten its surface divided by area of flattening (A), i.e., P = W/A. Fixed-force applanation (W fixed, P ∝ A) — measuring area of corneal flattening was difficult and not reproducible always; not done any more. Fixed-area applanation (A fixed, P ∝ W) — Goldmann modernised the concept. **Fixed-area applanation tonometers:** (a) **Goldmann** — double prism mounted on slit lamp; biprism applanates central 3.06 mm diameter corneal surface after topical anaesthesia; two fluorescent semicircles viewed through prism with cobalt blue filter; end point when inner edges of two semicircles just meet; IOP obtained by multiplying dial reading by 10. (b) **Perkin's** — handheld; same Goldmann biprism; no slit lamp required. (c) **Pneumatic** — measures IOP from air pressure required to applanate fixed corneal area; diaphragm with sensing nozzle, air pressure transducer, recording on paper strip. (d) **Air-puff** — non-contact; central cornea flattened by jet of air; good for mass screening. (e) **Pulse air and tono-pen** — computerised contact/pocket tonometer; both can measure IOP in any posture. **Advantages and disadvantages:** indentation — advantages: small, reliable, low price, relatively accurate, easy to master, can be done in opaque corneas; disadvantages: shape and weight of instruments not standardised, reflex contraction of extraocular muscles may falsely raise IOP, accommodation while measuring falsely lowers IOP, ocular rigidity interferes with IOP readings, expulsion of intraocular blood during indentation influences IOP measurement. Applanation — advantages: since very thin area of central cornea applanated, ocular rigidity has no influence on IOP; IOP measurement can be altered per central corneal thickness (per nomogram scale); may be handheld/non-contact (least infective for mass screening); disadvantages: requires slit lamp biomicroscope, expensive, requires clear cornea, relatively difficult to master; thicker corneas give falsely high IOP, IOP cannot be corrected per pachymetry; huge difference in IOP measurement if there is one scale reading difference on either side. **Newer advances:** tonometry independent of corneal variables — dynamic contour tonometry of Pascal, Reichert Ocular Response Analyser. However higher cost and lack of practical feasibility still makes CCT-corrected Goldmann applanation tonometer the gold standard in IOP measurement.

column2: Write short notes on hyphema.
column4: **Definition:** clinical condition characterised by presence of blood in anterior chamber either in settled or diffuse form. **Causes:** (1) traumatic ocular injuries (most common); (2) iatrogenic post-operative (trauma to iris or ciliary body); (3) infective — herpes zoster iritis, gonococcal iritis; (4) spontaneous — rubeosis iridis; (5) intraocular tumours — retinoblastoma, iris melanoma, juvenile xanthogranuloma, metastatic tumours; (6) blood dyscrasias — leukaemia, haemophilia, thrombocytopenia, von Willebrand's disease, sickle cell haemoglobinopathy; (7) miscellaneous — myotonic dystrophy, haemoglobinopathy. **Pathophysiology:** most common source of bleeding is tear in anterior face of ciliary body; most frequently ruptured vessels — vessels of major arterial circle of iris, choroidal arteries and veins crossing suprachoroidal space between ciliary body and episcleral venous plexus. Histopathology — core of aggregated RBCs surrounded by pseudocapsule of fibrin-plated coagulum. **Symptoms:** dimness of vision (sudden onset), ocular pain, redness, lacrimation. **Signs — grading (traumatic hyphema):** grade 1 (microhyphema) — circulating RBCs only under slit lamp; grade 2 — settled blood < 1/3 of AC; grade 3 — settled blood 1/3 to half of AC; grade 4 — settled blood > half of AC; grade 5 — total clotted blood in entire AC, dark red (eight ball/black ball hyphema, resembling dark eighth ball in snooker). Pupillary examination gives clue to posterior segment involvement; IOP raised proportional to grade and duration of hyphema; risk of corneal endothelial staining proportional to grade and duration; slit lamp to evaluate open globe injury (surgical drainage without primary closure contraindicated). **Management — investigations:** USG B-scan (opaque media, posterior segment); VEP (optic nerve damage); blood — complete hemogram, coagulation and bleeding profile (rule out blood dyscrasias); UBM (suspected iris and ciliary body tumours). **General measures:** absolute bed rest in large hyphema in propped-up position; smaller hyphemas — limited out-of-bed activity, sitting/semi-upright posture including sleeping; protective eye shield; avoid oral/topical NSAIDs (antiplatelet action). **Medical:** (1) **IOP-lowering measures** — topical beta-blockers with topical and/or systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors depending on presenting IOP; **avoid pilocarpine** (promotes further inflammation by disrupting blood-aqueous barrier, may lead to posterior synechiae); **avoid topical PG analogues** (inflammatory potential); **avoid alpha agonists** in children and sickle cell haemoglobinopathy; IV hyperosmotic agents temporarily for IOP spikes, avoided in sickle cell haemoglobinopathy. (2) topical potent steroids (reduce inflammation and future risk of secondary haemorrhage). (3) cycloplegics — topical 1% atropine reduces risk of secondary haemorrhage and posterior synechiae. **Surgical intervention — paracentesis for clotted blood:** persistently raised IOP > 50 mmHg > 5 days; total eight-ball hyphema; grade III or more hyphema with risk of endothelial staining; hyphema obscuring posterior segment analysis with suspected optic neuropathy or intraocular tumours; children < 2 years with hyphema obscuring pupillary zone (amblyopia prevention); haemoglobinopathy with lower threshold for surgical evacuation (higher risk of IOP-induced optic nerve damage). **Laser photocoagulation:** gonioscopically guided laser photocoagulation of visible bleeding points after 5–6 days may prevent secondary haemorrhage. **Complications:** (1) **secondary haemorrhage** — 2–7 days after initial event; lysis and retraction of clot and fibrin within traumatised vessels; increased size/reappearance of hyphema, fresh layer of blood over older darker clot, dispersed RBCs over settled darker clot; high chance of secondary glaucoma. (2) **corneal endothelial blood staining** — risk factors: larger grade, secondary haemorrhage, prolonged clot retraction, sustained IOP increase (> 25 mmHg for > 6 days), previous endothelial dysfunction. (3) **secondary glaucoma** — clogging of trabecular meshwork with deformed RBCs (ghost cell glaucoma), inflammation-induced PAS development, pupillary block with iris bombe, inflammatory glaucoma. (4) **optic atrophy** — risk increases if IOP > 50 mmHg for 5 days or > 35 mmHg for 7 days. **Recent advances:** antifibrinolytic agents (systemic aminocaproic acid/tranexamic acid or topical aminocaproic acid) in high risk of secondary haemorrhage; do not prevent other complications and may delay clot reabsorption; systemic use with antiemetics.

column2: Write short notes on hypermature/Morgagnian cataract.
column4: **Definition:** final stage of cataractogenesis where mature cataract either liquefies and swells up or shrinks down. **Pathogenesis — two types:** (1) **Morgagnian hypermature cataract** — entire lens cortex liquefies; small nucleus floats in bag of milky fluid; nucleus changes position with change of position of head; deep anterior chamber and iridodonesis. (2) **Sclerotic hypermature cataract** — disintegration of cortex and escape of fluid through anterior lens capsule; lens becomes shrunken, wrinkled, thickened anterior capsule; deep anterior chamber and iridodonesis. **Diagram contrast:** sclerotic cataract — shrunken nucleus with minimal cortex, shallow anterior chamber; hypermature — liquefied cortex, floating nucleus, deep anterior chamber. **Management:** urgent cataract surgery with in-the-bag PCIOL insertion is treatment of choice. **Pre-operative investigations:** PPBS; IOP estimation; patency of lacrimal drainage pathway; cardiological fitness (ECG, BP); biometry (IOL power calculation). **Pre-operative management:** IV 20% mannitol 300 ml IV 1–2 hours before surgery to reduce IOP; oral acetazolamide 500 mg at HS night before and morning of surgery; E/D flurbiprofen 1 drop BD/TDS × 5 days before surgery; ensure adequate pupillary dilatation (prone to peripheral posterior synechiae — homatropine and atropine instead of conventional tropicamide-phenylephrine); peribulbar block meticulously with minimal volume of LA to reduce risk of IOP elevation. **Intra-operative challenges:** IOP control before beginning surgery; SICS or phacoemulsification depending on corneal status (specular microscopy; avoid phacoemulsification in compromised corneas); **Argentinian flag sign** — capsulorhexis run-over due to high intracapsular pressure (linear bifurcation of capsular opening giving visual picture similar to Argentine national flag); methods to prevent capsulorhexis run-over — **spiral rhexis** (begin small, spirally increase very cautiously), **double rhexis** (initially 1–2 mm complete rhexis, then suction milky cortex with biway Simcoe cannula or bimanual I/A, then cut margin of rhexis with vannas scissors and extend with Utrata forceps), highly cohesive viscoelastic substance injection (reduce intracapsular pressure, flatten anterior capsule, prevent peripheral extension), decompression of intracapsular pressure with 26G needle before beginning capsulorhexis; high risk of capsular bag dialysis due to inadequate capsulorhexis size and pre-operative zonular weakness; high risk of posterior capsular rent due to absence of protective epinuclear plate during phacoemulsification. **Post-operative challenges:** dislocation/subluxation of IOL in immediate post-operative period in PCR or partial capsular bag dialysis; long-term anterior capsular phimosis in small or eccentric rhexis; increased risk of CMO.

column2: Write short notes on capsulotomy.
column4: **Definition:** surgical manoeuvre to create central opening in anterior capsule of crystalline lens of adequate size for nuclear management during cataract surgery. **Types:** (1) **Can-opener technique** — multiple small radial cuts for 360° at peripheral part of anterior capsule guided by dilated pupillary margin; nucleus taken out through linear opening, cortical matter washed out; rest of capsulotomy completed thereafter. (2) **Continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC)** — anterior capsule torn in circular fashion guided by dilated pupillary margin with irrigating bent needle cystotome or Utrata capsulorhexis forceps (26G needle bent twice in opposite directions to convert into irrigating bent needle cystotome); size — 5–5.5 mm for phaco, 6–6.5 mm for SICS. (3) **Manually modified capsulorrhexis** — approximately 24–48 radial point punctures for 360° in peripheral anterior capsule with needle cystotome; closely placed point punctures joined together to convert into modified capsulorrhexis. (4) **Femtosecond laser-assisted capsulotomy** — multiple pre-operative radial anterior capsular punctures made with femtosecond laser; intra-operatively anterior capsular tag removed with McPherson/Utrata forceps. **Advantages of capsulorrhexis over capsulotomy:** better tensile strength to capsular bag during nuclear management; less chance of capsular bag dialysis and posterior capsular rent; central CCC of adequate size with no PCR is must pre-requisite for premium IOL insertion. **Advantages of capsulotomy over capsulorrhexis:** easy to learn; less time consuming; in case of rhexis run-over conversion to capsulotomy is viable; useful in fibrosed anterior capsule; useful in large black/brown cataract; easier in small pupils. **Disadvantages of capsulotomy:** gives less tensile strength during nuclear management; mimics cortical fibres during cortical wash → more chance of capsular bag dialysis or PCR. **Disadvantages of capsulorrhexis:** difficult in small pupils, fibrosed anterior capsules, Morgagnian cataracts, large brown/black cataract; difficult to learn; peripheral extension common. **Special note:** femtosecond laser-assisted anterior capsulotomy is a promising alternative reducing learning curve of manual CCC; long-term studies yet to confirm superiority.

column2: Write short notes on small incision cataract surgery (SICS).
column4: **Principle:** form of extracapsular cataract extraction; creation of self-sealing triplanar entry wound; after opening anterior capsule, nucleus and cortical matter removed; in-the-bag PCIOL placement. **Indications:** removal of cataractous lens. **Anaesthesia:** children — general anaesthesia; adults — peribulbar block (2% lignocaine + 0.5–0.75% bupivacaine + 5 IU hyaluronidase + 0.1 in 1 lakh adrenaline injected in peripheral orbital space). **Principle surgical steps:** (1) **superior rectus bridle suture** — fixes globe in downgaze, counter-traction during nucleus delivery; (2) **peritomy and scleral exposure** — Tenon and conjunctiva dissected 10–2 o'clock, wet field cautery to expose sclera sufficiently for wound construction; fornix-based conjunctival flap; (3) **scleral incision** (1st plane) — plane of scleral incision (1/3 to half thickness), 1.5–2 mm behind superior limbus, 5.5–7.5 mm long (straight/frown) depending on nature of cataractous lens; instrument — No. 15 blade; (4) **2nd sclero-corneal plane** — extends 1–1.5 mm into clear cornea; instrument — crescent knife; (5) **3rd plane of internal corneal incision** — instrument — 3.2 mm angled keratome; (6) **side port entry** at ~9 o'clock — valvular stab clear corneal entry for injecting trypan blue, anterior capsulotomy, cortical wash, dialing IOL into bag; (7) **anterior capsulotomy** — types: can-opener (radial cuts 360°), envelope/linear capsulotomy, continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis; (8) **hydro procedures** — hydrodissection (BSS under peripheral anterior capsule to separate corticonuclear mass from capsule), hydrodelineation (BSS into peripheral cataractous lens to separate nucleus from epinuclear plate); (9) **nuclear prolapse** — prolapse of nucleus from capsular bag into AC initiated by hydro procedures and completed by dialing rest of nucleus by Sinskey's hook dialer; techniques to prolapse nucleus from AC into exterior through triplanar wound — irrigating/wire vectis, phaco sandwich, fish hook, Blumenthal's, phaco fracture, visco prolapse; (10) **aspiration of cortical matter** — Simcoe's biway I/A cannula preferably through side port for better AC volume maintenance; (11) **PCIOL insertion** — IOL inserted with McPherson's forceps, dialed into bag with Sinskey's hook/dialer; AC maintained with viscoelastic; (12) thorough removal of viscoelastic material to prevent secondary glaucoma; (13) AC maintained with BSS, wound closed, side port hydrated, conjunctival flap repositioned. **Complications — pre-operative:** general anxiety; local anaesthesia related (retrobulbar haemorrhage, oculocardiac reflex with heart block, inadvertent globe perforation, spontaneous crystalline lens dislocation, subconjunctival haemorrhage). **Intra-operative:** laceration of superior rectus muscle; incision-related (button-holing, premature entry, scleral disinsertion); Descemet's detachment; iris tissue prolapse; iridodialysis; escape of capsulorhexis into periphery; inadequate rhexis size; eccentric rhexis position; posterior capsular rupture with vitreous prolapse into AC; capsular bag dialysis; nucleus drop; expulsive choroidal haemorrhage. **Post-operative — early:** hyphaema, iris tissue prolapse through wound, shallow/non-formed AC, striate keratopathy, TASS, endophthalmitis. **Late:** CMO, pseudophakic bullous keratopathy, posterior capsular opacification, retinal detachment, secondary glaucoma, delayed endophthalmitis (Propionibacterium), subluxation/dislocation/pupillary capture of IOL.

column2: Write short notes on posterior capsular opacification (PCO).
column4: **Definition:** delayed post-operative complication of cataract surgery in which there is proliferation of anterior capsular cells into posterior capsular surface leading to opacification with or without resultant dimness of vision; also known as after cataract. **Causes:** proliferation of anterior capsular epithelial cells into posterior capsular surface across in-situ PCIOL even after uncomplicated cataract surgery; inadvertent incomplete posterior capsular polish; proliferation from persistent cortical matter remaining after surgery. **Types:** (1) **dense membranous after cataract** (usually paediatric); (2) **Soemmering's ring** — thick ring-shaped pacification behind iris in peripheral part; (3) **Elschnig's pearls** — central vacuolated subcapsular epithelial cell cluster resembling soap bubbles/pearls; (4) **fibrosis type PCO** — due to fibroblastic metaplasia of epithelial cells developing contractile qualities. **Treatment:** (1) dense membranous after cataract — surgical removal preferably through pars plana approach; (2) Soemmering's rings — serial observation as visual dimness not usually associated; (3) all PCO causing significant dimness — **laser posterior capsulotomy by Nd:YAG laser** (neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet); wavelength near infrared 1064 nm; solid-state system with four energy levels; rare earth metal neodymium doped with YAG (Y₃Al₅O₁₂), Y ions replaced by Nd³⁺ ions, doping concentration 0.7% by weight. **Technique:** accurate focusing and minimal energy; initial power 1 mJ/pulse, may be increased; first puncture aimed at visual axis centre; cruciate pattern using single-pulse shots; size of capsulotomy should match approximate size of dilated pupils under scotopic conditions (4–5 mm in pseudophakic eyes); capsulotomy margin should not exceed margin of optic to prevent vitreous strands prolapsing into AC; total energy < 80 mJ to prevent post-laser IOP spikes and CMO. **Post-laser follow-up:** IOP-lowering agents × 2 weeks; short course of soft topical steroids × 10 days; topical antibiotics × 1 week; post-laser applanation tonometry at 1 week; if no improvement in vision — fundus examination and OCT macula for CMO. **Complications:** pitting of IOL (may or may not be visually consequential), IOP spikes (usually transient), CMO (incidence decreases proportionally if laser before cataract surgery), subluxation/dislocation of IOL, endothelial laser burn, rarely retinal detachment. **Prevention:** in paediatric cataract, posterior capsulorhexis with 2 mm limited anterior vitrectomy during cataract surgery (PCO chance nearly 100% in < 20 years age group); complete cortical wash and posterior capsular polish; in-the-bag PCIOL placement; square-edged IOL prevents migration of anterior epithelial cells across optic into posterior capsule (round-edged allows cells to grow in, square-edged blocks growth in visual axis).

column2: Describe early post-operative complications of cataract surgery.
column4: **Complications — hyphaema:** clinical features — dimness of vision, redness, pain; diffuse or settled blood in AC with/without raised IOP. Management — rest in head-elevated posture, oral/systemic/topical IOP-lowering drugs, topical steroids, topical cycloplegics; surgical intervention if IOP > 50 mmHg, endothelial staining, hyphema > 50% AC volume, not resolving even after 1 week. **Striate keratopathy:** due to endothelial damage during surgery; dimness of vision, pain, photophobia; Descemet's folds with varying stromal oedema. Management — mild cases resolve spontaneously; hypertonic saline eye drops and ointment, topical steroids, topical/oral IOP-lowering agents, topical cycloplegics. **Flat anterior chamber:** (a) wound leak — Seidel's test positive; pressure bandage with oral acetazolamide (may lead to AC formation); surgical exploration with suturing of wound may be required. (b) ciliochoroidal detachment — negative Seidel's test; on USG B-scan convex-bordered detached ciliochoroidal complex (kissing choroids); usually cured within 4 days with pressure bandage and oral acetazolamide; suprachoroidal drainage with air injection in AC in persistent cases. (c) pupillary block — adhesions of IOL with iris; if persistent, PAS → secondary angle-closure glaucoma; usually treated with topical mydriatics, topical/oral/IV IOP-lowering agents; if not relieved, laser peripheral iridotomy. **Toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS):** sterile inflammation of anterior segment post-operatively; immunological reaction to chemicals attached to IOL, chemicals attached to instruments, denatured drugs, retained foreign body. Symptoms: dimness of vision, pain, photophobia beginning < 24 hours; signs: cells and flare in AC, KPs on endothelium, iris pigment scatter, transpupillary membrane formation (severe). IO — first-order vessels and fundal glow usually visible; USG B-scan normal posterior segment. Treatment similar to acute anterior uveitis — topical highly potent corticosteroids (1% prednisolone acetate), topical cycloplegics, topical IOP-lowering agents, oral steroid (10 days short course 1 mg/kg) in non-resolving cases with no systemic contraindications. **Acute bacterial endophthalmitis:** most common — Staph epidermidis, Staph aureus; others — Pseudomonas, pneumococci, streptococci, Corynebacterium. Severe dimness of vision, ocular swelling, pain, lacrimation, photophobia (within 1–7 days); swelling of lids, chemosis of conjunctiva, gaping of wound, diffuse corneal oedema, hypopyon in AC. IO — no fundal glow; USG B-scan — hyperechoic collections in vitreous. Treatment protocol per EVS: presenting vision only PL+ → immediate PPV; better than PL → 1st dose intravitreal injection + vitreous sampling; no improvement in 48 hours → repeat intravitreal injection per culture sensitivity; if immediate PPV available after repeat → immediate PPV. Drugs for intravitreal injection — vancomycin 2 mg/0.1 ml, ceftazidime 2 mg/0.1 ml, amikacin 0.4 mg/0.1 ml (optional); topical reconstituted vancomycin and ceftazidime with fortified amikacin may be used; systemic antibiotics limited role; systemic steroids doubtful (if started, 24–48 hours after controlling acute inflammation); topical strong cycloplegics and IOP-lowering agents supportive. **Special notes:** successful management of early post-operative complications plays important role in final visual rehabilitation; in clinico-investigative dilemma between TASS and acute bacterial endophthalmitis, better to instil first dose of intravitreal injection (latter is much more visually damaging).
