column2: Write short notes on biometry.
column4: **Definition:** procedure to calculate exact dioptric power of IOL to be implanted during cataract surgery; three steps — (A) keratometry (mean corneal radius of curvature); (B) USG A-scan (AP axial length); (C) dioptric power of IOL via statistically obtained mathematical formulas. **A) Keratometry:** objective method to measure central corneal radius of curvature; principle — from size of image formed by a convex mirror, radius of curvature can be calculated; anterior surface of cornea behaves as a convex mirror (first Purkinje image); keratometer uses principle of **visible doubling** to obtain exact measurement of image size. **Types:** (1) **Javal-Schiotz model** — four images seen initially; exact keratometric value obtained by coinciding a and b images together (positive coincidence); need to rotate 90° to obtain keratometric reading of horizontal and vertical meridians. (2) **Bausch & Lomb model** — circular mires; negative coincidence; simultaneously obtains radius of curvature in both meridians. **B) USG A-scan:** measured by applanation method (more accurate) and immersion technique; measures time required for sound waves to travel from cornea to retina; unidimensional amplitude scan displaying reflecting echo strengths as vertical deflections along Y-axis on graph progressing along X-axis; echo pattern — corneal echoes, echoes from anterior and posterior lens surface, tall retinal echoes, echoes from orbital fat. Probe should point toward macula with no fluid bridge between two and no inadvertent central corneal depression; automatic mode of software algorithm better; axial length of both eyes measured for comparison; scan with maximal axial length within range selected if using manual mode; axial length > 25 mm should raise suspicion of posterior staphyloma. **C) IOL power calculation — by basis of derivation:** (1) **theoretical formula** — based on mathematical principles around schematic eye; reliable only within 22–24.5 mm range; examples — Binkhorst, Gill's, Clayman's. (2) **regression formula** — retrospective analysis of post-operative visual outcomes; **first generation:** SRK-I (Sanders-Retzlaff-Kraff), P = A − 2.5L − 0.9K, where P = dioptric IOL power, A = constant for IOL type (provided by manufacturer), L = axial length in mm, K = average keratometric value in dioptres; also performs only for eyes with 22–24.5 mm range. **Second generation:** SRK-II (A constant modified on basis of axial length), Modified SRK-II (further stratification of A constant modification per axial length). **Third generation:** hybrid of theoretical and regression — Holladay I & II (suitable for normal and 24.5–26.0 mm large eyeballs), Hoffer Q (best for eyes < 24.5 mm short eyes). **Fourth generation:** more universal application — Haigis formula (more universal but requires triple optimisation, operationally cumbersome), SRK/T (non-linear theoretical optical formula empirically optimised for post-operative AC depth, retinal thickness, corneal refractive index; highly accurate for extremely long eyes > 28 mm). **Recent advances:** **Optical Biometer (IOL Master)** — highly accurate non-contact optical biometry based on partial coherence interferometry; measures axial length, corneal curvature, in-built software with internationally accepted IOL power formula; not operable for very high-grade cataract. **Paediatric population:** IOL power calculation based principally on axial length measurement (keratometric values not reliable in growing corneas — Dahan's rule). Immersion technique better choice for aphakic eyes. Vitrectomised eyes — modification of formulae per vitreous substitute used. Post-cornea-based refractive surgery — only Haigis formula applicable; all other formulas need customised modification per corneal tomography.

column2: Describe retinal arterial occlusive disease (CRAO/BRAO) with clinical features and management.
column4: **Blood supply of retina:** inner retina supplied by central retinal artery; outer retina supplied by ciliary arteries through choriocapillaries; both branches of ophthalmic artery. **Causes of central retinal artery occlusion:** **emboli** (most common — atheromatous carotid artery plaque; three morphological types: Hollenhorst plaque — small yellow refractile cholesterol emboli; greyish-white elongated fibrin-platelet aggregates; non-scintillating white calcific particles); **thrombus**; **arteritis** — giant cell arteritis, SLE, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, polyarteritis nodosa, migraine, systemic hypotension. **Precipitating causes for embolic occlusion:** cardiac arrhythmia (especially atrial fibrillation), mitral valve prolapse, thrombophilic disorders (hyperhomocysteinaemia, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, inherited coagulation disorders), sickle cell haemoglobinopathy, Susac syndrome (retinocochleocerebral vasculopathy — retinal artery occlusion due to microangiopathy + sensorineural deafness + encephalopathy). **Clinical features — amaurosis fugax:** transient painless monocular vision loss, often described as 'curtain coming down', lasts few minutes, frequency varies, may accompany ipsilateral transient ischaemic attacks; urgent cardiovascular and neurological assessment required. **BRAO:** may be asymptomatic if central vision spared; sudden painless altitudinal or sectoral visual field loss; RAPD may be present; pale oedematous (ground glass) sectoral retina; **cattle trucking/box-car appearance** (attenuation of arterioles and veins with sludging and segmentation of blood column); embolus occluding retinal artery branch usually at bifurcation points. **CRAO:** sudden monocular painless profound dimness of vision; VA severely reduced except if macular perfusion preserved by cilioretinal artery; if vision is No PL — suspect giant cell arteritis or ophthalmic artery occlusion; RAPD present, sometimes total afferent pupillary defect (amaurotic pupil); globally pale retina, retinal oedema develops over several hours; **cherry-red spot** (orange reflex from underlying intact choroid at foveola; if cilioretinal supply present, macula may appear normal); peripapillary opaque and swollen retina; emboli visible in 20% cases. **Long-standing cases:** optic atrophy, sheathing of retinal vessels, RPE changes, patchy retinal atrophy, retinal and disc neovascularisation (2%), iris neovascularisation (rubeosis iridis) in ~4–5 weeks leading to neovascular glaucoma. **Management — systemic evaluation:** smoking history; rule out systemic symptoms of giant cell arteritis; BP monitoring/control; cardiac consultation (arrhythmia, valvular heart disease); CRP and ESR (GCA); carotid artery duplex scanning (high-resolution real-time USG with Doppler flow — rule out carotid stenosis and thrombus); for young patients with no detectable risk factors — 24/48 hour Holter, blood tests (homocysteine, thrombophilia screening, plasma protein electrophoresis for multiple myeloma, lipid profile, TFT, autoantibodies, syphilis/HIV serology, blood cultures for endocarditis); neuroimaging (MRI), orbital imaging, HRCT chest. **Ocular treatment (if < 24 hours):** ocular massage with three-mirror goniolens (mechanically collapses arterial lumen, improves flow, dislodges emboli); anterior chamber paracentesis with 27G needle (0.1–0.2 ml aqueous, no ocular massage after, strict asepsis); IOP lowering (E/D apraclonidine 1%/timolol 0.5% or tab acetazolamide 500 mg BDPC); sublingual isosorbide dinitrate (vasodilation); rebreathing into paper bag (respiratory acidosis-induced vasodilation); carbogen inhalation (95% O₂ + 5% CO₂ prevents oxygen-induced vasoconstriction); IV mannitol 300 ml stat and 100 ml TDS; thrombolysis (rTPA, streptokinase, urokinase — intra-arterial via internal carotid or IV, with physician); trans-luminal Nd:YAG laser thrombolysis (vitreous haemorrhage as complication). **Systemic treatment:** risk of cerebrovascular accident very high after CRAO/BRAO/amaurosis fugax; refer and follow up with neurologist and cardiologist. **Follow-up:** weekly up to 1 month; monthly up to 6 months; check anterior segment neovascularisation at every visit after 3–4 weeks.

column2: Write short notes on ocular ischaemic syndrome.
column4: **Definition:** chronic eye disease resulting from chronic ocular hypoperfusion secondary to ipsilateral atherosclerotic carotid artery stenosis. **Risk factors:** aged patient, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease; more common in males. **Symptoms:** gradual dimness of vision over weeks/months; intermittent amaurosis fugax; ocular and periocular pain; worsening of vision with sudden exposure to bright light (bright light amaurosis fugax); persistent after-images. **Signs:** diffuse episcleral congestion; corneal stromal oedema; AC flare and cells; IOP low due to chronic hypoperfusion; cataractous lens; **iris neovascularisation (rubeosis iridis)** leading to neovascular glaucoma; arteriolar attenuation; venous dilatation; cotton wool spots; neovascularisation of disc with proliferative retinopathy; spontaneous arterial pulsation; flame-shaped haemorrhage; macular oedema. **Investigations — systemic:** FBS/PPBS/HbA1c, lipid profile, thyroid profile; carotid imaging — carotid duplex USG scan, digital subtraction angiography, MR/CT angiography. **Ocular:** FFA (delayed choroidal filling, prolonged arteriovenous transit time); OCT macula (macular oedema). **Treatment:** (1) E/D prednisolone acetate 1% QID for anterior segment inflammation; (2) E/D homatropine 1 drop BD; (3) pan-retinal photocoagulation if neovascular glaucoma develops; (4) intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide/anti-VEGF agents for macular oedema; (5) carotid endarterectomy or stenting (complete obstruction — extracranial-intracranial arterial bypass grafting); (6) systemic risk factor control by physician. **Prognosis:** poor — 5-year mortality from cerebral or cardiac illness is 40%.

column2: Write short notes on hypertensive eye disease.
column4: **Retinopathy — preclinical hypertension signs:** reduced retinal arteriolar calibre; increased venular tortuosity. **Grades of hypertensive retinopathy:** (1) **Grade I** — generalised mild retinal arteriolar narrowing. (2) **Grade II** — focal arteriolar narrowing with arteriovenous nipping at crossing points; arteriolar walls appear opacified (copper wiring). (3) **Grade III** — features of grade II plus dot/blot/flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages, hard exudates, macular oedema, chronic macular oedema leading to macular star formation, cotton wool spots. (4) **Grade IV** — features of grade III plus **optic disc oedema** (correlates with malignant hypertension). **Choroidopathy (rarely in accelerated hypertension in young adults):** Siegrist streaks (linearly arranged flecks along choroidal vessels); Elschnig spot (small black spots surrounded by yellow haloes indicating focal choroidal infarcts); exudative retinal detachment (mostly bilateral, seen in eclampsia).

column2: Write short notes on branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO).
column4: **Pathophysiology:** atherosclerotic thickening of branch retinal arteriole → compression of venule at arteriovenous crossing point → exacerbated by common arteriovenous adventitial sheath → intravenous endothelial cell loss, turbulent venous blood flow and thrombus formation → elevation of venous pressure and stagnation of blood flow distal to obstruction → sectoral retinal hypoxia → damage to capillary endothelial cells → retinal oedema, haemorrhage and neovascularisation (via VEGF). **Risk factors:** dyslipidaemia, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, glaucoma and ocular hypertension, age > 65 years, oral contraceptive pills, smoking, increased chance of RVO. **Rare risk factors:** dehydration, myeloproliferative disorders, thrombophilia, vasculitis. **Symptoms:** asymptomatic if macula not involved; sudden painless loss of vision if macula involved; metamorphopsia. **Signs:** **superotemporal quadrant** most commonly involved; site of occlusion may be identified at an arteriovenous crossing point; sectoral ischaemic retina filled with haemorrhage; macular oedema and haemorrhage. **Common sites of BRVO and relation to macular involvement:** site 1 at disc (macular involvement present); site 2 superotemporal or inferotemporal (macular involvement present); site 3 superotemporal away from disc (macular involvement may or may not be present); peripheral sites (macular not involved); site 6 away from disc nasally (macular involvement absent). **Investigations — systemic routine:** CBC, FBS/PPBS/HbA1c, lipid profile, plasma protein electrophoresis (rule out multiple myeloma), urea/creatinine, TFT (higher prevalence of thyroid disease), comprehensive cardiovascular check, chest X-ray (sarcoidosis, TB), CRP (vasculitis, inflammatory disorders), plasma homocysteine (homocysteinaemia), thrombophilia screening, autoantibodies (RA, Wegener's), serum ACE (sarcoidosis), syphilis serology, carotid artery imaging (exclude ocular ischaemic syndrome). **Selected investigations — indications:** bilateral RVO, RVO in < 60 years, H/O thrombosis elsewhere, negative routine investigations. **Ocular — FFA:** detects areas of capillary non-perfusion, site of obstruction, vessel pruning; may be diagnostic in late or subtle cases. **OCT:** detects macular oedema. **Treatment:** (1) control of systemic risk factors especially hypertension (reduces cardiovascular and cerebrovascular complications); (2) if no macular involvement — 3-monthly observation; (3) if macular oedema: intravitreal anti-VEGF agents (ranibizumab, aflibercept), intravitreal dexamethasone implant (increased risk of glaucoma and cataract), focal macular laser at areas of leakage guided by FFA, intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide (increased risk of glaucoma and cataract); combination of laser and intravitreal injection reduces frequency of latter and treatment cost (optimal regimen yet to be defined). **Complications:** neovascularisation of disc (NVD) and NVE occurs in 8% by 3 years (sectoral photocoagulation required); NVI and neovascular glaucoma (less chance than CRVO); vitreous haemorrhage; chronic macular oedema; cataract formation; glaucoma. Most BRVO has good prognosis.

column2: Write short notes on central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO).
column4: **Pathophysiology:** central retinal vein and artery possess common adventitial sheath at crossing point posterior to lamina cribrosa → atherosclerotic changes in artery compress adjoining vein → central retinal venous thrombus formation → pan-retinal hypoxia → capillary endothelial cell damage → pan-retinal haemorrhages, oedema and neovascularisation (via VEGF). **Risk factors:** hypertension, diabetes mellitus, age > 65 years, glaucoma and ocular hypertension, oral contraceptive pills, dyslipidaemia, increased chance of RVO; rare — dehydration, thrombophilia, vasculitis, myeloproliferative disorders. **Clinical features — non-ischaemic CRVO (80%):** mild visual dimness > 6/60; RAPD absent or present in mild grade; less tortuosity and dilatation of vessels; less haemorrhages and cotton wool spots; less oedema; macular involvement less; optic disc involvement less; visual field defect less; FFA — less area of non-perfusion (< 10 disc diameters); prognosis better; chance of NVI/NVG less. **Ischaemic CRVO (20%):** profound visual dimness > 6/60; marked RAPD; marked tortuosity and dilatation of vessels; profound oedema with cystoid changes; extensive haemorrhage and cotton wool spots; profound macular oedema and hyperaemia; optic disc involvement commonly present; extensive areas of non-perfusion (> 10 disc diameters); worse prognosis; increased chance of NVI and NVG. **Investigations — systemic routine:** CBC, FBS/PPBS/HbA1c, lipid profile, plasma protein electrophoresis, urea/creatinine, TFT, cardiovascular check, chest X-ray, CRP, homocysteine, thrombophilia screening, autoantibodies, serum ACE, syphilis serology, carotid imaging. **Selected — indications:** bilateral RVO, RVO in < 50 years, H/O thrombosis elsewhere, negative routine. **Ocular — FFA:** non-ischaemic CRVO — delayed AV transit time, good retinal capillary perfusion, less leakage, capillary non-perfusion < 10 disc diameter; ischaemic CRVO — marked delay in AV transit time, capillary non-perfusion area > 10 disc diameter, extensive leakage. **OCT:** detects and quantifies macular oedema; monitoring response. **Treatment — indications:** VA worse than 6/9; central macular thickness > 250 μm. **Modalities:** (1) **intravitreal anti-VEGF agents** — CRUISE study (monthly ranibizumab × 6 months better than placebo); COPERNICUS study (aflibercept 'as and when needed' basis, monitored clinically and by OCT); (2) **intravitreal dexamethasone implant** — GENEVA trial (initial vision improvement at 2 months but returns to baseline at 6 months); COMRADE trial (at 6 months, vision improvement by ranibizumab better than dexamethasone implant); (3) **intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide** — chronic macular oedema not responding to conventional therapy; complications: sudden IOP rise and cataract; (4) focal lasers — not beneficial except in some younger patients; (5) **pan-retinal photocoagulation** for neovascular glaucoma.

column2: Write short notes on retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).
column4: **Definition:** bilateral proliferative retinopathy occurring in premature infants with low birth weight and often with history of exposure to high concentration of oxygen. **Etiopathogenesis — primary risk factors:** low gestational age (< 32 weeks), low birth weight (< 1.5 kg), baby born prematurely, supplemental oxygen therapy. As baby grows, increased metabolic demand leads to unregulated production of VEGF → aberrant neovascularisation and progressive fibrovascular proliferation → ROP development. **Probable risk factors:** phototherapy, sepsis, apnoea, shock, blood transfusion. **Clinical features — international classification of ROP (ICROP):** by zones and stages into Type 1 and Type 2. **Stages:** stage 1 — demarcation line at junction of avascular and vascular retina; stage 2 — demarcation ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation into vitreous cavity; stage 3 — demarcation ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation; stage 4a — subtotal retinal detachment not involving macula; stage 4b — subtotal retinal detachment involving macula; stage 5 — total retinal detachment. **Zones:** Zone I — imaginary circle drawn on posterior pole with optic disc as centre, radius twice distance between centre of optic disc and fovea; Zone II — imaginary circle with optic disc as centre, radius distance between centre of disc and nasal ora serrata; area between zone I and this imaginary circle is zone II; Zone III — residual temporal crescent beyond radius of zone II. **Plus disease:** signifies tendency of progression; dilatation and tortuosity of blood vessels involving at least two quadrants of posterior fundus (or 6 clock hours) with any stage of ROP; may be associated with poorly dilating pupils, iris neovascularisation, vitreous haze; **pre-plus disease** — dilatation and tortuosity more than normal but not meeting plus disease criteria. **Aggressive posterior ROP (AP-ROP)/rush disease:** posterior location, severe plus disease, ill-defined nature of retinopathy with vascular loops, haemorrhages; requires immediate treatment otherwise rapidly progresses to stage 5. **Type classification:** **Type 1** — any ROP stage in Zone I with plus disease; Zone I non-plus with stage 3 and beyond; Zone II stage 2 or 3 with plus disease; requires treatment within 72 hours. **Type 2** — stage 1 or 2 in Zone I without plus disease; stage 3 ROP within Zone II without plus disease; requires weekly follow-up. **Management — screening (best way to prevent childhood blindness):** **primordial prevention** — premature infants not exposed to oxygen concentration > 30%, prevention of neonatal sepsis, acidosis and asphyxia; **screening criteria** — all premature babies < 34 weeks gestational age; all babies with birth weight < 1750 g; **screening tools** — indirect ophthalmoscope with 20D lens and scleral depressor, wide-field retinal imaging; **screening protocol** — begin 4–7 weeks postnatally with subsequent review 1–3 weeks according to severity. **Treatment:** (1) **laser photocoagulation** — 810 nm diode or double-frequency Nd:YAG (532 nm) with laser indirect delivery system; peripheral avascular retina lasered; weekly follow-up till regression; (2) **intravitreal anti-VEGFs** — indications: primary modality for AP-ROP, AP-ROP with hazy media (improvement of visualisation for laser), ROP progressing despite laser; (3) **pars plana vitrectomy** — stage 4a and 4b (lens-sparing PPV improved visual outcome); stage 5 (poor visual outcome even with early PPV). **Follow-up:** successfully treated ROP children prone to refractive error, strabismus, amblyopia; cycloplegic refraction at 6 months of age.

column2: Write short notes on diabetic retinopathy.
column4: **Definition:** retinal changes seen in patients with diabetes mellitus. **Risk factors:** duration of diabetes (most important), type I more risk than type II, sex (more in females), poor metabolic control, heredity (recessive trait without sex linkage), pregnancy, smoking, obesity and dyslipidaemia, hypertension, anaemia. **Pathogenesis:** endothelial cell damage, RBC deformation and aggregation, increased stickiness of platelets, increased plasma viscosity → loss of capillary pericytes → hard exudates (microaneurysms and capillary leakage) + microvascular occlusion → retinal ischaemia → retinal oedema + arteriovenous shunts (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, IRMA) → neovascularisation. **Classification (ETDRS):** (1) **Normal fundus.** (2) **Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR):** very mild (only microaneurysm); mild (any or all: microaneurysm, retinal haemorrhage, hard exudates, cotton wool spots); moderate (severe retinal haemorrhage in 1–3 quadrants, venous beading restricted in one quadrant, cotton wool spots in 1–3 quadrants, mild IRMA in one quadrant); severe (4-2-1 rule — severe retinal haemorrhage in all 4 quadrants OR significant venous beading in ≥ 2 quadrants OR moderate IRMA in ≥ 1 quadrant); very severe (≥ 2 criteria of severe NPDR). (3) **Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR):** mild-moderate (NVD or NVE but not sufficient to meet high-risk PDR criteria); high-risk (any: NVD > 1/3 disc area, any NVD with vitreous haemorrhage). (4) **Advanced diabetic eye disease** (stage of serious vision-threatening complication): non-resolving/recurrent vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, intractable neovascular glaucoma. **Diabetic macular oedema:** most common cause of visual impairment in diabetics; diffuse retinal oedema from extensive capillary leakage; localised from focal capillary leakage from microaneurysms and dilated capillary segments. **Types:** focal maculopathy (well-circumscribed retinal thickening with complete/incomplete rings of exudates; angiography shows good macular perfusion); diffuse maculopathy (diffuse retinal thickening commonly with cystoid changes; angiography shows diffuse capillary non-perfusion at fovea and elsewhere); ischaemic maculopathy (disproportionate loss of VA despite normal-looking macula; angiography shows diffuse capillary non-perfusion at fovea and posterior pole/periphery). **Clinically significant macular oedema (ETDRS):** retinal thickening within 500 μm of centre of macula; exudates within 500 μm of centre with retinal thickening (may be outside 500 μm); retinal thickening ≥ one disc area (1500 μm) any part within one disc diameter of macula centre. **Investigations — systemic:** blood — FBS/PPBS/HbA1c/lipid/urea/creatinine/complete hemogram; urine — microscopic, 24-hour urinary protein, albumin-creatinine ratio. **Ocular:** FFA (areas of neovascularisation, leakage, capillary non-perfusion); OCT (retinal thickening, cystoid spaces). **Management — general measures:** patient education and awareness for routine follow-up; strict glycaemic control per physician; control of hypertension, dyslipidaemia, anaemia; discontinuation of smoking; tab fenofibrate 200 mg OD irrespective of statin use (shown to reduce DR progression). **Diabetic macular oedema:** (1) laser photocoagulation — mainstay till recent past; diode/argon laser; reduces risk of visual loss by 50%; focal/grid laser per angiographic findings; (2) intravitreal anti-VEGF — ranibizumab 0.5 mg/0.05 ml monthly × 3 months; aflibercept 2 mg/0.05 ml monthly × 3 months; (3) intravitreal triamcinolone (intractable oedema); (4) pars plana vitrectomy for TRD.

column2: Write short notes on vitreous haemorrhage.
column4: **Definition:** any collection of blood within vitreous cavity. **Classification:** sub-hyaloid, pre-retinal, intragel haemorrhage (anterior VH, mid VH, posterior VH, total VH). **Causes:** (1) acute posterior vitreous detachment associated with retinal tear or avulsion of peripheral retinal vessels; (2) proliferative retinopathy in diabetes mellitus, retinal vein occlusion, sickle cell disease, Eales disease, vasculitis; (3) miscellaneous retinal disorders — retinal artery macroaneurysms, telangiectasia, capillary haemangioma; (4) trauma; (5) systemic disorders — bleeding disorders, Terson syndrome (intraocular + subarachnoid haemorrhage secondary to intracerebral aneurysmal rupture). **Symptoms:** small haemorrhage — sudden onset floaters and diffuse blurring without affecting VA; dense haemorrhage — sudden painless loss of vision (may be painful in trauma). **Signs:** distant direct ophthalmoscopy — small: black shadow against red glow; dense: no red fundal glow; indirect ophthalmoscopy — small: presence of blood in vitreous cavity; dense: non-visualisation of fundus; USG B-scan particularly helpful in diagnosing vitreous haemorrhage and excluding underlying retinal tear/detachment (hyperechoic reflections); A-scan overlay shows hyperechoic lens shadow and shadow of vitreous haemorrhage. **Treatment — without underlying retinal detachment:** bed rest in head-elevated posture to allow haemorrhage to settle down; indirect ophthalmoscopy to find and treat cause once blood settles; vitrectomy if not absorbed after 3 months or immediately if associated with RD. **With underlying retinal detachment:** immediate vitrectomy to clear haemorrhage and reposition detached retina. **Complications:** complete absorption within 4–8 weeks; organised haemorrhage/recurrent bleeding; tractional retinal detachment; vitreous liquefaction degeneration and ghost cell glaucoma.

column2: Write short notes on uses of laser in eye.
column4: **Properties of laser:** monochromatic (narrow beam of single wavelength, coloured light); polarised (in one plane, efficiently passing through ocular media); coherent (each wave in phase with subsequent); collimated (all rays parallel). **Commonly used lasers in ophthalmology:** argon (488/514 nm, argon gas, blue-green); krypton (647 nm, krypton gas); diode (810 nm, diode crystal); diode frequency-doubled Nd:YAG (577 nm, coloured Sienna, both diode and Nd:YAG crystals); Nd:YAG (1064 nm, neodymium-doped YAG crystals); excimer (193 nm, helium and fluorine gas); femtosecond (1053 nm, neodymium-glass platforms). **Uses by therapeutic effect:** (1) **Photochemical/photoradiation** — exogenous photosensitising agents accumulate in target tissue and produce cytotoxic free radicals when excited by near-infrared laser; e.g., photodynamic therapy with verteporfin and diode laser; collagen cross-linking with riboflavin and UVA light. (2) **Photothermal** — laser light absorbed by endogenous tissue pigments (Hb, melanin, xanthophyll) released as heat, target tissue destroyed by photocoagulation or photovaporisation; e.g., argon laser trabeculoplasty of POAG, pan-retinal photocoagulation for diabetic retinopathy and retinal vascular disorders and neovascular glaucoma, laser goniotomy for developmental glaucoma, argon laser corneal suture lysis. (3) **Photodisruption/photomechanical** — laser exposure ionises electrons of target tissue to plasma state, exerts cutting/incising effect; e.g., Nd:YAG uses — capsulotomy for PCO, laser iridotomy for angle-closure glaucoma, membranectomy for pupillary membranes, laser vitreolysis to cut vitreous strands in AC; femtosecond uses — refractive (corneal flap in LASIK, tunnel for intracorneal ring segments, astigmatism-correcting arcuate incisions, small incision lenticule extraction/SMILE, presbyopia-correcting corneal surgery), femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery (wound construction, capsulotomy, nucleofractise). (4) **Photoablation** — laser light of very short wavelength breaks molecular bonds of biological tissues into small molecules that diffuse away; e.g., excimer laser uses — PRK, LASIK for corneal refractive error correction, phototherapeutic keratectomy for band-shaped keratopathy.

column2: Write short notes on retinoblastoma.
column4: **Definition:** common paediatric malignant tumour arising from neurosensory retina of one or both eyes. **Demography:** confined to infancy mostly; mostly unilateral; no sex predisposition; more common among whites. **Genetics:** RB gene located 13q14 with two alleles; 10% familial, 90% sporadic. **Familial (autosomal dominant):** both mutations occur in same retinal cells after fertilisation in embryo; unifocal/unilateral tumours; no predisposition to non-ocular tumours; cannot be passed to offspring. **Sporadic:** first mutation in one of two alleles of RB genes in germ cells before fertilisation; second hit in other allele post-zygotic phase; usually multifocal and bilateral; predisposition to non-ocular tumours (pinealoblastoma); 40% of offspring affected due to variable penetrance. **Clinical manifestations:** leucocoria (most common), strabismus (second most common), painful red eyes, defective vision, asymptomatic, orbital cellulitis, unilateral mydriasis, heterochromia iridis, hyphema. **Diagnosis:** bilateral fundus examination with 360° scleral indentation by indirect ophthalmoscope; tumour patterns — endophytic, exophytic, mixed, diffuse infiltrating (older children, poor prognosis), placoid thickness of retina; RET cam (wide-angle fundus camera — useful in accurately documenting and monitoring response); USG B-scan (irregular mass with high internal reflectivity indicating intralesional calcification); CT (extraocular extension, pinealoblastoma detection); MRI (optic nerve involvement, intracranial extension). **Classification:** **International Classification of Retinoblastoma (logical flow of sequential tumour staging correlated with outcome of newer therapeutic modalities):** Group A — small tumour (< 3 mm in basal dimension/thickness); Group B — large tumour (> 3 mm basal/thickness, macular location < 3 mm from foveola, juxtapapillary location < 1.5 mm from disc, clear subretinal fluid < 3 mm from margin); Group C — focal seeds (C1 subretinal seeds > 3 mm from margin, C2 vitreous seeds < 3 mm from retinoblastoma, C3 both subretinal and vitreous seeds < 3 mm); Group D — diffuse seeds (D1 subretinal seeds > 3 mm from retinoblastoma, D2 vitreous seeds > 3 mm, D3 both); Group E — extensive retinoblastoma (occupying > 50% of globe, neovascular glaucoma, opaque media, invasion of optic nerve/choroid/sclera/orbit/anterior chamber). **Staging (clinico-histopathological prognosticating survival after enucleation):** stage I — no enucleation but one or both eyes may have intraocular RB; stage II — post-enucleation, tumour completely resected; stage III — post-enucleation with microscopic residual tumour (IIIa regional extension — overt orbital retinoblastoma; IIIb periocular/cervical lymph node extension); stage IV — metastatic disease (IVa haematogenous metastasis; IVb CNS involvement). **Management (highly individualised):** (1) **Group A/B:** focal cryotherapy/thermotherapy, transpupillary thermotherapy, followed by standard 6-cycle chemotherapy or plaque brachytherapy; for large tumours or small tumours in visually crucial areas not visually salvageable: followed by 6-cycle chemotherapy or plaque brachytherapy; if residual tumour large and non-regressing — bilateral: EBRT; unilateral: enucleation. (2) **Group C:** large tumours — focal cryotherapy, thermotherapy, transpupillary thermotherapy, followed by standard 6-cycle chemotherapy or plaque brachytherapy. (3) **Group D:** unilateral/bilateral with visual prognosis — high-dose chemotherapy with sequential aggressive focal therapy, periocular carboplatin for vitreous seeds; without visual prognosis — primary enucleation if unilateral. (4) **Group E:** primary enucleation; evaluate histopathology for high-risk factors. (5) **High-risk factor on HPE (stage II):** baseline metastasis evaluation, 6-cycle adjuvant chemotherapy, high-dose adjuvant chemotherapy with orbital EBRT for tumours recurring in orbit (secondary orbital RB). (6) **Extraocular tumour stage IIIa (primary orbital RB):** metastasis evaluation, high-dose chemotherapy 3–6 cycles, enucleation/exenteration followed by EBRT and continuation of high-dose chemotherapy for 12 cycles. (7) **Stage IIIb (regional lymph node):** metastasis evaluation, neck dissection, 12-cycle high-dose chemotherapy + EBRT. (8) **Stage IV:** very poor survival — palliative care with high-dose chemotherapy + EBRT.

column2: Write short notes on abnormal pupillary reflexes.
column4: **Afferent pathway defects:** (1) **Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)/Marcus Gunn pupil:** carries important clinical significance, most important clinical clue to diagnosis; detected by swinging flashlight test — bright light shone in one eye then shifted to other; normally both pupils constrict equally or maintain previous constriction (consensual response); second eye remains tightly constricted; in large retinal or optic nerve lesion, when light shifted to affected eye pupil fails to maintain constriction or dilates (afferent pathway of that eye affected). (2) **Wernicke's hemianopic pupillary response:** lesion in optic tract (carries fibres of ipsilateral temporal retina and contralateral nasal retina) — no direct and consensual reflex when light shown on temporal half of retina of affected side and nasal half of retina of normal side. **Efferent pupillary defects:** absence of direct and consensual light reflex along with absent near reflex on affected side. Causes: brainstem lesion (midbrain); third nerve lesion (infranuclear 3rd nerve palsy can cause abnormal dilatation of pupil with outward and downward deviated eyeball due to unopposed LR and SO; initial presentation of compressive mass lesion may be isolated pupillary involvement without muscle involvement); lesion in ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves (Adie's tonic pupil — light reflex absent or slow and slow/tonic near response with accommodative paresis); iris injury (secondary to surgery, accidental or homicidal trauma); drugs (cycloplegics — atropine, homatropine, cyclopentolate, tropicamide; sympathomimetics — phenylephrine). **Light-near dissociation:** light reaction to pupil absent but near response (pupillary constriction during accommodation) present; **Argyll Robertson pupil** — caused by neurosyphilis involving rostral midbrain; unless complicated by retinal disease, vision usually preserved; light reflex absent but near reflex present.

column2: What are the signs of optic nerve dysfunction? Write down the differential diagnosis of different types of scotomas of eye.
column4: **Signs of optic nerve dysfunction:** (1) dimness of vision (in some cases VA may be preserved); (2) RAPD detected by swinging flashlight test; (3) dyschromatopsia (impaired colour vision) tested by Ishihara chart; (4) reduced contrast sensitivity; (5) reduced light brightness sensitivity; (6) characteristic visual field defect. **Differential diagnosis of scotomas:** (1) **Central scotoma** — demyelinating optic neuropathy, toxic optic neuropathy, nutritional optic neuropathy, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, compressive optic neuropathy. (2) **Enlarged blind spot** — papilloedema, congenital optic nerve disorders. (3) **Scotomas respecting horizontal meridian** — anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, optic disc drusen, glaucomatous optic neuropathy. (4) **Scotomas not respecting vertical meridian** — tilted discs.

column2: Classify optic neuropathy.
column4: **Classification by etiology:** (1) **Inflammatory** — optic neuritis. (2) **Hereditary** — Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. (3) **Ischaemic** — anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (non-arteritic and arteritic); posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy; diabetic papillopathy. (4) **Toxic** — various toxins/drugs. (5) **Nutritional** — vitamin B complex deficiency. (6) **Traumatic.** (7) **Compressive** — secondary to orbital lesion. (8) **Infiltrative** — sarcoidosis, metastatic, neoplastic. (9) **Papilloedema** — secondary to raised intracranial pressure.

column2: Define optic neuritis. Classify it and describe clinical features
column5: **Definition:** inflammatory, progressive optic neuropathy due to loss of insulating myelin sheath of optic nerve; frequently associated with similar demyelination of white matter tracts of brain, brainstem and spinal cord. **Classification — by site:** (1) **Retrobulbar optic neuritis** — optic disc remains normal; most common in adults; associated with multiple sclerosis. (2) **Papillitis** — predominant involvement of optic nerve head; most common in children. (3) **Neuroretinitis** — papillitis with involvement of retinal nerve fibre layer and macular star formation; rare. **By etiology:** (1) **Demyelinating** — associated with multiple sclerosis. (2) **Parainfectious** — following viral infection or immunisation. (3) **Infections** — cat scratch disease, syphilis, Lyme disease, cryptococcal meningitis, herpes zoster infection. (4) **Non-infectious** — sarcoidosis, SLE, polyarteritis nodosa. **Pathophysiology:** myelin sheath progressively phagocytosed by microglial cells and macrophages → fibrous tissue deposition in form of plaques by astrocytes → disruption of neural conduction. **Clinical spectrum (demyelinating diseases involving visual pathway):** (1) isolated optic neuritis — demyelination of optic nerve without systemic involvement; (2) multiple sclerosis — idiopathic demyelinating disease involving white matter of CNS; female predilection; manifests 3rd–4th decade; relapsing-remitting course; (3) Devic disease (neuromyelitis optica) — bilateral optic neuritis progressing within weeks into transverse myelitis; rare autoimmune; antibody against aquaporin-4 protein in astrocyte cell membranes; (4) Schilder disease — rare progressive in children (< 10 years); potentially lethal (death within 1–2 years); bilateral progressive optic neuritis with generalised demyelination. **Symptoms:** uniocular visual impairment; white or coloured flashes (phosphenes); pain around eye exacerbating on ocular movement (present in 90%, may precede or accompany visual loss); frontal headache. **Signs:** BCVA 6/18 to 6/60 (may be worse); red-green colour vision defect; RAPD; mostly retrobulbar optic neuritis shows normal posterior segment; temporal disc pallor of fellow eye indicates prior attack. **Investigations:** (1) Humphrey visual field — diffuse depression, altitudinal field defect (respects horizontal meridian); (2) VEP — prolonged latency and decreased amplitude; (3) MRI — STIR (short T1 inversion recovery, low signal from fat, high from water; ideal for retrobulbar optic neuritis), FLAIR (fluid attenuated inversion recovery, better visualisation of periventricular plaques suggestive of MS), gadolinium-enhanced T1 (enhancement of optic nerve); (4) lumbar puncture and CSF protein electrophoresis — oligoclonal bands. **Prognosis:** vision worsens up to 3 weeks; after 3 weeks rapid initial recovery then slow over 6–12 months (self-resolving); 90% recover to 6/9 or better; 10% develop chronic optic neuritis with slowly progressive loss; mild red-green colour defect and RAPD may persist. **Associated multiple sclerosis — systemic features:** spinal cord (sphincter disturbance, sensory loss, motor weakness); brainstem (diplopia, nystagmus, dysarthria, dysphagia); cerebral (hemianopia, hemiparesis, dysphasia); psychological (depression, mood swings, intellectual deterioration); **Lhermitte sign** (electrical sensation on flexion of neck); **Uhthoff phenomenon** (sudden worsening of vision on exercise or increased body temperature). 15-year risk of MS following acute monocular optic neuritis — 50% without MRI lesion (reduced to 25% with one or more MRI lesions — increased to 70%); association with HLA DR15 and DQ6. **Treatment:** (1) visual recovery is self-limiting; (2) pulse methylprednisolone IV followed by oral prednisolone × 10 days speeds up visual recovery for 2–3 weeks and delays onset of clinical MS; (3) oral prednisolone without preceding IV methylprednisolone increases risk of relapse; (4) risk-benefit of steroid therapy evaluated well (TB ruled out, concurrent glycaemic control ensured); methylprednisolone sodium succinate 1 g IV daily × 3 days → from 4th day tab prednisolone 1–1.5 mg/kg at 8 AM ODPC × 11 days with PPI. **Disease-modifying agents for MS:** first episode with MRI-proven/clinically proven MS — interferon beta 1b 250 mg SC alternate day, interferon beta 1a 30 mg IM weekly, or glatiramer acetate 20 mg SC daily; relapsing active MS — natalizumab 300 mg IV monthly, mitoxantrone 12 mg/m² IV every 3 months (max 140 mg/m²), alemtuzumab, cladribine, fingolimod; progressive MS — ocrelizumab 300 mg IV repeated after 2 weeks, then 600 mg IV every 6 months.

column2: Write short notes on ischaemic optic neuropathy.
column4: **Types:** (1) **Non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION):** pathogenesis — partial or total infarction of optic nerve head secondary to occlusion of short posterior ciliary arteries. Risk factors — small optic nerve head (crowded disc), high hypermetropia, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, collagen vascular disease, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, hyperhomocysteinaemia, sudden hypotension, post-cataract surgery, sleep apnoea syndrome. Symptom — sudden painless uniocular dimness of vision. Signs — diffuse hyperaemic disc swelling, peripapillary splinter haemorrhages, pale swollen disc, moderate reduction in visual acuity. Investigations — FBS/PPBS, lipid profile, physician referral for BP control and systemic disease. Prognosis — self-limiting, VA may improve, recurrence rate 6%, fellow eye involvement 10% after 2 years. (2) **Arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION):** pathogenesis — occurs due to giant cell arteritis (GCA); 50% of patients have polymyalgia rheumatica (pain and stiffness in proximal muscle groups); GCA is granulomatous (necrotising) arteritis affecting large and medium arteries — superficial temporal, ophthalmic, posterior ciliary, proximal vertebral. Risk factors — smoking, low body mass index, early menopause, age > 50 years, women. Diagnosis — American College of Rheumatology criteria: age ≥ 50 years, new onset headache, temporal artery tenderness or reduced pulsation, ESR > 50 mm/h, temporal artery biopsy showing vasculitis. Ocular features — sudden severe uniocular dimness of vision, periocular pain. Investigations — CBC (elevated platelets, normocytic normochromic anaemia), ESR and CRP (raised), LFT (abnormal in 1/3), temporal artery biopsy (steroid treatment never withheld if biopsy delayed; ideally performed within 3 days of starting steroids; at least 2.5 cm of artery collected), colour Doppler USG of temporal artery, colour Doppler USG/MRA/PET of extracranial large vessels (rule out dissecting aneurysm of aorta). **Treatment:** visual loss in affected eye is irreversible; treatment done to prevent fellow eye — IV pulse methylprednisolone 1 g/day × 3 days followed by tab prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg ODPC × 4 weeks, then tapered over 2 months.

column2: Write short notes on optic atrophy.
column4: **Definition:** advanced damaged state of optic nerve occurring due to axonal degeneration in the afferent visual pathway between retina and lateral geniculate body. **Types:** (1) **Primary optic atrophy** — occurring without antecedent swelling of optic nerve head; causes — optic neuritis, optic nerve compression due to tumours and aneurysms, hereditary optic neuropathies, trauma, nutritional/toxic optic neuropathy; signs — clearly demarcated margins, flat white disc; **band atrophy** — due to lesions in optic chiasma or tract there is both nasal and temporal pallor. (2) **Secondary optic atrophy** — occurring with antecedent long-standing swelling of optic nerve head; causes — chronic papilloedema, papillitis, anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy; signs — obscured disc margin, greyish raised white optic disc, peripapillary retinochoroidal folds (Paton lines). (3) **Consecutive optic atrophy** — occurring secondary to disease of inner retina; causes — retinal vascular occlusion, excessive PRP, retinitis pigmentosa. (4) **Glaucomatous optic atrophy** — occurring in end-stage glaucoma.

column2: What are the causes of optic disc oedema? Outline the clinical features and management of papilloedema.
column4: **Causes of optic disc oedema:** papilloedema; accelerated hypertension; anterior optic neuropathy; Leber hereditary optic neuropathy; disc oedema secondary to intraocular disease (retinal vein occlusion, chronic uveitis, posterior scleritis, ocular hypotony, methanol poisoning). **Diseases mimicking optic disc oedema (pseudo-papilloedema):** tilted optic disc, optic disc drusen, crowded optic disc in high hypermetropia, peripapillary myelinated nerve fibres. **Papilloedema — definition:** swelling or oedema of optic disc/optic nerve head secondary to raised intracranial pressure. **Systemic features:** headache (especially morning, worsens with bending and head movement), nausea, deteriorated alertness, psychological symptoms. **Ocular clinical findings (always bilateral and symmetrical):** (1) **early stage** — visual acuity preserved, mild disc hyperaemia, preservation of optic cup, circumpapillary retinochoroidal folds (Paton lines). (2) **established stage** — visual acuity preserved, severely hyperemic disc, obscured disc margin, loss of physiological cup. (3) **chronic stage** — VA may be reduced, visual field constricted, elevated pale disc, no haemorrhage, no cotton wool spots, corpora amylacea (drusen-like crystalline deposits on disc surface). (4) **secondary optic atrophy stage** — same as secondary optic atrophy, obscured disc margin, greyish raised white optic disc, peripapillary retinochoroidal folds. **Investigations:** (1) MRI — rule out space-occupying lesions; (2) USG B-scan — measures external diameter of optic nerve head (ONSD); at 3 mm behind globe, ONSD > 5.7 mm indicates papilloedema; in lateral gaze ONSD reduces 10% in fluid-accumulated optic nerve head oedema; (3) lumbar puncture — detects raised intracranial pressure; should be done after neuroimaging rules out brainstem SOL (LP contraindicated due to risk of brain herniation).

column2: Write short notes on idiopathic intracranial hypertension (benign intracranial hypertension/pseudotumour cerebri).
column4: **Definition:** clinical condition characterised by raised intracranial tension with no associated detectable cause. **Risk factors:** obese young adult females; oral contraceptive pills; SLE; obstructive sleep apnoea; Lyme disease. **Systemic features:** persistent headache; nausea and projectile vomiting; pulsatile tinnitus; cranial nerve palsies. **Ocular features:** bilateral papilloedema; vision usually retained but 1/4 cases end up having variable degrees of permanent visual impairment. **Investigations:** MRI — slit-like ventricles, empty sella syndrome (flattening of pituitary gland); MRV — rule out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; USG B-scan — increased ONSD (optic nerve sheath diameter). **Treatment:** (1) weight loss; (2) ophthalmologist monitors vision and identifies early signs of optic nerve compression; (3) medical management by neurologist — acetazolamide, furosemide, digoxin; (4) if optic nerve compression — optic nerve fenestration (guarded visual prognosis); (5) IV mannitol or lumbar puncture only if severe exacerbation of ICT; (6) IV or oral steroids — controversial role.

column2: Write short notes on binocular single vision.
column4: **Definition (Romano and Romano):** state of simultaneous vision with two seeing eyes, neither of which needs necessarily be normal, which occurs when an individual fixes attention on an object of regard. **Prerequisites:** (1) both eyes must have proper fixation; (2) simultaneous overlap of visual fields of both eyes to a large extent; (3) image formed by retina of each eye must be closely similar in size, shape, colour, intensity; (4) normal retinal correspondence; (5) normal ocular movements and ocular reflexes. **Developmental milestones:** at birth — roving eyes with no central fixation; 1 month — fixation reflex starts to develop; 4 months — fixation reflex established; 6 months — macular stereopsis and accommodation reflex established; 6–7 years — full establishment of BSV and visual acuity. **Grades and tests:** (1) **Stage I — simultaneous perception:** signals transmitted by two eyes to visual cortex perceived at same time; does not imply both eyes seeing same object or superimposition of unrelated images; test — synaptophore-based plates (simultaneous perception of both eyes of a bird inside cage). (2) **Stage II — fusion:** ability to superimpose two incomplete but similar images to form one complete image; test — synaptophore-based plates (right eye incomplete + left eye incomplete; both eyes see complete image). (3) **Stage III — stereopsis:** ability to perceive third dimension (depth perception); tests — Titmus stereo test (polaroid material with two targets imprinted, polarised 90° to each other; house fly, animals, circle test; threshold of fine stereopsis quantified in seconds of arc; more reliable than Titmus — devoid of monocular clues); TNO random dot test (booklet with seven stereographic plates containing stereoscopic figures hidden within nonstereoscopic figures; requires red-green spectacles; first three plates for presence of gross stereopsis, rest for quantification of stereopsis); Lang test (panographic presentation of stereoscopic images in same plate; cylindrical lenses imprinted on surface causing unilateral disparity; does not require spectacles — popular among children; card held 40 cm in front of subject); Frisby test (does not require glasses — useful in small children; three stereoscopic cards with four squares of small random shape; one square in each plate has disparately placed circle); Random Dot E-test (three cards, held 50 cm in front of eye, polaroid glasses required; devoid of monocular clues — more reliable than Titmus); optokinetic nystagmus test currently considered test of stereoscopic potential in infants. **Two-pencil test:** primitive test to see presence or absence of gross stereopsis; stereopsis present if patient can appose both tips with both eyes open.

column2: Discuss differential diagnosis and management of esotropia in a 2-year-old child.
column4: **Differential diagnosis:** (1) **Concomitant strabismus** — infantile esotropia, accommodative esotropia, essential acquired non-accommodative esotropia, sensory esotropia, consecutive esotropia, esotropia associated with syndromes. (2) **Incomitant strabismus** (not very common) — hypoplasia/absence of 6th nerve nucleus, birth trauma, traumatic injury to LR or VI nerve, VI nerve palsy as false localising sign for intracranial lesions. **Evaluation:** (1) **history** — acute onset (incomitant), gradual onset (concomitant); infantile esotropia 2–4 months, manifests within first 6 months; accommodative esotropia 2–3 years; essential acquired non-accommodative after 6 months. (2) **slit lamp** — rule out sensory deprivation by cataract, ptosis, aphakia, retinoblastoma, retinal pathologies. (3) **uniocular and binocular ocular movements** in all cardinal positions of gaze. (4) **direct cover test and alternate cover test** — if primary deviation = secondary deviation, explore concomitant causes; if secondary > primary, explore incomitant causes. (5) **pupillary light reflex** — health of optic nerve up to visual cortex. (6) **estimation of angle of deviation** — Hirschberg corneal reflex (1 mm deviation = 7°; 45° at limbus, 70° at medial/lateral canthus, 30° at midpoint of pupillary border and limbus, 15° at pupillary base); prism bar cover test (PBCT — prisms with increasing strength with apex toward direction of deviation, alternate cover test until no refixating movement; near and distance in all cardinal gazes; measures deviation in prism dioptres); Krimsky's test (similar to PBCT, done with point source of light, prisms in front of normal eye); synaptophore (precise and accurate). (7) **assessment of sensory functions** — grade of BSV (Worth's four dot test: all four lights seen = BSV present; two red lights only = RE suppression; three green lights only = LE suppression; green and red lights alternate = alternating; two red + three green = presence of diplopia); retinal correspondence (synaptophore — subjective and objective angles of squint; normal retinal correspondence — subjective = objective; abnormal retinal correspondence — subjective < objective, angle of anomaly; harmonious ARC — angle of anomaly = objective angle; non-harmonious — smaller than objective angle); sensory fusion. (8) **in incomitant squint** — CT scan and MRI of brain and orbit; Hess chart. **Treatment:** (1) **cycloplegic refraction** — accommodative esotropia corrected by refractive correction with bifocal glasses (miotics in young children not tolerating bifocals); full refractive correction before planning surgeries. (2) **occlusion therapy for amblyopia** — normal eye occluded, patient encouraged to see through squinting eye to prevent strabismic amblyopia worsening; occlusion schedule — up to 2 years: 2 days normal eye: 1 day amblyopic; 3 years: 3:1; 4 years: 4:1; 5 years: 5:1; 6 years onwards: 6:1; amblyopic eye also occluded in older children to prevent amblyopia development in normal eye; continue until at least 8 years. (3) **squint surgery** — principles for esodeviation: bilateral MR recession (weakening), or unilateral MR recession + LR resection (strengthening); observations — bilateral surgery preferred with better results; 1 mm MR recession corrects roughly 2–3 PD, 1 mm LR resection corrects 2 PD; MR maximally recessed up to 7 mm; LR maximally resected up to 8 mm; surgery at early age (< 1 year) for better outcome. (4) **pre- and post-operative orthoptic exercises** (manual and synaptophore-based) to prevent and overcome suppression. (5) **incomitant/paralytic squint** — deviation must remain stable for at least 6 months before surgical intervention; treatment of underlying cause. (6) **sensory esotropia** — address cause of stimulation deprivation (cataract surgery, retinoblastoma management, PPV for posterior segment pathology).

column2: Describe approach to a patient with headache in ophthalmology OPD.
column4: **Definition:** headache is pain in any region of the head; may appear as sharp pain, throbbing sensation or dull ache; can develop gradually or suddenly; may last from less than an hour to several days. **Ophthalmological causes:** uncorrected refractive errors, ocular motility disorders, defects of accommodation, defects of convergence, ocular infections and inflammations, glaucoma, migraine. **Uncorrected refractive errors:** commonly young people present with dimness of vision; myopia — patients hold book closer to see better, more convergence, more headache; hypermetropia — more ciliary muscle activity to overcome error causes headache; astigmatism, anisometropia, imbalance of accommodation cause headache; management — cycloplegic refraction with correction. **Ocular motility disorders:** phoria (latent squint — discrepancy between deviation and amplitude of motor fusion; break fusion by occlusion to reveal); intermittent tropia; vertically incomitant horizontal heterotropia; management — optical (refraction under cycloplegia: exophoria under-correct by equal + power, esophoria maximum + power/bifocals, hyperphoria decentred lens, cyclophoria correct astigmatism), orthoptic (exercises with prisms or synaptophore). **Defects of accommodation:** decreased (presbyopia, insufficiency of accommodation, ill-sustained accommodation) — near vision glass with accommodative exercises; increased (excessive accommodation, spasm) — atropine eye drops with lens use for near vision. **Defects of convergence:** insufficiency (primary, high hypermetropia, myopia, presbyopia, muscle imbalance); spasm (functional, head trauma, pituitary tumours); management — insufficiency: refraction, convergence exercises, base-in prism; spasm: prolonged atropine, psychiatric workup. **Ocular infections and inflammation:** episcleritis (sectoral congestion, blanches on pressure, mild discomfort, recurrent history); scleritis (severe pain, photophobia, lacrimation, clear cornea, AC cells); hordeolum (lid swelling, purulent discharge); keratitis (corneal ulcer, peripheral ulcerative keratitis, Mooren's ulcer); uveitis (dimness of vision, severe pain, photophobia, lacrimation, ciliary congestion, AC cells/flare, constricted immobile pupil, KPs); orbital causes (preseptal cellulitis, orbital cellulitis, orbital pseudotumor); optic neuritis (middle-aged female, dimness, decreased colour, decreased contrast, pain on EOM). **Glaucoma:** acute angle-closure (ciliary congestion, corneal oedema, vertically oval mid-dilated non-reacting pupil, high IOP, mild AC reaction, other eye angle closed); chronic angle-closure (dull boring ocular pain, raised IOP, angle closure); lens-induced glaucoma (phacolytic, phacomorphic, phacotopic, phacoanaphylactic); inflammatory glaucoma; neovascular glaucoma; POAG. **Management:** angle-closure — urgent peripheral iridotomy; lens-induced — definitive lens extraction; other glaucomas — evaluation with antiglaucoma therapy. **Migraine:** U/L headache with/without aura, associated with nausea/vomiting, photophobia/phonophobia, recurrent; MR angiography — absence of communication between hemi-cranial circulation not uncommon; treatment — oral NSAIDs, caffeine, sumatriptan in acute attacks; calcium channel blocker (flunarizine), beta-blocker (propranolol), TCA (amitriptyline), topiramate prophylaxis.
