column2: Write short notes on vitamin A deficiency/keratophthalmia.
column4: **Definition:** xerophthalmia includes all ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency from structural changes in conjunctiva and cornea to physiological changes in retinal rods and cones. **Etiology:** dietary deficiency (e.g., protein-energy malnutrition); defective absorption from gut (e.g., measles infection). **Classification and clinical features:** (1) **XN (night blindness)** — earliest symptom in children. (2) **X1A (conjunctival xerosis)** — one or more patches of dry, lustreless, non-wettable conjunctiva in interpalpebral area (sand banks at receding tide). (3) **X1B (Bitot's spot)** — raised silvery white foamy triangular patch of keratinised epithelium, situated on bulbar conjunctiva in interpalpebral area; usually bilateral and in temporal quadrant. (4) **X2 (corneal xerosis)** — earliest change punctate keratopathy beginning from lower nasal quadrant; lack-lustre cornea. (5) **X3A and X3B (corneal ulceration/keratomalacia)** — colliquative necrosis: X3A < 1/3 corneal involvement, X3B > 1/3 corneal involvement; appearance of small peripheral ulcers with circular steep margins sharply demarcated → large central ulcers → total corneal melt. (6) **XS (corneal scars)** — healed stromal defects produce scars of different densities and locations. (7) **XFS (xerophthalmic fundus)** — seed-like raised whitish lesions scattered uniformly in central retina. **Treatment — prophylactic (WHO recommendation):** < 6 months: 50,000 IU orally single dose; 6–12 months or older < 8 kg: 1 lakh IU orally every 3–6 months; 1–6 years: 2 lakh IU orally every 6 months. **India-specific supplementation:** 1st dose 1 lakh IU at 9 months along with measles vaccine; 2nd dose 2 lakh IU at 18 months with DPT/OPV booster; 3rd dose 2 lakh IU at 2 years. **Therapeutic:** < 1 year or < 8 kg: 1 lakh IU orally / 50,000 IU IM stat and repeated after 24 hours and 4 weeks later; > 1 year: 2 lakh IU orally / 1 lakh IU IM stat and repeated after 24 hours and 4 weeks later; reproductive-age women irrespective of pregnancy: till stage X1B — 10,000 IU vitamin A sugar-coated tablet orally OD × 2 weeks; stage X2 (corneal xerosis) or worse — same dose as > 1 year infants. **Local ocular therapy:** artificial tear substitute; bandage soft contact lens; topical antibiotics for secondary infection. **Treatment of cause:** PEM, diarrhoea, sepsis.

column2: Write short notes on Vision 2020: The Right to Sight.
column4: **Introduction:** global initiative launched by WHO in Geneva on 18th February 1998 in collaboration with consortium of Task Force of International NGOs to effectively combat blindness. **Objectives:** (1) reduce global burden of blindness by 2020; (2) eliminate avoidable blindness by 2020. **Partners:** WHO; Task Force of International NGOs — International Agency for Prevention of Blindness (IAPB), ORBIS International, Sight Savers International, Lions Club International Foundation. **Implementation strategy:** four phases of 5-year plans — 1st phase 2000–2005, 2nd phase 2005–2010, 3rd phase 2010–2015, 4th phase 2015–till date. **Strategic approaches:** disease prevention and control; training of eye health personnel; strengthening existing eye care infrastructure; use of appropriate and affordable technology; mobilisation of resources. **Five major blinding eye diseases:** (1) **cataract** — aim to eliminate avoidable blindness by 2020 by cataract extraction with IOL; increasing cataract surgery rate (CSR — number of cataract surgeries per million per year); prevalence 0.5–1 per 1000 among children 0–15 years; target 32 million cataract surgeries by 2020. (2) **onchocerciasis** — no onchocerciasis in India; aim eliminate blindness by 2020; strategy community-directed treatment with annual doses of ivermectin. (3) **childhood blindness** — priority area; causes: vitamin A deficiency, measles, ophthalmia neonatorum, congenital cataract and glaucoma, ROP; measles immunisation and vitamin A supplementation; strengthening school eye screening; promoting surgical intervention. (4) **trachoma** — aim eliminate visual impairment due to refractive errors and other causes of low vision by 2020; strategy awareness, screening, provision of refractive services, affordable optical services, low vision assessment and low vision aids; SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial hygiene, Environmental changes); trachoma blindness no longer public health hazard in India; GET 2020 (Alliance for Global Elimination of Trachoma by 2020 organised by WHO). (5) **refractive errors and low vision.** **In India, three more conditions included under Vision 2020:** diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, corneal blindness. **Human resource development:** increase number of ophthalmologists per million; equitable distribution urban/rural; training and distribution of mid-level ophthalmic personnel (MLOP); management training. **Proposed infrastructure pyramid:** centres of excellence (COE) — professional leadership, strategy development, CME, research and quality assurance; training centres — tertiary eye care including retinal, glaucoma, corneal surgeries, training and research; service centres — cataract surgery, other anterior segment surgeries, refraction, functional referral network; vision centres — refraction, primary eye care, school eye screening, functional referral network.

column2: Describe the effect of blunt trauma on the eye (cricket ball injury).
column4: **Structures involved — signs, symptoms, treatment:** (1) **eyelids** — though rare, may result in partial/full-thickness defect involving skin and subcutaneous tissue; traumatic ptosis; non-marginal: close normally with 6-0 vicryl; marginal: apposition of grey line + 3-layered closure with 6-0 vicryl; conservative treatment with tetanus prophylaxis in exposed wound and systemic antibiotics. (2) **sclera and conjunctiva** — lamellar laceration, subconjunctival haemorrhage, conjunctival chemosis; dimness of vision, photophobia, pain; managed with topical antibiotics and patching. (3) **cornea** — corneal abrasion, lamellar corneal laceration, tears in Descemet's membrane, acute corneal oedema, blood staining of cornea; dimness of vision, photophobia, pain; erosions treated conservatively with topical antibiotics, patching and corneoloed; Descemet's tear — topical steroids and IOP-lowering agents; corneal blood staining — urgent paracentesis and AC wash. (4) **lens** — traumatic cataract (concussion cataract), subluxation/dislocation, traumatic absorption (young children), Vossius ring (circular ring of brown colour on anterior capsule due to impact of iris); cataract surgery with capsular support devices (hooks, tension rings); anterior dislocation — lensectomy + anterior vitrectomy + scleral-fixated IOL; posterior dislocation — PPV + phacofragmentation + scleral-fixated IOL implantation. (5) **iris and ciliary body** — traumatic mydriasis/miosis, rupture of pupillary margin, iridodialysis (D-shaped pupil), anteflexion/retroflexion of torn iris, traumatic aniridia (iris floats as ball in AC), radiating tear of iris; mydriasis/miosis require observation; any tear requires surgical reconstruction (pupilloplasty/iridoplasty); traumatic aniridia may require surgical removal of displaced iris and rehabilitation with aniridia contact lens; cycloplegic + steroids (cyclopentolate 1–2% and prednisolone acetate 0.12–1%). (6) **anterior chamber** — cells (WBC) and flare in AC under slit lamp (anterior uveitis); hyphaema (settled blood in AC, clot — 8-ball hyphema, diffuse); dull aching/throbbing pain, photophobia, onset mainly 3 days, blurred vision; management — bed rest, avoid strenuous work, propped-up posture, avoid patching (to check rebleed), cycloplegic (1–2% atropine TDS), avoid antiplatelets/anticoagulants, topical steroids, mild analgesics, IOP control with topical antiglaucoma drugs; indications for surgical intervention — corneal blood staining, significant visual deterioration, hyphaema > 50% in 8 days, IOP > 60 mmHg × 48 days or > 26 mmHg × 5 days, children (amblyopia). (7) **angle of anterior chamber** — angle recession and later angle-recession glaucoma; may precipitate acute glaucoma attack; long-term glaucoma monitoring, laser trabeculoplasty, trabeculectomy with antimetabolites ± glaucoma shunt devices, medical IOP lowering. (8) **retina and choroid** — commotio retinae (Berlin's oedema — milky white elevated posterior pole with cherry-red spot; dimness, may be asymptomatic; observation, spontaneous resolution within 6 weeks; visual prognosis poor if fovea involved; anti-VEGF intravitreal if CNVM develops); traumatic choroidal rupture (yellow/white crescent-shaped subretinal streak concentric to optic disc after severe trauma; rarely CNV; laser photocoagulation; anti-VEGF if CNVM); retinal break/detachment (if media clear — diagnosed by indirect ophthalmoscopy; if hazy — USG B-scan; breaks asymptomatic; RD if involves macula — sudden dimness, defective PR; breaks require barrage laser for sealing; RD requires surgical intervention with PPV); traumatic macular hole (lamellar or full-thickness; due to injury or during resolution of Berlin's oedema; diagnosis confirmed by OCT macular scan; if no RD — observation; if RD — immediate surgical intervention); surgical repair of macular hole; sudden dimness of vision. (9) **vitreous** — vitreous haemorrhage with/without RD; **Shafer sign** (pigment cells floating in anterior vitreous). (10) **optic nerve** — traumatic optic neuropathy (severe dimness, RAPD +ve, pulse methylprednisolone if within 48 hours, trans-ethmoidal optic nerve decompression, poor prognosis); optic nerve avulsion (complete/incomplete). (11) **orbit** — blowout fracture of orbital floor (diplopia, pain, subcutaneous emphysema; mild no entrapment on neuroimaging — observation; tissue entrapment with symptomatic diplopia — surgical correction with titanium plate); proptosis due to orbital haemorrhage; enophthalmos due to tissue entrapment through fracture line. **N.B.:** globe rupture may occur in blunt trauma with or without risk of intraocular/orbital foreign body; posterior segment evaluation and neuroimaging of brain and orbit to be done even in asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic cases.

column2: Write short notes on alkali burn of the eye.
column4: **Introduction:** alkali burn is a potentially blinding chemical assault on eyes and requires immediate ophthalmological intervention. **Mode of injury:** domestic accidents, agricultural accidents, chemical laboratory accidents, chemical warfare injuries, deliberate chemical attacks (more common with acids), self-inflicted chemical injuries (malingerers, psychopaths). **Agents:** liquid ammonia (most harmful), lime, caustic soda/potash. **Mechanism of injury:** alkalies decrease collagen synthesis by reducing ascorbate levels; hygroscopic extraction of water from cells; alkalies dissociate and saponify fatty acids of cell membrane → total cellular necrosis → destruction of cell membrane structure; alkalies combine with lipids of cells during cellular necrosis producing soluble compounds which cause softening and gelatinisation of tissue → deep tissue penetration. **Hence alkali burns are more dangerous than acid counterparts.** **Clinical features — grading by Roper-Hall (old) and Dua's (newer, more appropriate):** Roper-Hall — Grade I: clear cornea, no limbal ischemia, excellent prognosis; Grade II: hazy cornea, iris details visible, < 1/3 limbal ischemia, good prognosis; Grade III: opaque cornea, iris details not visible, 1/3–1/2 limbal ischemia, good to guarded prognosis; Grade IV: opaque cornea, no visibility of iris/pupils, > 1/2 limbal ischemia, poor to very poor prognosis. Dua's — Grade I: 0 clock hours, 0% conjunctival involvement, very good; Grade II: < 3 hours, < 30%, good; Grade III: > 3–6 hours, > 30–50%, good; Grade IV: > 6–9 hours, 50–75%, good to poor; Grade V: > 9–12 hours, 75–100%, poor to very poor; Grade VI: 12 hours, 100%. **Clinical course — three stages:** (1) **acute stage** (immediate to 1 week) — destruction of conjunctival and corneal epithelium; variable limbal ischemia; alkali-induced pH alteration leading to intraocular cell death; bimodal IOP rise (first peak hydration/shortening of collagen fibrils; second peak aqueous outflow obstruction). (2) **early reparative stage** (1–3 weeks) — replacement of destroyed cells and ECM; grade I/II: epithelial regeneration with clearing of stroma and synthesis of collagen; grade III+: epithelial regeneration does not begin/progress, stroma hazy, retrocorneal membrane formation, stromal ulceration from proteases. (3) **late reparative stage** (> 3 weeks) — grade I/II complete healing; grade III+: necrosis and melting with long-term complications. **Management — primary goals:** prevention of complications, restoration of intact epithelium, control of inflammatory reaction, support of reparative process. **Immediate:** irrigation with non-toxic liquid for minimum 30 minutes (tap water, normal saline, Ringer's lactate, BSS — efficacy same); pH measured from conjunctival cul-de-sac; if pH > 7 — stop; if pH < 7 — continue irrigation till normalises; after irrigation, thorough examination by double eversion of eyelid under topical anaesthesia — remove embedded particulate matter (lime particles removed by cotton-tip applicator). **Acute phase drug treatment:** topical steroids (severity-appropriate frequency; continue for 10 days then rapidly taper if epithelium not intact or ulcer developed); E/D 1% medroxyprogesterone acetate when steroids cannot be used for initial 10–14 days (suppresses corneal neovascularisation and ulceration); topical NSAIDs when epithelium intact (promptly discontinue if epithelial healing not as expected); broad-spectrum topical antibiotics (secondary bacterial infection); topical cycloplegics (ciliary spasm); antiglaucoma medications (IOP spikes — PG analogues avoided); tab ascorbate 500 mg QDS × 2 weeks + E/D 10% ascorbate hourly; tab doxycycline 100 mg BDPC × 2 weeks (inhibits MMP, prevents collagen destruction); liberal hourly preservative-free ATS drops/ointment; topical 20–40% autologous serum (improves epithelial healing). **Non-pharmacological:** bandage contact lens (prevents windshield wiper effect of eyelids); forniceal sweeping with ointment-coated glass rods twice daily or symblepharon ring (advanced injuries). **Intermediate-term:** mechanical debridement of necrotic tissue; amniotic membrane transplantation (grade II–III); tenoplasty/conjunctiva-Tenon advancement flap; BCL with tissue adhesives for small corneal perforation; therapeutic keratoplasty for melting corneas. **Late rehabilitation:** ocular surface rehabilitation (symblepharon lysis, fornicoplasty, cicatricial ectropion/entropion correction); limbal stem cell transplantation; optical penetrating keratoplasty (deferred until 18 months–2 years due to high failure); keratoprosthesis (recurrent corneal melting or PKP failure); management of secondary glaucoma.

column2: Write short notes on anti-VEGF agents.
column4: **Table of agents:** monoclonal antibody — bevacizumab 1.25 mg/0.05 ml; antibody derivative — ranibizumab 0.5 mg/0.05 ml; aptamer — pegaptanib 0.3 mg/90 μl; human recombinant fusion VEGF trap proteins — aflibercept 2.0 mg/0.05 ml. **Uses:** wet ARMD; macular oedema; diabetic macular oedema/proliferative diabetic retinopathy; macular oedema in retinal vein occlusion or neovascular retinopathy; myopic choroidal neovascularisation. **Side effects:** pain; bleeding (subconjunctival or vitreous haemorrhage); retinal tear leading to detachment or lenticular injury leading to cataract; endophthalmitis; increased intraocular pressure. **Contraindications:** fibrovascular proliferation threatening macula; active ocular or periocular inflammation; known hypersensitivity to drugs; uncontrolled hypertension; cardiovascular disease; pregnancy and lactation; pre-pubescent children.

column2: Write short notes on pilocarpine.
column4: **Source:** extracted from plant Pilocarpus microphyllus and related species; cholinomimetic agent with strong muscarinic action and weak ganglionic action. **Mechanism of action in eye:** stimulates muscarinic receptors of both ciliary muscle and circular muscle of iris to contract → changes direction of forces in iris → lessens ratio of iris with lens → central change of iris mass → pupillary block or iridolenticular contact broken → iridocorneal angle (angle of anterior chamber) freed → pupil constricted. If IOP is very high in acute attack of angle-closure glaucoma, pilocarpine fails to act. **Uses — as drops (2%):** causes 15–20% reduction of IOP; (1) after initial control of IOP by systemic medications, to release possible iridocorneal contact in acute angle-closure glaucoma attack (2% eye drop 3–4 times/day); (2) to prepare eye before laser peripheral iridotomy or surgical iridectomy in affected eye and prophylactically in fellow eye (2% eye drop at 10–15 minute intervals × 2–3 times); (3) long-term treatment in plateau iris syndrome (2% eye drop TDS). **As intracameral injection (1%):** to constrict pupil during surgery to check for vitreous strand in AC; to perform surgical iridectomy in cases of suspected future pupillary block by vitreous. **Side effects — ocular:** induced myopia; brow ache; reduction in peripheral vision and dim light vision; epiphora (direct lacrimal stimulation and punctal stenosis); iris pigment epithelial cysts; cataract formation; bleeding during surgery; increased iridocyclitis in post-operative patients; paradoxical angle-closure in phacomorphic angle-closure. **Systemic:** diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, increased salivation, bronchospasm.

column2: A 65-year-old patient presented with gradual painless dimness of vision in both eyes during last 2 years. Discuss the differential diagnosis and management.
column4: **Causes/differential diagnosis:** (1) disorders of refraction — especially presbyopia; (2) disorders of conjunctiva — progressive pterygium involving pupillary area; (3) disorders of cornea — corneal degenerations; (4) disorders of lens — senile cataract; (5) disorders of retina — diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, chorioretinal degeneration; (6) disorders of optic nerve — optic atrophy. **Approach to diagnosis — history:** occupation mandating significant outdoor activity → risk of progressive pterygium and senile cataract from UV exposure; Type II diabetic for long duration (> 5 years) or Type I diabetic → risk of diabetic retinopathy; known diabetic nephropathy or significant systemic involvement (post-CABG, CVA) → more risk of diabetic retinopathy; known POAG → risk of glaucomatous optic atrophy; past ocular trauma. **Ocular examination:** (1) **pinhole vision** (2 mm diameter) — if vision improves = uncorrected refractive errors or optical media opacities (immature cataract, vitreous haemorrhage, steroid hyalosis); if vision same as presenting = dense cataract or retino-optic pathway defects; if vision deteriorates = macular pathology. (2) **PAM testing** — tests retinal acuity in eyes with other media problems; projects Snellen eye chart via narrow beam converging to a 0.1 mm opening in less dense areas/windows within the media (e.g., cataract); identifies patients with coexisting ocular diseases (retinal or optic nerve pathologies) who may benefit from cataract surgery. (3) **Pupil examination** — sluggish direct reflex = retino-optic pathway; RAPD identified by neutral density filters = pathology of retinal ganglion cell layer and/or retino-optic pathway. (4) **keratometry** — irregular readings indicate irregular astigmatism secondary to corneal opacities (corneal degenerations) or progressive pterygium involving visual axis. (5) **slit lamp anterior segment** — cornea: progressive pterygium involving pupillary area, axial corneal degenerations (fatty/lipoid keratopathy — whitish/yellowish deposits secondary to corneal infections, trauma, glaucoma, chronic iridocyclitis; hyaline degeneration — hyaline spherules in superficial stroma secondary to old keratitis, long-standing glaucoma, trachomatous pannus; band-shaped keratopathy — calcific degeneration, calcium salts in Bowman's membrane and superficial stroma secondary to chronic uveitis, keratitis, ocular trauma, chronic renal failure, hypercalcaemia; age-related BSK can happen even in healthy corneas). (6) **lens examination** — slit lamp gives idea of location, morphology, sometimes etiology; cortical cataract, nuclear sclerosis grade I–IV, posterior subcapsular, anterior polar, anterior subcapsular, posterior polar; old KPs in corneal endothelium with iris pigment dispersion over anterior lens capsule and polychromatic lustre with bread-crumb appearance = complicated cataract; poor pupillary dilatation with pseudoexfoliative material on lens capsule and iris = cataract with pseudoexfoliation syndrome; subluxated/dislocated cataracts indicate poorer visual prognosis. (7) **posterior segment** — if dense cataract or corneal opacity, media not optically clear → USG B-scan (shallow RD, vitreous haemorrhages, exudates); if media clear → morphological assessment by 90D lens, 78D lens, indirect ophthalmoscope; diabetic retinopathy (dot/blot haemorrhages, exudates, IRMA, CSME, PDR or advanced diabetic eye disease); ARMD (drusen with pigmentary change at macula, geographic atrophy, wet ARMD). **Ocular investigations:** OCT (diabetic macular oedema with multiple optically clear cystic spaces; rupture of Bruch's membrane with macular morphology loss indicates choroidal neovascularisation due to wet ARMD); FFA (areas of retinal non-perfusion and leakage due to neovascularisation). **Management:** (1) **corneal degenerations** — clear lens and viable posterior segment: PKP or DALK (DALK preferred over PKP due to lesser chance of rejection and complications); with significant cataract: triple procedure (PKP/DALK + cataract extraction + IOL in bag); nonviable retino-optic pathway: no available treatment. (2) **progressive pterygium** — pterygium excision with conjunctival autografting (suture/glue/autoblood fixation) ± mitomycin C; corneal transplantation (PKP/DALK) if significant corneal involvement. (3) **cataract** — phacoemulsification with PCIOL insertion (preferably multifocal IOL) posterior chamber foldable IOL. (4) **diabetic retinopathy** — with significant cataract: pre-cataract/intraoperative anti-VEGF intravitreal injection to control diabetic macular oedema; post-cataract serial monthly OCT-guided intravitreal anti-VEGF; PDR: PPV + phacoemulsification; without significant cataract: anti-VEGF monthly guided by OCT + focal laser + PRP for PDR. (5) **ARMD** — dry ARMD: dietary supplements and antioxidants, cessation of smoking; wet ARMD: intravitreal anti-VEGF injections. (6) **refractive error** — presbyopia: +2.50 to +2.75 Dsph near addition; myopia: concave lens; hypermetropia: convex lens; astigmatism: cylindrical lens; refractive surgeries — presbyopia: femtosecond laser-assisted PRESBYOND; myopia: SMILE/LASIK; hypermetropia: hyperopic LASIK; astigmatism: astigmatic LASIK/toric IOL after cataract extraction.
column6: Gradual Painless Dimness of Vision — Differential Diagnosis

column2: Enumerate the possible causes of sudden painful dimness of vision in a 35-year-old female patient. Briefly discuss the signs
column3: symptoms and management of any one cause.
column5: **Causes:** (1) **Disease of cornea** — corneal ulcer. (2) **Glaucoma** — acute angle-closure glaucoma. (3) **Ocular injury** — mechanical blunt trauma, perforating and penetrating ocular trauma, chemical injury by acids/alkalis. (4) **Diseases of uvea** — acute anterior uveitis. (5) **Diseases of optic nerve** — retrobulbar optic neuritis, orbital apex syndrome (Tolosa-Hunt syndrome). **Acute angle-closure glaucoma (detailed example):** symptoms — severe pain, nausea/vomiting, rapidly progressive diminution of vision, redness, photophobia, lacrimation; often in evening due to mid-dilated pupil in dusk; may have past history of intermittent subacute attacks. Signs — lid oedematous; conjunctiva chemosed and congested (ciliary + conjunctival vessels); cornea oedematous; anterior chamber shallow with cells and flare; angle closed; iris discoloured; pupil unreactive, mid-dilated, vertically oval; IOP markedly elevated (40–70 mmHg); optic nerve head oedematous and hyperaemic; fellow eye shows shallow AC and narrow angle. **Management:** (1) **medical** — supine position; measure IOP; if > 40 mmHg: IV mannitol 20% 1 g/kg + IV acetazolamide 500 mg + E/D pilocarpine 2% every 30 min × 2 hours + E/D timolol 0.5% BD + E/D prednisolone acetate 1% QID + oral acetazolamide 250 mg QDS + analgesic + antiemetics; if < 40 mmHg: E/D pilocarpine 2% every 30 min + E/D timolol 0.5% BD + E/D prednisolone acetate 1% QID + oral acetazolamide 250 mg QDS. (2) **prophylactic treatment of normal fellow eye** — prophylactic laser peripheral iridotomy after instilling 1% pilocarpine. (3) **surgical** — peripheral iridotomy when PAS < 50% of AC angle; filtration surgery when PAS > 50%; clear lens extraction when medical therapy fails or non-compliance.

column2: What are the causes of red eye? Write in brief about their diagnosis and management.
column4: **Causes of red eyes:** (1) **Diseases of conjunctiva** — acute conjunctivitis, subconjunctival haemorrhage. (2) **Diseases of cornea** — keratitis, corneal ulcer. (3) **Diseases of uvea** — iridocyclitis. (4) **Glaucoma** — acute angle-closure glaucoma, lens-induced glaucoma. (5) **Ocular injuries.** (6) **Endophthalmitis.** (7) **Panophthalmitis.** **Diagnosis and management — conjunctivitis:** (a) **diagnostic pearls** — conjunctival congestion marked in bacterial (moderate in viral and chlamydial); marked chemosis in bacterial and allergic; huge subconjunctival haemorrhages in viral haemorrhagic and some bacterial; discharge — purulent/mucopurulent (bacterial), watery (viral), ropy (allergic), frank mucopurulent (chlamydial); papillae most common in allergic (cobblestone/pavement stone pattern; Horner-Tranta spots); follicles more prominent in lower palpebral conjunctiva and lower fornices in viral (chlamydial — follicles resembling boiled sago grains in upper tarsal conjunctiva and upper fornix; Herbert follicles in limbal area); pseudomembrane more common in advanced bacterial and viral; typical pannus in chlamydial; preauricular lymphadenopathy most common with viral (sometimes bacterial); cytoplasmic inclusion bodies in pox viral and chlamydial, nuclear inclusion bodies in herpetic. (b) **management** — bacterial: topical 4th-generation fluoroquinolone eye drop and ointment + supportive (conjunctival sac irrigation, dark goggles, SOS anti-inflammatory and analgesic drugs); enteroviral and adenoviral: no specific treatment; HSV: acyclovir eye ointment; chlamydial: tetracycline eye ointment + oral tetracycline 250 mg BD × 3–4 weeks. **Keratitis and corneal ulcer:** (a) **diagnostic pearls** — ulcerative (bacterial, fungal, protozoal) vs nonulcerative (mainly viral); bacterial corneal ulcer: yellowish-white area oval/irregular, floor covered with necrotic material, margins swollen and overhanging, peri-ulcer stromal oedema; Staph/Strep — oval densely opaque, peri-ulcer clear cornea; Pseudomonas — irregular margin, peri-ulcer ground-glass appearance, greenish mucopurulent exudation; Enterobacteria — shallow ulcer, ring-shaped peri-ulcer corneal infiltrate; protozoan: central/paracentral ring-shaped infiltrate with stromal opacities; HSV: superficial punctate keratitis, dendritic ulcer, geographic ulcer, disciform keratitis (delayed hypersensitivity to HSV antigen); herpes zoster: punctate epithelial lesions, peripheral microdendritic ulcers, nummular and disciform keratitis, characteristic skin lesions. (b) **management** — bacterial: topical fluoroquinolone eye drop and ointment; non-responding: culture sensitivity-guided reconstituted fortified drops; HSV: acyclovir eye ointment; HZO: oral and topical acyclovir; topical steroids in viral keratitis when active lesions absent; cycloplegics for pain and photophobia. **Iridocyclitis:** (a) **diagnostic pearls** — loss of iris pattern, muddy iris, keratic precipitates, iris nodules, cells and flare in AC, posterior synechiae, sterile hypopyon, complicated cataract. (b) **management** — investigations for granulomatous and non-granulomatous causes; topical corticosteroids, mydriatics, cycloplegics and IOP-lowering drugs. **Acute angle-closure glaucoma:** (a) **diagnostic pearls** — acute pain, redness, dimness; lid oedematous; corneal oedema; mid-dilated vertically oval fixed pupils; conjunctival chemosis; shallow anterior chamber; gonioscopy — closed angle. (b) **management** — systemic IV hyperosmotic agents; topical pilocarpine and IOP-lowering drugs (PG analogues avoided); oral acetazolamide; YAG peripheral iridotomy of affected eye when corneal oedema subsides; prophylactic YAG PI in fellow eye if occludable angle; lens-induced glaucoma: cataract extraction with in-the-bag PCIOL insertion.

column2: What are the causes of seeing rainbow halo around light? Describe the management of one such cause having severe pain in the eye.
column4: **Causes of rainbow halo:** (1) acute angle-closure glaucoma; (2) immature cataract; (3) mucopurulent conjunctivitis; (4) corneal oedema due to different causes like bullous keratopathy. **Management of acute angle-closure glaucoma:** **history** — severe pain (acute onset), photophobia, redness, sudden dimness of vision; past history of repeated attacks; may have YAG laser peripheral iridectomy in affected eye or fellow eye; may have history of pharmacological pupillary dilatation or prolonged dark room activity. **Examination:** (1) visual acuity — acute sudden painful dimness suggests acute attack; (2) **Fincham's stenopaeic slit test** (differentiates coloured halos from cataract vs glaucoma) — stenopaeic slit moved across patient's eye while patient looks at bright point source of light giving rise to halo; halo caused by immature cataract breaks into a fan whose blades seem to move (peculiar disposition of lens fibres causing diffraction of light parallel to meridian of slit); halo caused by glaucoma remains unchanged or becomes little faint. (3) anterior segment evaluation under slit lamp — lids may be oedematous; ciliary congestion; conjunctival chemosis; variable degree of diffuse stromal oedema; mid-dilated vertically oval fixed pupils not reacting to light or accommodation; if corneal oedema less, gonioscopy shows completely closed angle; shallow anterior chamber; may have non-patent peripheral iridotomy scar; IOP very high (40–70 mmHg); fellow eye may also show shallow AC with occludable angle. **Management:** (1) **medical** — supine position; measure IOP; if > 40 mmHg: IV mannitol 20% 1 g/kg + IV acetazolamide 500 mg + E/D pilocarpine 2% every 30 min × 2 hours + E/D timolol 0.5% BD + E/D prednisolone acetate 1% QID + oral acetazolamide 250 mg QDS + analgesic + antiemetics; if < 40 mmHg: E/D pilocarpine 2% every 30 min + E/D timolol 0.5% BD + E/D prednisolone acetate 1% QID + oral acetazolamide 250 mg QDS. (2) **prophylactic treatment of normal fellow eye** — prophylactic laser peripheral iridotomy after instilling 1% pilocarpine. (3) **surgical** — peripheral iridotomy when PAS < 50% of AC angle; filtration surgery when PAS > 50%; clear lens extraction when medical therapy fails or non-compliance.

column2: Write short notes on uses of atropine.
column4: **Mechanism of action:** competitive antagonist of parasympathetic acetylcholine muscarinic receptors; inhibits circular pupillary sphincter muscle → mydriasis (radial dilator muscles unopposed); paralyses ciliary muscles → complete loss of accommodation. **Topical formulations:** 1% atropine sulphate ophthalmic solution; 1% atropine sulphate ophthalmic ointment. **Dosage:** for wet retinoscopy TDS × 3 days; for therapeutic purposes up to TDS till resolution of symptoms. **Adverse effects — ocular:** pain and stinging on application (especially children/elderly due to systemic absorption from nasal mucosa); blurring of vision; photophobia; decreased lacrimation; superficial keratitis with prolonged use; conjunctival hyperaemia and chemosis after topical use; allergic conjunctivitis due to hypersensitivity; eyelid chemosis due to hypersensitivity in very small children. **Systemic:** fever (especially children), hypotension, arrhythmia (usually transient), CNS complications (ataxia, restlessness, delirium, hallucinations, somnolence), dry mouth, dysphagia, constipation (transient after topical application), hypersensitivity reactions. **Uses as mydriatic — diagnostic:** posterior segment evaluation especially in small children and patients not dilating well with standard mydriatics (tropicamide, phenylephrine); mydriatic provocation test in suspected angle-closure glaucoma. **Uses as mydriatic — therapeutic:** adequate and maximal pupillary dilatation in small children requiring cataract surgery or posterior segment surgery; maximal pupillary dilatation in adults poorly responding to conventional mydriatics before cataract and/or posterior segment surgeries; to prevent development or break already established posterior synechiae in anterior uveitis; to relieve pupillary block due to anterior dislocation of microspherophakic lens (**inverse glaucoma**). **Uses as cycloplegic — diagnostic:** objective refraction (wet retinoscopy) in children < 5 years and high hypermetropic adults (1% ointment preferred; peak effect 2–3 days; retinoscopy on 4th day after TDS × 3 days; effect remains till 20 days; post-cycloplegic subjective verification after 3 weeks; tonus allowance ~1D). **Therapeutic:** relieving ocular pain due to ciliary muscle spasm in acute corneal ulcer, acute anterior and intermediate uveitis, acute keratitis, acute endophthalmitis, accommodative convergent squint, relieving accommodative spasm in neovascular glaucoma; as penalisation treatment for amblyopia. **Contraindications:** cautiously used in angle-closure glaucoma, Down syndrome, spastic paralysis, or any other CNS disorders; infants with systemic adverse reactions to atropine sulphate have increased susceptibility. **Recent advancement:** low-dose atropine sulphate ophthalmic solution reduces myopic progression in children by slowing axial elongation.

column2: How will you counsel a patient with known glaucoma?
column4: **Glaucoma is a potentially blinding disorder:** affects peripheral vision initially; visual acuity and central vision affected only at advanced stage; at advanced stage treatment options are few and outcome poor. **Glaucoma counsellor:** treating ophthalmologist is best counsellor (busy clinic may not permit); any hospital staff trained in glaucoma counselling (optometrists, nurses, social welfare officers, community health workers are good candidates); **glaucoma care team** comprising ophthalmologist (complete control and overview of patient care and counselling), glaucoma nurse (pre and post-operative care, rapid assessment of complications), glaucoma-trained optometrist (vision test, applanation tonometry and other glaucoma diagnostic tests), glaucoma counsellor (comprehensive counselling, maintenance of glaucoma register). **Purpose of counselling:** help patient understand current status of glaucoma; understand long-term and short-term prognosis; accept status of 'guarded visual prognosis' (amount of visual disability occurred will remain — treatment will prevent further deterioration); make informed decision regarding treatment options (medical, surgical, both with clinician's advice, adjunct laser); improve compliance and adherence to medical treatment (lifelong); find additional requirements beyond glaucoma services (diabetic retinopathy clinic, low vision clinic); alleviate fear regarding glaucoma and improve quality of life. **Glaucoma counselling:** development of personal relationship based on trust with patient and caregivers; counsellor should be good listener and allow patient to express in own vernacular words; unearth patient's understanding of current disease status (bridge the gap); **two pillars** — choosing appropriate treatment modalities and lifelong adherence/compliance: surgery reserved for failure of maximal medical therapy, non-compliance, severe adverse reactions; laser as adjunct to medical therapy; laser PI to normal eye in acute attack of angle closure; correct method to instil topical medications; explain possible ocular and systemic adverse reactions of anti-glaucoma medications; explain glaucoma drugs should not be discontinued during hospitalisation, personal grief, hearsay advice; sudden discontinuation can worsen glaucomatous damage; explain lifelong follow-up to stop progression and preserve useful vision; eye-drop dispensing aids for better compliance; glaucoma has genetic predisposition (runs in families) — counsel for glaucoma screening of first-degree relatives; breaking bad news for patients with advanced glaucoma and proper visual rehabilitation with low vision aids.

column2: How will you counsel an adult patient for correctly applying eye drops and eye ointment?
column4: **Topical administration** of eye drops and ointments are pillars of ophthalmic drug therapy indicated for various ophthalmological diseases and post-operative care. **Principle:** topical medications must have same priority as systemically administered drugs; prior knowledge of possible immediate and long-term adverse effects (e.g., pupillary dilator drops can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma); potential drug interactions between co-administered topical or systemic drugs (e.g., topical timolol may reduce effect of insulin); **'5 C's'** of topical drug administration — correct time of instillation, correct eye to be instilled, correct person to be instilled, correct strength of instillation, correct route of instillation. **Prerequisites:** confirm patient is not allergic/sensitive to drug; for dilator drops, counsel regarding loss of accommodation and photophobia; in open globe injury, ensure topical formulations are preservative-free; ensure whether prevention of systemic absorption is required; confirm date of expiry; explain properly. **Strategies to avoid systemic absorption:** keeping eye closed for slow count of 60 after administration; digital pressure to tear drainage system at nasal corner of closed eyelids after administration; in high-risk cases, punctal plugs for complete safeguard. **Procedure for eye drop instillation:** comfortable positioning with head support; hand wash/sanitisation to prevent cross-infection; on first post-operative day, sterile gloves or aseptic non-touch technique; cleaning crusty or purulent deposits with cotton buds dipped in sterile saline; gentle agitation of bottle for proper admixture; reminder of transient blurring and stinging post-administration; gentle pulling down of lower eyelid (create space) and ask patient to look up (prevent direct administration over sensitive cornea), then instil **one drop** (not more) — conjunctival cul-de-sac volume ~30 μl, one drop ~100 μl, ~70 μl overflows into cheeks (instillation of more than one drop causes drug wastage); post-instillation strategies to prevent systemic absorption; wipe excess from **cheeks, not from eyes**; **alternate closed-eye strategy (Alster et al, 2000):** topical drop administered into closed eyelid at nasal corner, then patient opens eye allowing drug to enter; **remove contact lens before administration**. **Multiple eye drops:** time gap between two drops ≥ 5 minutes; order of administration — first: local anaesthetics, mydriatics and cycloplegics, miotics; second: sympathomimetics, tear substitutes, NSAIDs, steroids; third: antimicrobials (if multiple — antibiotics, antifungals) and anti-inflammatory (e.g., antihistaminics); fourth: antiglaucoma; **all eye ointments last**. **Procedure for eye ointment instillation:** comfortable positioning with head support; hand wash; on first post-operative day, sterile gloves or aseptic non-touch technique; cleaning crusty deposits; reminder of transient blurring and stinging; gentle pulling of lower eyelid; a thin ribbon of ointment instilled in lower fornix (if self-administering, patient may squeeze a blob into lower fornix if ribbon technique difficult); patient closes eyes and excess wiped from cheeks; before administering next topical therapy (≥ 2 hours), eyelid must be cleaned thoroughly. **Documentation:** even in home and self-administration, documentation of drops is always a must. **Eye drop dispensing/compliance aids:** specifically indicated in old patients self-medicating, patients with arthritis in small joints of hands, highly expensive drops (prevent loss), patients at high risk of adverse reaction (prevent excessive drug application); commonly used — autodrop (all bottle sizes, accurate position, no pressure application), auto squeeze (same features), opticare (2.5–15 ml bottles, pressure application required), opticare arthro (severe osteoarthritis or limited hand/shoulder movement; size 5 for 2.5/5 ml bottles; size 10 for 10/15 ml bottles), rubber eye drop bottle opener (open cap with minimum squeeze action).

column2: How will you counsel a patient with low vision approaching permanent blindness?
column4: **Definition (WHO):** low vision = best corrected vision in better eye less than 6/18 to perception of light and will not improve with any further medical or surgical intervention. **Pathway:** detection of low vision and confirmation of diagnosis by ophthalmologist → evaluation by low vision optometrist → prescription of appropriate low vision aid → rehabilitation (visual, social, vocational). **Common causes:** advanced diabetic eye disease, wet ARMD (CNVM), advanced glaucoma, polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, failed corneal graft, optic atrophy. **Low vision optometrist:** ophthalmic assistant trained in rehabilitation of patients with low vision; under guidance and supervision of treating ophthalmologist can act as low vision counsellor. **Roles of low vision counsellor:** (1) **first job** — explain clinical condition of patient's eye and communicate that no further improvement in vision is possible even with any medical or surgical intervention (**breaking the bad news**); while breaking bad news — no false hope, visual prognosis explained in vernacular language preferably with visual anatomical tools, patient's near relatives must be present, in case of psychological setback refer to psychological counsellor and follow up. (2) **detailed interview** regarding visual goals, professional activity, socio-economic status, psychological status, educational status, educational/socioeconomic status of caregivers. (3) **detailed visual analysis** — assessment of distant vision by telescopic aids; assessment of near vision by optical low vision aids (hand-held or stand magnifiers, high bifocals, prism glasses, hand magnifiers, telescopes) and non-optical aids (reading stand, writing guide, typoscope); ideal LVA should provide maximum vision with compromising mobility, balanced magnification with minimum decrease of working distance and field of vision, be simple/lightweight/portable/flexible; after using prescribed LVA patient should feel independent and increased adaptation to daily life; counsellor must make patient aware of goals of LVA prescription. (4) In one-eyed patient or others where complex telescopic-based LVA prescribed, motivate for adherence. (5) Counsellor must make patient aware of home lighting condition (many patients complain LVA functions more in clinic than at home — due to room light). (6) Explain maintenance of LVA, when/where/for which activities to use. (7) Maintain register of low vision patients with periodic follow-up. (8) Guide patient regarding disability certificate and other benefits.
column6: Counselling a Patient with Low Vision

column2: How will you counsel and rehabilitate a child with low vision?
column4: **Extremely challenging situation.** **Causes of low vision in children:** congenital disorders of retino-optic pathway, high refractive errors, amblyopia; many are irreversible and progressive despite medical/surgical management. **Low vision counsellor for children:** assume role of caring friend and not professional guide; assist actively in comprehensively rehabilitating the child in society; help family come to terms with child's disability; integrated educational, social, parental counselling and vocational rehabilitation. **Vision stimulation:** encouragement for use of vision through visual stimulation vital in children with low vision; strong colourful lights or toys used as visual stimulation; stimulates visual areas of brain to maximise visual development; counsellor must explain that visual stimulation helps child use remaining vision more effectively (does not strengthen eye muscles or cure primary eye disease). **Parental counselling:** every child and parent is unique; parents have huge role in helping child gain organisational skill required for successful rehabilitation; counsellor acts as bridge between parents and children; frequent group meetings of parents with low vision children very useful (share ideas, difficulties, unique parenting solutions); guide parents to achieve scholarships and concessions per government rules. **Integrated educational rehabilitation:** counsellor plays important role in finding appropriate educational mode; options — blind school (now called special schools), integrated education (now considered best approach — low vision students trained in normal schools with normal students; school must have appropriate learning/teaching environment for blind and low vision students; specially trained teachers; school staff and teachers must inculcate appropriate behaviour training to normal students in interacting and integrating with low vision students; braille, large prints, low vision aids, audio books must be provided), special education (for those children only who are not achieving through integrated education). **Vocational rehabilitation:** customised plan for each child depending on physical and visual status to develop an employment when child attains adulthood; vocational rehabilitation team should regularly visit offices employing persons with visual disability. **Social rehabilitation:** ability of person to function in various social situations towards satisfaction of needs and right to achieve maximum richness in participation in society; **daily living activities** — counsellor guides visually impaired child to perform all daily activities independently and safely with least external assistance; **orientation and mobility** — training helps visually impaired child navigate through world efficiently, effectively and safely.
column6: Counselling and Rehabilitating a Child with Low Vision

column2: Discuss the role of counselling in an eye care hospital.
column4: **Psychological barrier to taking advice** — ophthalmologist communicates about disease and possible treatment options → counselling plays catalytic role influencing patients to undergo surgical and medical treatment for potentially blinding eye problems. **Types of counselling:** (1) **paternalistic approach** — avoids explicit counselling about potential risks as long as medicolegal requirements of valid informed written consent met; counsellor guides patient to choose treatment modality. (2) **non-paternalistic or patient autonomy approach** — counsellor acts as provider of information; patient chooses with responsibility about future treatment; explicit documented counselling about procedure. (3) **hypothetical or gold standard approach** — adequately informs patient about treatment options to allow reasoned decision without causing undue anxiety. **Beneficial effects of counselling in eye care hospitals:** escalation of awareness of common eye diseases among patients and community; counsellor guides patient from entry till departure — quality of patient care services improves as a whole; breaks psychological barrier on behalf of patients — increases number of patients accepting medical or surgical treatment; increases patient's follow-up visits — chronic eye diseases like glaucoma get better monitoring, long-term effect on prevention of irreversible blindness; compliance and adherence to treatment protocols increase; reduces rate of post-operative infections (counsellor demonstrates correct method of eye drop and ointment instillation and cleaning operated eye); increases patient satisfaction rate and ultimately patient inflow; counsellor creates awareness about various eye diseases in community — voluntary glaucoma screening, voluntary diabetic retinopathy screening, voluntary retinal check-up for myopes, voluntary eye check-up of children by parents; **acts as public relations officer** — smoothens disputes between hospital and patients, bridges communication gaps; vital role in community outreach programmes and camps (ophthalmologist evaluates patient and advises cataract surgery at base hospital, spectacle correction, medical treatment, referral to base hospital for specialty treatment). **Role of counsellor in screening camp/outreach programme:** explain cause of blindness, treatment options, natural history of disease if not treated, necessity and urgency of referral to base hospital, mode of curative treatment prescribed at camp, importance of adherence/compliance/follow-up, health education on primary eye care. **Effectiveness assessed through indicators:** patient satisfaction score, surgery acceptance rate, spectacle acceptance rate, specialty referral acceptance rate, surgery follow-up acceptance rate.
column6: Role of Counselling in Eye Care Hospital

column2: How will you counsel a patient for refractive surgery (LASIK)?
column4: **LASIK** — cornea-based outpatient surgical technique utilising accuracy and precision of computer-controlled excimer laser to alter shape of cornea and correct refractive errors permanently. **Role of counsellor:** (1) **identify ideal candidate** — age 20–40 years, healthy cornea, stable refraction for last 12 months, no coexisting ocular disease; LASIK better avoided in pregnancy, poorly controlled hypertension. (2) **educate patient about principle** of surgery, benefits, side effects. (3) **educate about types of surgery** — flap-based (explain flap-related complications); lenticule-based (SMILE — additional use of femtosecond laser; costly; suitable for sports and military personnel occupationally more prone to flap-related complications). (4) **clear doubts and misconceptions** — SMILE vision correction takes about a week, flap-based LASIK vision correction immediate post-operative; after 40 years patient requires presbyopia glasses or presbyopia-correcting surgeries; retinal complications of myopia remain. (5) **bridge gap between patient's pre-operative expectation and post-operative clinical outcome.** (6) **counsel patients not suitable for LASIK** — thin corneas, > −6D myopia, high hypermetropia — advise alternative lens-based procedures. (7) **pre-operative counselling** — discontinue contact lens use one week prior; wear spectacles till laser procedure; wear comfortable clothing (no garment pulled over head, avoid zippers and buttons); remove mascara from eyelid margin; no perfumes (excimer laser very sensitive to odour); any barrage laser to retina (seal retinal breaks) at least one month prior. (8) **explain surgical procedure** — 30–60 minutes; both eyes operated under topical anaesthesia same day; no eye patch. (9) **post-operative counselling** — avoid watching television, reading, computer work, physical heavy exertion for one week; shower and baths may be taken normally; avoid splashing water directly over eye for 2 weeks; avoid rubbing or wiping eyes for 3 months; avoid swimming and hot tubs for 2 weeks; avoid eye make-up, lotions and after-shave for one week; use sunglasses for a month outdoors (light sensitivity); driving and limited professional activities can resume from immediate post-operative day. (10) **follow-up schedule:** 1st post-op, 1 month post-op, yearly follow-up.

column2: Discuss the role of counselling in detection and management of diabetic retinopathy.
column4: **Scenario I — recently diagnosed young (< 30 years) diabetic with no DR:** explain diabetes if uncontrolled damages blood vessels in different organs (eye, heart, kidney, brain) — microvascular complications; even with good glycaemic control microvascular complications can progress; **duration of diabetes** is single most important risk factor for DR progression; emphasise strict diabetic control (poor/fluctuating blood sugar → faster DR progression); regular yearly DR screening is best way to monitor microvascular complications; counsellor acts as bridge between treating physician and ophthalmologist — explain importance of liaison; regular check-up with physician for screening of microvascular complications in heart, kidney, brain; coexisting hypertension, dyslipidaemia, hypothyroidism must be diagnosed and controlled (additive retinal damage); fluctuating blood sugar causes vision problems — refraction done when blood sugar well controlled; cataractogenesis increases if diabetic control poor (metabolic/sugar cataract). **Scenario II — 40-year-old with 5 years duration, mild-moderate NPDR:** same points as scenario I plus coexisting hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, anaemia, hypothyroidism must be strictly controlled and regularly monitored (uncontrolled → further retinal damage); explain various stages of DR with clinical pictures and emphasise where he/she is currently standing; explain need for ocular diagnostic tests (OCT, FFA — painless; systemic adverse effects of fluorescein dye explained); explain possible future treatment modalities (break misconceptions about laser; indications and complications of laser and anti-VEGF intravitreal injections); emphasise regular follow-up and adherence; counsellor as bridge between physician and ophthalmologist. **Scenario III — 50-year-old with severe NPDR with diabetic macular oedema, advised FFA:** explain stages of DR with clinical photographs, demonstrate current stage and severity; FFA advised to determine exact location of involvement and establish severity; invasive procedure requiring venepuncture; dye (fluorescein) injected into vein, once it reaches retinal vessels photographed with special camera; test done 3 hours after last meal; FFA is diagnostic invasive investigation and will not cure disease — ophthalmologist decides further treatment modality; detailed history of allergy (especially seafood), bronchial asthma, diabetic nephropathy (fluorescein nephrotoxic, GFR may reduce up to 10 ml/min per session — clearance from nephrologist), cardiac fitness from physician, anxiety neurosis; explain signs of fluorescein dye allergy (nausea, vomiting, dyspnoea) and alert doctors if occurs. **Scenario IV — 55-year-old woman with PDR advised PRP:** explain laser is intense highly energetic beam of light that slows/ceases DR progression and stabilises vision; will prevent further vision loss but will not cause improvement; during procedure patient should fixate vision as directed and not move eyes (wrong delivery → affect vision); regular follow-up and adherence; laser is outpatient day care procedure, no restricted water use. **Scenario V — 50-year-old lady with severe NPDR + DMO, advised intravitreal ranibizumab:** explain microvascular complications damaged retinal vessels at central retina; damaged vessels lead to fluid accumulation; anti-VEGF agents prevent visual loss; different agents, safety, efficacy, cost; patient allowed to choose freely without coercion; severe cardiovascular compromise → cardiological clearance; prior CVA → neurological/physician clearance; ocular bioavailability of IV drugs poor — intravitreal required; drug delivered through 30G needle (very thin) with topical anaesthesia; minimal discomfort (pain scale less than blood sample); asepsis maintained for at least 7 days post-injection; monthly follow-up; OCT macula scans to monitor therapeutic response. **Scenario VI — 70-year-old with advanced diabetic eye disease (ADED):** explain stages with clinical photograph; if untreated can turn into permanent blindness; requires surgery followed by laser (intra or post-operative) to preserve residual vision; document 'guarded visual prognosis' — even with treatment vision will not improve significantly; PPV under local anaesthesia, duration 1–2 hours; probable complications per vitreo-retinal surgeon; if intraoperative C3F8 gas used as vitreous substitute, patient must lie prone or head-down post-operatively; strict glycaemic, BP, cholesterol control to prevent further retinal damage; adherence with treating physician for monitoring microvascular complications in kidney, heart, brain; counsellor as liaison between physician and vitreo-retinal surgeon; develop positive attitude; help patient accept low vision and guide towards low vision aids; encourage and ensure regular follow-up.

column2: A 40-year-old gentleman with pathological myopia has come to your OPD. How will you counsel the patient for future course of management?
column4: Before initiation of treatment: (1) counsel about basic optics of myopia preferably with simple picture; explain that degree of myopia in his case is abnormal. (2) Counsel about **degenerative basis** of pathological myopia. (3) Explain necessity for **periodic retinal examination** — examine retinal periphery for identification and barrage laser sealing of peripheral retinal breaks and tears; examine central retina to rule out macular pathology like CNVM; rule out coexisting ocular morbidities like POAG. (4) Counsel about **premonition signs of retinal detachment** — flashes of light especially during eye movements, sudden increase in number of floaters, cobweb-like large black rings, black curtain-like sensation in certain parts of visual field, sudden complete loss of vision (painless) if RD involves macula. (5) Counsel for possible **refractive surgery options** and their potential benefits and adverse effects. (6) Counsel to **avoid tobacco products** (increase chance of CNVM). (7) Counsel about **genetic basis** of pathological myopia — any offspring must be followed up for myopia. (8) Counsel to **avoid trauma to eye** and in case of even minor trauma, undergo dilated fundus examination to rule out traumatic retinal breaks.

column2: A 50-year-old pathological myopia patient has presented with fresh retinal detachment. How will you counsel the patient?
column4: (1) Explain need for **immediate surgical intervention** for best possible visual outcome. (2) Explain type and nature of RD with visual prognosis — shallow peripheral RD: good prognosis; recurrent RD: bad prognosis; total RD with macular involvement: bad prognosis; RD with PVR changes: poor prognosis. (3) Need for using **C3F8 as vitreous substitute** — explain post-operative prone position. (4) If **silicone oil** used as vitreous substitute — patient counselled that second surgery required after 3 months to remove silicone oil; if silicone oil retained > 3 months, risk of glaucoma and cataract. (5) Counsel about nature and duration of surgery. (6) Counsel about **premonition signs of RD** to save the other eye.

column2: Discuss the role of genetic counselling in ophthalmology.
column4: **Definition:** process to educate patient and near family members on inheritance pattern, genetic testing, management, prevention and medical and psychological implications of genetic diseases; ensures patient and family make informed choices. **Genetic counsellors:** any of — medical graduates and/or postgraduates, clinical geneticist, social worker/nursing personnel (after proper training); genetic counselling training imparted in India by **Board of Genetic Counselling of India** (non-government organisation). **Role of genetic counsellor:** imparts basic education regarding inheritance pattern, natural history of disease and available treatment options; assesses social and psychological implications of disease on family and patient; guides patient and family to appropriate rehabilitation and support groups. **Challenges of genetic counselling in India:** absence/shortage of counsellors (ratio 1:14 million); limited access to genetic services; inadequate knowledge of genetics among physicians; absence of legal regulations on genetic discrimination; lack of recognition, low professional income with poor regulatory implications of genetic counselling at ground level; religious, cultural and linguistic challenges. **Principles of genetic counselling (Walker et al):** education (patient should have sufficient information); complete disclosure (no selective withholding of information to influence patient's decision); empowering (post-counselling patient should feel encouraged to proceed with his/her decision); non-directive (options provided in neutral manner); universal (equal access to genetic services); justice (protection of patient's privacy and confidentiality); voluntariness (patient ought to decide for themselves and their families whether genetic testing is required).

column2: Write short notes on inherited ophthalmic diseases and role of genetic testing.
column4: **Purpose of genetic testing:** (1) confirm diagnosis in affected individual where phenotype–genotype correlations have been recognised; (2) determine carrier status of an individual; (3) ascertain predisposition to late-onset disease or establish presymptomatic diagnosis; (4) pre-implantation diagnosis, prenatal diagnosis, newborn screening. **Types of genetic testing:** (1) **cytogenetic tests** — analyses number and morphology of chromosomes; detects chromosomal duplications, deletions, insertions, translocations. (2) **karyotype** — chromosomes rearranged in predetermined fashion called karyogram/idiogram; useful to detect trisomies. (3) **FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridisation)** — combines cytogenetic and molecular techniques. (4) **SKY test (spectral karyotype)** — hybridisation molecular cytogenetic technique; different chromosome pairs dyed with different colours. (5) **SSDGE/SSCP (single-strand DNA gel electrophoresis / single-strand conformational polymorphism)** — allele-nonspecific test using PCR. (6) **DGGE (denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis)** — allele-nonspecific test requiring PCR to amplify double-stranded DNA molecules. (7) **RFLP (restriction fragment length polymorphism)** — allele-specific tests using restriction endonuclease enzymes. (8) **Dedicated DNA microarrays** — allele-specific test requiring matrix hybridisation platform reactions; useful to detect Leber congenital amaurosis, Usher syndrome, recessive retinal dystrophies. (9) **Direct DNA sequencing** — next generation sequencing technology (International HPA Map Project); ability to make genetics-based precise molecular diagnosis; WES (whole exome sequencing analysis) gives molecular diagnosis with immediate application to reduce differential diagnosis ambiguity (used for rare and ultra-rare disorders); interpretation — pathogenic, likely pathogenic, benign, variants of unknown sequence (VUS) must be reported and uncertainty explained to patient. (10) **Prenatal genetic screening** — amniocentesis (20–30 ml amniotic fluid, 16–18 weeks gestation, risk of fetal death 0.5%); transabdominal/transvaginal chorionic villous sampling (10–14 weeks gestation, risk of fetal death 1%); cordocentesis (higher than 20 weeks gestation, risk of fetal death 2–5%). **Disorders with ophthalmic manifestations requiring prenatal screening:** Fabry's disease, cystinosis, galactosemia, gangliosidosis type 1 and 2, homocystinuria, globoid cell leucodystrophy (Krabbe's disease), metachromatic leucodystrophy, Niemann-Pick disease, Refsum's syndrome.

column2: Write short notes on grief counselling.
column4: **Definition:** grief is mental state where one experiences personal loss or any other distressing situation; **grief counselling** is communication between grief counsellor under Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programme (HCRP) and near relatives of a recently deceased or about-to-decease or brain-dead person admitted in ICU or elsewhere in hospital, to encourage organ donation with special reference to cornea after death of concerned person. **Grief counsellor:** Eye Bank Association of India (EBAI) started HCRP for increasing availability of donor corneal tissue; HCRP needs successful co-ordination between ICU/hospital staff, eye bank staff and grief counsellor (synchronisation). **Eligibility:** any literate person can act as grief counsellor; must be professionally trained from recognised eye bank training centre with certificate of completion; in case of non-availability of separate grief counsellor, hospital nurse or social workers can also do grief counselling (with proper training); medical graduates, postgraduates and postdoctoral can also do grief counselling (exempted from separate training). **Roles:** grief counselling; sensitisation of hospital staff for eye donation; installing posters for eye donation; installing public awareness systems for eye donation in patient waiting area; celebrate Eye Donation Fortnight with hospital staff, patients and patient's near relatives. **Steps of grief counselling (on event of death/imminent death):** hospital staff informs grief counsellor (or starts to act as grief counsellor if unavailable) → introduces self to patient's near relatives → conveys **condolences** for death (after appropriately judging situation — sudden death, young patient, head of family, only earning member, long-standing terminally ill) → discusses briefly about situation of corneal blindness and availability of donor tissue (not didactic lecture but short appealing description of 'demand-supply mismatch'; pictures and electronic aids with prior permission) → asks family members (after appropriate yet prompt time) whether they would like to donate eyes of deceased — no coercion, no fear, no monetary benefit, no physical or verbal altercation. **In case of positive response:** inform nearest eye bank personnel immediately; take valid written consent from nearest relative present; facilitate process to obtain death certificate; switch off fan near deceased; elevate head end of deceased; close eyelids and apply ice packs; explain process of eye retrieval to relatives and assure no facial disfigurement. **Post-counselling roles:** maintain confidentiality regarding donor and recipient; issue certificate of appreciation to donor family; provide promotional pamphlets and relevant contact number of eye donation centres; keep contact and motivate donor family members for further donations in future.

column2: How will you counsel the parents of a 5-year-old child for periodic eye examination?
column4: Preschool children are more vulnerable to vision-threatening ocular morbidities because: children unaware of visual symptoms; even if aware, incapable of verbally expressing accurately; there has to be a concerned caregiver (mostly parents) to bring child and maintain logistic liaison with healthcare system. Hence, **care providers/parents of preschool children require proper counselling** to realise importance of periodic eye examination. **Diseases of utmost importance:** (1) **uncorrected refractive error** — most common cause of preventable blindness among children; 4–5% of all children have same kind of refractive error; may be myopia (most common) or hypermetropia with/without astigmatism; symptoms — holds books/toys very close to eyes, difficulty identifying faces of known family members from distance, sits very close to television, squeezes eyes to see distant objects, headache, squinting of eye. (2) **strabismus** — misalignment of eyes due to lack of neuromuscular binocular coordination; causes: heredity, uncorrected refractive error, cataract, post-ocular injuries; progressively eyes turning out, in, up or down either in isolation or combinedly. (3) **white pupillary reflex** — potentially vision-threatening and may be life-threatening (ocular tumours like retinoblastoma); common causes: cataract, PHPV, Coats disease, retinoblastoma. (4) **paediatric glaucoma** — rare entity; genetic predisposition; clinical triad blepharospasm, photophobia, lacrimation; large cloudy corneas. (5) **amblyopia** — vision in one or both eyes reduced without structural abnormality; commonly called 'lazy eye'; causes: strabismus, uncorrected refractive error in one or both eyes, cataract, central corneal opacity, severe blepharoptosis. **Role of counsellor (all counselling in vernacular language):** explain parents about nature, severity and visual prognosis of detected ocular morbidity preferably using eye models; explain importance of regular and continuous use of glasses for child; break common social myths for regular glass use; explain possibility of increment of power of refractive error despite all efforts; explain 'red flag signs' of immediate eye examination of child indicating ophthalmic emergency; explain role of voluntary periodic (6-monthly or at least yearly) eye check-up; explain risks of amblyopia and its long-term effect on visual fitness for certain career opportunities; break common social myths regarding strabismus (certain societies believe persistence of strabismus is good sign for economic upliftment, especially among children); customised counselling for parents of girl child.
column6: Counselling Parents for Periodic Eye Examination

column2: Write short notes on school eye screening programme.
column4: **Introduction:** 1976 — National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI) started by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India; 1994 — School Eye Screening Programme became integral part of NPCBVI. **Initial target population:** 5th–10th Standard students (10–14 years) till 2009 (for administrative, logistic and social ease of implementation); from 2009 — eye screening of all children from class 1 onwards. **Objectives:** in liaison with Department of Primary and Secondary Education, identification and mapping of location of schools in districts; collection of information regarding number of students and teachers in each school; identification of teachers in each school capable of eye screening; training of selected teachers for eye screening of children; maintenance of referral chain for students suspected of ophthalmic morbidities requiring intervention by ophthalmologist; prescription of glasses and disbursal of free spectacles to students with refractive errors; maintenance of register for students with ophthalmic morbidities. **Organisation and implementation:** **agency** — District Health Society (DHS) in collaboration with Department of Primary and Secondary Education; **time zone** — April–September of each year (to avoid hamper of cataract services from October); **chain of implementation** — screening of students by trained teachers in each school (suspect students) → on fixed date ophthalmic assistant from nearby BPHC (Block Primary Health Centre) visits individual schools for confirmation of suspect students, prescription for glass to students with refractive error, providing free spectacles to children with refractive error, identification of students with ophthalmic morbidities and proper referral, identification and rehabilitation of students with irreversible blindness, maintaining and following up referral register; in case of non-availability of ophthalmic assistant, medical graduates or nursing personnel from nearby BPHC can also perform this. **Role of trained teachers:** from each school, one or two teachers selected for one-day training course in ophthalmic morbidity screening; preference to women teachers (counteract gender inequality); preference to teachers with spectacle or prior history of preventable blindness (more motivated); after successful completion, teachers provided with a kit to screen children in respective schools — contains 6 m (20 feet) measuring tape, referral card, booklet containing basic information of paediatric ocular morbidities, standard vision screening E chart (field chart — four lines with single E letter; chart rotated at least 3 times for each optotype; child asked to identify which side of E is 'open'; if child identifies correctly twice for smallest optotype, only then vision recorded; chart simple, less confusing for non-technical person, does not give opportunity to memorise optotypes from near distance; if child reads 6/9 optotype, teacher records vision as 'good', otherwise 'not good'); Snellen visual acuity confirmation done by ophthalmic assistants. **Provision of spectacles:** one of the most attractive pillars; District Health Society makes Memorandum of Understanding with reputed local optician by official tender for 6 months (optician from district itself); monitoring of quality of spectacles by Chief Medical Officer of Health or assigned deputy. **Sustainability and quality issues:** community-based effective paediatric eye care programme is challenge even in developed countries; coordination between Health Department and Education Department; maintenance of effective referral ladder; social and visual rehabilitation of children with low vision; effective interaction between District Hospital and Medical Colleges for training of ophthalmologists and ophthalmic assistants in paediatric eye care.

column2: How will you counsel a patient before cataract surgery?
column4: Patient and near relative need following to be explained by counsellor: (1) exact nature of cataract and urgency to undergo cataract surgery. (2) Any pre-existing ocular disease which can have devastating intra or post-operative complications — known glaucoma: pre/intra/post-operative IOP control very essential; known diabetes: pre/post-operative glycaemic control essential; known hypertension: pre/intra/post-operative BP control essential; ongoing medications for diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia should be continued even on day of surgery; any pre-existing pathology in lacrimal sac must be addressed first before cataract surgery (pathological myopia, high hypermetropia — risks explained). (3) Patients with pre-existing posterior segment pathology — diabetic retinopathy, retinal vascular occlusion with macular involvement, ARMD — must be explained about **guarded visual prognosis** after cataract surgery. (4) Patients with poor pupillary dilatation (due to synechiae, floppy iris, medications, prostatomegaly) — risks and basic knowledge about pupillary expander use explained. (5) Pre-existing cardiac condition (IHD, arrhythmia) — importance of thorough cardiac check-up before cataract surgery; patients on blood thinners (antiplatelet or anticoagulants) must stop at least 5 days prior in consultation with physician. (6) Dense cataracts with poor or no view of posterior segment — post-operative guarded visual prognosis. (7) High-risk consent from physician and anaesthetist — systemic risks and requirement of ICU. (8) Topical and local anaesthesia including risk-benefit ratio. (9) Types of cataract surgery including risk-benefit ratio for each in context of his/her cataract situation. (10) Patients must know: cataract surgery is not a minor procedure; cataract surgery has known complications; spectacles may be required after cataract surgery. (11) Patients with claustrophobia or mental illness must be identified and counselled for general anaesthesia. (12) Post-operative care after cataract surgery must be counselled in detail. (13) Operation-related 'anxiety disorder' addressed adequately in balanced manner to avoid complications. (14) **Informed written consent** regarding surgery must be explained to patient in language he/she comprehends (preferably mother tongue) — verbatim. **Counselling types:** paternalistic approach (avoids explicit counselling about potential risks as long as medicolegal requirements of valid informed written consent met; counsellor guides patient to choose treatment modality); non-paternalistic/patient autonomy approach (counsellor acts as provider of information; patient chooses with responsibility about future treatment; explicit documented counselling); hypothetical/gold standard approach (adequately informs patient about treatment options to allow reasoned decision without causing undue anxiety).
