column4: Answer

column2: Explain why: PCO develops after cataract surgery.
column4: In cataract surgery the posterior capsule, capsular equatorial rim (where zonules are attached), and rim of anterior capsule (after capsulorrhexis) or part of cut margins of anterior capsule (after capsulotomy) are kept for easy and safe placement of PCIOL in the capsular bag. **Causes:** (1) growing equatorial cells; (2) remaining cortical matter or cortical lens fibres or cells on the posterior capsule; (3) placement of PCIOL in sulcus or partly in the capsular bag; (4) hydrophilic IOLs; (5) not using posterior square-edged IOLs; (6) rigid PCIOL insertion without washing with balanced salt solution; (7) putting IOL in developmental cataract surgery without primary posterior capsulorrhexis and anterior vitrectomy to clear central area. These are all responsible for development of PCO. Aqueous imbibition and free growth of remaining cortical/equatorial cells behind the PCIOL occurs after cataract surgery leading to PCO.

column2: Explain why: IOP may rise following long-term treatment of vernal conjunctivitis.
column4: Steroid eye drop is the treatment of choice in management of vernal conjunctivitis. **Long-term treatment of vernal conjunctivitis by steroid eye drop causes raised IOP by:** (1) induction of physical and mechanical changes in the microstructure of trabecular meshwork (TM); (2) deposition of substances (extracellular matrix) in TM; (3) inhibition of proteases and endothelial phagocytosis. All three lead to **increased aqueous outflow resistance** → rise of intraocular pressure.

column2: Explain why: Continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis (CCC) is better than 'can-opener type' anterior capsulotomy.
column4: CCC is one of essential parts of small incision cataract surgery (SICS) or phacoemulsification, while can-opener type capsulotomy is done in extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE), which is not preferred nowadays. **Reasons CCC is better:** (1) capsulotomy provides weak support against intracapsular bag manipulation during cataract surgery (hydrodissection, nucleus manipulation) in SICS or phacoemulsification — capsulotomy may extend to equatorial part of capsular bag or even posteriorly leading to intra-operative vitreous loss; (2) CCC directly helps in putting IOL in capsular bag without injuring capsular rim (whereas rim may be injured in can-opener capsulotomy); (3) CCC helps keep IOL in the centre, whereas decentration of IOL is not uncommon in can-opener capsulotomy.

column2: Explain why: Pterygium can recur after simple excision.
column4: Simple excision of pterygium without any conjunctivo-limbal autograft or stem cell-rich amniotic membrane transplantation leads to absence of mechanical barrier provided by limbal stem cells. The situation cannot prevent conjunctiva from growing across the limbal border and encroaching inside the cornea, leading to recurrence. **Stem cells at the limbus** provide a junctional mechanical barrier by providing a separate group of epithelium and prevent free growth of conjunctival epithelium into the cornea. So, simple excision without replacing limbal stem cell lining leads to pterygium recurrence.
column6: Recurrence of Pterygium After Simple Excision

column2: Explain why: Corneal oedema can develop after endothelial damage / intraocular surgery.
column4: Corneal dehydration mainly depends upon active endothelial pump mechanism, e.g., Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump, bicarbonate-dependent ATPase pump, Na⁺/H⁺ pump. Any form of endothelial damage leads to loss of these dehydrating pump mechanisms in the cornea. Water is imbibed inside the cornea and dehydration status is lost, leading to **corneal oedema formation**.

column2: Explain why: Control of blood sugar (in diabetic patients) prior to cataract surgery is important.
column4: In diabetic patients, blood sugar must be controlled before cataract surgery because: (a) uncontrolled blood sugar makes intraocular chambers and fluids susceptible to growth of organisms, which may lead to **post-operative endophthalmitis**; (b) uncontrolled blood sugar makes surgical site prone to develop wound infection, which may in turn lead to endophthalmitis; (c) uncontrolled blood sugar causes **delayed wound healing**, so post-operative recovery period is prolonged. Hence, control of blood sugar is an integral part of cataract surgery preparation.

column2: Explain why: Syringing of lacrimal passage is important in chronic watering from eye.
column4: Watering from eye may be due to hyperlacrimation (increased tear secretion) or epiphora (decreased drainage of tear). In chronic watering the most common cause is epiphora. To search for the level of blockage in lacrimal passage in epiphora, **syringing** is performed: (a) fast or immediate regurgitation of clear fluid along with **soft stop** (at tip of syringing cannula) — common canalicular block; (b) slow regurgitation of clear serous fluid or muco-pus or mucus-mixed clear fluid with **hard stop** (at tip of cannula) — nasolacrimal duct (NLD) block; (c) fluid going to nose and throat — watering is not due to blockage in lacrimal passage; (d) fluid passing through NLD with simultaneous regurgitation — partial blockage of NLD. Depending on these findings, treatment plan can be fixed.

column2: Explain why: Cycloplegics are used in treatment of uveitis/iridocyclitis.
column4: Uveitis = inflammation of uveal tissue; anterior uveitis = inflammation of iris and pars plicata of ciliary body. Ciliary and iris muscles become irritated and hyperactive, leading to constriction of pupil. **Roles of cycloplegics:** (a) relieves ciliary spasm and iris-sphincter spasm, which reduces pain, redness and ocular discomfort; (b) breaks pre-existing posterior synechiae or prevents development of synechiae; (c) gives additional benefit of examining vitreous and fundus by dilating the pupil; (d) reduces exudation by decreasing vascular permeability. Hence, cycloplegics are considered first-line drugs in anterior uveitis/iridocyclitis.

column2: Explain why: No sutures are needed in small incision cataract surgery (SICS).
column4: In SICS, a **tri-planar sclerocorneal tunnel** is made for delivery of cataractous crystalline lens and insertion of PCIOL. This tri-planar sclerocorneal tunnel acts as a **self-sealing wound**. Sclera provides the 1st plane, cornea provides the 2nd and 3rd planes, and the geometry of the tunnel creates a valve-like seal that holds the anterior chamber. Hence, no suture is required after completion of surgery.

column2: Explain why: Viscoelastic substances are used liberally during cataract surgery.
column4: Viscoelastic substances or ophthalmic viscosurgical devices have several uses in different steps of cataract surgery. They are used liberally to: (a) protect the corneal endothelium from intra-operative injuries; (b) protect iris and lens from intra-operative injuries; (c) create intra-AC space for movement of instruments; (d) prevent corneal surface from dryness and improve visibility during surgery.

column2: Explain why: Steroids are contraindicated in corneal ulcer.
column4: Steroids are contraindicated in corneal ulcer because: (a) topical steroids reduce local immunity, which in turn reduces anti-inflammatory response that normally occurs against invading organisms in corneal ulcer — so ulcer progresses to involve whole cornea, though from signs it may look like responding because of reduced anti-inflammatory response; (b) steroids cause secondary rise of intraocular pressure, and raised IOP is the commonest cause of non-healing corneal ulcer.

column2: Explain why: Glaucoma can develop if cataract becomes hypermature.
column4: Hyper-mature cataract may lead to **lens-induced glaucoma** by: (a) **phacolytic glaucoma** — in hyper-mature Morgagnian variety, lens proteins leak into anterior chamber and are engulfed by macrophages; these swollen macrophages block the trabecular meshwork, leading to secondary open-angle glaucoma; (b) **phacotopic glaucoma** — hyper-mature cataract may subluxate anteriorly and block the pupil or push iris anteriorly, causing secondary angle-closure glaucoma.

column2: Explain why: Viral conjunctivitis is associated with lymphadenopathy.
column4: Viral conjunctivitis mainly involves the lymphoid follicle in the palpebral and forniceal part of conjunctiva. So in viral conjunctivitis a **predominantly follicular reaction** is seen in conjunctiva. This lymphoid reaction stimulates more lymphoid cells to proliferate in the draining lymph nodes (submandibular and preauricular). Secondly, in viral conjunctivitis, due to local immunity suppression, superadded bacterial infection may also take place — this aggravates lymphoid cell proliferation in draining lymph nodes. Hence, viral conjunctivitis is associated with lymphadenopathy.

column2: Explain why: Presbyopia develops after the age of 40 years.
column4: Presbyopia is physiological age-related decrease of amplitude of accommodation or age-related receding of near point of accommodation. Near point of an emmetropic eye is at **25 cm at 40 years** with +4 dioptres of amplitude of accommodation. Near working distance of emmetropic eye is usually 25 cm. As age increases beyond 40 years, near point recedes further (e.g., 33 cm at 45 years), so working accommodation will not suffice to work at 25 cm distance. Hence, presbyopia develops after age 40. **Factors:** (a) age-related changes in the lens — decreased lens capsule elasticity, increased sclerosis of lens; (b) age-related decline in ciliary muscle power.

column2: Explain why: An un-operated case of cataract can cause glaucoma.
column4: Human crystalline lens-induced glaucoma or sudden rise of IOP is mainly due to the following mechanisms: (a) **phacomorphic glaucoma** — most common type of lens-induced glaucoma; swollen and cataractous lens pushes iris forward to close angle of anterior chamber (secondary closed-angle glaucoma); (b) **phacolytic glaucoma** — in hyper-mature Morgagnian cataract, liquefied cortex proteins leak out into anterior chamber; proteins are engulfed by macrophages and these swollen macrophages block trabecular meshwork (secondary open-angle glaucoma); (c) **phacotopic glaucoma** — hyper-mature cataractous lens may subluxate or dislocate anteriorly, blocking the pupil or angle of anterior chamber (secondary closed-angle glaucoma).

column2: Explain why: Headache may occur from uncorrected hypermetropia.
column4: In hypermetropia, parallel light rays from infinity focus behind neurosensory retina when accommodation is at rest. Uncorrected hypermetropia leads to an optical setup where patient cannot see at distance as well as near, with near vision dimness more prominent. To overcome this dimness at both distance and near, patient uses accommodation to increase convergence power of lens so image focuses on neurosensory retina. This **extra accommodative effort produces hyperactivity of ciliary muscles**, leading to headache — more evident during near work.

column2: Explain why: Cataract surgery can cause against-the-rule astigmatism.
column4: Traditionally cataract surgery is performed by surgeon sitting at head end of patient, i.e., main sclerocorneal tunnel (SICS) or phacoemulsification main port is made **superiorly**. Against-the-rule (ATR) astigmatism means vertical meridian is flat and horizontal meridian is steep (horizontal meridian more curved). After cataract surgery, when wound healing has taken place, the **vertical meridian becomes flatter** (making horizontal meridian relatively steeper). So, superior surgical wound always makes the eye prone to develop against-the-rule astigmatism.

column2: Explain why: Episcleritis may occur recurrently.
column4: Episcleritis occurs due to: (a) idiopathic cause; (b) systemic diseases — gout, rosacea, connective tissue disorders, psoriasis; (c) hypersensitivity reaction to endogenous allergen — staphylococcal or tubercular protein; (d) rarely due to some infection — herpes, Borrelia infection. Since the causes include **chronic diseases and chronic presence of endogenous allergens**, episcleritis may recur.

column2: Explain why: For keratoplasty
column3: cornea cannot be collected from every dead body.
column5: Though eye donation is encouraged as much as possible by awareness programs, strict guidelines are followed regarding donor cornea utilisation for keratoplasty. **Diseases that can be transmitted through donor cornea:** Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (prion disease); hepatitis; herpes simplex virus; syphilis, tuberculosis, smallpox, malaria; HIV, SARS-CoV-2. **Patients who died of the above infections cannot be considered as donors and cornea cannot be collected from them.** Additional contraindications include viral encephalitis/encephalitis of unknown origin, rabies, active meningitis, progressive encephalopathy, active septicaemia. A post-mortem blood sample must be non-reactive to HIV, HBsAg, anti-HCV, syphilis, COVID-19 before tissue is released.

column2: Explain why: Atropine is the mainstay of treatment of acute anterior uveitis.
column4: Atropine as the strongest cycloplegic in acute anterior uveitis: (a) relieves iris sphincter and ciliary spasm, giving rest to them; (b) prevents formation of posterior synechiae and can break already formed synechiae; (c) reduces vascular permeability, so exudation is also reduced; (d) increases blood supply to anterior uvea, so more antibodies are delivered and more toxins are absorbed. Hence, atropine is the mainstay of treatment of acute anterior uveitis.

column2: Explain why: Dacryocystitis must be treated before cataract surgery.
column4: Dacryocystitis (chronic or acute) is a **contraindication for cataract surgery**. Acute dacryocystitis must be treated with systemic antibiotics and subsequently re-evaluated regarding dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR); chronic dacryocystitis must be evaluated for DCR before cataract surgery. Dacryocystitis in any form is a **potential source of infection** which can easily contaminate the cataract surgery wound; subsequent **endophthalmitis** may develop in such cases. So dacryocystitis must be treated before cataract surgery.

column2: Explain why: Intraocular pressure rises in hyphema.
column4: Hyphema means blood in anterior chamber. Mechanisms: (a) hyphema produces blockage of trabecular meshwork, which in turn reduces aqueous humour drainage; (b) hyphema usually occurs after trauma (accidental, surgical) or neovascularisation of iris — in all cases aqueous humour (sometimes turbid) production increases in a situation of blocked trabecular meshwork; (c) in low-grade hyphema with anterior chamber inflammation, macrophages come into AC and engulf RBCs — these block the trabecular meshwork. Hence, IOP rises in hyphema.

column2: Explain why: Visual impairment in proptosis.
column4: Proptosis occurs in benign conditions (thyroid eye disease, non-specific orbital inflammation) or due to primary orbital mass effect or secondary deposits. **Vision loss in proptosis occurs due to:** (1) **exposure keratopathy** leading to vision-threatening corneal ulcer and subsequent scarring or melting; (2) **compressive optic neuropathy** due to compression on optic nerve leading to optic nerve conduction pathway defect; (3) **choroidal folds** involving posterior pole due to pressure effect on posterior part of globe.

column2: Explain why: Center-involving nebular opacity causes more defective vision than localised leucoma away from pupillary area.
column4: Nebula is a faint opacity due to superficial scars where Bowman's layer and superficial stroma are involved. A nebular opacity in **central cornea** produces more discomfort due to formation of blurred images as a result of **irregular astigmatism**. A leucoma away from central cornea completely cuts off light entry into the eye, so blurring or discomfort never happens. Hence central nebula causes more defective vision than peripheral leucoma.

column2: Explain why: Posterior polar or posterior subcapsular cataract causes more difficulty in near vision.
column4: Near vision is maintained by accommodation — anterior bulging of crystalline lens, convergence of eyeball, constriction of pupil. Posterior polar cataract (PPC) or posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC) primarily involves posterior pole of crystalline lens or central posterior cortex. During near vision **pupil constricts**, and light entry occurs **only through central axis** which is obscured by existing PPC or PSC. During distant vision, pupil comparatively dilates, allowing more light entry through peripheral part of pupil; light rays then pass through non-cataractous zone of posterior part of crystalline lens, improving vision over near. Hence, PPC or PSC causes more difficulty in near vision.

column2: Explain why: Cycloplegia is needed in paediatric refraction.
column4: Any kind of refractive error in children must be assessed after cycloplegia. (A) In children inherent ciliary muscle tone is highest and provides up to +1D of hypermetropia (**latent hypermetropic part**) — this inherent muscle tone must be neutralised to get proper refractive status. (B) Accommodative effort corrects some part of hypermetropic refractive status (**facultative hypermetropic part**) — this must be neutralised to relieve accommodative effort. So, in children cycloplegic refraction is done not only in hypermetropia but also in myopia, to neutralise ciliary muscle tone and accommodative effort.

column2: Explain why: High hypermetropia in aphakia.
column4: Aphakia is clinical condition where there is absence of lens. Human crystalline lens provides **+16D** (approximate) of refractive power of whole eyeball (+44D from cornea; total emmetropic eye ~ +60D). In aphakia, this +16D is lost and refractive power of eyeball becomes ~ +44D. Generally ≥ +5D is considered high hypermetropia; in aphakia the refractive status is always > +10D (considering initial status as emmetropia). So, in aphakia we get a high hypermetropic status of the eye.

column2: Explain why: Pterygium is more common on nasal aspect of interpalpebral area.
column4: Pterygium occurs more commonly on nasal side of interpalpebral area for the following reasons: (A) actual mechanism still unknown; (B) ultraviolet rays (UVr) of sunlight falling on temporal part of cornea/limbus undergo **total internal reflection**, traverse through cornea, and pass nasal limbus; then UVr hits nasal bridge and reflects back towards nasal limbus — limbal stem cells are ever-dividing cells that differentiate into various cell linings; these dividing cells are exposed to UVr **twice** on nasal side in fractions of seconds → stem cells lose pluripotent power and become normal epithelium unable to provide mechanical barrier against growing conjunctival epithelium; (C) nasal side has **lowest volume of tear film lake** and less tear re-surfacing than temporal side → comparative dryness increases chance of limbal stem cell destruction; (D) sun-exposure and exposure-related dryness occur more in interpalpebral area.

column2: Explain why: Unilateral cataract (with good vision in other eye) needs IOL implantation rather than aphakic spectacle correction.
column4: Modern cataract surgery is always considered a refractive surgery; keeping aphakia is not recommended for many reasons even in high myopic cases. If IOL is not given and high hypermetropic condition aphakia is corrected by glasses, there will be: (A) spherical aberrations; (B) **Jack-in-the-box phenomenon** (sudden appearance and disappearance of objects in visual field); (C) **roving ring scotoma** (ring scotoma, inside and outside which patient can see); (D) **pin cushion effect** (peripheral expansion or broadening of images with central narrowing); (E) unilateral aphakic glass and other eye minimum/zero power glass may lead to diplopia in binocular vision; (F) keeping aphakia may lead to free vitreous movement and vitreous fixation at pupillary margin (capsular bag collapses if IOL not put) → free vitreous movement may lead to retinal complications (retinal tear, CME) and pupillary block by vitreous → secondary glaucoma; (G) diminished peripheral vision. So, in many ways aphakia should not be kept as far as visual correction is concerned after cataract surgery. If PCIOL cannot be given (posterior capsular complications, loose zonules, loose bag) — sulcus-supported, scleral-fixated, or iris-claw lens must be given.

column2: Explain why: Near vision improves with nuclear cataract.
column4: As a result of presbyopia, near point recedes further as age increases beyond 40 years. So, at the age of development of senile cataract, patient is already presbyopic. Nuclear cataract is one morphological variety of senile cataract where **nuclear sclerosis** occurs. As nuclear sclerosis develops, **refractive index increases** and patient starts becoming myopic (refractive status shifts toward myopic side). So, near point starts to return toward pre-presbyopic stage and sometimes comes nearer. Hence, near vision improves with myopic shift in nuclear cataract (**second sight**).

column2: Explain why: Vitamin A is essential for good vision.
column4: Vitamin A is essential for good vision because: (A) with active form of vitamin A (**retinol**), protein **opsin** binds to form **rhodopsin** — pigment present in rod cells of retina responsible for night vision; (B) hypovitaminosis A results in **goblet cell dysfunction** — goblet cells secrete mucin, an integral part of tear film; dry eye (though not directly related to dimness of vision initially) in late stage causes corneal involvement and dimness of vision. Hence, vitamin A is essential for good vision.

column2: Explain why: Corneal endothelium is the metabolically most active layer of cornea.
column4: Corneal endothelium is the most important layer controlling fluid transport through cornea to maintain corneal transparency. It has multiple enzyme systems — Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump, HCO₃⁻-dependent ATPase pump, Na⁺/H⁺ ATPase pump. As cornea is avascular, major supply of glucose and other nutrients comes via simple diffusion or active pump mechanism from aqueous humour. These endothelial pumps play an active role in transport, and **anaerobic glycolysis** takes place in cornea. So, endothelium is the most important and major metabolically active layer of cornea. (Corneal epithelium is ~10 times thicker than endothelium, so requires more supply of metabolic substrates, and is also more metabolically active than endothelium — but the endothelium's continuous pump function is what maintains corneal clarity, which is why it is regarded as the most metabolically critical layer for corneal transparency.)

column2: Explain why: Sutures are not needed in small incision cataract surgery.
column4: In SICS there are two entry points — one is the **side port** and the other is the **tri-planar sclerocorneal tunnel**. Side port is ~1.2 mm in length and width; tunnel is usually ~6.5 mm. The sclerocorneal tunnel has two parts — external scleral part and internal corneal part; the entry into anterior chamber is made from the corneal part and it **seals by itself** (chamber can be formed with air or balanced salt solution after cataract surgery). Side port is sealed by **stromal hydration** after cataract surgery. Hence, no sutures are needed.

column2: Explain why: Biometry is done before cataract surgery.
column4: Biometry is performed during pre-operative assessment for all patients undergoing cataract surgery. Measurements obtained are used to **calculate the power of intraocular lens** for each patient. Several formulas are used — SRK I, SRK II, SRK/T, Hoffer Q, Haigis, Barrett's formula. SRK II: P = A − 2.5L − 0.9K. It should **not be done on the day of surgery**, as contact procedure may increase chance of contamination.

column2: Explain why: Pterygium is more common on nasal side.
column4: Pterygium is a triangular-shaped mass arising from conjunctiva growing upon the cornea and encroaching it, usually due to **elastotic degeneration** of subconjunctival tissue. Cause is usually high-altitude or hot climate with excessive exposure to sun rays and dust. It is more common on nasal side because the **temporal side of conjunctiva gets protection from UV rays of sunlight due to the nasal bridge** — so the nasal side, which is not protected from UV rays, develops pterygium more commonly.

column2: Explain why: Ocular viscoelastic substances are needed in cataract surgery.
column4: Ocular viscoelastic devices have following properties — **viscosity, elasticity, pseudoplasticity, coat-ability**. Composition: 2% hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) and 1.4% chondroitin sulphate; may be cohesive or dispersive. They are needed in almost all steps of cataract surgery: during **capsulorrhexis**, during **nucleus delivery**, during **implantation of IOL**, and most importantly to **maintain the anterior chamber** in all steps of surgery. They have a very important role in **coating the endothelium** and protecting it.

column2: Explain why: Cycloplegics are used in treatment of corneal ulcer.
column4: Cycloplegics like 1% atropine sulphate and 2% homatropine are used in treatment of corneal ulcer to: (A) reduce ciliary spasm and provide relief from pain; (B) dilate the pupil so posterior synechiae do not occur; (C) increase blood supply to iris so more antibodies reach there, helping to treat the condition.

column2: Explain why: Ocular injury with alkali is more dangerous than acid.
column4: **Mechanism of injury by alkali:** alkalies are lipophilic and therefore penetrate tissues more rapidly than acids; they **saponify fatty acids of cell membranes**, penetrate corneal stroma and destroy proteoglycan ground substance and collagen bundles; damaged tissues then secrete proteolytic enzymes which lead to further damage. **Mechanism of injury by acid:** acids are generally less harmful than alkalies; they cause damage by **denaturing and precipitating proteins** in tissues they contact — the coagulated proteins act as a barrier to prevent further penetration. One exception is hydrofluoric acid, where the fluoride ion rapidly penetrates the full thickness of cornea and causes significant anterior segment destruction.

column2: Explain why: Homonymous hemianopia occurs in optic tract lesion.
column4: Optic tract on any side carries ipsilateral temporal fibres of optic nerve and contralateral nasal fibres. So any lesion at this level will cause **nasal field defect on the same side and temporal field defect on opposite side**, leading to same-sided homonymous hemianopia.
column6: Homonymous Hemianopia in Optic Tract Lesion

column2: Explain why: Iris shadow is absent in mature cataract but present in immature cataract.
column4: Iris shadow is seen in immature cataracts as some areas of the clear cortex are still not opacified and light rays can pass through and get reflected, so there is shadow formation. In mature cataract the crystalline lens is **totally opacified** so light rays cannot pass — hence no shadow formation.

column2: Explain why: Diplopia is absent in comitant squint but present in paralytic squint.
column4: Comitant squint is a type of squint where angle of deviation is the same in all directions of gaze, but in paralytic squint it is different in different gazes. In paralytic squint, two different images are formed on the fovea (or on non-corresponding visual points), so **diplopia** occurs. In comitant squint, the same images are formed on corresponding visual points, so there is **no diplopia**.

column2: Explain why: Good glycaemic and blood pressure control is necessary before cataract surgery.
column4: Recommended to have **CBG < 200 mg/dL** on the day of surgery. Good glycaemic control is necessary because high sugar can cause several complications — diabetic retinopathy increases chances of post-operative endophthalmitis and post-operative macular oedema; in SICS, the tunnel wound may not heal quickly. **BP < 160/80** is needed because otherwise intraoperative bleeding from wound site can occur, making surgery difficult, and it can also cause other systemic complications.

column2: Explain why: Regular eye examination is essential for diabetic patients.
column4: Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus can cause diabetic retinopathy, which can cause severe vision loss. The most common cause of vision loss in diabetes is **macular oedema**. DR can be non-proliferative or proliferative. Disease usually starts with formation of **microaneurysms** which leak, causing dot-blot haemorrhages and other features of DR. **Vitreous haemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment** are the most severe forms. To prevent these, regular check-up is very essential and depends on stage of disease.

column2: Explain why: Oral potassium chloride is prescribed along with systemic acetazolamide.
column4: Oral acetazolamide is used to lower IOP. **Mechanism:** carbonic anhydrase inhibitor — reduces formation of aqueous humour and lowers IOP; also acts as a diuretic. The major side effect of systemic acetazolamide is **hypokalaemia**. So it is advised to take potassium chloride syrup when a patient is on systemic acetazolamide.

column2: Explain why: Prophylactic peripheral laser iridotomy is done in the fellow eye of a patient of acute congestive glaucoma.
column4: Patient of acute congestive glaucoma presents with severe pain in eye, vomiting, and blurring of vision. Treatment consists of IOP-lowering agents and systemic mannitol; after control of IOP, gonioscopy should be performed to see the angle. **Studies have shown that the fellow eye of a patient of acute congestive glaucoma is also prone to an angle-closure attack.** So a prophylactic peripheral iridotomy is done in the fellow eye.

column2: Explain why: Cycloplegic relieves pain in acute iridocyclitis.
column4: Cycloplegics like 1% atropine sulphate and 2% homatropine are used in acute iridocyclitis to: (A) reduce ciliary spasm and provide relief from pain; (B) dilate the pupil so posterior synechiae do not occur; (C) increase blood supply to iris so more antibodies reach there, helping to treat the condition.

column2: Explain why: Pupillary examination and dilation is essential before cataract surgery.
column4: Pupillary examination and dilation is essential before cataract surgery because: **poor dilatation of pupil** indicates that iris expansion devices have to be given during surgery — it can cause difficulties in nucleus delivery, and in phacoemulsification chopping may be a little difficult; iris expansion devices like iris hooks or BHEX iris expansion device may be needed. Also, examination before cataract surgery is essential to prognosticate surgery — any fundus abnormality (diabetic retinopathy, hypertensive retinopathy, other fundus pathology) indicates vision will not improve after cataract surgery, and patient may need other modalities of treatment after cataract surgery.

column2: Explain why: Pterygium may cause significant decrease in vision.
column4: **Mechanism of vision loss in pterygium:** (A) it causes **with-the-rule astigmatism** — increase in astigmatism can cause visual loss; (B) a large pterygium crossing from one side to another can **obscure the pupillary axis**, causing severe vision loss.

column2: Explain why: Dacryocystitis must be treated before any intraocular surgery.
column4: Dacryocystitis is inflammation of lacrimal sac typically occurring secondarily to obstruction within nasolacrimal duct, with backup and stagnation of tears within sac. It must be treated by DCT or DCR before cataract surgery or any intraocular surgery because **regurgitation of fluid or pus from lacrimal sac can cause endophthalmitis** and loss of vision, and may ultimately lead to **panophthalmitis**.

column2: Explain why: Phacoemulsification is advantageous compared to SICS in some cataracts.
column4: (A) In phacoemulsification the main wound is 2.8–3.2 mm, so **astigmatism is less** if incision is planned properly; (B) size of capsulorrhexis is smaller (5–5.5 mm) → **better centration of IOL**; (C) **post-operative recovery is fast**; (D) it can be done under **topical anaesthesia** — so risk of peribulbar block seen in SICS is not present.

column2: Explain why: Amblyopia is more common in hypermetropia.
column4: Amblyopia is more common in hypermetropia, astigmatism, and anisometropia because in both conditions **near vision is also poor** along with distant vision. A child's visual world is limited to 3–4 feet from him/her. In myopia, near vision is good, so at least the child has something to focus on and see. But in hypermetropia, near vision is also blurred, so it is more amblyogenic.

column2: Explain why: IOL implantation is preferred over aphakia.
column4: **Problems in aphakia:** (A) severely reduced visual acuity; (B) increased chance of retinal detachment; (C) cystoid macular oedema; (D) no protection from UV rays; (E) optical aberration (roving ring scotoma); (F) relative spectacle magnification; (G) unilateral aphakia in children is a potential cause of amblyopia. That is why it is important to implant an IOL rather than keeping the patient aphakic.

column2: Explain why: Untreated diabetes mellitus for 10 years can cause blindness.
column4: Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus can cause diabetic retinopathy, which can cause severe vision loss. **Most common cause of vision loss in diabetes is macular oedema.** DR can be non-proliferative or proliferative. Disease usually starts with formation of microaneurysms which leak, causing dot-blot haemorrhages and other features of DR. **Vitreous haemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment** are the most severe forms. To prevent this, regular check-up is very essential and depends on stage of disease.

column2: Explain why: Long-term steroid use can cause glaucoma.
column4: Steroid-induced glaucoma is a form of **open-angle glaucoma**. Precise mechanism for IOP elevation after steroid intake is not very clear, but primarily it occurs due to **reduced facility of aqueous outflow**. Steroids cause accumulation of **polymerised glycosaminoglycans (GAGs)** in the trabecular meshwork — these polymerised GAGs produce outflow resistance. Steroids also increase production of **extracellular trabecular meshwork protein**, which increases outflow resistance.

column2: Explain why: RAPD has several clinical implications.
column4: RAPD is seen in asymmetric lesions of the pre-chiasmal optic nerve starting from the retina, but can occur anywhere in the afferent pupillary pathway including optic tract and pretectal afferent fibres in dorsal midbrain. **Conditions leading to RAPD:** lesions of optic nerve (optic neuritis, glaucoma, compression, infection); lesions of optic chiasm; lesions of optic tract; lesions of pretectum; lesions of retina/posterior segment; large retinal detachments; ischaemia (ischaemic CRVO or CRAO); dense macular lesions (chorio-retinal scar). Testing of RAPD is done by **swinging flashlight test**.

column2: Explain why: Convex lens is used in treatment of presbyopia.
column4: Presbyopia is irreversible loss of accommodative ability of eye occurring due to ageing. Accommodation refers to ability of eye to increase its refractive power of crystalline lens to focus near objects on retina. Significant decrease in accommodative power occurs between ages 20 and 50. **Symptoms:** gradual onset of blurred near vision (often first presenting symptom), headache, squinting, increased light requirement. **Management:** corrective glasses lenses — separate reading glasses, contact lenses, bifocals, or progressive lenses — all of which are **convex** (plus) lenses that supplement the eye's reduced accommodation for near work.

column2: Explain why: At end of cataract surgery
column3: viscoelastic should be thoroughly removed from anterior chamber.
column5: At end of cataract surgery, viscoelastic should be thoroughly removed from anterior chamber; otherwise in post-op period it may cause **raise in intraocular pressure** and may result in **corneal oedema**, causing decreased vision and delayed post-operative recovery. In case of **toric IOL implantation**, remaining viscoelastic in the bag may cause **rotation of IOL** and can hinder the purpose of toric IOL implantation.
column7: Viscoelastic Removal at End of Cataract Surgery

column2: Explain why: B-scan USG is done before operation of mature cataract.
column4: In cataract surgery, pre-operative **dilated fundoscopy** is done to prognosticate surgery. In mature cataract the media is **totally opaque**, so dilated fundoscopy cannot be done — that is why **ultrasonography B-scan** is done to rule out gross retinal pathology like retinal detachment or vitreous haemorrhage, which has impact on visual outcome.

column2: Explain why: Progressive lenses are preferred over bifocal lenses.
column4: Main difference: **bifocal lenses only provide distance correction and near correction — no correction is provided for intermediate distance**. In **progressive lenses**, intermediate vision is also improved. Secondly, bifocal lenses have distinct zones for distant and near vision, whereas progressive lenses do not, so they are more **cosmetically acceptable** to the patient.

column2: Explain why: Increased IOP is the most important factor for diagnosing glaucoma.
column4: IOP is considered the most important **risk factor** for development of POAG, and remains the only known **modifiable** risk factor. IOP-related mechanisms of optic nerve damage are very important in pathogenesis of POAG. By definition, patients with POAG have raised IOP; raised IOP is an important risk factor for progression to POAG from ocular hypertension; and is the only common clinical finding in a wide variety of secondary glaucomas. IOP seems to be important even in **normal-tension glaucoma**, as reduction of IOP was shown to reduce risk of progression in these patients (Collaborative Normal Tension Glaucoma Study).

column2: Explain why: In chalazion surgery
column5: Chalazion is a lipo-granulomatous inflammation of the meibomian gland occurring due to obstruction of the meibomian gland opening; most commonly affects the upper eyelid. During incision, a **vertical incision** is always given to prevent damage to adjacent meibomian glands or meibomian gland ducts in the tarsal plate. A transverse incision would cut many unrelated meibomian ducts, leading to evaporative dry eye due to lack of superficial oily layer of tear film. A vertical incision only severs the affected meibomian duct.

column2: Explain why: Corneal sensation is checked in viral keratitis.
column4: Symptoms of viral keratitis are pain, redness, watering, blurring of vision. Signs: dendritic or disciform keratitis may be present with circumciliary congestion. **Corneal sensation is typically reduced in viral keratitis and not hampered in bacterial or fungal keratitis** — so it is important to test corneal sensation in suspected viral keratitis for proper diagnosis and treatment.

column2: Explain why: Tropicamide is preferred over tropicamide plus phenylephrine in hypertensive patients.
column4: Phenylephrine is an **alpha-1 adrenoreceptor agonist**. Tropicamide plus phenylephrine is used to dilate pupil and maintain dilation. But phenylephrine can cause **rise in blood pressure** after absorption through nasal mucosa due to its adrenergic action — so in hypertensive patients it is better to avoid phenylephrine and use tropicamide alone.

column2: Explain why: Presbyopia starts around 40 years.
column4: Presbyopia is irreversible loss of accommodative ability of eye occurring due to ageing. Significant decrease in accommodative power occurs between ages 20 and 50 years. At 40 years of age, our near point recedes **beyond emmetropic near work distance (35 cm or 14 inches)**. So presbyopia starts after 40 years. **Symptoms:** gradual onset of blurred near vision (often first presenting symptom), headache, squinting, increased light requirement. **Management:** corrective glasses lenses — separate reading glasses, contact lenses, bifocals, progressive lenses.

column2: Explain why: Cataracts in diabetic patients develop in the pre-senile age group.
column4: Cataracts in diabetic patients develop in the pre-senile age group due to the **polyol pathway**. Several studies have shown conversion of sugar to **sorbitol** via action of **aldose reductase**. Sorbitol being osmotic adsorbs water into lens fibres, leading them to swell and opacify. There is also release of various **free radicals** within lens epithelial cells (LEC), leading to apoptosis of these cells and cataract formation. In Type 1 DM patients, there is formation of **'snow-flake' cataract** very early on, characterised by fluid-filled cysts under anterior capsule and intumescence of lens.

column2: Explain why: Anterior chamber is deep in buphthalmos.
column4: In primary congenital glaucoma or buphthalmos, patients present with **large corneal diameter, deep anterior chamber, and raised IOP**. The scleral tissue in young children is **highly elastic and stretchable** — as a result of which, under high intraocular pressure, it is stretched, leading to increased axial length (myopic shift) as well as a deep anterior chamber.

column2: Explain why: Cataract surgery is difficult in small pupil.
column4: Cataract surgery is one of the most commonly performed ophthalmic procedures worldwide; it generally produces predictable results, but in certain cases surgery can be challenging. In patients with small pupils, several steps become difficult: **staining of anterior lens capsule**; getting a **decent-sized continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis**; proper **hydroprocedures** cannot be done; **nucleus management** (both SICS and phacoemulsification) becomes challenging; **inadvertent injury to iris** can occur. In addition, if patient has past history of **uveitis with posterior synechiae** between iris and anterior lens capsule, these need to be released prior to initiating nucleus management. Patients with **pseudoexfoliation syndrome** pose challenges due to poorly dilating pupils with weakened zonules.

column2: Explain why: Exacerbation of asthma in COPD patients after application of topical timolol maleate for management of glaucoma.
column4: Patients with COPD have chronic bronchitis leading to narrowing of bronchioles. Timolol being a **non-selective beta-blocker** blocks beta receptors in both ocular tissues and bronchioles. **β₂ receptors** are adrenergic receptors that help in bronchodilation — blocking them leads to **bronchoconstriction**, exacerbating asthma in COPD patients.

column2: Explain why: Pupil is small
column4: and sluggishly reacting in acute anterior uveitis.
column6: In acute anterior uveitis there is inflammation in uveal tissue of anterior chamber (iris and ciliary body). This results in release of inflammatory cells, increased permeability of vascular structures, and temporary damage to tissues by immune system. As a result of this sudden inflammation both **constrictor and dilator pupillae muscles are stimulated** — constrictor pupillae tone is higher than dilator pupillae, so pupil becomes constricted. Due to exudation iris becomes **water-logged and oedematous**, so pupillary reaction becomes sluggish. **Irregular pupil** is due to exudation in pupillary margin and pre-existing posterior synechiae.

column2: Explain why: Raised IOP causes corneal oedema.
column4: Raised IOP exerts pressure on the **endothelial side of cornea**. The transparency of cornea is largely maintained due to **endothelial Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump** which drives out aqueous humour that enters the cells. In raised IOP, endothelial pump action is affected, resulting in its dysfunction — and as a result there is **corneal oedema**.

column2: Explain why: Astigmatism occurs after SICS.
column4: In SICS a **large (usually 5–7 mm) sclerocorneal tunnel** needs to be made to remove the entire nucleus in toto. This results in **flattening of corneal curvature** along that meridian, inducing astigmatism — called **surgically induced astigmatism (SIA)**. Larger the size of nucleus, larger the sclerocorneal tunnel, hence larger the SIA.

column2: Explain why: Peribulbar block is safer than retrobulbar block.
column4: Basic difference between retrobulbar and peribulbar block: **retrobulbar block deposits anaesthetic drugs within the muscle cone**, while in **peribulbar anaesthesia the drugs are deposited outside the muscle cone**, thus giving a margin of safety. In peribulbar blocks there is lesser risk of: retrobulbar haemorrhage; optic nerve compression; extraocular muscle injury/haematoma; globe perforation; lesser risk of central retinal artery occlusion; optic nerve injury; oculocardiac reflex.

column2: Explain why: Hyphema may need paracentesis.
column4: Hyphema is accumulation of blood in anterior chamber. Paracentesis is a surgical procedure where a clear corneal incision is made with a lance-tipped blade to enter and clear out contents of anterior chamber. **Indications for paracentesis in hyphema:** corneal staining with blood; raised IOP > 60 mmHg for ≥ 2 days, or > 50 mmHg for ≥ 5 days, or > 35 mmHg for ≥ 7 days, or > 25 mmHg for ≥ 24 hours in sickle cell anaemia; globe injury; suspected foreign body; active bleeding; recurrent/persistent hyphema; patients with sickle cell haemoglobinopathies; young patients (to prevent amblyopia).

column2: Explain why: Leukocoria needs detailed investigation.
column4: Leukocoria is appearance of a **white pupillary reflex in children**; often the only sign seen by parents in an otherwise healthy-looking child, and may be indication of a serious underlying cause. **Causes of leukocoria:** retinoblastoma; retinal detachment; Coats disease; persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV); congenital cataract; ocular toxocara or toxoplasma; retinopathy of prematurity; corneal opacity due to various causes (infective keratitis, corneal dystrophies like CHED 1 or 2, buphthalmos, sclerocornea); familial exudative vitreoretinopathy. To rule these out, a battery of tests and investigations must be undertaken — clinical, pathological, microbiological, radiological.

column2: Explain why: Recurrent chalazion needs refractive examination.
column4: Chalazion is a non-infective granulomatous lesion of meibomian gland. **Uncorrected refractive errors in children, especially uncorrected myopia, cause the child to constantly rub his/her eyes**, resulting in blockage of glands and non-granulomatous inflammation of glands leading to chalazion. Also, already-present chalazion can lead to **mechanical pressure on cornea leading to astigmatism**. Hence, chalazion and uncorrected refractive errors are associated.

column2: Explain why: Syringing is done before lacrimal sac surgery.
column4: Syringing is done before lacrimal sac surgery to **assess patency of canaliculi**. Syringing through lower punctum: if fluid regurgitates from the **upper punctum**, the block may be at common canaliculi/lacrimal sac/nasolacrimal duct; if fluid regurgitates from **only the lower punctum**, the block is probably at the lower canaliculus — **such a patient will not benefit from DCR surgery**.

column2: Explain why: Visual acuity is measured from 6 metres and 20 feet.
column4: Visual acuity is measured at distance of **6 m or 20 ft** in a standard Snellen's chart because at this distance the light rays coming from the lowest line of Snellen's chart (from uppermost point and lowermost point) travelling to the patient will be **parallel to each other** — so the patient will not need to accommodate to view the optotypes.

column2: Explain why: Vitamin A is essential for maintaining good vision.
column4: Vitamin A is transported in blood as **all-trans retinol** bound to a carrier protein (fat-soluble vitamin, needs carrier for water solubility). It becomes available to photoreceptors after crossing Bruch's membrane. All-trans retinol is converted to **11-cis retinol** by enzymes, then oxidised to **11-cis retinal** by retinal dehydrogenase. 11-cis retinal binds to **opsin** in photoreceptor cells to form **photopigments** (rhodopsin and iodopsin). During phototransduction, 11-cis retinal is converted to all-trans retinal, released from opsin, converted to all-trans retinol by retinol dehydrogenase in cytoplasm, transported to RPE where converted to 11-cis retinol. From there transported back to photoreceptors where converted to 11-cis retinal by dehydrogenase for regeneration of visual pigments.

column2: Explain why: DCR is contraindicated in atrophic rhinitis.
column4: In atrophic rhinitis the nasal mucosa is **dry and atrophic** along with severe crusting. This prevents proper healing after DCR operation. Also, the ostium may get **fibrosed or infected easily** as these patients are more prone to infection. Hence, it is a **relative contraindication** to external DCR.

column2: Explain why: Pupillary examination is a helpful guide for different neuro-ophthalmological lesions.
column4: The pupillary pathway involves an afferent and an efferent pathway. **Afferent** fibres travel along optic nerve, chiasma, optic tract up to superior colliculus at pretectal nucleus in midbrain, from where it leaves tract and enters midbrain. It then gives parasympathetic fibres to both **Edinger-Westphal nuclei**, which send fibres to ciliary ganglion via 3rd cranial nerve, finally supplying iris sphincter and dilator muscles. Any lesion along this tract can cause anomalies in pupillary reflex. Lesions in afferent pathway (any cause of optic atrophy, diabetes, hypertension, compressing mass, aneurysm) can lead to **RAPD**. Lesion at pretectal level (neurosyphilis, Parinaud's syndrome) can lead to **light-near dissociation**. Lesions posterior to ciliary ganglion can lead to **atonic pupils (Adie's pupils)**. Lesions affecting sympathetic fibres supplying pupil can lead to **Horner's syndrome**.

column2: Explain why: Screening for low vision in children is essential under school programme.
column4: Screening for low vision is essential under school programme to: detect refractive errors as early as possible and prescribe appropriate spectacle correction; early detection of defects in colour vision; early detection of any signs of dysfunction of ocular motility (squint); early detection of loss of stereopsis, any nystagmus; prevent development of amblyopia; spread awareness among parents; detect early signs of congenital causes of visual loss like corneal opacity, cataract and refer patient accordingly; detect any white pupillary reflex and early referral (may save life of patient).

column2: Explain why: Enucleation is not done in panophthalmitis.
column4: Enucleation is surgical procedure involving removal of entire globe and intraocular contents with preservation of all other periorbital and orbital structures; labor-intensive surgical option. Panophthalmitis is a rapidly progressive suppurative process encompassing all structures of globe with extension into orbital structures. **Enucleation in panophthalmitis will expose the central nervous system through optic nerve to infective organisms** — though it ensures complete removal of globe and proximal optic nerve, infection may gain access to CNS, causing life-threatening CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis).

column2: Explain why: DCR operation is not done before 4 years in a child with congenital dacryocystitis.
column4: DCR in children < 4 years is a challenging entity because of **minimally developed paranasal sinus structures**, anatomical variations, and related anaesthetic complications. The **valve of Hasner** is the most common site of obstruction in infants; congenital dacryocystitis resolves by 6–12 months of age spontaneously or by **Criggler massage**. DCR could be an option when massaging and repetitive probing have failed. Anatomical variation of nasal cavity in children causes insufficient size of osteotomy, cicatricial ostium closure, adhesions in ostium, synechiae between ostium and nasal septum, and granuloma formation in post-operative period. However, **endoscopic DCR provides better surgical outcome**.
column6: DCR Age Limit in Congenital Dacryocystitis

column2: Explain why: Coloured haloes are seen in immature cataract not in mature cataract.
column4: Coloured halos around lights are a common complaint of patients with **immature senile cataract**. It is due to **prismatic dispersion of light** as it passes through a cataractous lens, due to differences in refractive indices of lens fibres. Cataractogenesis involves degeneration and opacification of lens fibres with formation of **water clefts and protein aggregates**, causing unequal diffraction of light. As lens fibres undergo complete opacification in mature cataract, lens fibres become completely opaque to light passing through — thus vision deteriorates further to light perception in patients with mature cataract. For uniformly opaque lens fibres, **coloured halos are not seen in mature cataract**.

column2: Explain why: Congenital dacryocystitis in infant is mostly cured by lacrimal sac massage whereas in adult acquired chronic dacryocystitis it is not.
column4: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLDO) is a common cause of congenital dacryocystitis leading to epiphora in infants; usually caused by a **membranous block at the valve of Hasner** covering the nasal end of the nasolacrimal duct. The caudal end of the nasolacrimal duct is the **last to canalize**. Lacrimal sac compression/Criggler massage creates **hydrostatic intraluminal pressure** in the nasolacrimal duct by obstructing the common canaliculus; this is followed by increasing pressure downward, causing rupture of the membranous obstruction. Resolution occurs until 18 months of age when correct technique is practised. However, massage serves only **symptomatic relief** in adult acquired chronic dacryocystitis, which is due to suppurative infection of sac and **necessitates surgical intervention**.

column2: Explain why: Fungal hypopyon has a convex border.
column4: Fungal organisms invade corneal stroma following an epithelial defect. They proliferate and incite an inflammatory reaction, leading to tissue necrosis. **Filamentous fungi penetrate intact Descemet's membrane**. So fungal hypopyon is an **infected hypopyon with fungal hyphae** along with inflammatory exudates. This results in thick and immobile hypopyon with an **upper convex border continuous with the ulcer through hyphae**. Infection in anterior chamber is difficult to eradicate. Fungal ulcer is characterised by: fixed hypopyon (45–66%); dry texture with grey-white infiltrates; creamy exudates at base; feathery margins (70%); satellite lesions (10%); immune ring; deep stromal abscess; endothelial plaque.

column2: Explain why: Latanoprost is not prescribed in acute congestive glaucoma.
column4: Intraocular pressure-lowering effect of latanoprost is produced by **enhancing outflow of aqueous via the uveoscleral pathway**. Access to this pathway may be **hindered in acute congestive glaucoma due to 360° posterior synechiae**. Moreover, relaxation of ciliary muscle may cause **shallowing of anterior chamber**, leading to an attack of pupillary block. The IOP-lowering effect is maximum for a single agent (27–35%), with peak effect 12–24 hours after instillation — too slow for the acute attack. Hence, latanoprost is not prescribed in acute congestive glaucoma.

column2: Explain why: Granulomatous uveitis is clinically different from non-granulomatous uveitis.
column4: **Granulomatous uveitis** is characterised by insidious onset and chronic course; **circumciliary congestion** is often mild/absent; **iris nodules (Koeppe's and Busacca's)** are more common; **keratic precipitates** are medium-large in size, oval/oblong, confluent, resembling mutton fat (yellow and greasy, mashed potato appearance); KPs undergo pigmentation and cause alteration of endothelium leading to prelucid halos; **posterior segment involvement** is more common. **Non-granulomatous uveitis** is differentiated by sudden onset and acute course; severe ciliary congestion; no iris nodules; KPs are small-medium, white-hydrated, circular; KPs are dehydrated and flattened; posterior segment involvement is less common. Causes differ — granulomatous uveitis: infectious or non-infectious causes (TB, leprosy, sarcoidosis); non-granulomatous: usually idiopathic or immunologic. Treatment differs — granulomatous: treatment of cause (systemic) with ocular immunosuppression and cycloplegia; non-granulomatous: ocular immunosuppressives and cycloplegics.

column2: Explain why: Untreated hypermetropia can cause convergent squint.
column4: Untreated hypermetropia (usually > +2.00D, average +4.00D) leads to **accommodative esotropia**. This occurs due to **failure of fusional divergence mechanism** to compensate for convergence caused when a person with hypermetropia accommodates to clear a blurred image. A normal **AC/A ratio** is the hallmark of refractive accommodative esotropia. Most often presents between 2 and 4 years of age. Esotropia is initially intermittent, manifesting when child is tired or focusing for near. Suppression in young children can lead to **amblyopia**. Decompensation of an initially well-controlled deviation in few cases may require change in refractive correction or surgical intervention.
